MLT.name: Malta
MLT.summary:
Malta is among the safest countries in the world for transgender visitors. It has ranked first for LGBTI legal rights in its region every year since 2015: gender identity and expression are protected from discrimination in law, legal gender recognition works by self-determination, and 'X' gender markers are available on passports. Conversion therapy is banned and the constitution guarantees LGBTI equality.

Malta records one of the lowest rates of physical or sexual victimisation of LGBTIQ+ people in its region, and the national police force has adopted hate-crime procedures for sexual-orientation and gender-identity incidents. A foreign government's diplomatic guidance describes the country as a safe environment for foreign LGBT travellers, and no government travel advisory flags trans-specific concerns.

Residual risks are minor: non-physical harassment (including online) is more common than violence and tends to be under-reported, and — in the unlikely event of arrest — prison practice has been found to lag the country's progressive law. The lag is documented, with an improving record: in May 2018 the civil court awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each after finding the authorities had "knowingly and repeatedly" held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers and suffered insults and "continuous sexual abuse and violence"; since the 2013 gender-law reform, trans and gender-diverse inmates transfer to the female section and now receive individual cells there, though a 2024 University of Malta study still records misgendering by officers and clothing and healthcare gaps.
MLT.outOfScopeNotes:
Petty crime around nightclubs and tourist spots, and general regional terrorism guidance, are ordinary travel risks that affect everyone.

Routine border handling of trans visitors is not documented beyond the asylum-seeker case, and no source describes visa or document scrutiny for trans visitors specifically.

Prison axis: the 2024 study rests on four interviews spanning 25 years; the earlier separate-dormitory segregation is documented from that study alone; no source in this record documents current solitary or special-unit practice for trans prisoners beyond what the study describes, and the abuse documented in the 2018 ruling predates the post-2013 reform practice.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page for Malta, scoring national compliance by category on the map's red-to-green scale: asylum, civil-society space, intersex bodily integrity, legal gender recognition, hate crime and hate speech, and equality body.

Equaldex data for Malta: homosexuality legal, marriage legal, gender change with no restrictions, nonbinary recognised, hate-crime protections cover SOGI, discrimination illegal, full ban on intersex infant surgery, conversion therapy banned, bathroom access protected. 84% rate it a 'good place' for gay people; but Maltese rank #1 of 30 EU regions for hiding being LGBTIQ at work.

Legal status: same-sex conduct legal since 29 January 1973; civil unions since 2014 and same-sex marriage since 2017; gender change without surgery; full adoption since 2014; open military service; discrimination protections cover sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Academic chapter (Routledge Companion to Gender and Crime, 2025, Mary Grace Vella): Malta records one of the lowest SOGIE physical/sexual victimisation rates in the EU27, yet LGBTIQ+ people still report a higher share of harassment and online hatred, and reporting of violence to the Malta Police Force remains significantly low despite institutional reforms.

University of Malta dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024): four interviews with current and former transgender inmates at the Correctional Service Agency, covering a 25-year cohort, found gaps in healthcare, legislation and knowledge, alongside problems after release, and found Correctional Service Agency practice out of sync with national gender-identity legislation.

ICJ (30 July 2025): ICJ and partners filed observations in M.S. v. Malta at the ECtHR — an LGBTI asylum seeker detained on arrival in Malta in April 2023 received a return decision and removal order to Bangladesh in May 2024; submissions raise ECHR Articles 3/5/13 (non-refoulement, detention conditions, individualised assessment before detention). Direct evidence of how LGBTI arrivals are treated at Maltese borders.

MaltaToday (15 April 2014): parliament approved the constitutional amendment naming gender identity — Malta the first European state to do so — and introduced civil unions in the same sitting; Transgender Europe was among the first NGOs to applaud gender identity as a protected ground in the highest legal text.

sources.title: Seven transgender prison inmates awarded €5,000 each in damages for 'truly disgusting' treatment (Malta Today)
sources.summary: Malta Today (29 May 2018): the Maltese civil court (Judge Silvio Meli) awarded seven transgender inmates of Corradino prison €5,000 each (€4,000 for breach of rights plus €1,000 for damage to personal dignity) after the prison authorities held them in the male section, where they shared cells with male inmates, were forced to use the men's showers (often forgoing washing) and suffered insults and 'continuous sexual abuse and violence'. The court found the authorities had 'knowingly and repeatedly' placed them in situations of high risk of sexual and psychological violence; the only alternative offered, transfer to the female section, would have cost them the work and study opportunities they needed to pay for hormone therapy, and female inmates and warders were said to be hostile, so they stayed in the male section. The director of prisons was ordered to pay; the Aditus Foundation human-rights NGO represented the seven women.

sources.title: The lived experiences of transgender inmates at Malta's Correctional Service Agency (Oriana Vidal, University of Malta, 2024)
sources.summary: University of Malta master's dissertation (Oriana Vidal, 2024) interviewing four current and former transgender/gender-diverse inmates of Malta's Correctional Service Agency (CSA), a cohort spanning the last 25 years. It records that after Malta's 2013 gender-law reform CSA practice allowed TGD inmates to transfer to the female section, whereas earlier practice had segregated them in a separate dormitory (staff described the rationale as 'the risks of pregnancies'); participants now receive individual cells in the female section but report residual misgendering by officers (masculine birth names), gender-appropriate clothing and healthcare gaps, and conclude that CSA practice, policies and procedures lag Malta's progressive national gender-identity law. It also cites the 2018 newspaper report (Agius, Malta Today) of seven TGD inmates winning a court award after rights breaches including strip searches, showering-privacy issues and being treated as males.

ISL.name: Iceland
ISL.summary:
Iceland ranks first of 121 jurisdictions surveyed by Equaldex as a good place for gay and lesbian people, at 93 per cent. Same-sex sexual activity is legal for men and women, same-sex marriage is recognised, gender change carries no restrictions, and non-binary identity is recognised in law.

Legal gender recognition operates through a self-determination process introduced by the 2019 reform, which replaced an earlier statute that had itself been among the most progressive in Europe. Reporting on that reform by the Reykjavík Grapevine in August 2019 records that, alongside the liberalisation, campaigners including the chair of Trans Ísland continued to map practical obstacles that the change did not resolve.

Statutory protections cover discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity, hate-motivated offences, and access to sex-segregated facilities. Equaldex also records a full ban on intersex infant surgery and a ban on conversion therapy. Outright International's Iceland profile, last updated 12 March 2026, describes the legal framework as progressive while noting acknowledged gaps in protection, and confirms that LGBTI organisations can register.

Reporting routes exist at national level. 112.is, Iceland's national emergency service, treats hate crime as an umbrella term covering offences committed from prejudice or hatred and publishes guidance for victims and perpetrators, alongside a dedicated page on abuse against queer people that states queer people are more likely to be victims of violence.

Recorded incidents have risen even as the statutory framework has widened. Police-recorded potential hate crimes numbered 16 in 2023, three times the previous year, 11 in 2024, and 7 in the current year at the time of reporting. Samtökin 78, the queer rights organisation, is publicly calling for stronger hate-crime legislation in response.

For British visitors, the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office states that same-sex sexual activity is legal and same-sex relationships are recognised in Icelandic law, and links dedicated LGBT+ traveller advice.
ISL.outOfScopeNotes:
The specific statutory penalties attaching to hate-motivated offences and to discrimination are not stated in the available inventory; the sources confirm that the protections exist without giving sentencing ranges.

Whether the police-recorded potential hate crimes from 2023, 2024 and the current year resulted in charges or convictions is not sourced here, so outcomes downstream of recording remain unresolved.

The scope and conditions of the ban on intersex infant surgery, including any age limit or consent threshold, are not detailed in the inventory; only Equaldex's characterisation of it as a full ban is available.

Two sources intended to document legislation directly, the OSCE hate-crime legislation and national-frameworks pages for Iceland, yielded no usable findings in this pass, so the underlying statutory text was not examined.

The extent to which the Equality Complaints Committee's procedures differ from the criminal hate-crime route in timing, remedy and evidentiary threshold is not sourced, and neither is the practical accessibility of the 2019 gender recognition process to foreign nationals or visitors.

A visitor weighing the two should treat the legal assessment and the incident counts as separate evidence.

ESP.name: Spain
ESP.summary:
Ley 4/2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado on 28 February 2023, establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, Spain stands alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from Organic Law 6/2022 rather than from Ley 4/2023. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. Ley 4/2023 did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In Vigo, a Tribunal de Instancia used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over WhatsApp messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In Valencia, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and Spain is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
ESP.outOfScopeNotes:
A December 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group, the only country where a majority supported unrestricted change of legal gender designation, with restroom support above 70 per cent alongside Argentina and India and 25 per cent of respondents saying they knew a trans person. This data predates the 2023 law by nearly seven years and cannot be read as a measure of current conditions; it is retained only as a dated public-attitude baseline.

The source inventory contains no material on entry or visa rules, gender markers on passports or residence documents, border or airport screening practices, or the recognition of foreign gender markers in Spain. These remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

Also not sourced: variation in Civil Registry practice between Spanish provinces, hate-crime reporting rates and complaint volumes, and the placement policy applied to trans people in immigration detention or prisons. No source in the inventory addresses whether the facility rules stated in national law are applied uniformly by private venues.

sources.summary: Official text of Ley 4/2023 (28 Feb 2023), 'real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantee of LGTBI rights', BOE. Article 43: any person of legal age 16+ may request rectification of the registry gender mention themselves before the Civil Registry - the administrative self-identification route visitors and residents use; law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12-16.

Human Rights Watch (16 Feb 2023): parliament passed the 'Trans Law' - gender recognition now by self-identification through a simple administrative process, ending the prior requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment. Also expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual 'normalising' surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures in healthcare, employment and housing; recognition possible from age 12 under conditions. Joins Argentina, Ireland, Portugal, Uruguay and peers.

Spanish criminal-law firm analysis (Jun 2026): disentangles which statute does what - 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Criminal Code; the hate-speech aggravation (Art. 22.4 CP) and Art. 510 CP penalties (1-4 years plus 6-12 month fine) come from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 reformed offences against sexual freedom (Arts. 132, 173, 178-181, 189 bis). Useful for reading actual enforcement: gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence.

Euro Weekly News (9 Jul 2026): Spain's framework for facility access rests on legal gender self-determination, while the UK is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the EHRC statutory code, with restrictions applied case-by-case rather than as a blanket ban. Access rules therefore differ on either side of the Channel.

Intrepid Travel LGBTQIA+ country guide: rates Spain a safe and welcoming destination for LGBTQIA+ travellers, especially tourist hubs Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting attitudes can be more conservative outside big cities and that same-sex marriage plus protective laws apply. Advises knowing local conditions before going (venues, regional variation).

Turespana (national tourism institute) B2B page: names Spain's 8 flagship LGBTQ+ destinations - Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera) - and the 'Destinations for Diversity' certification for open, safe, welcoming, discrimination-free spaces. Practical destination map for trip planning.

La Razon (Jul 2026): Vigo's Tribunal de Instancia applied the discrimination aggravating circumstance for transfobia for the first time, in a misdemeanour threats case - messages threatening a trans woman sent by WhatsApp; the author was fined EUR 300. First instance-level precedent that gender-identity aggravation is being applied in practice.

Observatorio de delitos de odio (8 Jan 2026, reporting Las Provincias): a juvenile gang in a Valencia park harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison, two minors were separately judged. Documents actual sentence outcomes for gender-identity-motivated violence.

UK Foreign travel advice, Spain (safety and security): official UK government view that Spain is 'a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers' with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings (counterfeit money treated as a serious offence). Baseline official safety framing for a UK-issued passport holder.

Wikipedia overview: same-sex marriage and full adoption rights since 2005; legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation; LGBTQ military service and MSM blood donation since 2005; Spain recognised as one of the world's most LGBT-friendly countries. Backbone timeline for the record.

BuzzFeed News / Ipsos-style 23-country survey (Dec 2016): Spain ranked most trans-supportive of the 23 - the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, restroom support over 70% (with Argentina and India), and 25% of respondents knew a trans person. Dated public-attitude baseline predating the 2023 law.

ESP.tangentialFactors:
Facility rules differ on either side of the Channel. Euro Weekly News reports that the United Kingdom is moving toward stricter single-sex-space rules on biological-sex lines under the Equality and Human Rights Commission statutory code, with restrictions applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban, while Spain's framework continues to rest on legal gender self-determination. A trans visitor moving between the two jurisdictions therefore faces different facility regimes.

Intrepid Travel rates Spain a safe and welcoming destination for LGBTQIA+ travellers, particularly in Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, while noting that attitudes can be more conservative outside large cities and advising travellers to check local conditions and venues before going. The guide also notes that same-sex marriage and protective laws apply.

The national tourism institute, Turespana, names eight flagship LGBTQ+ destinations for trip planning: Madrid (Chueca), Barcelona, Valencia, Seville, Cadiz, the Canary Islands (Maspalomas Pride), Sitges and Torremolinos (La Nogalera), alongside a Destinations for Diversity certification for open, safe, welcoming and discrimination-free spaces.

The UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's travel advice for Spain describes the country as a generally tolerant and progressive place for LGBT+ travellers, with active communities and social venues, alongside standard crime warnings such as the fact that counterfeit money is treated as a serious offence. This is the baseline official safety framing available to a UK passport holder.
ESP.localsOnly:
Ley 4/2023 extends beyond gender recognition. Human Rights Watch records that the law expands assisted reproduction, strengthens sexuality education, bans non-consensual normalising surgeries on intersex children, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, and adds anti-discrimination measures covering healthcare, employment and housing.

The resident-facing timeline includes same-sex marriage and full adoption rights since 2005, legal gender change without surgery or sterilisation, LGBTQ service in the armed forces and MSM blood donation since 2005.

Consent rules for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16 are set by the 2023 law, which is the framework parents and guardians in Spain work under rather than a visitor-facing rule.
ESP.blindSummary:
The national trans equality law of 28 February 2023 establishes real and effective equality for trans persons and guarantees LGTBI rights. Under its Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative route that replaces the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis and two years of medical treatment. The law also regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16, and recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions. With administrative self-declaration, the state stands alongside several peer states in permitting self-identification.

Access to sex-separated facilities rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules.

Transphobic motivation operates as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing under Article 22.4 of the Criminal Code, and the hate-speech provision at Article 510 carries one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months; both derive from a separate organic law on hate crimes rather than from the 2023 statute. Gender expression appears in no article of the Criminal Code, so a gender-expression-based hate crime has no free-standing offence. The 2023 law did reform the offences against sexual freedom at Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Courts are applying the aggravation in practice. In one city, a court of first instance used the transfobia aggravation for the first time, in a misdemeanour case over messaging-app messages threatening a trans woman, and fined the author EUR 300. In another city, a juvenile gang that harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park to mock them produced a six-month prison sentence for the only adult defendant, while two minors were judged separately.

Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have applied since 2005, and the state is recognised in comparative rankings as among the most LGBT-friendly countries.
ESP.blindOutOfScope:
a December 2016 survey of 23 states ranked this state/province the most trans-supportive of the group, the only one where a majority supported unrestricted change of legal gender designation, with restroom support above 70 per cent alongside two peer states and 25 per cent of respondents saying they knew a trans person. This data predates the 2023 law by nearly seven years and cannot be read as a measure of current conditions; it is retained only as a dated public-attitude baseline.

The source inventory contains no material on entry or visa rules, gender markers on passports or residence documents, border or airport screening practices, or the recognition of foreign gender markers in the state. These remain unresolved and are not sourced here.

Also not sourced: variation in Civil Registry practice between provinces, hate-crime reporting rates and complaint volumes, and the placement policy applied to trans people in immigration detention or prisons. No source in the inventory addresses whether the facility rules stated in national law are applied uniformly by private venues.

NLD.name: Netherlands
NLD.summary:
Visa and border treatment of transgender visitors is set out in the official WorldPride Amsterdam 2026 safety and travel guidance: visa requirements depend on nationality alone, with gender identity playing no part in the application, and a passport carrying a gender marker that differs from the marker assigned at birth or an 'X' marker is accepted provided it was officially issued. No additional gender documentation may be demanded at the border. The Netherlands ranks 13th on the ILGA Rainbow Map 2026.

Discrimination on grounds of gender identity is prohibited under Dutch law, and since 1 July 2025 a discriminatory motive is written into criminal law as a ground for increasing penalties, alongside expanded rights for victims and protection of victim data. Same-sex marriage is legal, non-binary people are legally recognised, conversion therapy is banned and access to sex-segregated facilities is protected, so a trans traveller's relationship status raises no entry or registration issue.

Official victimisation figures published by the Dutch government show that more than 10% of LGBTIQ+ people have experienced physical or sexual violence, rising to 17% of transgender people and 22% of intersex people. The 2023 National Programme against Discrimination and Racism recorded a sharp rise in incidents of verbal abuse, intimidation and violence, and in 2022 one third of discrimination reports reaching the police concerned sexual orientation.

Reported anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination is climbing in measurable terms. Police figures relayed by Transgender Netwerk record 4,800 reports concerning LGBTQIA+ people last year, 7.5% above 2024 and 81% above the 2,654 recorded in 2022. Reports specifically about transgender people rose 51% within a single year, from 264 to 399, while COC describes the trend as extremely worrying and notes that only six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination followed last year's reports.

Pride-period conditions carry their own documented incident load. During the opening of WorldPride Amsterdam in July 2026, more than 70 people filed discrimination reports through the RITA platform, most of them festival-goers leaving the Milkshake festival and participants in the Pride Walk; RITA states that these reports represent only a fraction of the total. Mayor Halsema told the city council that discrimination and violent incidents will be handled as a priority during World Pride, with police, enforcers and organisers agreed to act quickly, and recent Prides drew 25 to 45 anti-LGBTQIA+ incident reports covering vandalism, theft, discrimination, insults, intimidation and serious assault, typically with perpetrators leaving the scene before intervention.

Practical reporting infrastructure is extensive for the event. Amsterdam broadened its Safer Spaces reporting points for anti-LGBTQIA+ violence across the Nieuwe Kerk, the Stedelijk Museum, the Stadsarchief, hotels and a central RITA location, with 1.4 million visitors expected. The capital remains among the safer large European cities for ordinary street crime, and the combination of legal protection, priority police response and multiple physical reporting channels gives a trans visitor clear routes to assistance.
NLD.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether hate-crime law covers gender identity is unresolved across sources: Equaldex records hate-crime protections as covering sexual orientation only, while the government's own July 2025 measures make any discriminatory motive a ground for increased penalties in criminal cases. The scope of the aggravating-factor rule as applied to gender identity is not specified in the available material.

RITA has stated that the 70-plus discrimination reports filed at the opening of WorldPride 2026 are only a fraction of the total, so no reliable count of incidents during the event exists. Recent Pride baselines of 25 to 45 reports are themselves reported figures rather than measures of underlying incidence.

Official Dutch victimisation statistics for transgender people (17% experiencing physical or sexual violence) and the report trend (transgender-specific reports up 51% in a year) come from different collection systems and cannot be directly compared. The discrepancy between 4,800 reports and six convictions for anti-LGBTQIA+ discrimination last year is unexplained in the source material.

NJCM records that no official figures exist on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and that the placement guidelines under drafting by DIZ were unpublished as of February 2024. The current status of those guidelines and of the minister's response to the advice is not documented in the available inventory.

sources.title: NJCM adviseert demissionair Minister voor Rechtsbescherming over plaatsing van transgender gedetineerden (Nederlands Juristen Comité voor de Mensenrechten)
sources.summary: The Netherlands Jurists Committee for Human Rights (NJCM), criminal-law working group, announced (site date 22 Feb 2024) that it had advised the caretaker Minister for Legal Protection on the placement of transgender detainees: no law or regulation currently governs their placement, which NJCM calls worrying and undesirable. The note highlights the group's vulnerable position (international research documents human-rights violations including discrimination and sexual violence), the absence of official figures on the number of transgender detainees in the Netherlands, and the relevance of CPT standards, pointing to the full letter (PDF) to Minister Weerwind (21 Feb 2024).

sources.title: Advies plaatsing transgender gedetineerden — brief aan de Minister voor Rechtsbescherming (NJCM Werkgroep Strafrecht, 21 februari 2024)
sources.summary: NJCM letter to Minister Weerwind (Leiden, 21 Feb 2024) documenting Dutch placement practice for transgender detainees: there is no law, regulation or official policy governing their placement — the Penitentiary Principles Act only separates male and female detainees — and DJI (Prison Service) confirmed placement is based on the gender designation in the BRP (municipal records) together with case-by-case factors (gender-related physical features, the detainee's own preference, offence background, physical/mental health), while DIZ said it was (unpublished) drafting guidelines. Transgender detainees are frequently placed on an 'Extra Care Facility' (EZV) wing, generally to protect them from other detainees, where they sit alongside people with intellectual disabilities and sex offenders. The letter cites documented cases: a trans woman initially held on a regular male wing at arrival then moved to an EZV; a parole-board appeals ruling (21 Mar 2016, 15/4323/GB) on a trans woman first placed in a men's institution before transfer to the women's prison at Nieuwersluis, who reported intimidation, threats, assaults and molestation in the men's prison; and sentencing rulings by the Limburg court (17 Oct 2017, ECLI:NL:RBLIM:2017:10624, trans woman facing placement in a men's prison) and The Hague appeals court (29 Jun 2020, ECLI:NL:GHDHA:2020:1108, trans man in a women's prison) treating a wing not matching the detainee's gender as making imprisonment considerably heavier. NJCM asks the minister to create CPT-aligned rules placing transgender detainees by gender identity.

USA.name: United States
USA.summary:
Travel documents are the sharpest risk. Since January 2025, Executive Order 14168 makes all federal identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth: the X marker was eliminated, the passport agency stopped processing markers not matching birth sex, and new applications list only M or F per supporting documents — mismatched documents have left trans travellers stranded abroad, passports have been confiscated or blocked at application, and the ACLU has sued over the policy (Lambda Legal maintains guidance on documentation). In February 2025, under Executive Order 14201, the State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sporting events, flagging applicants internally as 'SWS25', and stated that applicants whose declared gender does not match sex assigned at birth may be permanently banned as fraud.

Entry and screening can be hostile in practice: airport screening (secondary screening, body scanners, pat-downs) risks outing trans travellers; a trans traveller was detained at the border for weeks and then deported in January 2025, and a border officer faces a lawsuit over alleged sexual contact with a trans traveller at a major airport.

Facilities and care are federal flashpoints: the same executive order bars trans people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and the January 2025 order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care (EO 14187) has led institutions to pause services — a visitor needing care during a trip may find access reduced. The military ban (EO 14183) and schools order (EO 14190) complete the 2025 federal package; several orders are enjoined or blocked in court, so the operative position shifts with litigation.

Beyond the federal layer, exposure is state-by-state: bathroom bans cover trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in 9 states plus 1 territory, and in some states trans bathroom use is a criminal offence in certain circumstances — a trans student was handcuffed in a women's restroom at a state capitol in April 2025 in what attorneys called the first known arrest under such a law. Kansas invalidated birth certificates and licences not matching birth sex, promoted as a template other states may copy. Dated state-level guidance flags 4 states as do-not-travel for trans people as of July 2026 (Idaho the latest).

Foreign governments now warn their own citizens: at least eight European states, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidance for trans and non-binary citizens entering the US in 2025, following documented detentions of European citizens over visa issues.

BRA.name: Brazil
BRA.summary:
Brazil pairs a broad legal framework for LGBTI people with persistent violence against them in practice. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since 2013, the Supreme Federal Tribunal removed the surgical requirement for legal gender change in 2018, the age of consent is equal regardless of sexual orientation, and a federal anti-discrimination framework covers sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

After the Supreme Court's 2019 ruling, constitutional and federal criminal provisions prohibit discrimination and hate crimes on SOGI grounds, with transphobia punishable on the same footing as racism. Courts have applied those provisions to commercial conduct: the 27th Private Chamber of the São Paulo Court of Justice upheld a moral-damage award against a nightclub that refused entry to a trans woman wearing women's clothing, affirming the compensation ordered at first instance in Barra Bonita. An expat legal guide updated in April 2026 confirms that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a trans visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at entry and in family matters.

The protective text of the law does not describe what people routinely encounter. Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records that LGBTIQ people still face significant violence and discrimination despite the constitutional and criminal provisions. A May 2024 investigation documented 'boa noite, Cinderela' drink-spiking robberies in which LGBTQIA+ people are targeted in São Paulo nightlife, in a city preparing for a Pride event that draws thousands of tourists. In the October 2024 municipal elections, close to 1,000 transgender candidates stood across every state of the country and received death threats and intimidation, while the number of trans officeholders tripled compared with the previous cycle.

Protection machinery has also widened. An analysis of case law from 2022 records lower courts pressing the Superior Court of Justice toward unanimously extending the remedies of the Maria da Penha Law and the Feminicide Law to trans women, bringing trans people within the country's violence-prevention statutes.

Detention carries a specific and contested regime. National Council of Justice Resolution 348 of 13 October 2020, amended by Resolution 366 of 20 January 2021, governs where LGBTI people who are arrested or imprisoned are housed. A person is recognised as LGBTI for these purposes by self-declaration before a judge, including at a custody hearing. On arrest the place of deprivation of liberty is fixed by a judge in a reasoned decision after the person has been consulted about their preference; the judge must set out the available male, female and LGBTI-specific units and ask trans, travesti and intersex people whether they prefer custody in a female, male or specific unit, and within it the general population or a specific wing or cell. The declared preference is recorded, a later change of placement is possible, and transfers are prioritised where there is violence or a serious threat. LGBTI-specific living spaces may not be used as disciplinary isolation, and compulsory transfer as punishment is prohibited.

Practice does not reliably follow that framework. A peer-reviewed census of travestis and transgender women held in Rio de Janeiro state prisons, carried out between April and June 2021, interviewed 138 self-declared travesti and trans-woman inmates inside eleven units treated as masculine in the metropolitan region. It documents that in that system travestis and trans women are housed in units operated as masculine, with some held in so-called neutral or security units, and treats placement in male units as a double punishment compounded by recurring violations of basic rights. The same study notes a 2015 Rio de Janeiro state law granting parity of treatment with cisgender women in women's units, covering hair length, feminine clothing, accessories and cosmetics, and national norms from 2014 and 2020 that permit people to be housed where they choose, including in units denominated masculine.
BRA.outOfScopeNotes:
Access to sex-segregated facilities such as restrooms and changing rooms is not addressed by any source in the present inventory. Whether official guidance affirms a trans person's right to use facilities matching their identity, and on what legal basis, remains unresolved here.

The gap between the National Council of Justice's placement rules and conditions on the ground is documented for one state system only. Whether Resolution 348 and Resolution 366 are applied as written at custody hearings elsewhere in the country is not sourced in this inventory, and the Rio de Janeiro census covers eleven units in one metropolitan region rather than the national prison population.

The enforcement record for the 2019 hate-crime provisions is illustrated by a single civil damages ruling against a nightclub. Criminal prosecutions and convictions for transphobia under those provisions are not sourced here.

The travel advisory material in the inventory concerns general crime, gang activity and demonstrations. It offers no trans-specific assessment, so the extent to which official advisories address anti-LGBTI violence is unresolved.

RUS.name: Russia
RUS.summary:
Russia presents severe legal and physical risks for transgender visitors, and the situation has deteriorated sharply since 2022. Legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023; the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation; and the expanded "propaganda" law criminalises any public expression — including, explicitly, anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who violate these laws face arrest, up to 15 days' detention, and deportation, and official national government warnings explicitly tell LGBT travellers of this.

Official assessments from a foreign body conclude that trans people specifically are likely to face treatment amounting to persecution in Russia. Enforcement has produced over a hundred "extremism" convictions for displaying LGBT symbols or participation, bar raids, and the death in custody of a man who ran travel tours for gay customers. Enforcement focuses on public expression and activism rather than private existence, and same-sex activity itself is not criminalised — a discreet visitor is not automatically targeted — but there is effectively no police protection, and detention carries placement by passport sex.

One region, Chechnya, where quasi-Sharia governance applies, is in a separate and graver category of danger for anyone perceived as LGBT.
RUS.outOfScopeNotes:
Official travel advisories from a foreign government (the US State Department) and most Western governments advise against all travel to Russia regardless of any personal characteristic, due to the risk of wrongful detention, the war in Ukraine, and arbitrary law enforcement.

Unresolved or unverifiable: the travel-advisory page itself could not be retrieved at research time (the underlying highest-level advisory includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers); the death-in-custody case has no published outcome; exact current conviction totals and detention counts are not published, so visitor exposure is assessed from dated records.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation/gender identity and expression (v2.0, June 2025; page updated 12 Aug 2026) affirms that LGBT+ people in Russia, including the autonomous republic of Chechnya, constitute a particular social group under the refugee convention, setting the assessment standard for UK asylum claims. External-protection framework, dated 2025-26.
US State Department travel advisory for Russia is Level 4, Do Not Travel, and includes warnings relevant to LGBT travellers.

Human Rights Watch (30 Jun 2025): Russian courts have issued 101 'extremism'-related convictions for alleged participation in the 'International LGBT Movement' or displaying its alleged symbols; the charges span administrative and criminal codes, and HRW calls on governments to offer safe haven to those fleeing Russia.

Meduza (19 Jun 2025): after the Supreme Court's 2023 designation of the non-existent 'international LGBT movement' as extremist, cases under Russia's propaganda laws have grown eighteenfold over the past decade, and fines under those statutes brought over 60 million rubles ($765,300) into the state budget in the past two years alone.

The Moscow Times (23 Jun 2025): arrests, club raids and extremism charges defined LGBTQ+ life in Russia through 2025 — a St Petersburg queer woman describes waking up to find herself 'a second-class citizen' after the Supreme Court's extremist designation.

AP (Dec 2024): 'Russian man arrested for allegedly running LGBTQ+ travel agency found dead in custody' — detained on extremism-related charges over an LGBTQ+ travel business, found dead in a pretrial detention facility.

BBC Russian (27 Jul 2024): follows 'Ada', a transgender woman lured by relatives in summer 2021 to a Siberian conversion-therapy centre near Novosibirsk. Held for nine months, forced to take testosterone, pray and do manual labour, she escaped when police responded to a phone she found. A documented account of coercive conversion practice against trans people in Russia.

About 100 patrons at one venue were ordered to face walls, searched and photographed, and at least two other venues were raided the same night, showing the speed of the post-ruling crackdown.

SAU.name: Saudi Arabia
SAU.summary:
Saudi Arabia is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a transgender person to be discovered in. Under its uncodified Sharia legal system, same-sex conduct is punishable in theory by death, flogging, or long imprisonment, and transgender expression itself is criminalised through "imitation of the opposite sex" and public-morality provisions that police and the morality police enforce with broad discretion. There is no legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care is banned.

Enforcement is documented and brutal: trans women have been arrested, detained, and tortured on morality grounds; a Pakistani trans woman died in custody in Riyadh in 2017 after a raid; men have been arrested for cross-dressing videos posted online. Amnesty International reported in 2026 that visitors have been imprisoned after unfair trials over social media posts — including posts published before they entered the Kingdom — and device inspection at the border is an established risk.

The tourism authority's "everyone is welcome" messaging reflects official interest in visitors' money, not any change in law. Any practical safety depends entirely on never being discovered, including digitally; detention would be in facilities matching passport sex, with no consular leverage able to prevent mistreatment.
SAU.outOfScopeNotes: Missile and drone attacks on infrastructure, and the general risk of detention without charge for any visitor, affect all travellers.

sources.summary: LegalClarity (4 Jun 2026): Saudi Arabia criminalises same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity with no codified penal code — judges apply an uncodified sharia interpretation; penalties range from flogging and lengthy imprisonment to death in the most severe cases; visitor-facing explainer of the laws, how enforcement works and rules for visitors.

Outright International Saudi Arabia overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): criminal penalties are based on Shari'a; same-sex relations illegal for men and women; no legal gender recognition; LGBTI organisations cannot register anywhere in the country.

Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute Saudi Arabia profile (MENA Trans Archives): deviating from traditional gender norms is itself treated as a criminal offence in Saudi Arabia, with provisions applied through enforcement against gender-nonconforming people.

Wikipedia 'LGBTQ rights in Saudi Arabia' (fetched 2026): same-sex conduct illegal with penalties including capital punishment, indeterminate prison terms, flogging and fines; no gender-identity recognition, no discrimination protections, no same-sex relationship recognition; law uncodified on a Wahhabist interpretation of sharia (Quran/Sunnah), with documented enforcement cases and living conditions.

BBC News: 'Meeno' — Mohammad Amin, a Pakistani transgender woman — died in Saudi custody after a roundup with 34 others in Azizia prison, Riyadh; Pakistani activists say she was beaten with clubs and hosepipes aggravating a chronic heart condition, while Saudi authorities attributed the death to a heart attack; family and trans-rights activists dispute the official account. Directly relevant to how Saudi enforcement treats trans people.

Gulf News (25 Oct 2021): five Saudi men were arrested in the Northern Borders province after filming themselves in women's clothing and posting the footage on social media — cross-dressing/gender-nonconformity enforced as a criminal matter.

Amnesty International (29 Jun 2026, updated 17 Jul 2026): documents visitors imprisoned over social media posts — including a business analyst arrested at Riyadh airport on 31 Aug 2024 as he was returning to the UK with his family, targeted for posts published before he even arrived in the country. Enforcement reaches travellers for expression, not only conduct on the ground.

UK FCDO Saudi Arabia safety advice (current): same-sex relations are illegal although legal action is uncommon; couples should avoid public affection; VisitSaudi states all visitors are welcome and privacy will be respected; being transgender is not recognised — trans travellers could face difficulties with dress codes and access to medical care.

A3M Global Monitoring LGBTQ+ Risk Map (2024/25): Saudi Arabia appears among the least safe destinations for LGBTQ travellers in a ranking that also lists Somalia, Yemen, Uganda, Afghanistan, UAE, Tanzania, Malaysia and Pakistan.

The Guardian (April 2005) by Brian Whitaker: 'Saudis' tough line on gays' - dozens of Saudi men caught dancing and 'behaving like women' at a Jeddah party described as a 'gay wedding' were sentenced to a total of 14,200 lashes plus up to two years' jail, after a closed trial without defence lawyers; HRW's Scott Long: 'Prosecuting and imprisoning people for homosexual conduct are flagrant human rights violations.'

AFG.name: Afghanistan
AFG.summary:
Afghanistan under the Taliban is the most hostile environment on this map for a transgender person. No legal protection on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity existed before the 2021 takeover and none exists after it, according to the EUAA COI Report of February 2026. The Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice Law of 31 July 2024, in its Article 22, obliges the regime's overseers to prevent listed evils including lesbianism and homosexuality "even if with one's own spouse", placing same-sex conduct under continuous moral surveillance alongside adultery and gambling.

Criminalisation is layered. The Human Dignity Trust country profile, updated 19 January 2026, records that Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women: Penal Code 2017 provisions on "sodomy" and "inciting sodomy" carry up to two years' imprisonment, while the Code's Sharia-reference clause permits the death penalty for same-sex activity. Amnesty International, cited in the EUAA COI Report, states that same-sex relations are punishable by death, and reporting from October 2021 records the same conclusion as applied by the ruling movement.

Enforcement has intensified and is public. OHCHR reported in March 2026 that UN human-rights experts condemned a surge in corporal punishment, with at least 1,110 people flogged during 2025 alone, nearly double the 2024 figure, and warned that women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for moral crimes including adultery, illicit relationships and sodomy. OutRight International reported in February 2023, from interviews conducted with LGBTIQ Afghans still in the country in September and October 2022, that Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in the early months of rule, using physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations; the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed such punishments on social media.

Detention is documented as abusive. CNN reported in November 2024 first-person accounts of arbitrary detention, beatings and sexual abuse in Taliban custody as the crackdown intensified. The Human Rights Watch and OutRight report of 26 January 2022, based on 60 interviews, found that Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes, that abuse by family, neighbours and partners surged after the takeover, and that many went into hiding or fled. Reporting from Kabul in October 2021 documented street attacks on men coded as gay, with victims changing their clothing and confining themselves indoors.

Visibly transgender people carry the gravest risk. The JURIST feature of 8 November 2024, drawing on the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen, reports systematic persecution after August 2021 and notes that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework. Transgender residents describe years of hiding in windowless rooms. A discovered trans visitor would be processed by the same apparatus as local LGBTIQ people: moral-police surveillance under the 2024 law, arbitrary detention, corporal punishment, and abuse in custody, with no legal recognition, no protection machinery, and no consular recourse that operates for LGBTIQ detainees.
AFG.outOfScopeNotes:
The relative weight of the Penal Code's two-year maximum against the Sharia-reference death penalty in actual sentencing is not resolved in the inventory; the sources state both provisions without indicating which is applied in a given case, and no conviction-level data is available here.

No sourced material addresses how a trans visitor's passport gender marker is read at entry, whether visa applications or arrival screening ask questions that would disclose gender history, or what consular assistance a foreign mission would attempt for a detained dual-national or foreign trans person. The claim of no consular recourse rests on the general absence of protection machinery rather than on a documented consular case.

The inventory does not establish whether the 2024 Morality Law's provisions apply with identical force in every province, nor does it document enforcement against foreign nationals specifically; all first-person accounts sourced here concern Afghan residents or those who fled.

Reporting on detention abuse in November 2024 and on the flogging totals in March 2026 carries dates but no figures for LGBT-specific detentions, so the scale of trans detainees remains unquantified.

sources.summary: EUAA Country Guidance: Afghanistan, section 3.17 'LGBTIQ persons' (profile last updated Jan 2023, in guidance May 2024): treats LGBTIQ Afghans as persons perceived to transgress religious/social norms, alongside minors without support networks and persons facing the death penalty — the asylum-framework basis for assessing Afghan LGBTIQ protection claims in the EU.

EUAA COI Report — Afghanistan Country Focus, section 4.5 (Feb 2026): no legal protections for sexual orientation or gender identity before or after the 2021 takeover; the 'Morality Law' of 31 Jul 2024 specifically prohibits lesbianism, anal intercourse and enabling same-sex relationships; per Amnesty International, same-sex relations are punishable by death.

Human Rights Watch / OutRight report (Jan 26, 2022), 43 pages based on 60 interviews with LGBT Afghans: Taliban members and their supporters attack, threaten and expel LGBT people from their homes; family, neighbour and partner abuse surged after the takeover; many went into hiding or fled.

OutRight International report (Feb 14, 2023), 22 interviews Sep-Oct 2022 with LGBTIQ Afghans still in-country: Taliban security officials pursue gay men and trans women more systematically than in early rule, with physical and sexual assault, arbitrary detention and public flogging for alleged same-sex relations — punishments the Taliban Supreme Court has confirmed on social media.

DW feature (Oct 2, 2021): profiles a trans man and a gay friend in their mid-20s hiding in Kabul after the Taliban takeover, stating that under Taliban rule LGBTQ people face the death penalty and their only option is to leave; documents street attacks on men coded as gay (clothing changed, confinement indoors).

JURIST feature (Nov 8, 2024) summarising the Rainbow Organization of Afghanistan (formed by Afghan LGBTQ refugees in Bremen): reports systematic persecution after Aug 2021, noting that even the post-2001 constitution provided no protective framework and that visibly transgender individuals face the gravest risks including exploitation and violence.

Translation of Article 22 of the Taliban's Promotion of Virtue and Prevention of Vice (PVPV) Law, dated 31 Jul 2024: the overseer must prevent listed 'evils' including lesbianism and homosexuality 'even if with one's own spouse', codifying moral surveillance over same-sex conduct alongside adultery, gambling and other offences.

OHCHR press release (Mar 2026): UN human-rights experts condemn the Taliban's surging use of public corporal punishment — at least 1,110 people flogged in 2025 alone, nearly double 2024 — warning women, girls and LGBT+ people face heightened punishment for 'moral crimes' such as adultery, 'illicit relationships' and 'sodomy'.

Human Dignity Trust country profile (updated Jan 19, 2026): Afghanistan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women; Penal Code 2017 provisions on 'sodomy' and 'inciting sodomy' carry up to two years, while the Penal Code's Sharia-reference clause allows the death penalty for same-sex activity.

GBR.name: United Kingdom
GBR.summary:
The United Kingdom's post-April 2025 Supreme Court regime now operates through statutory and quasi-statutory machinery rather than executive decree. In August 2026 the equality watchdog's code on single-sex spaces came into force, giving organisations compliance examples for restricting toilets, changing rooms and similar facilities to one sex. The code is the daily, nationwide consequence of the ruling: trans visitors use facilities designated by biological sex, and organisations are instructed on how to lawfully enforce that division.

Prison placement has been litigated to the same end. On 19 June 2026, in For Women Scotland v Scottish Ministers [2026] CSOH 59, Lady Ross of the Outer House, Court of Session, ruled the Scottish Prison Service's non-statutory custody guidance unlawful, holding that sex segregation in prisons must rest on a lawful basis; the guidance had allowed some trans prisoners to be held in prisons matching their gender identity rather than their sex at birth. The preceding hearing had been told by the challengers that housing trans prisoners by sex at birth would breach human rights and create an unacceptable suicide risk, while government lawyers defended individual risk assessments as a flexible safeguard. Any visitor arrested in the United Kingdom should therefore expect placement by sex at birth, with contested suicide-risk arguments surrounding that outcome.

Searching and strip-searching follow the same rule. British Transport Police amended its strip-searching policy after the Supreme Court ruling, with trans women searched by officers of their sex at birth as an interim position; the prior policy had permitted a trans woman staff member to conduct an intimate search of a woman holding a Gender Recognition Certificate. Police Scotland's interim guidance of 25 June 2025 states that in custody and stop-and-search, any search involving removal beyond a jacket, gloves, headgear or footwear is conducted on the basis of biological sex, though where a person's lived gender differs, efforts will be made to provide an officer of that lived gender on request.

The direction of travel is a court- and watchdog-led rollback rather than executive hostility, and it is contested at international level: on 18 August 2026 UN human rights experts warned that UK revisions to the Equality Act 2010 risk discriminating against and excluding transgender people.
GBR.outOfScopeNotes:
Surrey Police's FOI-released searching/biological-sex policy (a Surrey and Sussex document) could not be retrieved at research time because the source returned HTTP 403; its contents are therefore unverified here and no claim in this record rests on it.

Whether the interim search policies issued by British Transport Police and Police Scotland have been made permanent, or replaced by a national consolidated policy, is not sourced in this inventory. The inventory also does not record whether the Scottish Prison Service issued replacement custody guidance after the 19 June 2026 ruling, nor whether the reported revisions to the Equality Act 2010 have been enacted in the form the UN experts criticised.

DEU.name: Germany
DEU.summary:
Custody placement is the sharpest documented exposure for a trans visitor. German prisons operate under statutory separation with a binary men and women housing model, and placement corresponding to a prisoner's gender identity has been practised only in exceptional cases; the Criminological Research Institute of Lower Saxony gives that reading of § 170(2) of the Lower Saxony correctional act as the operating rule and runs a research project on the situation of transgender people in prison. Several states have amended their prison statutes in recent years to accommodate legally recognised gender diversity, and a new § 17 of the Rhineland-Palatinate prison act took effect on 1 March 2026 with no press coverage at all.

How the exception is applied in practice remains unsettled. In August 2025 the chief prosecutor for Halle stated that Marla-Svenja Liebich, whose gender entry was changed to female at the end of 2024 under the Self-Determination Act, would serve an 18-month sentence for incitement at Chemnitz women's prison with placement reviewed at intake. After her extradition from Czechia in July 2026 she was transferred to a men's prison despite being legally registered as a woman since 2025; authorities cited the safety of prisoners at the women's facility, and critics called the gender change an abuse of the self-determination law.

DW reported on 23 August 2023 that German prisons offer few safe spaces for trans inmates, a finding illustrated by the case of climate activist Penelope Frank of Last Generation, legally recorded male, who faced assignment to a men's prison if convicted. The Berlin prison service maintains an official page in German with information and contacts for trans, inter and non-binary persons held across the city's facilities.

Screening is a documented flashpoint. In June 2025 the DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a legal complaint under Germany's Equal Treatment Act over a screening at Frankfurt Airport on 23 November 2024, in which officers allegedly deliberately disregarded her gender identity; she characterised the incident as a targeted, degrading act of transphobic harassment and gave Resident Advisor a copy of her statement to the airport.

Access to women-protected facilities has been contested since the Self-Determination Act took effect on 1 January 2025. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline issued in January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off a debate about registered trans women's access, in which trans woman Alessia Dorigo argued that claiming a trans identity on a whim is unrealistic. Tagesspiegel Queerspiegel reported on how Berlin saunas and similar venues now treat trans women, after months of public argument over women-protected spaces and fears that the self-declaration route would be misused.

Reporting and support machinery exists for hostility encountered in country. The STOP the HATE campaign site, run by the Prevention and Empowerment organisation in northern Germany, provides a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
DEU.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether identity-based placement is applied uniformly across the 16 states is unresolved in these sources. No national figure for the number of trans prisoners, and no data on the outcomes of intake placement reviews, is sourced here.

The legal weight of the Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline against the Self-Determination Act is unresolved. The sources document the debate and individual venue practice, but no court ruling on whether a private association may restrict women's saunas by sex characteristics is available.

The outcome of BASHKKA's complaint under the Equal Treatment Act is not sourced, and no source states whether Frankfurt Airport screening procedures were revised after 23 November 2024.

Whether a visitor's gender marker is checked at entry in general, as distinct from the documented airport incident, is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

JPN.name: Japan
JPN.summary:
Most visitors to Japan report little direct hostility or discrimination in daily contact, particularly in major tourist destinations, and the everyday risk posture for a transgender traveller is low. LGBTQ visibility remains limited, social attitudes can be reserved, and legal equality still lags behind other developed countries.

The statutory framework is the Act on Promotion of Public Understanding of Diversity of Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity. The official translation defines gender identity, obliges the government to publish the annual implementation status of policies promoting understanding of sexual orientation and gender identity diversity, and sets out the national basic plan. Parliament enacted the law in June 2023 after months of debate.

No national anti-discrimination statute stands alongside that Act, and no statutory guarantee against violence on grounds of gender identity exists. Full marriage equality for same-sex couples is also absent, so a trans visitor's marital or partner status has no national recognition to rely on.

On workplace and facilities access, Japan's Supreme Court ruled in July 2023 that government restrictions on a transgender employee's use of restrooms were illegal. The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry was found to have violated public-service law by barring a transgender woman from the women's bathroom at work. She had challenged the denial in 2015, and a Tokyo district court ruled for her in 2019 on the basis of her important legal interest in living by her self-identified gender, awarding damages; the Supreme Court upheld that outcome.

On legal documents, a Japanese court has ruled unconstitutional the requirement of sterilising surgery for a change of gender on official documents, in the case brought by Gen Suzuki against the surgical precondition for a legal gender-marker change. Visitors should note that the ruling addresses the surgical precondition itself; the wider procedural route for marker changes and its application to foreign documents is not described in these sources.

Bathhouses are the most concrete everyday friction point. Onsen, sento and super-sento establishments can be daunting for non-binary and trans visitors, and guides aimed at gender-diverse travellers set out LGBTQ+-friendly venues, private-bath and co-ed-pool options and the etiquette involved. First-person accounts from trans travellers published in 2023 describe what to expect from venue norms and transition-related concerns in practice.
JPN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in these sources: whether Gifu Prefecture adopted a policy on clothing, hair and housing for trans inmates after the bar association's September 2023 warning, and whether any national prisons directive now governs placement by legal sex.

Unresolved: the current statutory procedure for changing a gender marker after the surgery requirement was struck down, and whether the ruling extends to documents presented by foreign nationals at entry.

Not sourced in this inventory: any account of immigration or border screening that could reveal a traveller's trans status, visa application questions on gender, or entry refusal on that basis. Nor is there sourced material on the availability of gender-affirming medication to short-term visitors, insurance coverage for it, or access to competent care beyond the bathhouse and venue guidance.

The onsen and bathhouse material is drawn from guidebooks and first-person travel writing rather than official regulation, so the practical norms it describes are reported expectations, not enforceable rules.

THA.name: Thailand
THA.summary:
The Immigration Bureau operates 'Welcome Pride by Immigration', launched 5 August 2024 to mitigate the concerns of foreign LGBTQ+ travellers whose passports do not match their current appearance or gender. It is the entry-friction measure a trans visitor most needs to know about before arrival.

Same-sex marriage has been legal since 22 January 2025, following the bill's final Senate reading in June 2024, making Thailand the first country in Southeast Asia to do so; the statute uses gender-neutral 'marriage partners' terms. Marriage equality closes the practical gaps that previously excluded couples from property regimes, succession, hospital visitation and pension survivor claims.

Legal gender recognition remains absent. There is no mechanism to change the sex marker on a birth certificate, national ID or passport, and title prefixes remain locked to the sex assigned at birth. Advocates at the 2025 'Pride in Action' forum urged the government to expedite a gender-recognition law after marriage equality, and Human Rights Watch found no route for transgender people to obtain legal documentation reflecting their gender identity, with even affirmative measures such as first-name changes leaving discretionary power with officials.

Thai law has no hate-crime designation. When a Chinese tourist murdered a trans woman in Pattaya in April 2025, after she refused his request for sex, the community called it a hate crime, but bias-motivated violence is handled as an ordinary offence with no enhanced penalties and no data collection. LGBTQ+ groups called urgently for new hate-crime protections in the aftermath.

Detention carries specific exposure. The Department of Corrections has separated LGBT prisoners from other inmates nationwide since 1993, and at Pattaya Remand Prison transgender inmates are held in a dedicated block apart from cisgender men; one trans woman stopped by police, expecting to be placed with men because her documents still carried the title Mr., was instead held in the separated wing. Elsewhere, transgender women usually face a choice of men's cells or solitary confinement.

Social acceptance runs ahead of the legal framework. Trans people report greater societal acceptance and higher company positions than is typical in the West, and gender variance is visible in mainstream culture.
THA.outOfScopeNotes:
Legal gender recognition is still pending after marriage equality; no enactment date or draft status is established in the available sources.

The enforcement record of the 2015 anti-discrimination law is described as incomplete, but the sources do not quantify complaints, rulings or penalties.

The status of the Min Buri LGBT prison pilot after its 2016 announcement is not resolved in the inventory, and the proposal for an exclusively-LGBTQ facility has no reported outcome.

The Outright International country overview underpinning the legal-status read was last updated 12 March 2026; other items date from 2017, 2021 and 2025, so the currency of individual claims varies.

The 2025 Pattaya killing is documented through community and press accounts; the inventory does not report the judicial outcome or whether any charge beyond the ordinary offence was brought.

sources.title: Thailand Separates LGBTQ Inmates, Considers Segregated Prison (NBC News/AP)

MEX.name: Mexico
MEX.summary:
Extending legal recognition to trans people remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported in March 2025 that many states now operate administrative legal gender recognition procedures, while calling on the remaining states to adopt them and warning that implementation varies sharply from one state to another. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

Barriers are documented concretely. A 2024 Human Rights Report on Tabasco found that delays and refusals in name and gender recognition leave trans residents with documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying everyday discrimination in banking, health care and policing; the same report set those barriers against killings, including a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Legislative gains are real and recent. Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law criminalising transfemicide in July 2024, named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished; activists describe the statute as critical to their sense of safety. Twenty-two of 32 states offer administrative legal gender recognition, Nayarit and Mexico City have criminalised transfemicide, marriage equality is nationwide, and constitutional anti-discrimination protections apply throughout the country.

The death toll contradicts the statutory picture. Transgender Europe's monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicides in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100 in the same period. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and killings of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding year. In early 2024 the Associated Press counted at least three transgender people killed, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which prompted street protests by LGBTQ+ organisations. Seventy-one trans or gender-diverse people were killed in a single recent year, the second-highest count in the Americas.

Impunity is the decisive variable. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and state authorities to step up prevention and punishment of violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Organised crime is increasingly involved in these killings, and the victims are overwhelmingly local trans women, frequently sex workers and activists, and migrants in transit rather than foreign visitors.

Independent analysis reinforces the gap between statute and enforcement. Writing for the LSE USAPP in November 2024, Caroline Beer found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and cautioned explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence including murder and torture.

For a trans visitor, ordinary risk in heavily policed, progressively governed destinations and central Mexico City tends toward harassment rather than attack, though that assessment sits against an unusually severe national baseline. Global Affairs Canada advises a high degree of caution throughout the country because of high levels of criminal activity and kidnapping, with avoid non-essential travel advisories covering Baja California Sur and the northwestern mainland coast, and the advice was recently revised for Hurricane Polo. Violence against trans people is also highly concentrated by region.

Tourism infrastructure is developed. Intrepid Travel notes that same-sex marriage was legalised in 2009 with Mexico City as the pioneer, that Zona Rosa serves as the capital's gay hub with an annual Pride march and LGBT-friendly hotels, bars and tours, and that Cancún operates as a mainstream LGBTQ+ destination; the same guide records Oaxaca's indigenous muxé third-gender tradition and advises caution outside tourist hubs.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights phrased its impunity warning conditionally, stating that impunity may reach alarming levels, and its 2024 appeal to federal and state authorities is a recommendation rather than a report of completed investigations. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 dispatch likewise documents implementation gaps between states without quantifying them.

MEX.tangentialFactors:
Regional comparison sets the scale of the problem. Mexico's count of 52 transfeminicides between October 2022 and September 2023 trailed only Brazil's 100, placing the country second in the Americas for a single recent year at 71 trans or gender-diverse victims. Human Rights Watch's March 2025 dispatch frames the domestic question as one of coverage rather than principle, since the states that lack recognition procedures are the ones where document mismatch drives the worst outcomes.

Coahuila's 2007 approval of gay civil unions by a 20–13 vote made it the third jurisdiction in the Americas to do so, after Mexico City and Buenos Aires, and the statute barred adoption and custody for those couples; the measure drew a PRI deputy's description as a sensible response to discrimination and a PAN attack on the family argument. That history indicates how uneven and contested subnational equality law has been across states.

MEX.localsOnly:
Residents can seek administrative legal gender recognition in 22 of the 32 states, and Human Rights Watch's March 2025 dispatch presses the remaining states to establish procedures, noting that implementation gaps persist between states and that document requests without recognition expose applicants to discrimination, violence and humiliation. The Tabasco research shows what those gaps cost in practice: mismatched documents impede access to work, banking and public services.
