BRN.name: Brunei
BRN.summary:
Section 198 of Brunei's Syariah Penal Code creates the trans-specific offence of "a man posing as a woman or vice versa". Official guidance on the code states that it binds all persons in the country including tourists, and travel agents are briefed to that effect.

The US State Department's 2017 report on human rights practices in Brunei describes the provision as banning men from dressing as women and women from dressing as men "without reasonable excuse", with no known convictions recorded in 2017. Morality provisions covering cross-dressing were among those enforced under the code at that time, while the sharia implementing regulations had not been issued.

Human Rights Watch's #OUTLAWED survey places Brunei among at least two countries, with Oman, whose national laws expressly criminalise "posing as" or "imitating" a person of a different sex. That trans-specific offence appears in only nine of the countries that criminalise gender expression, against at least 67 countries that criminalise same-sex relations. A state-sharia analogue exists in Malaysia.

Stage three of the Syariah Penal Code took effect on 3 April 2019 under the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, which was brought into force in stages. It provides for death by stoning for anal sex, adultery and abortion, amputation for theft, and 40 strokes of the cane for lesbian sex. Homosexuality was already an offence carrying up to 10 years' imprisonment under the previous law. The 2017 State Department report separately records that 'liwat' between men carries death by stoning if implemented.

The code applies chiefly to Muslims, roughly two-thirds of an estimated population of 420,000 to 450,000. First-person reporting published as the penalties took effect describes anonymous accounts of a climate of fear and no assurance of enforcement against foreigners.

The sultan stated that Brunei's capital-punishment moratorium covers the new sharia provisions. The country has carried out no execution since 1957, and a freshness check dated 27 September 2026 found the law still in force with the 2019 moratorium intact. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights urged Brunei to halt the code, Human Rights Watch described it as barbaric, and the United Nations and foreign governments condemned it.

The 2017 State Department report also records LGBTI-reported discrimination in employment, housing, recreation and services.
BRN.outOfScopeNotes:
Four sources in the inventory could not be retrieved at research time and returned HTTP 403: the Norwegian government's hosted copy of Brunei's Penal Code including the Syariah Penal Code provisions, the Human Dignity Trust's April 2019 briefing on implementation of the Syariah Penal Code Order 2013, a France24 report of April 2019 on fear among Brunei's gay community, and an SSRN paper on the sharia penal code. Their specific claims remain unresolved against the primary text.

No source in the inventory reports a conviction under Section 198 after 2017; the only conviction figure available is the US State Department's "no known convictions" finding for 2017, and whether that position has since changed is unresolved.

Whether the sharia implementing regulations that were unissued in 2017 have since been made is not sourced here, and no source addresses legal gender recognition, the text or marker on identity and travel documents, visa or border screening that could expose a visitor's gender history, bathroom or facility rules, access to transition-related healthcare, or recognition of partners or marriages. These gaps are not findings of permissiveness.

Population estimates differ between sources, with 420,000 and 450,000 both appearing in the inventory, and the Muslim share is given as roughly two-thirds.

PRT.name: Portugal
PRT.summary:
Portugal remains one of the safer destinations in Europe for transgender visitors. Homosexuality is legal, same-sex marriage has been legal since 2010, gender-affirming care is available, legal gender and name change is possible without restriction under the 2018 self-determination law, self-declaration is available from age 16, bathroom access matching a person's gender is protected, discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is illegal, conversion therapy has been banned since 2024, and surgical intervention on intersex infants is prohibited.

The Penal Code treats sexual orientation and gender identity as explicit grounds for aggravated offences. Under Articles 132, 144 and 145, an assault determined by hatred on those grounds is aggravated and punishable by up to four years, and organising discrimination on those grounds carries penalties of one to eight years.

That baseline is under direct legislative pressure. On 20 March 2026 the Assembly of the Republic approved on first reading three bills tabled by the governing PSD, the far-right Chega and the CDS-PP, by 124 votes to 79. The package targets the 2018 self-identification law directly. One bill would reinstate a mandatory medical opinion for any change of legal gender and name, undoing the reform that replaced medical certification with self-declaration. The bills were referred to the Committee on Rights, Freedoms and Guarantees.

The rollback package also threatens the statutory ban on forced medical interventions on intersex children, according to ILGA-Europe's assessment of the draft legislation. Committee-stage analysis by the Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality warns that the bills worsen suffering and negative outcomes for trans people, and defends the existing discrimination-prevention duties of schools.

As of the most recent reporting none of the three bills has become law. The measures sit at committee stage after a first vote, and the Justice Ministry continues to process legal gender and name changes under the 2018 framework.

The ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map 2026 places Portugal 12th, down one position, with a score of 67 percent. The rating reflects the absence of any new affirmative legislation since the 2024 ban on conversion practices, and the draft bill threatening self-determined legal gender recognition and the intersex intervention ban. Portugal scores below Malta, Iceland and Belgium and above most other European states.
PRT.outOfScopeNotes:
The three bills are at first reading and committee stage. Their final content, the committee's report, the second reading and any presidential or constitutional review are unresolved, and reporting does not establish whether the mandatory medical opinion, the changes to the intersex provision, or any restriction on hormone treatment for minors will survive in enacted form.

The precise division of measures across the three separate bills is not consistently specified across sources. The mandatory medical opinion is attributed to the package; a ban on hormone treatment for minors is described for one of the bills in political reporting but is not separately confirmed by the committee or rights-group documents cited here.

The Rainbow Map 2026 score of 67 percent and the 12th-place ranking predate any adoption of the rollback, and the projected loss of at least four places is a projection by signatory organisations rather than a published score. Whether the rating will be revised after the legislative process concludes is unresolved.

The outcome of the Ombudsman's request for constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C is not stated in the source material, and no ruling on the provision's compatibility with the constitution is available here.

The European Parliament written question E-001183/2026 records an inquiry to the Commission; no Commission reply or any binding effect on the national legislative process is documented in the inventory.

PRT.tangentialFactors:
The political contest over the bills has been unusually public. The psychologists' professional order and trans rights organisations describe the package as a retrocesso, a backwards step, and the socialist opposition invoked the 2006 murder of Gisberta, a trans woman killed by youths in Porto, against the rollback, drawing a protest response from Chega's Hugo Soares.

Six European LGBTI organisations, IGLYO, ILGA-Europe, OII Europe, TGEU, EL*C and Bi+ Equal, issued a joint statement warning that the three bills debated on 19 March and voted on 20 March 2026 would seriously attack trans and intersex rights, bodily autonomy and legal gender recognition. They calculate that adoption would cost Portugal at least four places on the Rainbow Map, dropping it below Sweden, the Netherlands, Ireland and France, and reversing its position as a European reference point.

The rollback has reached European-level scrutiny. A European Parliament written question, E-001183/2026, formally asks the Commission about the repeal process for the 2018 gender self-determination law and its consequences for the health and safety of transgender people in the country.

Public opinion runs against the legislative direction. Equaldex records high public support for same-sex parenting, ranked first among 30 European peer jurisdictions, while the same source records gender change with no restrictions, gender-affirming care legal, a full ban on intersex infant surgery, hate-crime protections covering sexual orientation and gender identity, and protected bathroom access.

The Ombudsman, Provedoria da Justiça, has requested constitutional review of Penal Code Article 176-C, which criminalises acts contrary to sexual orientation, gender identity or gender expression. The institutional watchdog is questioning the hate-speech provision itself rather than expanding it, a challenge running alongside rather than against the rollback bills.
PRT.localsOnly:
Justice Ministry data show legal sex and name changes climbing back toward the high-water mark recorded two years earlier, with the largest number recorded in the capital district, according to Expresso. The uptick occurred before any tightening takes effect, so residents are completing changes under the existing self-declaration route while it remains in force.

The Commission for Citizenship and Gender Equality assessed the bills in committee and concluded that they worsen suffering and adverse outcomes for trans people. The same analysis defended the discrimination-prevention duties already imposed on schools, and found the Bloco de Esquerda bill on the subject compatible with those human-rights obligations.

Residents benefit from protections that remain in force regardless of the bills: the 2018 self-determination route to legal recognition, the 2024 conversion-therapy ban, the prohibition on intersex infant surgery, aggravated-offence penalties for hatred-motivated crime, and the Ombudsman's standing to bring constitutional challenges against Penal Code provisions.

Constitutional review of Article 176-C is a domestic institutional process available to residents through the Ombudsman, distinct from the parliamentary rollback and from European-level questions raised by MEPs.

IRL.name: Ireland
IRL.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Ireland rests on the Gender Recognition Act 2015 (No. 25 of 2015), commenced on 4 September 2015 by S.I. 369/2015 and amended by subsequent statutory instruments through 2026. Adults change their legal gender by self-declaration, with no psychological evaluation or medical requirement, and the operative text is the statute itself rather than any discretionary approval process.

GCN's anniversary reporting records that Ireland is one of only 11 European countries permitting gender recognition through self-determination without a psychological evaluation requirement, with activists marking the milestone while flagging gaps that remain. A Guardian retrospective of 23 December 2025, marking the decade since the Act, carries first-person accounts of self-declaration and updated documents and frames the statute as a move away from Ireland's Catholic past, alongside renewed calls over remaining gaps in trans rights and healthcare.

The Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 explicitly covers gender identity and sex characteristics as protected characteristics. Garda reports of hate crimes rose 15% in 2025, with racism and xenophobia recorded as the most common motives, according to an Irish Times report of August 2026. A University College Dublin study published on 3 July 2025 found that discrimination against sexual and gender minorities in Ireland has increased, documenting a rise in prejudice despite the protective statutory framework.

Access to gender-affirming care is constrained by waiting times rather than by a legal prohibition. The Journal's April 2025 investigation reports years-long waiting lists for multidisciplinary assessment at the National Gender Service, with some trans people turning away from official channels as a result; the HSE defends its comprehensive multidisciplinary model of care.

Equaldex records gender change as legal with no restrictions, but no legal recognition of non-binary identity, gender-affirming care that is legal yet restricted for minors, no statutory ban on conversion therapy, and no ban on intersex infant surgery. Hate-crime protections there cover sexual orientation and gender identity, while employment and housing discrimination protections cover sexual orientation only.

Belong To LGBTQ+ Youth Ireland operates an anonymous online hate-crime reporting form alongside rights information and links to protections under the Equal Status Acts, giving young LGBTQ+ people a route to report incidents short of a formal complaint.
IRL.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposed limitation on the effect of a Gender Recognition Certificate during imprisonment has since been enacted, and what the amended text would provide, is unresolved in the available sources; only its passage at first legislative stage as of late 2025 is documented.

Enforcement of the Criminal Justice (Hate Offences) Act 2024 in cases where gender identity is the recorded motive is unresolved: the published statistics break down hate-crime reports by overall motive, with racism and xenophobia most common, and no trans-specific charge or conviction data is sourced here.

The Telegraph's September 2024 account of Ireland backing down on hate-speech laws amid the trans debate was paywalled (HTTP 402) and could not be read at research time; no claim from it is carried into this record. Two further sources, the Garda hate-crime statistics release for 2025 and a Diaspora Support page on returning to Ireland, were too thin to yield findings.

The reported rise in discrimination rests on a single UCD study; its methodology, sample and the specific categories of discrimination measured are not detailed in the inventory and remain unverified.

BEL.name: Belgium
BEL.summary:
Belgium is among the more protective jurisdictions in Europe for transgender visitors. Discrimination, hate crimes and hate speech on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are prohibited; same-sex marriage and adoption are legal; and legal name and gender-marker change rests on self-determination.

Since 1 January 2018, under the Law of 25 June 2017, transgender people have been able to change their registered gender and first names by declaration to the civil registrar, without medical conditions. The Federal Justice Department records that the Constitutional Court partially annulled that law on 19 June 2019 and that, pending replacement provisions, applications continue to be handled under the current procedure.

Hate crime and hate speech on grounds of gender identity are criminal offences, and transphobia is recorded as a hate-crime motive. One qualification matters for expectations of the justice system: the OSCE/ODIHR national framework page states that hate crimes are not defined in Belgian legislation and that no code exists to record them as such, so breaches of non-discrimination law that constitute criminal offences are prosecuted under general provisions.

Belgium passed Europe's first femicide law in 2023, covering all gender-based homicide and including protections for gender minorities, and a 2023 law banning conversion practices. Medically unnecessary surgeries on intersex infants remain legal, although a Brussels court held a hospital accountable for non-consensual interventions.

The principal visitor-facing risk is violence rather than law. The equality bodies Unia and the Institute for the Equality of Women and Men reported in May 2025 that violence and intimidation targeting LGBTQI people are rising, with gay men and transgender people especially affected. Of 136 sexual-orientation discrimination cases Unia handled in a year, 35% involved physical assault and 35% serious intimidation. An RTBF investigation documented a recurring pattern in which perpetrators use fake dating-app profiles to arrange meetings, then ambush victims in isolated locations to rob, humiliate or assault them; police have recorded an alarming number of incidents, many unreported through fear or shame. A case against three men accused of targeting at least eight victims went to the Brussels Criminal Court in May 2025.

The formal-law position is confirmed by the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map country page, which scores Belgium across legal gender recognition, hate crime, equality and non-discrimination, family law, civil society, asylum and intersex protection.

FRA.name: France
FRA.summary:
The risks documented for transgender travellers in France concentrate in two settings: detention and the border. In everyday movement, accommodation and services, the country's own oversight bodies record persistent discrimination rather than legal prohibition.

Prison placement follows no statutory rule. Where a trans woman is held is decided by the gender inscribed on her identity documents, with each facility improvising: special units, or isolation that restricts contact with other inmates. Treatment varies between establishments, and accounts collected in a BuzzFeed News feature of 12 January 2018 describe heightened assault vulnerability and suicide risk under those arrangements.

France's national custodial-inspection authority, the CGLPL, examined roughly 40 referrals from trans detainees since 2010, together with ministry and association input, and issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 finding serious and persistent violations: placement by birth sex, isolation, and exposure during strip searches. It recorded no marked improvement since its 2010 opinion despite the 2016 legal gender-recognition reform, and issued binding guidance for places of deprivation of liberty.

The national preventive mechanism explained to the Association for the Prevention of Torture that a new opinion was needed precisely because the 2010 opinion produced no marked improvement, because the gender-recognition law and its terminology had changed, and because coverage now extends to intersex and non-binary detainees. Its findings rest on a decade of letters from detained trans people and identify structural problems in the isolation of vulnerable detainees and in suicide prevention.

That practice remained current in 2025. Louna, a trans woman detained for opposing the A69 motorway works, has been held since mid-October 2024 in the Tarbes men's prison and kept in isolation since October. Her incarceration was put to the Keeper of the Seals in oral question no. 219 in the French National Assembly, arguing that the case exposes a prison system unable to guarantee conditions for trans detainees; placement remains under parliamentary scrutiny.

At entry points, trans women have faced questioning of their identity documents in public. Giovanna Rincon's first-person account in StreetPress of 7 March 2017 describes ten minutes of routine humiliation by French border police at the airport, questioned in front of other travellers, documenting identity-document friction for trans travellers arriving in France.

The Défenseur des droits issued a new framework decision on trans rights, confirming persistent fundamental-rights violations drawn from case files and association testimony. It cites the EU Fundamental Rights Agency's 2023 survey, in which 64% of trans people in France report identity-related discrimination, and sets out official guidance for service providers.

For partner recognition, the legal baseline dates from the marriage-equality law in force by late May 2013; CNN reported France's first same-sex wedding on 29 May 2013, performed days after the law took effect.

The border incidents are documented through a single first-person account of 7 March 2017; no more recent equivalent account of document checks at French entry points is present in the sources, so the current frequency of such treatment is not established here.

Not sourced: any rule or practice governing bathroom and changing-facility access for visitors in France generally, as distinct from the hostel dormitory dispute reported in August 2024.

Not sourced: whether visa or entry screening asks questions that could disclose a traveller's trans status, and whether gender markers on foreign passports are accepted without additional scrutiny.

Not sourced: access to hormone therapy, continuity of care, or姓名-related documentation for trans detainees, and how the CGLPL's binding guidance is enforced when a facility departs from it.

The referral figure of roughly 40 cases since 2010 is an approximation given by the CGLPL; the count of facilities operating special units or isolation is not quantified in the sources.

An advocacy organisation reported in August 2024 a hostel incident in which a foreign guest who objected to a man in the female dormitory bathroom was threatened with a charge of transphobia by the manager. The report comes from an organisation with a stated position on sex segregation, and it concerns hostel dormitory rules rather than a legal requirement.

Advocacy and oversight bodies, not only state institutions, drive the record here: the international NGO's interview and the national custodial-inspection authority's opinion both rest on accumulated letters and referrals from detained trans people and on association testimony collected over more than a decade.

CHE.name: Switzerland
CHE.summary:
Legal gender recognition in Switzerland operates by self-declaration. Since 1 January 2022 any person registered in a Swiss municipality can change their sex marker and/or first name by personal declaration before a civil registrar, with no surgery and no court proceeding. In the first months of the route about 350 people had used it.

Same-sex marriage has been in force since 1 July 2022 under the 'Marriage for All' reform, which also opened adoption and IVF to same-sex couples; the reform was approved by 64.1% of voters in referendum.

Public incitement to hatred, denigration or discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation has been punishable under Article 261bis of the Criminal Code since 1 July 2020. That provision does not cover gender identity, so a person targeted specifically for being trans does not receive the criminal-law aggravation available on sexual-orientation grounds. The Criminal Code contains no general hate-crime provision; offences are addressed through the anti-discrimination provisions instead.

Recorded anti-LGBTIQ+ violence is rising. Monitoring by the LGBTIQ Helpline reports roughly six hate crimes per week, 309 cases in the reference year, with reports up fivefold since 2020. OSCE/ODIHR's 2024 Hate Crime Report records that Swiss police do not record bias motivation and that national recording does not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes, so official statistics understate the picture.

On 28 January 2026 the Federal Council adopted Switzerland's first National Action Plan to combat hate crimes against LGBTIQ persons, covering 2026 to 2030. Its three pillars are support and protection of victims, prevention of hate crime, and monitoring of violence, with the Federal Office for Gender Equality coordinating implementation.

Non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is recognised in Swiss law, and same-sex couples have been able to marry since 1 July 2022.

Placement of transgender detainees is governed cantonally rather than nationally. The canton of Basel-Stadt's detention law, adopted by the Grand Council on 13 November 2019, requires separation of female and male detainees and states that the gender identity of the detained person is respected as far as possible, with the prison directorate permitted to deviate from the separation rules in consultation with the referring authority. No federal trans-prisoner placement rule is recorded and no Swiss case law on the question is recorded; placement practice varies by canton.
CHE.outOfScopeNotes:
The numeric value of the ILGA-Europe Rainbow Map index for Switzerland is not present in the inventory and is therefore not stated here.

No federal rule governing the placement of trans prisoners is recorded, nor is any Swiss case law, specialised trans units in places of detention, or federal practice on solitary confinement for trans prisoners; whether such material exists elsewhere is unresolved.

Entry and visa rules, border or airport document screening, gender markers on passports and other identity documents, access to gender-affirming healthcare, and rules on access to sex-segregated facilities such as bathrooms are not addressed by the sources supplied and remain unsourced for this record.

The hate-crime figures derive from LGBTIQ Helpline monitoring rather than police statistics, and official police recording does not code bias motivation, so the relationship between the two data sets is unresolved.

AUT.name: Austria
AUT.summary:
Outright International's country overview, updated March 2026, records a permissive statutory baseline: same-sex relations have been legal since 1971, marriage equality has applied since 2017, and same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2016.

Legal gender recognition is available without mandatory medical procedures. A person may obtain an 'X', indeterminate or absent gender marker, and intersex people may choose 'diverse', 'inter' or no designation at all.

The non-binary marker carries a documented restriction. The Constitutional Court ruled in June 2018 that official documents must reflect gender identity accurately, and Austria issued its first 'X' passport and 'divers' birth certificate in 2019; the Interior Ministry limited 'divers' registration to applicants holding a medical panel certificate of intersexuality.

The Equal Treatment Act covers discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, and recent amendments broadened 'gender' to encompass gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics.

Violence is an active and documented risk. In March 2025 police uncovered a network that used fake dating-platform accounts to lure at least 17 gay, bisexual and queer people to remote locations, where masked groups ambushed them, filmed the attacks and falsely accused them of being paedophiles. Fifteen people aged 14 to 26 were arrested, and investigators state that the real victim count is considerably higher.

National police data for 2025 records 6,751 suspected hate crimes, 7,327 prejudice motives and 1,575 victims of prejudice-related violence, with official and media commentary acknowledging that the figures under-record.

A visitor who is detained falls under national rules on the housing of transgender prisoners, set out in Justice Ministry answer to parliamentary question XXVIII. AB 774 of May-June 2025, a German-language document. A 2025 Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report covers the legal framework for LGBTIQ people in Austrian prisons, including gender self-determination and anti-discrimination protection.
AUT.outOfScopeNotes:
Hate-crime totals for 2025 are police figures, and under-recording is acknowledged in the sources; the split between rising homophobic and falling transphobic incidents rests on that same administrative data.

Whether an 'X' or 'divers' marker on a foreign passport is accepted at Austrian border control, and how gender markers are screened on entry, is unresolved: the inventory contains no source stating a border or visa position on markers.

The precise scope of the Interior Ministry's restriction of 'divers' registration to holders of a medical panel certificate of intersexuality, including any subsequent change to that policy, is unresolved in these sources.

Justice Ministry answer XXVIII. AB 774 is available only in German and is cited here for its subject and date rather than for a reviewed reading of its provisions.

The rejected sauna petition and the Ministry of Education rules on outside sex-education providers are reported in a single source and are not corroborated elsewhere in the inventory.

DW report (March 2025): Austrian police arrested 15 people (aged 14-26) over a wave of hate attacks in which at least 17 LGBTQ people were lured via fake dating-platform accounts to remote locations, ambushed by masked groups, filmed, and falsely accused of being paedophiles. Investigators believe the real victim count is much higher.

ITA.name: Italy
ITA.summary:
Outright International records same-sex relations as legal throughout Italy for men and women. That legal baseline has not prevented recurring violence against LGBT people, and in particular against transgender people. ILGA-Europe's 2026 Annual Review documents that homophobic and transphobic violence continued in 2025, including organised dating-app entrapment schemes in which groups lure victims and then assault or rob them. Progetto Gionata characterises transphobia as the most severe and most widespread discrimination confronting transgender people in Italy, which is consistent with the pattern of violence recorded by monitors rather than with isolated incidents.

The most serious traveller-specific finding is the sexual assault of young transgender tourists in Campania. ANSA reports that the convictions for the assault were upheld on appeal in April 2026, an outcome that affirms accountability for violence against trans visitors, while also confirming that the assault took place and that the victims were targeted while in Italy. Organised entrapment schemes of the kind ILGA-Europe records for gay men present a comparable risk surface for transgender visitors who use dating and hookup applications, where victims are deliberately isolated before being attacked.

Police violence against transgender people is documented and has been prosecuted. On 5 July 2024 tgcom24 reported that a Milan traffic officer was sentenced to ten months in prison for stopping and then beating a transgender woman with batons. The conviction shows that such conduct reaches criminal sanction, and it also shows that transgender people in Italy face the risk of physical violence from the officers who stop them.

Transgender people who are detained in Italy are held in an institutional environment that monitor reports describe as lacking consistent gender-affirming provision. The Ludwig Boltzmann Institute national report of July 2025 sets out the legal and policy framework governing LGBTIQ detainees in Italy, the pathways available for gender affirmation in custody, and the treatment of same-sex relationships in prison. A 2026 study in Frontiers in Psychiatry, drawing on a thematic analysis of transgender identity and psychiatric care in Italian prisons, records systemic gaps and institutional challenges in the care provided to incarcerated trans people.

The political and institutional climate is openly hostile. POL.name: Poland
POL.summary:
Poland is broadly workable with two genuinely traveler-relevant weaknesses. In detention, documented severe failures involve foreign trans people directly: a Vietnamese trans woman was held in a male immigration-detention center with her hormone-therapy needs ignored for three months, until the border authorities ordered her release after intervention, and the European Court of Human Rights found in 2024 that the country violated a trans prisoner's rights by denying her hormone therapy. There is no specialized trans prison section.

Socially, the climate was deeply hostile under the previous government ("LGBT-free zones") and is improving under the current coalition — a hate-speech reform draft appeared in March 2025, and in June 2024 the directive blocking recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad was revoked — but a low baseline persists: Pride marches have been violently attacked (Białystok 2019), online anti-LGBT harassment is documented (Amnesty 2025), and rural areas draw harassment warnings.

Bathrooms are unrestricted and there is no cross-dressing statute. Gender-marker documents run through the civil-status-records regime, whose sufficiency a 2024 scholarly analysis questions. A government travel advisory lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, and major cities are calmer than rural areas.
POL.outOfScopeNotes: Passport theft, unofficial-taxis overcharging, and general urban crime affect all travellers.

sources.summary: Association for Legal Intervention news (13 Mar 2024): a regional court had placed a transgender Vietnamese woman in a guarded centre for male foreigners; after NGO intervention the Border Guard commander ordered her release. Her hormone therapy had been interrupted for three months because the centre refused medication supply; the case also documented her prior violence and sexual-assault history. Evidence Polish detention practice can endanger trans detainees' health until challenged.

TGEU (16 Jul 2024): on 11 July the ECtHR found Polish prison authorities violated Article 8 (and rejected Article 3) by denying a trans prisoner hormone replacement therapy; damages of EUR 8,000 ordered. Directly relevant precedent: trans prisoners in Poland can litigate medication denial and win.

Amnesty International report 'A Thousand Cuts' (2025): documents technology-facilitated gender-based violence against Poland's LGBTI community on X, including LGBT-free-zone legacy (2019-23), lack of legal inclusion, and X's policy reversals (misgendering/deadnaming rule removed Apr 2023, reinstated 2024). Online abuse climate, not visitor law.

HRW World Report 2025 (Poland, events of 2024): LGBT-rights reform under the Tusk government was 'slow and insufficient'; in June 2024 Justice Minister Bodnar revoked the Ziobro directive that had blocked recognition of same-sex marriage certificates obtained abroad, and in September the ECtHR ruled Poland's lack of partnership recognition leaves couples in a 'illegal vacuum' violating their rights, calling for a recognition framework.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (Jan-Dec 2024): Deputy Justice Minister Smiszek announced a hate-speech law extending protection to gender identity and sexual orientation; March draft Penal Code amendment raised penalties for anti-LGBTI hate speech/violence, passed Government Legislation Centre in May but approval was postponed; a second bill followed in late October; Prosecutor General set up a special response team with new guidelines for law enforcement.

Global Affairs Canada travel advisory for Poland lists sexual orientation among reported harassment motives alongside physical appearance and foreigner status, links general LGBTQ2+ travel guidance, and notes visa-free entry for tourists staying up to 90 days.

Przeglad Sejmowy 2024/5, Podgorska-Rykala & Kepa: scholarly legal analysis of Poland's administrative regime for transgender persons under the Civil Status Records Law, Population Register Act and Identity Cards Act; asks whether citizens are equally treated and whether protection is sufficient, especially on civil status. Evidence of how gender-marker documents work in practice in Poland.

HRW news release (18 Mar 2007): the then government proposed fast-track legislation 'punishing anyone who promotes homosexuality' in schools - dismissal, fines or prison for teachers/students, banning LGBT organisations and safer-sex HIV education, with deputy minister Orzechowski announcing teachers who reveal homosexuality would be fired; HRW wrote to PM Kaczynski. Historical precedent for state-led school censorship.

HUN.name: Hungary
HUN.summary:
Hungary's statutory position on trans people has not changed with the political turnover of the 12 April 2026 election, in which Péter Magyar's Tisza party won 138 seats and ended 16 years of Viktor Orbán's government. Analysts describe the outcome as a restoration of the democratic baseline rather than a repeal of the legal architecture built during the previous era, and Tisza has not published an LGBTQ+ programme. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal in Hungary since 1961.

Legal gender recognition is explicitly prohibited. In May 2020, while ruling by emergency decree during the COVID-19 pandemic, the Orbán government pushed through a bill barring passports and identity cards from reflecting an acquired gender, including for people already legally recognised, and redefined the word nem (sex) in the civil code as immutable biological sex. Administrative refusal had already made recognition effectively impossible from 2018. Trans Hungarians therefore carry identity documents that do not match their presentation, and a visitor whose papers were issued under this regime should expect document checks to expose the mismatch at border control and in any transaction requiring identification.

One correction route operates at European level. In Case C-247/23 Deldits, judgment of 13 March 2025 on a reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration matter, the Court of Justice of the European Union held that Article 16 GDPR obliges the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where that data has changed and no longer satisfies the accuracy principle of Article 5(1)(d). In September 2024 the same court's Advocate General had called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries. Neither holding reinstates the domestic power to issue new documents bearing an acquired gender.

In April 2026 the Court of Justice ruled that Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ legislation, including the prohibition on gender change for under-18s argued under child-protection law, breached EU rules on several levels, and found a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty, which sets out the union's founding values. The judgment was delivered nine days after Hungarians voted.

Public assembly is the most contested area for a visitor. Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik identified restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue after the election and noted that anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds parliamentary majority, while the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar has raised questions about the pace of change. The 31st Budapest Pride, held in June 2026, was the first since Orbán was voted out; tens of thousands marched against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws still in force, and international coverage recorded community expectations that changes will be made.

Detention remains a documented exposure point. A 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, produced by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society as part of the EU-funded Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU project, sets out the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people held in Hungarian detention under the current legal and political climate. Human Rights Watch's World Report 2025 records that LGBT people in Hungary continue to face discrimination and demonisation.
HUN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this source set: whether the constitutional restriction on LGBTQ public events and the child-protection content legislation have been amended, suspended or left untouched in the months since the April 2026 election. The sources record the repeal mechanism and the organisers' demands, not the legislative outcome.

Unresolved: whether the Court of Justice holdings on registry rectification and on the under-18 gender-change prohibition have been applied in practice by Hungarian registry authorities, and how border and police officials treat documents that do not match presentation during routine checks. No source in this inventory reports enforcement data.

Not sourced here: access to gender-affirming healthcare, facilities and restroom access for visitors, and the operation of hate-crime or anti-discrimination protections in prosecutions. Any statement on those points would rest on material outside the current inventory.

The 2025 detention report is cited at the level of its subject and authorship; individual findings on conditions, complaints handling and staff conduct are not reproduced in this record.

sources.summary: France24 (June 2026) covers LGBTQ rights in Hungary after the election: 'we are very hopeful that changes will be made'.

AP (Jun 2026): 'Hungary holds its first Budapest Pride in the post-Orbán era' — tens of thousands march in the 31st Budapest Pride, the first since Viktor Orbán was voted out, against the backdrop of his era's anti-LGBT laws.

The Dissident analysis (April 2026) by Alejandra Caraballo: what Hungary's election (Tisza's 138 seats, ending Orbán's rule) actually means for LGBTQ people - a return to democratic baseline, not liberation. Details the 'constitutional architecture of erasure': the May 2020 total ban on legal gender recognition (redefining 'nem' as immutable biological sex), forcing trans Hungarians to carry mismatched documents.
Wikipedia's Hungary country overview states that legal gender change has been de facto impossible since 2018 and explicitly illegal since 2020, and that same-sex activity has been legal since 1961.

BBC News (April 2026): the European Court of Justice ruled Orbán-era anti-LGBTQ laws — including the under-18 gender-change ban argued under child-protection law — breached EU rules on several levels, significantly finding a breach of Article 2 of the EU Treaty (an unprecedented finding against founding values). The ruling came nine days after Hungarians voted in the election that ended Fidesz rule.

niHaplus (17 April 2026): after Fidesz lost power in the 12 April 2026 election ending 16 years of Orbán rule, Budapest Pride spokesperson Johanna Majercsik named restoration of the right to assembly as 'the most urgent issue' and said anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds majority; the Tisza party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights under Péter Magyar raises questions about the pace of change.

Hungarian Helsinki Committee / Háttér Society national report (2025) on LGBTIQ detainees in Hungary, part of the EU-funded 'Strengthening the rights of LGBTIQ detainees in the EU' project - the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people in Hungarian detention amid the current legal and political climate.

HRW World Report 2025 (Hungary): LGBT people continue to face discrimination and demonization; a 2020 law bans legal gender change for transgender and intersex people, and in September 2024 the CJEU Advocate General called on Hungarian authorities to correct a transgender refugee's gender marker in national registries.

ECJ judgment C-247/23 Deldits (13 March 2025), on reference from the Budapest High Court in an immigration case: Article 16 GDPR requires the national register authority to rectify recorded gender data where it has changed and no longer complies with the accuracy principle of Art 5(1)(d) — the operative authority for updating gender markers on official records.

BuzzFeed News (April 2020, Patrick Strudwick): while ruling by emergency decree during COVID, Orbán's government pushed a bill barring passports and ID cards from reflecting a person's acquired gender — even for those already legally recognized. This is the decree-level rollback that made legal gender recognition explicitly illegal in 2020.

Hungarian citizens cannot obtain legal gender recognition at all: the 2020 emergency-decree legislation removed the route and locked identity documents to sex assigned at birth, and the redefinition of sex as immutable biological sex in the civil code forecloses domestic litigation on the point.

Registry rectification under Article 16 GDPR remains available for correcting recorded gender data, following the Deldits judgment of 13 March 2025, but that mechanism addresses the accuracy of an existing record rather than authorising the issuance of a new passport or identity card.

Repeal of the anti-queer statutes is a two-thirds majority question in the National Assembly, and the Budapest Pride organisers have framed restoration of assembly rights as the first objective. The 2025 report by the Hungarian Helsinki Committee and the Háttér Society is the reference document on the treatment and rights of LGBTIQ detainees, produced under an EU-funded project covering the situation in Hungarian places of detention.

Human Rights Watch's 2025 country chapter documents continuing discrimination and demonisation of LGBT people in public life, which shapes how a resident's documents and presentation are read by officials even where no offence is committed.

Public assembly is the most contested area for a visitor. a spokesperson for the national Pride organiser identified restoration of the right to assembly as the most urgent issue after the election and noted that anti-queer laws can be repealed with a two-thirds parliamentary majority, while the incoming party's silence on LGBTQ+ rights has raised questions about the pace of change. The 31st Pride march, held in June 2026, was the first since the previous government was voted out; tens of thousands marched against the backdrop of the anti-LGBT laws still in force, and international coverage recorded community expectations that changes will be made.

Detention remains a documented exposure point. A 2025 national report on LGBTIQ detainees, produced by a national detention-monitoring NGO and a national LGBTQ+ organisation under a union-funded project on the rights of LGBTIQ detainees, sets out the situation and rights of LGBTIQ people held in places of detention under the current legal and political climate. GRC.name: Greece
GRC.summary:
Greece's statutory framework is among the stronger ones in the region. Law 5089/2024 legalised same-sex marriage in February 2024, making Greece the first state with a majority Orthodox Christian population to do so, and added SOGIESC equal-treatment guarantees covering social protection, education, healthcare, housing and goods and services. Civil unions have been available since 2015, with adoption and foster care permitted, and the age of consent is 15 for everyone. Legal gender change has been possible on a self-declaration basis since 2017. Conversion practices have been banned for minors and intersex genital mutilation criminalised since 2022, employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity has been prohibited since 2023, and hate-crime and hate-speech provisions cover gender identity. ILGA-Europe's Rainbow Map placed Greece 7th in its 2025 rankings.

There are no trans-specific restrictions at the border or on bathroom use, and legal gender recognition is available. The UK Foreign Office updated its Greece travel advice for LGBTQ+ travellers in April 2024, noting that same-sex relations are legal, civil unions date from 2015 and marriage from February 2024, and advising visitors to remain alert.

Enforcement and street-level violence tell a harder story. In March 2024 a mob of roughly 150 people attacked two transgender people in Thessaloniki; 21 people were arrested, 11 of them minors, and a masked attack on counter-protesters followed. The European Court of Human Rights found in Koutra and Katzaki v. Greece (2017) that police stopped and mistreated transgender sex workers and their lawyer in Athens in 2013, pulling them from cars in street stops, and that complaints against the officers were discontinued. In 2025 the same court condemned Greece for detaining an LGBTI Iranian refugee pending deportation, finding a violation of Article 3. In July 2025 the Crete Court of Appeal convicted three French tourists over a 2017 attack, and a criminal case was opened over an online post inciting discrimination against immigrants and LGBTI people.

The social climate lags the statute. EU Fundamental Rights Agency survey data from 2024 shows 63% of LGBTIQ respondents avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 average of 53%, 36% avoid certain locations for fear of assault against 29%, only 35% are open about being LGBTIQ against 51%, and 28% felt discriminated against at work against 19%. The Orthodox Church officially opposed marriage equality, and transphobic comments were directed at Greece's Eurovision contestants in 2024.

Trans-specific gaps remain measurable. The TGEU Trans Rights Index and Map 2025, which recorded backsliding outpacing progress across Europe for the first time, counts Greece at 21 of 32 indicators, with shortfalls including age restrictions on legal name changes, the absence of a national action plan, and no legal recognition of trans and non-binary parenthood.
GRC.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not state how Greek border officials handle a passport whose gender marker does not match the holder's presentation, whether additional document checks are applied to trans travellers, or whether any entry refusal or secondary screening on gender-identity grounds has been recorded. This is unresolved in the inventory.

No sourced material addresses access to hormone therapy or other trans-specific healthcare for short-term visitors, the availability of gendered facilities in tourist accommodation, or whether the healthcare equal-treatment guarantee in Law 5089/2024 has been tested in practice for a visitor.

The UK Foreign Office advice is reported as an alertness recommendation rather than a warning of a specific threat; the inventory does not reproduce the full text or any regional caveat it may contain.

Enforcement outcomes are unevenly sourced. The Thessaloniki arrests, the Crete appeal conviction and the discontinued police complaints in the 2017 Strasbourg judgment are documented, but there is no inventory data on conviction rates for gender-identity hate crimes nationally, nor on whether the criminal case opened over the discriminatory online post resulted in charges.

The TGEU count of 21 of 32 indicators is given without the full indicator list, so the eleven unmet measures beyond the three named cannot be enumerated from this inventory.

CZE.name: Czechia
CZE.summary:
Czechia's rules for legal gender recognition have been rewritten twice in eighteen months. On 24 April 2024 the Czech Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery disabling reproductive function, holding compulsory sterilisation for legal recognition unconstitutional; by June 2025 the surgery requirement had been dropped in practice. The European Court of Human Rights then found a violation of Article 8 against Czechia in T.H. v. the Czech Republic (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), holding the surgical and sterilisation conditions and the related civil-registry treatment incompatible with private-life rights and framing Convention-guaranteed gender recognition on self-determination, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe intervening.

Detention remains the weakest point for a trans visitor. Administrative courts clashed in public over the handling of an HIV-positive trans man in transition held by immigration police: in March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the Prague Municipal Court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward the detainee and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a person is 'potentially vulnerable' before deciding placement. Practice has not caught up with that standard. In November 2025 reporting, judges described Czech prisons as unprepared for trans people and lacking clear rules; the Supreme Court is pressing for a national prison concept that explicitly addresses the needs of people in or after transition, the human-rights commissioner is pushing a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry maintains that the existing framework is sufficient, with consultation ongoing.

Social hostility is measurable and politically amplified. The ILGA-Europe 'Being LGBTQ+ in Czechia' survey found 43% of respondents discriminated or harassed in the previous five years, over a third within twelve months, with trans and non-binary respondents reporting the highest rates, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. In 2024 the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, and the far-right SPD circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists' and 'give more to families, take it away from the deviants'.

Enforcement machinery exists but is thinly quantified. Police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, and LGBTI-motivated incidents appear in the bias breakdown; the OSCE/ODIHR 2024 Hate Crime Report notes that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in Parliament, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status.

Entry and protection channels carry no trans-specific obstacle on the record: the new Asylum Law includes sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and offers an opposite-gender interview option. Facilities and public-space conduct are not restricted by any trans-specific rule in the sources.

Where a visitor goes matters. Prague and Brno rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, queer districts in Vinohrady and Žižkov, and hostels providing concierge support, private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. In June 2023 a group disrupted Brno Pride drag story-time with homophobic slurs.

Partner recognition is unresolved. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2018 by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs (ANO, Pirates, KSČM, ČSSD, TOP 09, STAN) to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government and cleared committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with SPD, ODS, KDU-ČSL and ANO support estimated at 80–90%.
CZE.outOfScopeNotes:

Unresolved: whether the national prison concept or a binding regulation on trans detainees has been issued after the November 2025 reporting. The sources document competing positions between the Supreme Court, the human-rights commissioner and the Justice Ministry, with consultation ongoing.

Unresolved: the final status of the same-sex marriage bill. The inventory records committee clearance on 29 June 2023 and a constitutional ban proposal in second reading, with no later outcome sourced.

Unresolved: whether the 2024 hate-crime figures break out LGBTI-motivated incidents numerically. OSCE/ODIHR states that LGBTI-motivated incidents are included in the bias breakdown but also that recorded statistics do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other crimes.

Not sourced: the UK Foreign Office travel advice for Czechia produced no trans-specific safety finding, so no assessment from that channel is reflected here. The sources also do not address bathroom access, identity-document presentation at borders, or medication import rules beyond general traveller guidance.

Unresolved: whether the vulnerability-assessment standard set by the Supreme Administrative Court in the 2023 immigration-detention case is applied consistently by lower courts; the reporting documents disagreement between courts rather than a settled practice.

ECHR, T.H. v. the Czech Republic (App. no. 33037/22, judgment 12 Sep 2025): the Court found a violation of Article 8 regarding Czech legal-gender-recognition conditions — the surgical/sterilisation condition for official sex change and related civil-registry treatment held incompatible with private-life rights, with Transgender Europe and ILGA-Europe as third-party interveners; the Court's reasoning frames Convention-guaranteed gender recognition through self-determination. Definitive international-law datapoint for Czech LGR posture.

Deník/ČTK (22 Jun 2018, Czech): the caretaker government backed a same-sex marriage bill introduced by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs (ANO, Pirates, KSČM, ČSSD, TOP 09, STAN) to replace registered partnerships; the Jsme fér campaign welcomed it. Dated marker of the marriage-equality legislative trail still running (per ILGA-2024, bill passed committees June 2023).

CZE.localsOnly:
Legal gender recognition no longer requires surgery or sterilisation, following Constitutional Court judgment PL. US 52/23 of 24 April 2024 and the administrative change confirmed in June 2025. The Ostrava Regional Court ordered re-issued certificates and a diploma for a trans graduate in April 2023, an example of document correction being granted by an administrative court.

Prison placement remains governed by practice rather than a dedicated rule. The Supreme Court has demanded that the national prison concept explicitly address the needs of people in or after transition, the human-rights commissioner is pressing for a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry holds that the current framework is adequate; consultation is ongoing and no regulation has been issued.

Discrimination exposure is concentrated among trans and non-binary residents, who report the highest rates in the national survey: 43% discriminated or harassed over five years, more than a third within twelve months, 51% subjected to insults, assault or threats.

Residents seeking protection can invoke sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds under the new Asylum Law, which also provides an opposite-gender interview option.

Relationship recognition still runs through registered partnerships. The 2018 cross-party marriage bill cleared committees in June 2023 but no enacted marriage equality is recorded in these sources, and a constitutional ban proposal advanced to second reading.

Document and diploma reissue has been ordered by the Ostrava Regional Court, but no general administrative procedure for marker change is described in the sources reviewed.
CZE.blindSummary:
The state's rules for legal gender recognition were rewritten twice in eighteen months. On 24 April 2024 the national Constitutional Court, in judgment PL. US 52/23, struck down the requirement that an official sex change be conditional on surgery disabling reproductive function, holding compulsory sterilisation for legal recognition unconstitutional; by June 2025 the surgery requirement had been dropped in practice. The regional human-rights court then found a violation of Article 8 against the state in T.H. (Application no. 33037/22, judgment 12 September 2025), holding the surgical and sterilisation conditions and the related civil-registry treatment incompatible with private-life rights and framing guaranteed gender recognition on self-determination, with two international NGOs intervening.

Detention remains the weakest point for a trans visitor. Administrative courts clashed in public over the handling of an HIV-positive trans man in transition held by immigration police: in March 2023 the Supreme Administrative Court rebuked the municipal court for 'sarcastic moral lectures' toward the detainee and ruled that authorities must first assess whether a person is 'potentially vulnerable' before deciding placement. Practice has not caught up with that standard. In November 2025 reporting, judges described the national prisons as unprepared for trans people and lacking clear rules; the Supreme Court is pressing for a national prison concept that explicitly addresses the needs of people in or after transition, the human-rights commissioner is pushing a binding regulation, and the Justice Ministry maintains that the existing framework is sufficient, with consultation ongoing.

Social hostility is measurable and politically amplified. A national LGBTQ+ survey found 43% of respondents discriminated or harassed in the previous five years, over a third within twelve months, with trans and non-binary respondents reporting the highest rates, and 51% targeted by insults, assault or threats over five years. Politicians' anti-LGBT speech rose from 43% in 2018 to 71% in 2023, and 63% of respondents attributed rising intolerance to politicians. In 2024 the Justice Minister publicly stated that his goal was 'to prevent men from giving birth' after the Constitutional Court repealed the surgical prerequisite, and a far-right party circulated election leaflets promising to take money from 'LGBT activists' and 'give more to families, take it away from the deviants'.

Enforcement machinery exists but is thinly quantified. Police recorded 94 hate crimes in 2024, with 46 prosecuted and 42 sentenced, and LGBTI-motivated incidents appear in the bias breakdown; the international hate-crime monitoring body notes that recorded statistics still do not sufficiently distinguish hate crimes from other offences. The government has approved a Criminal Code amendment extending bias-motivated factors to disability, sexual orientation and gender identity, which remains pending in the national legislature, while a Constitutional Court ruling weakened 'particularly vulnerable victim' status.

Entry and protection channels carry no trans-specific obstacle on the record: the new Asylum Law includes sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds and offers an opposite-gender interview option. Facilities and public-space conduct are not restricted by any trans-specific rule in the sources.

Where a visitor goes matters. The largest urban centres rate highest for LGBTQ+ solo travellers, with formal nondiscrimination policies, designated queer districts and hostels providing concierge support, private rooms and organised socials; harassment risk concentrates in rural areas and late-night settings. In June 2023 a group disrupted a Pride drag story-time in a large city with homophobic slurs.

Partner recognition is unresolved. A same-sex marriage bill introduced in June 2018 by a cross-party group of 46 MPs from six parliamentary clubs to replace registered partnerships was backed by the caretaker government and cleared committees on 29 June 2023, while a constitutional ban on same-sex marriage moved to second reading with far-right, conservative and people's party support estimated at 80–90%.

SVN.name: Slovenia
SVN.summary:
Slovenia is among Central and Eastern Europe's most progressive destinations for trans visitors, with a cleaner documented profile than its neighbours. Legal gender recognition is depathologised (no surgery or psychiatric-diagnosis requirement), and a 2022 reform abolished local jurisdiction in the gender-change procedure — reducing involuntary outing through local bureaucracy. Comprehensive anti-discrimination law covers gender identity, same-sex marriage is legal (2022, via the Constitutional Court), and no far-right party is in government.

No severe traveler-axis incidents surfaced in research: no mob violence against trans people, no trans-tourist rape, no European Court case of police abuse, and no documented foreign-trans-detention case — unlike several neighbours (Greece's Thessaloniki mob, Italy's tourist-rape and Milan police beating, Czechia's trans-foreigner extradition mishandling, Poland's foreign-trans-woman-in-male-detention). The main caveats are a far-right youth campaign ("Two Sexes, One Truth"), an underreporting/trust gap in hate-crime reporting, and thinner detention-placement evidence for a small country.
SVN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is very low.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: Slovenia is regarded as among the most progressive countries in Central and Eastern Europe on LGBTIQ rights - same-sex relations legal nationwide, legal gender recognition possible, LGBTI organisations registerable - with comprehensive antidiscrimination laws enacted since 2016 explicitly covering sexual orientation and gender identity.
No substantive finding recorded.

Ministry of the Interior notice of 29 October 2022: the local-jurisdiction step in legal gender-change procedures was abolished on the recommendation of the Advocate of the Principle of Equality, so transgender persons are no longer exposed to involuntary disclosure of transgender identity in their local environment.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): Legebitra documented 17 cases of bias-motivated speech and TransAkcija documented 25 cases of direct bias-motivated incidents in 2023. After Pride, LGBTIQ+ organisations held a press conference about attacks and rising hate while the Prime Minister took three days to react and the Interior Minister made no statements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the Health Ministry officially confirmed to the Interdisciplinary Council for Gender Recognition that medical treatment is not required for legal gender recognition and formally asked the Interior Ministry to amend the relevant Civil Registry Act sub-article. The review also notes the death at 73 of a founder of Slovenia's grassroots LGBTI movement.

US State Department 2023 report on Slovenia: no laws criminalise consensual same-sex conduct and there were no reports of state-condoned violence, but authorities recorded violence incidents without tracking case numbers and local NGOs called violence against LGBTQI+ persons prevalent and under-reported. In June 2023 a woman wearing a rainbow flag was assaulted near the Ljubljana Pride route, marchers had eggs thrown at them and rainbow flags were burned on video.

ENACT national report of January 2025 (EU CERV-2023 project): civil society provides LGBTI hate-crime victims counselling, advocacy and safe spaces, but LGBTI persons using generic victim-support services face heteronormative hurdles. The report documents institutional shortcomings in the anti-LGBTI hate-crime framework.

UPI report of 25 July 2006: Slovenia passed a law legalising same-sex marriage but restricted the ceremony to the two partners plus a local community registration official - no friends or relatives. Gay and lesbian organisations welcomed the move as a concrete step while criticising the law as 'insufficient'.

Inquirer/AFP (Dec 2015): Pope Francis urged Slovenian politicians to 'support the family' four days before the referendum on the gay-marriage law adopted by parliament in March - the referendum (later lost) followed a conservative challenge.

SVN.tangentialFactors: Same-sex marriage legal since 2022 — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
SVN.localsOnly: The depathologised LGR regime and the 2022 local-jurisdiction reform are resident-facing administrative law.

SRB.name: Serbia
SRB.summary:
Serbia is a dangerous destination for trans visitors despite no criminalisation. The most acute documented traveler-axis risk is police: in February 2024 the interior ministry began investigating officers who beat, tortured and sexually harassed two LGBT people during a Belgrade apartment raid. About 105 sexual-orientation/gender-identity-motivated incidents were recorded in 2024, and Pride marches require heavy police protection.

The country is outside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreign travellers.

The bottom line for visitors: police-brutality risk and weak protection make it a high-risk destination despite no criminalisation, with the major-tourist city "conditionally" manageable under situational awareness.
SRB.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and border-corruption affect all travellers; the country is not inside the Schengen border-free travel area, so border checks apply to foreigners.

sources.summary: Balkan Insight (27 Feb 2024): Serbian authorities investigating allegations that police officers assaulted two LGBT people — a probe into police violence against LGBT citizens (outcome: investigation opened).

APT (Association for the Prevention of Torture) Serbia country page, national-preventive-mechanism recommendations: the Penal and Correctional Institution in Padinska Skela, Belgrade, shall let transgender women at intake choose a female officer for searches/body inspection rather than a male or combined search — a concrete custodial-rights finding for trans detainees.

HRW World Report 2025 (Serbia/Kosovo chapter): intolerance and violence against LGBT people remained significant concerns in Serbia in 2024; state response to July-August protests (activist arrests, smear campaigns) highlighted rule-of-law weaknesses.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Serbia: trans people face testosterone supply shortages (Testosteron Depo); a publication analysed 70 instances of politicians' hate speech (April 2023-April 2024); the Pride Info Centre was attacked in January and announced closure in September after 20+ attacks since 2018, none properly sanctioned; a Zoomer survey found three-quarters of trans/non-binary people fear job interviews due to anticipated discrimination.

US State Department 2018 Human Rights Report for Serbia: human-rights issues include government corruption, violence against journalists, and 'crimes including violence targeting Lesbian, Gay, Bisexual, Transgender, and Intersex (LGBTI) individuals'.

HRV.name: Croatia
HRV.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been legal in Croatia since 1977, and open military service is available. Registered life partnerships have existed since 2014, but a 2013 constitutional referendum barred same-sex marriage, and full same-sex adoption rights were confirmed only by a final court ruling in 2022. Hate-crime legislation covers sexual orientation and gender identity.

Legal gender recognition rests on a 2013 legislative amendment that allows a gender marker to be registered without altering sex characteristics. A Croatian legal analysis works through the Criminal Procedure Act, the Police Powers Act, the Customs Act and the law governing prison sentences to set out how police, customs and court officers must conduct searches of trans and gender-nonconforming people, and records case studies of the difficulties that arise in practice.

Formal protection outpaces enforcement. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report records minority representatives saying that anti-discrimination provisions covering employment, housing, education and health are not consistently enforced, and NGOs describing uneven judicial handling of discrimination cases, limited access to justice, and victims reluctant to report for fear of inefficiency and victimisation during trial; hate-crime investigations are flagged as inadequate. Zagreb Pride's 2018 documentation report on Council of Europe Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5 records under-reporting of homophobic and transphobic crimes alongside its compiled hate-crime data and case studies on hate speech, freedom of assembly, legal gender recognition, partnership recognition and employment discrimination. The European Commission's 2024 country report assessed transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including the sexual-orientation and gender-identity grounds.

Protection machinery has produced at least one concrete result: a Zadar prosecutor charged a man over the refusal of a gay couple's accommodation booking, an incident dating from 2018 and reported in ILGA-Europe's 2025 Annual Review.

Official hostility is visible in organised form rather than in street-level attacks. The same review reports escalating anti-gender disinformation, including a Croatian Parliament session on 'Gender Ideology' at which speakers spread misinformation and no LGBTI organisations were invited, and disruption directed at the first Pula Pride march the day before it took place. No case of mob violence, trans-tourist rape, police brutality or detention of a foreign trans visitor surfaced in the sources reviewed.

On the visitor axis, public displays of affection may draw unwelcome responses in less-populated cities, and gay venues have been described as virtually non-existent outside Zagreb, though new venues have opened in Split, Rijeka, Osijek, Hvar, Rab, Rovinj and Dubrovnik. Pride events are held in Zagreb, Split, Osijek, Karlovac and Pula, alongside the Balkans Trans Inter March.
HRV.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Zadar prosecution is not stated in the sources reviewed; only the charge and the 2018 date of the underlying incident are documented.

Whether the 2013 gender-marker registration route operates as a self-declaration process, and which documents it covers, is unresolved in this inventory; the 2018 Council of Europe report and the 2026 legal analysis address the framework from different angles without settling current practice at counters and border posts.

No source in this inventory reports a trans-specific violent offence against a visitor, and absence of such a case in the reviewed material is not evidence of absence on the ground.

Enforcement data post-dating the 2024 European Commission reporting period, which covered 2023, is not available here; the anti-gender and Pride-disruption accounts derive from a single monitoring review.

Search and detention practice for trans people is analysed in academic sources for 2013 onward, with no official statistical breakdown of how often officers deviate from the prescribed procedure.

EST.name: Estonia
EST.summary:
Estonia decriminalises same-sex relations nationwide and has had marriage equality since June 2023, the first Baltic state to reach that point, with joint adoption included. Opposition filed more than 700 amendments to block the bill and every one failed. Public support for marriage equality stood at 53% in 2023, reaching 75% among people in their twenties, against 34% in 2012.

Legal gender recognition remains medicalised. A psychiatric diagnosis and physiological alteration are required, and no nonbinary identity is recognised. Advocacy continues for recognition based on self-determination, and the national action plan adopted in 2025 commits the state to updating the legal framework so that gender identity and expression are protected.

Anti-discrimination coverage is uneven. Employment discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, as is discrimination in healthcare. One source records housing protection extending to gender identity while another records housing protection on sexual orientation only, a discrepancy the sources do not resolve. Hate-speech and hate-crime legislation does not include gender identity, and no hate-crime protection is recorded for trans people. Conversion therapy is not banned. Access to sex-separated facilities is recorded as protected.

The social climate is more guarded than the legal framework. In the 2024 EU FRA survey, 62% of LGBTIQ Estonians avoid holding hands with a same-sex partner against an EU-27 average of 53%, 40% avoid certain locations for fear of assault against 29%, and 38% are open about being LGBTIQ against 51%. Estonia ranks first among 30 EU regions for concealing LGBTIQ identity at work, while reported workplace discrimination sits below the EU average, 12% against 19%.

Official posture is supportive. In December 2025 Estonia adopted a national action plan for LGBTI equality spanning education, healthcare, employment and the legal system, approved by Economy Minister Erkki Keldo after roughly two years of preparation by the Equality Policies Department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs and Communications. It sets targets for inclusive curricula and for the physical and mental safety of LGBTIQ students and staff. Estonia joined 16 EU states urging Hungary to revise its anti-LGBTI laws, the foreign minister publicly supported Tallinn Pride, Estonian missions abroad flew rainbow flags, and Tallinn Pride was held on 31 May 2025.

The F&M Global Barometer of Transgender Rights records no known murders of gender-identity minorities in Estonia through 2024.
EST.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on whether housing discrimination protection covers gender identity or sexual orientation only. Equaldex records sexual orientation alone; the F&M Global Barometer records gender identity as included. This is unresolved in the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses gender markers on Estonian passports or identity documents as they would be presented by a foreign visitor, nor any entry, visa or border-screening practice that could disclose a traveller's trans status. Nothing here should be read as an assessment of entry screening.

No sourced material covers police conduct toward trans people, detention of foreign trans nationals, or reported incidents of violence against trans visitors. The absence of such material is not evidence that none occurs; the F&M no-murders figure is a national count through 2024, not a traveller-incident record.

The quality and coverage of hate-crime data collection in Estonia is not established by the inventory, beyond the 2018 compliance report identifying it as a topic of assessment.

The TGEU and ILGA-Europe compliance report dates from 2018 and has not been updated in the sources provided, so its findings on deprivation of liberty, asylum and sports cannot be treated as current.
