LTU.name: Lithuania
LTU.summary:
The country is broadly workable, at the lower end, with one of Europe's most restrictive legal-gender-recognition situations. Lithuania's Civil Code grants the right to medically change gender in principle, but no legal framework regulating the procedure has existed for 17 years — a deadlock the Constitutional Court refused to resolve in September 2025, perpetuating what an ECtHR body called a "distressing legal uncertainty."

Socially, a conservative climate is well documented: an MP called LGBT people "degenerated" and "spreading diseases" (his immunity was revoked), "traditional family values" groups disrupt peaceful protests, and an ombudsperson found police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to assembly. Trans people report systemic workplace harassment — open ridicule, isolation, and psychological abuse.

There is no criminalisation, and the national Pride in 2024 drew a large crowd of 15,000.
LTU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

sources.summary: LGL (Lithuanian Gay League) news (Sept 2025): the Constitutional Court refused to address Lithuania's 18-year trans rights gap - a significant setback; the Civil Code grants unmarried adults the right to medically change gender but implementing legislation has never been adopted, leaving trans people in legal limbo.

LGL news (Aug 2025): could courts finally end 17 years of legal limbo for transgender rights? - the Ukmergė Chamber of the Vilnius Regional District Court suspended a civil case on amending civil-status gender documents and referred the question of the laws' compliance with the Constitution to the Constitutional Court.

LRT (Sept 2025): Lithuania's Constitutional Court declined to examine a lower court's request to review the absence of legal provisions allowing trans people to change gender markers and personal identification codes in official documents.
LRT (May 2025): trans people in Lithuania detail workplace harassment - open ridicule, isolation and psychological abuse; systemic labour-market discrimination per experts.

LGL news (April 2024): the Seimas Ombudsperson found that police failed to guarantee the LGBT community's right to peaceful assembly - inadequate police response to hostile provocateurs at an LGL assembly; recommended measures to guarantee effective assembly rights.

Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, 'The Situation of Transgender People in Lithuania - Summary of the National Review 2024': the second national review, after 2019, covering legal framework, document changes, healthcare barriers, labour-market discrimination, data protection and public attitudes. It records the absence of a legal framework and of a strategic approach to trans rights.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Lithuania: systemic lack of targeted LGBTI hate-crime victim support; LGBTI asylum seekers from Cameroon granted protection after a four-year wait, with dire camp conditions and a psychologist convicted of coercing asylum seekers into sexual acts; prosecution of former MP Gražulis for anti-LGBTI ridicule complicated by his MEP immunity.

PinkNews (Sept 2013): Lithuania's parliament to consider five anti-gay and anti-trans bills - a ban on gender reassignment ('gender is determined genetically from the very moment of conception'), a same-sex adoption ban, fines up to €1,800 for organisers of events 'denigrating constitutional moral values', and legalisation of anti-gay speech.

PinkNews (July 2009): Lithuania's parliament passed a 'Section 28-style' law banning information on homosexuality in schools and media accessible to minors ('Law on the Protection of Minors'), overriding President Adamkus's veto 87-6; Amnesty called it 'a huge step backwards'.

LVA.name: Latvia
LVA.summary:
Latvia has no procedure for legal gender recognition. Transgender and nonbinary Latvians cannot obtain a corrected gender marker, and no targeted legislation has been adopted; coalition members of parliament said in June 2025 that trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." One trans immigrant interviewed by LSM stated that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples have been in force since 1 July 2024. They do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry.

There is no criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, and no legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities is documented in the sources.

The most significant institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14. A 2020 attack on a gay couple in Riga was not prosecuted as a hate crime even though the aggressor admitted using anti-gay slurs; the matter was reduced to a minor public-order offence carrying a lenient fine. The Court held that the failure to prosecute inhuman treatment and the discriminatory handling of the case violated the prohibition of inhuman treatment, the right to private life and the non-discrimination guarantee, and the Strasbourg Observers analysis of the judgment notes that states must investigate and punish hate-motivated attacks thoroughly as a positive obligation.

Enforcement failures are documented beyond that case. In Daugavpils, two people were attacked and police closed the matter until the Prosecutor General ordered the investigation reopened. Following the ECtHR ruling, the Prosecutor General also reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. Former MEP Tatjana Mamikins faced an investigation over homophobic posts and left for Russia.

Protection machinery does function in some channels. In 2025 an administrative court overturned the denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI applicant.

Public hostility remains visible from senior religious figures: in 2007 Cardinal Jānis Pujats of Riga described homosexuality as "total corruption in the sexual arena" and demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage and large counter-demonstrations against Pride.
LVA.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; ordinary crime is low.

TUR.name: Turkey
TUR.summary:
Turkey presents real, structured danger for trans visitors — institutionalised, presidential-level hostility that has become state policy. Police profile and detain trans women for identity checks (20 detained in Istanbul in July 2025), trans women have historically been frequent targets of torture and ill-treatment by police, and a trans woman attacked with a knife was herself detained (victim-criminalised). Transphobic attacks and Pride-event violence are documented, and foreign visitors must carry original passports at all times — creating outing risk at the frequent transit checkpoints. A draft law leaked in October 2025 would criminalise LGBT people — not yet passed but under active government consideration. The risk is concentrated in urban trans-visible contexts (Istanbul's Beyoğlu/Tarlabaşı) rather than package-holiday tourist zones, but the institutional hostility pervades.

The consequence axis of an arrest is severe and current: Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex — a transgender man was held in a women's prison — and a 2024 system-level profile documents LGBTI+ prisoners facing arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto isolation in solitary confinement with restricted healthcare access, frequent transfers, and complaints that are ineffective and can lead to further violence, with no policy or staff training to address LGBTI+ needs in a system described as built on a binary, heteronormative model. The December 2025 death of a transgender prisoner in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison moved the question to formal state-level contestation: rights groups demanded an independent investigation and changes to “detention practices affecting transgender prisoners,” accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers describe four trans inmates sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, a delayed medical response, investigators entering only two days later and witness statements not taken, and the case was raised in parliament on 12 December 2025. For a trans visitor — already profiled and detained for identity checks — arrest means placement by registered sex in a gendered facility under practices documented as segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched housing, in a system where the most recent custody death is under contested official handling.
TUR.outOfScopeNotes:
The October 2025 draft law is not yet passed — its enactment outcome is unresolved and under active government consideration. General terrorism and crime advisories affect all travellers to Turkey. No source in the record documents marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors separately from the general criminalisation risk described above.

Prison axis: no Turkish statute or regulation codifying trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in this record — the registered-sex placement finding rests on the December 2025 reporting, the segregation-and-isolation practice on the 2024 Prison Insider/CISST profile, and the December 2025 death's circumstances are contested with the investigation outcome unresolved.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (29 Oct 2025): a draft legislative package would effectively criminalise LGBT people under vague claims of protecting 'the family' and 'public morals' — framing the Erdoğan government has repeatedly used to legitimise stigmatisation; sets the reform backdrop as authoritarian drift. Key legislative-risk evidence for 2025-26.

Kaos GL (Feb 2026): the LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 records 313 violations in 2025 — about two-and-a-half times 2024 — dominated by detention (299 detention decisions: 256 on record, 43 off the record), plus systematic privacy attacks; frames hostility turned into state policy. Quantified annual evidence.

bianet (Aug 2025): Istanbul police detain ~20 trans women for ID checks amid profiling concerns - stopped on the street, while shopping or in cafés in Beyoğlu, held at Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station and released after 'General Information Gathering' (GBT) background checks; legal experts argue GBT checks violate ECHR Article 5; one detainee: 'They didn't fine us, but they documented us. The new law hasn't even passed yet, but they're already enforcing it on us.'

Turkish Minute (26 Feb 2026): covers the Kaos GL 2025 report — hundreds of cases documented via media monitoring and civil-society complaints; six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three classified as hate killings; transgender individuals disproportionately affected. Second reporting of the annual data.

Truth Justice Memory Center (Aug 2025): monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week — violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025; senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepened homophobia and transphobia, and discrimination against LGBTI+ people and their allies was entrenched. Event-monitoring evidence.

Kaos GL (Sept 2025): a new Health Ministry regulation risks profiling trans people — after a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular added 'gender reassignment' to official reasons for medical-board reports, hospitals were barred from the 'other' option and told to issue e-reports, with online framing contested as an 'LGBT opening'. Transition-access regulatory drift.

Kaos GL (Aug 2024): trans woman Yaşam was knifed by a 17-year-old in Bakırköy; the perpetrator was released while the victim was referred for arrest — activists call the detention asymmetry evidence of a state hate policy. Concrete 2024 violence + policing-asymmetry case.

Nomad Lawyer (2026): Turkey's passport-carrying rule for foreigners — original photo ID required at transit checkpoints in holiday destinations, with fines up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and detention warnings. Direct visitor-facing document-risk evidence.

Human Rights Watch (22 May 2008): launches the 123-page report 'We Need a Law for Liberation' from 70+ interviews over three years — documents a continuing history of beatings, robberies and abuse against gay men and transgender people in Turkey. Foundational historical evidence; dated (pre-2018 legal changes).

sources.title: Rights groups urge probe into 'suspicious' death of transgender prisoner in Turkey (Stockholm Center for Freedom)
sources.summary: SCF (18 Dec 2025): transgender prisoner Poyraz was found dead in his cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025, and Turkish rights groups (coordinated from Human Rights Association / IHD branches in Istanbul, Ankara, Izmir, Diyarbakir, Mersin and Aydin) demanded an independent investigation and changes to 'detention practices affecting transgender prisoners'. Kaos GL-cited accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers say four transgender inmates were collectively sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators only entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken; opposition MP Sevda Karaca (EMEP) raised the case in parliament on 12 December 2025. The case documents that Turkey holds trans prisoners in gendered facilities by registered sex (a trans man was held in a women's prison) and that trans-prisoner custody conditions were formally contested at the state level in late 2025.

sources.title: LGBTQI+ prisoners are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches (Kaos GL), reporting the Prison Insider 'Country Profile' on Turkey (with CİSST data)
sources.summary: Kaos GL (7 May 2024), covering the Prison Insider Country Profile report on Turkey prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association (CISST) and using ILGA World data: LGBTI+ prisoners in Turkish prisons are subjected to arbitrary body and strip searches and to de facto isolation, being placed in solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and sometimes refusing to go to hospital out of fear of other male prisoners during transfers. CISST observations quoted in the article state that there is no policy or staff training to identify and address LGBTI+ prisoners' needs, that Turkish prison administration is built on a binary, heteronormative system, that LGBTI+ prisoners are frequently transferred (disrupting visits and solidarity), and that complaints are ineffective and can lead to further violence. The piece documents that Turkey manages trans and LGBTI+ prisoners through segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement.

DNK.name: Denmark
DNK.summary:
Denmark permits legal gender recognition by self-declaration, with no medical evaluation required, a regime in force since 2014 and the first of its kind in Europe. Non-binary people may obtain an 'X' marker in passports, and trans people determine their own legal gender markers.

Discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics is prohibited. The Equal Treatment Act covers sexual orientation and gender identity in employment and services; workplace protection on the basis of gender identity has been in place since 2015, and fair-housing protection on that ground has held throughout the monitored period.

Same-sex couples may marry and adopt. Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships, in 1989, and marriage equality followed in 2012.

On 10 September 2024 the Danish Supreme Court held that serving a sentence in a men's prison department does not violate the human rights of a trans inmate. That judgment is the leading Danish authority on where trans detainees are placed, and it is the single most consequential ruling for a visitor who is remanded or convicted.

The Danish Institute for Human Rights reports that police under-investigate hate crimes and are not obliged to flag hate-crime motivation at the time a report is made, which bears directly on a visitor who is targeted. Its LGBT+ barometer records that 38% of homosexual and bisexual respondents report differential treatment based on gender, sexual orientation or appearance, and that hate speech directed at sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, or sex characteristics recurs every year.

Violence against trans people is documented. In July 2024 a migrant trans woman was murdered in a hotel room in Copenhagen. The UN Committee Against Torture, in its eighth periodic review, found that some trans people, QTIBIPOC and migrants report denial of access to spaces and services as well as threats.

Denmark's record on arrest and asylum is favourable on the available indicators: freedoms against arbitrary arrest based on gender identity were affirmed in every year from 2011 to 2024, and in February 2013 a Guatemalan trans woman became the first transgender person granted asylum in Denmark, refused return over her gender identity after citing police attacks and threats tied to her trans activism.
DNK.outOfScopeNotes:
Conversion-therapy status is unresolved in the sources. One source records a ban in force since 2023, while another states there is no ban and that a bill was revived in August 2026. The current legal position should be verified against the Danish statute before publication.

Whether Danish police have since been required to flag hate-crime motivation at the point of reporting is not sourced; the inventory only establishes the Danish Institute for Human Rights finding that no such obligation existed.

The scope of the Supreme Court's 10 September 2024 prison-placement ruling — whether it extends to pre-operative, non-binary or intersex detainees, and to remand rather than convicted prisoners — is not addressed in the available material.

The sources do not state whether Denmark's asylum practice toward trans claimants after the 2013 Fernanda Milan decision has been consistent; only that single early case is documented here.

sources.summary: Context/Thomson Reuters (25 Sep 2024): Denmark's self-ID law (gender change without medical evaluation, in force since 2014) is credited by activists with cooling the trans debate; Denmark was the first country to recognise same-sex partnerships (1989) and ranks among the world's best for LGBTQ+ rights.

NOR.name: Norway
NOR.summary:
Norway is very safe for trans visitors, with strong legal protections and official responses, but with a more acute violence context than its Nordic neighbours. There is no criminalisation, bathrooms are unrestricted, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction; anti-discrimination law covers gender identity; and the police operate a dedicated hate-crime unit with the security service providing annual Pride threat assessments.

Offsetting facts: a terrorist shot and killed two people at Oslo Pride in 2022 (the perpetrator, an ISIS sympathiser, was sentenced to 30 years); police-reported hate crimes against queer and trans people rose sharply in 2023 (up 18% overall, with trans-specific reports nearly doubling); and though the security service reports a significant decline in threats for 2025 Pride, hate-speech and intimidation risks persist.
NOR.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US travel update; general urban crime is very low.

A source was not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401), so the 2020 hate-speech ban's adoption details rest on the underlying news report. Underreporting means the official hate-crime figures understate the real level, which remains unverifiable.

sources.summary: Official Norwegian health-rights page (Gender Recognition Act): legal gender is determined by the individual's own perception of gender identity — self-declaration decided at the tax office — from age 16 alone, 6-16 with parents, under-6 only for documented congenital DSD; a 2017 regulation covers citizens resident abroad. For this record: the official, no-medical-intervention document-change route.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024) chapter on Norway: reported hate crimes rose 18% in 2023, with the largest increases in crimes motivated by sexual orientation, gender identity/expression and antisemitism; Zaniar Matapour sentenced to 30 years (the strictest penalty) for the 2022 Oslo Pride mass shooting; a drag bingo event sparked online threats; a knife attack on two people investigated as a hate crime.
Reuters report (2020): Norway outlawed hate speech against trans people through an amendment to the Penal Code. For this record: criminal liability for anti-trans hate speech.

NRK (May 2024, Norwegian): record numbers of hate-crime reports against queer and trans people in 2023, but the clearance rate fell from 52% to 45% and more cases were dropped; many victims report little trust in police, and a dedicated hate-crime group encourages reporting. For this record: rising reports with a documented, quantified drop in case clearance.

UiO C-REX research blog (Sept 2024): transphobic hostility in Norway manifests mainly among political extremists and religious fundamentalists — the Nordic Resistance Movement's 2017 Kristiansand march advocated 'crushing the gay lobby', and research interviews with far-right activists frame gender diversity as 'degeneracy'. For this record: organised ideological anti-trans hostility as a movement phenomenon, not street-level risk for ordinary visitors.

UiO C-REX (June 2025), HATECYCLE study of 3,000+ survey responses from LGBTQI people: only 8% of those who experienced a hate crime reported it to police — barriers include mistrust, procedural obstacles and fear of personal costs, and many who did report described dismissive treatment. For this record: official statistics undercount anti-LGBTQI hate crime by a wide margin.

OSCE/ODIHR frameworks page for Norway: hate crimes are defined as criminal offences motivated by hatred due to ethnicity, religion, belief, sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression, or disability; any offence so motivated is recorded under the framework. For this record: the statutory definition behind Norway's hate-crime counting.

Nordisk Post (Apr 2025): Norway's Police Security Service (PST) reports a 'significant decline' in threats against LGBTQ+ events and individuals over the past year, but warns hate speech and intimidation risks remain, especially during Pride — most threat actors aim to spread fear rather than act. For this record: current threat-level assessment from the security service.

Life in Norway resource page (updated Nov 2020): Norwegians generally hold liberal attitudes toward LGBT people; Norway was among the first countries with anti-discrimination laws; directory of national resources (FRI, Skeiv Ungdom, Transgender Association, Oslo Pride). For this record: social-climate context and the support-directory landscape.

SWE.name: Sweden
SWE.summary: Sweden is very safe. The one documented everyday-facility friction: a national swimming-pool chain's guidelines restrict trans persons' changing-room access — lawyers say this may violate discrimination law, so a trans visitor using such facilities may face exclusion. Brå (the crime-prevention council) reports roughly 6,700 LGBTQI-related hate-crime reports. Bathrooms as such are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and there is no rollback movement.
SWE.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is low.

One source could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403), so the parliamentary-approval step rests on the underlying summary of that entry. Whether the changing-room guidelines breach discrimination law is unresolved — only a legal opinion is on record.

sources.summary: A Library of Congress entry dated April 2024 records Sweden's parliament approving new acts on legal gender and on medical procedures performed on genitalia.

TGEU report of 16 July 2025: Sweden's new Legal Gender Recognition Act came into force on 1 July 2025, simplifying the procedure but falling short of a full self-determination model, with medical barriers remaining.
SVT reported in October 2025 that the swimming-pool chain Medley stopped trans customers from choosing their changing rooms, an everyday facility-access restriction affecting trans visitors.

Brå (National Council for Crime Prevention) report 2024:13: supplements Swedish hate-crime statistics with a descriptive analysis of persons suspected of offences where police identified LGBTQI-related hate-crime motives - the national dataset on anti-LGBTQI offending.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025): a bill would extend protection of victims of conversion practices when carried out through coercion, threats or sustained psychological pressure. In November the Church of Sweden decided new priests must be willing to marry same-sex couples, passing 141 votes at the 2025 Church Council.

Open-access article in Sexuality Research and Social Policy (4 February 2016, vol 13, pp 119-129): traces LGBT policy development in Sweden's military from 1944 to 2014 - the historical record behind current service conditions.

2019 edition of the Spartacus Gay Travel Index reported by Newsweek: Canada, Portugal and Sweden tied as the most LGBT-friendly travel destinations - third-party evidence on Sweden's standing as a visitor destination.

TT/The Local, 28 January 2017: Sweden's main national board decided transgender people will no longer be classified as 'mentally ill', the depathologisation step for trans residents' diagnostic status.

SWE.localsOnly: The 2025 LGR Act (medical examination still required) is a resident-facing process; the reform separated recognition from surgery requirements. FIN.name: Finland
FIN.summary: Finland is very safe for trans visitors. There are no documented severe trans-specific incidents (no tourist-rape, mob-violence or police-brutality case); bathrooms are unrestricted, there is no criminalisation, and the Schengen border poses no trans-specific friction. Record-level hate-crime reporting exists, but no incident series involving trans visitors is documented.
FIN.outOfScopeNotes:
No trans-specific travel advisory beyond its US update issued for outbound citizens; general urban crime is very low.

Official statistics register suspected offences as reported in police files — the legal code has no hate-crime category, so the true motive-based level is unverifiable from official figures. No marriage or partner-travel exposure for visitors beyond the general legal-equality baseline is documented in this record.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering 2025) chapter on Finland: record 1,808 suspected hate crimes in 2025 (+13% since 2023), with sexual orientation and gender identity recurrent motives (12% of cases); Finland's first conversion-practices case prosecuted as assault (convictions in March); Parliament endorsed a citizens' initiative to ban conversion practices (125-49) in March, though a full ban remained pending.

Finland's Police University College (Polamk, Nov 2025): record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offenses reported in 2024 — highest figure ever recorded; defamation and assault the most common types. The sexual-orientation/gender-identity-or-expression category climbed 72 -> 68 -> 126 -> 140 -> 215 -> 241 across the six reported years. The Criminal Code has no hate-crime category, so motive is only recorded in police reports — meaning SOGI-motivated incidents are counted via reported suspicion, not charge.

The Guardian (21 Mar 2025): Finland and Denmark updated their travel advice for transgender citizens travelling to the United States after reports of border difficulties following the US 'two genders' executive order. Denmark advises trans travellers to contact the US embassy in Copenhagen before departure over document issues. Finland's advice is outbound guidance issued to its own travellers, not an assessment of risk within Finland.

Investigate Europe, 'The Cruel Condition' (10 Sep 2025): Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden explicitly wrote infertility requirements into law for legal gender recognition; at least 11,000 people subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, Sweden first (1972, in force 40 years); the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025 — Finland's statutory sterilisation-era requirement is history, but the legacy cohort is documented.

Yle (28 Feb 2018): Parliament approved a citizens'-initiative-inspired change to the Maternity Act recognising both women in same-sex partnerships as mothers from the moment of the child's birth — second-parent registration fixed at birth rather than via adoption.

Yle (1 Mar 2017): same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in Finland. The western Finland register office alone had about 41 same-sex couples scheduled to marry in the first week. The operative date for marriage equality in Finland is 1 March 2017.

Yle (19 Sep 2013): the 'Tahdon2013' citizens' initiative for same-sex marriage collected 162,000+ certified signatures — largest Finnish initiative ever, far above the 50,000 threshold forcing parliamentary consideration; organiser target had been 250,000. The process route that produced the 2017 marriage law.

Sterilisation-era history is documented: a first such requirement took effect in 1972 and stayed in force forty years, at least 11,000 people were subjected to such conditions across the six countries investigated, and the last requirement was phased out at end-June 2025.

Resident discrimination and legal data: record 1,808 suspected hate-crime offences in 2024 (+13% since 2023, with sexual-orientation/gender-identity motives in about 12% of cases); the penal code has no hate-crime category, so motive is recorded in police reports only; same-sex marriage and joint adoption became legal in 2017; maternity registration from birth for two mothers was recognised in 2018; a citizens' initiative with 162,000+ certified signatures forced legislative consideration in 2013; and a first conversion-practices case was prosecuted as assault with convictions in March 2025.

The 2023 LGR reform made Finland the last member of the regional bloc to remove its sterilisation requirement — a policy-history note rather than a visitor-risk finding.

TWN.name: Taiwan
TWN.summary:
Taiwan is a progressive Asian destination — it was the first in Asia to legalise same-sex marriage (2019), the government is investing US$8.76 million to double gender-neutral public bathrooms by 2029, and a trans march in Taipei drew 3,000 participants in 2025. There are no documented severe incidents (no mob violence, trans-tourist rape, or organised dating-app predation).

The main gaps are legal-gender-recognition reform stagnation — a 2008 Ministry order still requires sex-reassignment surgery to change one's gender marker (blocking an estimated 90% of trans people, with only case-by-case court exceptions), and the government has been "floundering" on reform — and a rising anti-gender discourse movement that has produced online waves of hostility. A trans woman was outed during a police identity inspection (the Viva case), and Taipei has held a vigil for victims of anti-trans violence.

For a visitor, bathrooms are unrestricted (and being proactively expanded to gender-neutral), there is no criminalisation, and border/immigration poses no trans-specific friction. Taipei City has trans-friendly service guidelines.
TWN.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; earthquake/typhoon risks affect all travellers.

KOR.name: South Korea
KOR.summary:
South Korea does not criminalise gender identity or gender expression in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. The exception is the armed forces: Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among military personnel with up to two years' imprisonment, the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017. Transgender people are excluded from military service altogether.

Legal gender recognition is available and the requirement of surgery is falling. On 8 May 2024 a court ruled against mandating sex-reassignment surgery as a condition of changing legal sex status, holding for five plaintiffs assigned male at birth who had been on hormone therapy for years that forcing surgery violates physical integrity and that outdated judicial guidelines cannot ground dismissals. The Supreme Court has also allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Trans visitors have a documented, judicially enforced right to public restrooms. On 2 July 2024 the Seoul Central District Court issued a final, unappealed ruling that police advice telling a transgender plaintiff undergoing gender correction to avoid public restrooms for a period infringed personal rights, awarding 300,000 won in symbolic compensation against the state.

There is no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on these grounds. In healthcare, the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation in November 2023, after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients on the grounds that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage, which matters to a visitor travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court did issue a landmark 2024 ruling on same-sex partners' healthcare rights, extending a measure of recognition in that specific area.

For a visitor on the ground, Seoul's established LGBTQ+ neighbourhoods are broadly positive, but the surrounding context requires care: organised conservative opposition is active, no national anti-discrimination law exists, and Human Rights Watch records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people in its 2025 world report, which also notes a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
KOR.outOfScopeNotes:
The consequence axis of an arrest remains unresolved on the civilian side: no source in this inventory describes how transgender prisoners are housed in South Korea's civilian prison system. There is no birth-sex versus identity placement rule, no special unit, and no solitary or segregation practice recorded, and no civilian trans-prisoner case surfaced.

The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor entry on the Supreme Court's decision permitting a transgender person with minor children to change gender in the family relations register returned HTTP 403 and could not be retrieved at research time; the claim rests on the entry's title and metadata rather than the full text.

No source here reports a hate-crime statute or aggravated-penalty provision covering offences motivated by gender identity or sexual orientation, and none confirms whether police or prosecutors apply any such charging enhancement in practice. This is not sourced either way.

Whether a foreign visitor can present identity documents whose marker matches their presentation at Korean immigration is not addressed by any source in this inventory.

IND.name: India
IND.summary:
India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill in March 2026, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking; critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The baseline for entry and stay is mixed. Same-sex acts were decriminalised by the Supreme Court in 2018, and discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, interpreted to cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage and civil partnership are not available, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Criminal-law protection weakened in 2024. Replacing the Indian Penal Code with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita removed the gender-identity-specific offences that had shielded trans people from sexual violence, and trans communities report fear of a rise in assaults under the new code.

Checkpoint and document friction is documented across modes of travel. A trans woman at a Kolkata railway station alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her under the pretext of checking her gender. Transgender people arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam recounted degrading treatment in custody in interviews recorded in June 2024. At Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 in November 2024, CISF personnel stopped an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, although she presented a PAN card for verification. Passport authorities have required a trans applicant to sit a medical examination; the Allahabad High Court granted relief in February 2026.

The courts remain the strongest protection machinery. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, delivered by Justice N. Anand Venkatesh, followed police harassment of a same-sex couple and issued sweeping guidelines covering police sensitisation, a ban on conversion therapy, and directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. The UK Home Office's country note of December 2025 records only limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.

For a visitor, exposure concentrates at checkpoints and in police contact rather than in statute alone: recognition narrowed in March 2026, sexual-violence safeguards removed in 2024, and abuse at railway, airport and passport encounters documented in 2024 and 2026, set against high courts that have intervened repeatedly on behalf of trans and LGBT+ people.
IND.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state when the March 2026 amendment takes effect, whether rules or forms under it have been notified, or how it affects identity documents already issued to trans people.

Unresolved: whether the narrowed recognition scheme changes passport endorsements, visa applications or gender markers for foreign visitors is not addressed in any source here.

Unresolved: the inventory gives no figures on penalties for anti-trans violence under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, nor on prosecution rates for the offences the old Indian Penal Code did cover.

Unresolved: the frequency of airport, railway and passport incidents beyond the cited cases is not quantified, so the four documented encounters cannot be read as a rate.

Not sourced here: any count of state-level protection cells or other sub-national implementation machinery.

News outlet (16 Nov 2024): an openly transgender law student was stopped at an airport terminal by security personnel despite presenting identification for identity verification — a discrimination incident at a national airport checkpoint that drew outrage.

News outlet (6 Sep 2024): replacing the old penal code with a new criminal code removed legal safeguards that had protected trans persons from sexual violence — trans people fear a rise in assaults as the new code omits the identity-specific offences the old law carried.

Official policy note (Dec 2025): the parent nation bars discrimination on grounds including sex interpreted to cover gender identity; same-sex acts decriminalised by the supreme court in 2018; no same-sex marriage or civil partnership (courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units); limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic.
Note: not retrievable at research time (page removed); the underlying blog post (Feb 2026) covered a high court granting relief to a trans person asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities.

High-court judgment (7 June 2021): landmark case brought by a same-sex couple harassed by police — the court's sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTIQ persons, police sensitisation, banning conversion therapy, and directions to medical and education authorities.
IND.blindLocalsOnly:
Residents' legal recognition is now governed by the 2019 Act as amended in March 2026, which ties recognition to historically accepted socio-cultural groups and to intersex status rather than to self-identification. Trans residents who identified under the previous route face a change in how they evidence status for welfare schemes, employment and services.

The 2021 high court guidelines bind police forces on sensitisation, prohibit conversion therapy, and direct the national medical regulator and education authorities on treatment of LGBT+ people. These are domestic obligations with continuing effect on residents.

Discrimination on grounds including sex, read as covering gender identity, is prohibited in the fields the constitutional and statutory framework covers, and courts have recognised same-sex couples as family units for domestic purposes even though marriage and civil partnership remain unavailable.

Residents face the same custody and policing risks documented for travellers: the railway police detentions of June 2024 and the station incident are domestic-facing examples of treatment in police hands.
IND.tangentialFactors:
The March 2026 amendment is contested on opposite readings of the same text. The government frames the shift away from self-identification as widening welfare access and strengthening anti-trafficking protection, while opponents inside and outside Parliament, including LGBTQ-community protesters, read it as exclusion of trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people from legal personhood.

Assessments of police conduct diverge in degree rather than in fact. The UK Home Office's December 2025 note characterises police abuse of LGBT+ people as limited and not systemic, and likelier in conservative rural areas, while the incident record from Kolkata, Assam and Chennai shows specific, named encounters with railway police, airport security and passport officials. Urban checkpoints are not exempt from the pattern the country note treats as peripheral.

Courts and the legislature are moving in opposite directions. The Supreme Court's 2018 decriminalisation, the Madras High Court's 2021 guidelines and the Allahabad High Court's 2026 relief on passport medical examinations sit against a Parliament that narrowed recognition in the same period, so the protective floor is judicial rather than statutory.

Scale matters for expectations: an estimated two million transgender people live in India, and the 2026 amendment determines which of them can evidence legal recognition at all.

CHN.name: China
CHN.summary:
China is authoritarian without criminalising trans identity: there is no criminal offence attaching to being transgender, no law restricting bathroom use by gender identity, and courts have awarded compensation to a trans claimant. Against that, the legal framework offers no anti-discrimination protection, legal gender recognition is unavailable, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. A visitor should expect a state that does not prosecute trans people but does not protect them either.

The most directly visitor-relevant evidence concerns the border. In May 2025 the Thai trans YouTuber Nisamanee 'Nut' Lertvorapong alleged that Chinese immigration officials laughed at, mocked and questioned her during a family trip, posting video to Instagram with the statement that no one should be treated differently on the basis of gender. A visibly trans traveller should anticipate intrusive or humiliating handling by immigration officers, with no complaint mechanism on offer.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable in China, and gender-affirming surgery for adults requires parental consent, with proof of parental death where that applies; disagreements are pushed back into the family to resolve. This is a practical barrier for trans residents and for anyone staying long enough to need medical care.

Trans-specific violence and coercive treatment are documented. A New York Times investigation in December 2024 set out transgender 'conversion' practices in the country, and in November 2024 the 28-year-old performance artist Ling'er won a record monetary payout after being subjected to electroshock 'conversion' treatment under family pressure — the first successful legal challenge to such treatment by a trans person in China. She said she hoped the case would help other LGBTQ+ people protect their rights. The case shows both that the medical system has permitted forced commitment and electroshock, and that a court will now hear a claim.

Public expression is tightly constrained. Around Pride month in 2026 platforms scrubbed prominent LGBT social media accounts, foreign films and events with LGBT themes, which Human Rights Watch read as evidence of a deteriorating rights situation and deepening repression of expression and association. Displaying rainbow flags or accessories is no longer permitted even inside venues, and in August 2023 officials removed an LGBTQ+ anthem titled 'Rainbow'. The broadcast regulator SAPPRFT's 2016 guideline banning depictions of 'abnormal sexual behaviour', including same-sex romance, established the censorship baseline that has since extended from television to social platforms.

Foreign gender-nonconforming performers meet the same squeeze: a Zurich drag artist on tour found the space for queer subcultures shrinking first-hand in August 2026, and the cancellation of nationwide shows by the transgender dancer Jin Xing in early 2025 led observers inside the country to fear a wider crackdown. Visible queerness by a visitor, performer or resident carries a real risk of cancellation, refusal or removal rather than prosecution.
CHN.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of trans travellers, including whether officials inspect passport gender markers or ask transition-related questions at the border beyond the reported treatment of Nisamanee Lertvorapong. That question is unresolved here.

There is no sourced material on bathroom or facility access for visitors, on hate-crime or hate-speech protection for trans people, or on whether any anti-discrimination remedy exists outside the civil claim Ling'er brought. These are not established either way by the available sources.

Whether the parental-consent requirement for gender-affirming surgery applies to foreign patients treated in China, and whether it affects short-stay visitors needing emergency care, is not sourced and remains unresolved.

Enforcement is reported at national and platform level; variation between provinces and cities, and the practical treatment of trans residents by police outside documented cases, are not covered by the inventory.

MYS.name: Malaysia
MYS.summary:
Malaysia is dangerous — one of the few countries that criminalises gender expression per se. All 13 states and the Federal Territory prohibit "a man posing as a woman" under Sharia law (up to 3 years in jail, a fine, and caning). While these laws technically apply to Muslims, the enforcement climate affects all trans people: religious police conduct systematic raids on trans events — tipping off media in advance and sharing detainees' faces with tabloids (public outing and humiliation). Three trans women were killed in fewer than two months in 2019.

The political climate is shifting toward Islamist parties (a deputy minister urged the "deviant culture" label for LGBTQ; state-backed "rehabilitation" programs; dating-site blocking). For a non-Muslim foreign trans visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing law doesn't directly apply, but being caught in a raided venue, facing the enforcement climate, or being subject to Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping, applies to all including tourists) are real risks. There is no legal gender recognition.
MYS.outOfScopeNotes: General crime and Islamic-law compliance (alcohol, dress codes for religious sites) affect Muslim and non-Muslim travellers in different ways; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile — Malaysia: federal Penal Code section 377 criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 20 years plus whipping). Sharia enactments across the states prohibit 'cross-dressing' or 'males posing as females', including the Selangor and Kelantan codes and the Sharia Criminal Code (I) Enactment 2019 covering 'sodomy' and 'sexual intercourse against the order of nature'. The profile places Malaysia among jurisdictions that criminalise, and lists active litigation alongside cases from Mauritius and Namibia.

Human Rights Watch report (10 August 2022) 'I Don't Want to Change Myself', based on interviews with 73 LGBT people in Malaysia between 2018 and 2021 across seven states plus journalists and lawyers: every state and the federal territories (Kuala Lumpur, Putrajaya) maintain Sharia codes criminalising same-sex activity and gender nonconformity ('a man posing as a woman'), while the federal penal code punishes oral/anal sex with up to 20 years plus mandatory whipping. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, and LGBT events/media content were censored. The 2021 Nur Sajat case shows enforcement reach — 122 religious officers were mobilised to hunt her over 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and gained UNHCR protection.

Human Rights Watch (25 June 2019): a transgender woman was killed in Klang, a Kuala Lumpur suburb — the third such killing of a trans woman in Malaysia in fewer than two months — with the piece documenting violence against trans people alongside police mistreatment and impunity ('The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself').
Reuters (August 2023): growing fears among LGBT people in Malaysia as Islamist opposition forecloses reform.

The Diplomat (10 December 2025): on 28 November police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur and arrested 208 men under section 377B — the largest such raid since 2022 — with media pre-tipped and detainees' faces and personal details leaked, suspending 17 civil servants identified among them. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground under 377B, yet release was delayed; over 130 remained held at one point including 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid; on 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang. Documents current enforcement-and-exposure risks against queer spaces, including for foreign visitors.
Human Rights Law Centre case summary: the Malaysian High Court denied a request to declare the Sharia prohibition on cross-dressing unconstitutional.
United Nations Development Programme and the Asia Pacific Transgender Network have published a joint publication on Malaysia. The file is image-based and yielded no extractable text.

International Commission of Jurists (July 2020): Religious Affairs Minister Zulkifli Mohamad Al-Bakri announced he had given the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) 'full licence to carry out its enforcement actions' against transgender persons; the ICJ condemned the order, demanded its revocation and called for non-discrimination guarantees. Documents state-sanctioned targeting of trans people in the federal territories.

Malaysia4U legal guide (updated July 2026): sections 377A/377B criminalise 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' for any person regardless of gender or consent — maximum 20 years plus whipping — and apply to tourists; state Syariah offences (liwat, musahaqah, cross-dressing) apply only to Muslims (max 3 years, RM5,000 fine, 6 strokes). The Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and 16 Kelantan Syariah provisions in February 2024 on federalism grounds without decriminalising anything under the Penal Code; enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely targeted. No same-sex marriage or anti-discrimination law; sodomy first criminalised in 1871.

Human Rights Watch (24 September 2014) 'I'm Scared to Be a Woman': since the 1980s every one of Malaysia's 13 states has passed Sharia enactments institutionalising discrimination against trans people — all 13 bar Muslim men from 'dressing as women' and three also bar 'women posing as men' — enforced by state Islamic religious departments with no legal definition of transgender dressing. Documents the 2011 strip-search and sexual assault of Victoria by religious officials, repeated arrests (one woman over 20 times), routine rejection of gender-marker changes by the Registration Department (a 1982 National Fatwa Council fatwa ended domestic sex-reassignment surgery), and prison terms of four months to three years with male-ward sexual violence. Follows the mass arrest of 16 trans women at a wedding on 8 June 2014 that triggered the Negeri Sembilan constitutional challenge (Court of Appeal decision then expected 7 November 2014).

MYS.tangentialFactors: Section 377A (same-sex conduct, 20 years + whipping) applies to all including tourists — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.

Enforcement of these laws creates real risks for all trans people, with official raids on trans community events reported and the media tipped off in advance by the authorities. Political influence has grown for religious-conservative groups, and official rehabilitation programs for LGBT people exist.

For a foreign trans visitor who does not follow the country's religion, the religious offence does not apply directly, but same-sex conduct is a national criminal offence with severe penalties, applying to residents and international visitors alike. There is no legal gender recognition.

SGP.name: Singapore
SGP.summary:
Singapore is broadly workable — far safer than its neighbour Malaysia, with no criminalisation of trans identity, no religious police, and one of the world's lowest crime rates. Section 377A (which criminalised sex between men) was repealed in 2022, and the prison service reports no assaults against its 10 transgender inmates — unusually positive for axis-H. Singapore is also a regional medical hub with gender-affirming care available.

The main gaps: legal gender recognition requires genital surgery (expensive and restrictive), there is no anti-discrimination law (the 2025 Workplace Fairness Act explicitly excludes sexual orientation and gender identity), and over 65% of trans Singaporeans report negative workplace experiences. A radio code still groups homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" as lifestyles barred from the airwaves. Progress has "stalled" since the 377A repeal, with discrimination "quietly tolerated."

For a visitor: efficient border processing, very low street crime, unrestricted bathrooms, and no trans-specific police friction. The atmosphere is conservative but quietly accommodating in practice.
SGP.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is extremely low; no trans-specific travel advisory.

Outright International Singapore overview (updated March 2026): same-sex relations legal for men and women; legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations cannot register — registration remains the structural gap despite decriminalisation.

Straits Times (15 Nov 2023): the Singapore Prison Service reported 10 transgender inmates currently behind bars and no recorded cases of assault against transgender inmates — a rare official datum on trans prisoners in the system.

Pink Dot SG (8 Jan 2025): the new Workplace Fairness Legislation gives Singapore its first statutory anti-discrimination framework, but it stops short of covering LGBTQ+ workers — gender identity/expression are not protected grounds, leaving workplace exposure for trans staff.
Reuters feature (June 2023): Singapore's LGBT community feels safer as the end of the 377A ban brings change.

South China Morning Post (3 Jul 2025): a clause of the radio broadcast code grouping homosexuality with paedophilia and incest as forbidden 'lifestyles' sparked calls for review — a former radio DJ and actor argued the grouping 'has no place in a post-377A Singapore'. Media-regulation residue after decriminalisation.

F&M Global Barometers Singapore country profile: interactive scores across unified/gay/transgender rights indices and an LGBTQI+ perception index, 2011–2024, covering de jure protections and lived experience.

Intrepid Travel 'Is Singapore LGBTQIA+ friendly': describes a thriving LGBTQIA+ social scene — gay-friendly bars (e.g. Backstage Bar in Chinatown), pop-ups and exhibitions — alongside practical guidance on solo travel and room sharing for its own trips. Visitor-facing operator guidance.

SGP.tangentialFactors: The radio code grouping homosexuality with "paedophilia and incest" is a climate signal; the 2022 repeal of 377A removed partner-related criminal exposure for visitors.

IRN.name: Iran
IRN.summary:
Iran is among the most severe environments in the world for a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The Islamic Penal Code criminalises all same-sex activity for men and women, with penalties running from flogging to execution, and Human Rights Watch has recorded executions carried out for homosexual conduct, most recently documenting two men put to death in November 2005. The UK Home Office's December 2025 country report notes that convictions are also brought under more severe charges used as a pretext, and that the code contains no discrimination protections of any kind.

The country's position is bifurcated. Transsexuality is legally recognised, following a 1987 fatwa by Ayatollah Khomeini, and gender-reassignment surgery is permitted and may be state-subsidised after a diagnosis of "gender identity disorder." Recognition of a person's acquired gender, however, comes only after surgery, sterilisation and a lengthy legal process. Surgery is described by the UK Home Office as invasive and frequently carried out to a sub-standard level.

For a trans visitor the practical consequence is that legal recognition does not travel with you. An LGBT+ person living openly in Iran without recognised surgery is assessed by the UK Home Office as likely to face persecution, and the same report places trans people who have not completed the surgical and legal pathway under immorality and indecency provisions carrying imprisonment, fines and corporal punishment.

Custodial violence is documented. Ghazal Marzban, an imprisoned trans rights activist, recounted in an open letter published by HRANA being raped while held in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility. Public space is also restricted by administrative pressure: Tehran authorities issued a public warning instructing transgender people to avoid "busy" areas of the capital, an official advisory that narrows where gender-nonconforming people may appear.

Coercion shapes the recognition system itself. Reporting in 2025 describes pressure on Iranian trans people to conform to a binary transition or face legal penalty, with state funding for surgery presented as protection while functioning as the price of tolerance. Human Rights Watch's country analysis frames the same arrangement as state-funded surgery purchased at the cost of dignity. At the same time, foreign patients travel to Iran for the subsidised procedure, and trans medical tourism has grown into a visible industry.

Documented persecution is systematic rather than incidental. A 6Rang submission to the UN Independent Expert on Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity and Expression, filed in February 2025, surveyed 25 LGBTIQ+ people who had fled Iran and found 96% of them from ethnic minorities, describing forces driving displacement from the country. 6Rang's January–February 2025 submission to Iran's Universal Periodic Review separately catalogued human-rights violations against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender people, including violence and legal discrimination.
IRN.outOfScopeNotes:
The current status and terms of the Tehran advisory warning transgender people to avoid busy areas are not resolved here: the inventory confirms the warning was issued but does not establish whether it remains formally in force or how it is enforced.

The outcome of Ghazal Marzban's criminal case and her custody location at the time of the HRANA publication are not sourced in this inventory; the account of the assault in a Ministry of Intelligence detention facility is documented, the subsequent proceedings are not.

No source in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers for entry into Iran, airport treatment of trans travellers, or the availability of names and pronouns in official documents. Any statement about entry screening would be unsourced.

Figures specific to executions or imprisonments of trans people as distinct from same-sex conduct are not available here; the inventory supports execution records for homosexual conduct and imprisonment under immorality provisions for people without recognised surgery, but not a combined count.

The extent to which state-subsidised surgery meets clinical standards rests on the UK Home Office's characterisation of procedures as invasive and often sub-standard; no independent clinical audit is present in the inventory.

Whether the UPR and UN Special Procedures submissions produced any change in Iranian law or practice by the date of this record is unresolved; the inventory documents the filings, not their effect.

Trans people face restrictions on movement and assembly in practice as well as in law: Tehran authorities publicly instructed transgender residents to stay out of busy areas of the capital. Detention carries documented risk of sexual violence, as the account of activist Ghazal Marzban of rape in a Ministry of Intelligence facility demonstrates.

Displacement is a common outcome. 6Rang's February 2025 survey of 25 LGBTIQ+ people who left the country found 96% were from ethnic minorities, and its UPR submission documents the pattern of persecution, violence and legal discrimination that drives people out.

ISR.name: Israel
ISR.summary:
Israel does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct, and its legal framework carries anti-discrimination protections alongside publicly funded transition healthcare. Legal gender recognition runs through the courts, and as of 2025 registration of a person's previous name has been abolished for transgender people, removing the old-name traceability that previously followed a document change. Tel Aviv functions as a regional queer hub, and the country is widely regarded as the most progressive destination in its part of the world for trans visitors.

Border screening is the sharpest visitor-specific risk. A first-person account published by Haaretz in May 2023 documents a transgender traveller subjected to gender-identity humiliation at an Israeli airport, with security personnel insisting "if you don't undergo surgery, you're still a male". The Israel Police adopted a new regulation governing searches of transgender people in 2023, in response to complaints about humiliating searches of trans detainees and travellers. That change governs search protocol; it does not establish that border screening will be conducted with respect for a visitor's stated gender.

Violence against LGBT people rose in Israel during 2025, according to official data reported by the Jerusalem Post, and Ynet reported anti-LGBTQ violence reaching a record high, with dating-app traps and organised ambushes used to lure victims into assaults. Haaretz reported in February 2025 that inflammatory messaging from the United States was feeding into the local climate, with trans Israelis describing heightened fear as a result.

Custody remains the weakest point of the protection framework. Documentation in a law-journal article establishes that Israel's response to transgender prisoners' vulnerability has been isolation or segregation from the general prison population rather than placement in facilities matching gender identity, and trans women have at least at times been held in men's prisons. Courts have intervened case by case: in October 2019, following a petition by ACRI, an Israeli court ordered the Israel Prison Service to provide hormone-replacement therapy to a trans woman prisoner and transfer her from a male prison to a female one. She was initially housed in a separate wing of the women's prison, and ACRI prepared a further petition seeking her placement with the general population.

On partner recognition, a Channel 10 survey found most Israelis favour same-sex marriage while half of Members of the Knesset declined to state a position, including a culture minister who has marched in the Pride parade.
ISR.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory could not be used. The LegalClarity page on trans rights in Israel returned HTTP 404 at research time and its content is unresolved; nothing from it is reflected here.

A direct conflict between sources is unresolved: Outright International's profile states there is no legal gender recognition in Israel, while the Jerusalem Post reports that registration of a previous name has been abolished for transgender people. The inventory does not reconcile the two, and the scope of the 2025 change (whether it covers full marker change or only removal of the prior-name trace) is not sourced.

Not sourced: whether Israel issues a non-binary or third gender marker; whether the 2023 police search regulation extends to airport border screening or applies only to police searches in custody; trans-specific breakdowns of the 2025 violence statistics; and any post-2025 court rulings on prison placement.

The violence trend is documented at the aggregate LGBT level rather than the trans level. The sources do not break the assault totals down by victim gender identity.

ARG.name: Argentina
ARG.summary:
Argentina's statutory framework remains among the most permissive in the world for legal gender recognition. Law 26.743, passed by the Chamber of Deputies 167-17-7 and by the Senate on 9 May 2012 by 55 votes to one abstention, was promulgated on 24 May 2012 and allows a change of legal gender without surgery, hormone treatment or judicial approval. The United Nations described it as a pioneering step for transgender rights in the region. Argentina was also the first Latin American country to legalise marriage equality, in 2010, and anti-discrimination protection exists through a combination of national and provincial laws.

That framework has been narrowed by executive action. In February 2025 the government of President Javier Milei issued a decree modifying the Gender Identity Law as it applies to minors, and a second decree governing the housing of transgender people in prisons. Reuters reported that the decree bans gender-affirming surgery and hormone therapy for adolescents. Legal experts interviewed by Agencia Presentes called the measure illegal and unconstitutional and a setback for the rights of adolescents, and signalled an intention to seek judicial intervention.

Violence against LGBTIQ+ people reached a documented peak in 2025. The Observatorio Nacional de Crímenes de Odio recorded at least 227 hate crimes based on sexual orientation or gender identity over the year, a record, averaging one every 38 hours. Agencia Presentes described the figure as an inflection point in violence against LGBTIQ+ people in Argentina, with trans women bearing a disproportionate share of the harm.

Trans activists in Buenos Aires interviewed in April 2025, including representatives of organisations named for Diana Sacayán, killed in 2015, and for the activist Lohana Berkins, said the Milei government's policies had made the community more vulnerable to violence and described the situation as chaotic and desperate.

The judicial response to gender-motivated killing is contested. In April 2025 Argentina's Supreme Court left standing the life sentence imposed on Gabriel Marino for the 2015 murder of trans activist Diana Sacayán, while rejecting attempts to reinstate the travesticidio aggravating circumstance that an appeals court had removed in 2020. The gender-motivated aggravation is therefore not currently applied in that line of cases.

Outright International's country overview, updated in March 2026, records negative assessments for same-sex relations, gender recognition and the registration of civil-society organisations, an assessment of deterioration against the earlier statutory position.
ARG.outOfScopeNotes:

The inventory does not state whether the core self-identification provisions of Law 26.743 for adults remain fully operative after the decrees, or only the provisions touching minors and prison housing. The distinction is not sourced and should be verified against the decree texts.

No source records how the current framework is applied to foreign nationals seeking document changes or entry on the basis of a changed gender marker, and no data is available on screening of trans travellers at Argentine border points.

The removal of the travesticidio aggravating circumstance in 2020 and its rejection by the Supreme Court in 2025 are sourced to one case; whether the aggravator is unavailable across all gender-motivated homicide prosecutions is not established here.

ARE.name: United Arab Emirates
ARE.summary:
The United Arab Emirates subjects trans visitors to gender-document screening at the border. In 2025, two Israeli trans women were detained for hours at Dubai airport, X-rayed to check whether their genitals matched the female sex recorded in their passports, mocked by staff, and denied entry with their passports confiscated.

Entry refusals on identity grounds are documented across a decade. In August 2016 the trans media personality Gigi Gorgeous was denied entry and detained at Dubai airport. In March 2022 the Thai trans model Rachaya Noppakaroon, 2014 Miss Tiffany Universe runner-up, was stopped at Dubai immigration and interrogated for nine hours before being deported to Thailand ahead of her Expo 2020 appearance; her passport listed male sex while she lives as a woman.

The legal framework underpinning these encounters explicitly acknowledges and penalises nonconformity with traditional gender roles, and transgender expression or unconventional appearance frequently results in arrest, confinement or expulsion. A new federal criminal code enacted in early 2022 criminalised consensual same-sex relations with up to six months' imprisonment, and charges under it require a complaint basis.

There is no legal gender recognition in the UAE, so a visitor's documents cannot be brought into line with lived gender before travel. Foreign nationals also face prolonged custody: a Brazilian trans woman has been detained since September 2022, arrested after refusing a police-requested toxicology test, and in April 2023 she accused the consulate of negligence over her case.
ARE.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether genital X-ray screening at Dubai airport is a written procedure or an ad hoc practice by individual officers is not resolved by the available sources; the 2025 account establishes that it occurred, not that it is codified.

No source in the inventory gives conviction or sentencing data under the 2022 code's six-month provision, so the frequency of enforcement is unresolved.

The inventory does not address hate-crime protection, healthcare access, bathroom or facilities rules, or partner recognition for trans visitors; nothing should be inferred about those from the entries above.

Cairo 52 describes legal mechanisms penalising gender nonconformity without naming the specific articles relied on, so the statutory basis of those provisions remains unresolved here.

The outcome of the Brazilian detainee's case, and whether her consulate responded to the negligence allegation, are unresolved.

ZAF.name: South Africa
ZAF.summary:
South Africa has one of the world's most progressive constitutional frameworks for trans rights — it was the first country to ban discrimination on sexual orientation (1996), has a legal gender recognition procedure (the Alteration of Sex Description Act, 2003), marriage equality (2006), and an Equality Act prohibiting unfair discrimination on gender. The Equality Court recently ruled in favour of a trans inmate who was denied gender expression and healthcare in prison (the Mokoena case, November 2025), affirming the constitutional right to gender-affirming healthcare for inmates, and Correctional Services has developed a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners.

But there is a wide gap between law and lived reality. LGR is administratively difficult, expensive, and inconsistently implemented ("the Mariana Trench of transphobia"). A trans woman was brutally attacked in a Tshwane tavern (January 2025); a Grindr-hostage ordeal was reported (December 2024); and anti-transgender violence has been documented within the public health system. There is a legal debate about whether businesses can refuse trans people facility access under the Consumer Protection Act.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, private healthcare available, and Cape Town and Johannesburg have established queer scenes. The violence targets local trans communities, not tourists.
ZAF.outOfScopeNotes: South Africa's high general crime rate (violent crime, carjackings, muggings) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Full judgment, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Gauteng High Court, delivered ~14 Nov 2025): refusal to provide gender-affirming health care to a transgender inmate for whom it was prescribed falls below the required standard of health care; refusal to allow feminising clothing/accessories likewise impugned — binding equality-court remedies for detained trans persons.

Lawyers for Human Rights case summary (14 Nov 2025): the High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services — orders DCS to implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs for transgender inmates, and provide prescribed medical care.

SAHRC media statement (14 Nov 2025): welcomes the Gauteng High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case 2024/070075) under PEPUDA — orders compelling DCS to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense and to permit clothing/cosmetics expressing her gender identity.

GroundUp (6 Aug 2025): Correctional Services has a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but rights organisations doubt implementation; Lawyers for Human Rights represents a trans prisoner (NM) challenging conditions — pre-echo of the Nov 2025 Equality Court win.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): Civil Union Act in force 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits black lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people in townships.

GroundUp opinion (27 Jun 2025, Mikhail Petersen): ordinary administrative tasks are fraught with risk for trans people — medical requirements under the Alteration Act lock people out of legal gender recognition, binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; Gender Dynamix's 2024 report documents a trans woman denied filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID (police mockery).

MambaOnline (6 Jan 2025): 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo (make-up artist, Soshanguve→Winterveld) survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

OUT LGBT Well-being rights watch (Dec 2024): East London activists spotlighted trans healthcare access — memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long treatment delays; escalating hate violence with five LGBTQIA+ murders reported; also covers the Tshwane tavern attack (arrest made).

Academic article (PER/PELJ 2024) 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Door?': analyses whether gender-segregated bathrooms to the exclusion of transgender/non-binary persons constitute unfair discrimination under CPA s9 read with Constitution s9 — argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access; relevant to visitor facility anxiety.

Daily Maverick opinion (19 Jan 2026, Mikhail Petersen/Gender Dynamix): makes the legal gender recognition case — mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and even arrest threats for 'fraud'; defines LGR as changing marker/name on official documents to align with identity; argues recognition should be a right grounded in dignity.

IOL/SAPA: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence, citing the Constitution's equality clause — early (2010s-era) government recognition of LGBTI violence as a policy problem; historic context for the later Hate Crimes Act (2024).

ZAF.tangentialFactors: The Grindr-hostage ordeal (December 2024) is a caution for trans visitors using apps; the facility-access legal debate affects visitors' everyday exposure.
ZAF.localsOnly: The Alteration of Sex Description Act LGR procedure (difficult, expensive, inconsistently implemented) is resident-facing; the Mokoena prison case and the public-health-system violence concern residents.

IDN.name: Indonesia
IDN.summary:
Indonesia is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The national penal code signed in December 2022 took effect on 2 January 2026 and penalises consensual extra-marital sex between adults with up to two years' imprisonment. Because same-sex marriage is not permitted in Indonesia, this provision effectively criminalises all consensual same-sex relations; reporting indicates that prosecutions are selective rather than systematic.

The Human Dignity Trust country profile records that two provinces, Aceh and South Sumatra, criminalise same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, alongside national-level provisions targeting morality. In Aceh, where Sharia law applies, two men were publicly caned for a same-sex relationship in February 2025. Aceh's punishments are imposed under provincial religious law and reach anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors.

Enforcement also takes the form of venue raids.
