Official policy now frames LGBTQ+ people as a security matter. A presidential decree issued by President Prabowo Subianto in October 2025 lists nonmilitary threats and places LGBTQ+ people within national defence policy as risks to be monitored and controlled. Reporting from August 2026 ties that framing directly to a wave of vigilante attacks on transgender women, with mobs attacking trans people as the government codifies anti-LGBTQ+ attitudes into law. Commentators quoted by ABC News state that the regulation moved hostile rhetoric into the official doctrine of national defence policy.

PAK.name: Pakistan
PAK.summary:
Pakistan is dangerous for trans travellers — legally progressive on paper but severely undermined in practice. The 2018 Transgender Persons Protection Act is described as one of the most progressive pieces of legislation internationally, but the national religious court (the Shariat Court) gutted it in 2023, declaring provisions "un-Islamic". Transgender people face extreme violence: three trans women were shot dead in Karachi, the largest city of the country, 267 violence cases were documented in one state/province (Khyber Pakhtunkhwa), and police commit a documented "continuum of violence — from routine harassment to arbitrary detention, extortion, and abuse in custody." The jirga (tribal) system closes cases under family pressure.

Same-sex conduct is NOT clearly criminalised nationally (the Zina Ordinance is unclear; no known cases or executions). No trans-traveller-specific border friction or death in custody is documented. The 2020 rules introduced a neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but how document markers are treated at border crossings is undocumented.

For partner travel, no relationship or partner recognition is documented, so partner-based protections should not be assumed. The severity of social and police violence is the dominant risk.
PAK.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism risks, sectarian violence, and general crime in certain regions affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the precise criminal status of consensual same-sex conduct — the statutes cited in the sources differ and definitions are unclear — remains ambiguous; no prosecutions were documented.

Unresolved: how identity documents are treated at border crossings ('X' recognition-marker practice is undocumented).

sources.summary: AP (Nov 2024): 'Shooting kills 3 transgender women in Pakistan's largest city' — gunmen shot three transgender women at close range near Karachi, the second deadly attack on the community there in a week.

BBC (21 Sep 2025): police found bullet-riddled bodies of three transgender women shot dead by unidentified assailants on a roadside highway at Memon Goth, Karachi — latest in a continuing pattern of lethal violence; article notes estimates of ~500,000 transgender citizens facing social exclusion and abuse.

Justice Project Pakistan policy brief: despite notable legal advances (Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018), protections have not translated into safeguards against torture and ill-treatment in practice — the central challenge is implementation failure, not absence of law; brief makes custody/police safeguards recommendations.

UK Home Office country-policy note on SOGI, Pakistan, November 2025 (current-status authority): trans/intersex people protected under the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 though the Federal Shariat Court declared provisions 'un-Islamic' in 2023 leaving ongoing legal disputes; consensual same-sex acts criminalised under PPC s.377 (2 years to life, definition unclear, male-to-male sex), only men criminalised per Human Dignity Trust (Dec 2024); LGBT+ people unlikely to face state persecution.

Amnesty International (19 May 2023): reacting to the Federal Shariat Court's reserved verdict striking down sections of the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act 2018 — calls the ruling 'a blow to the rights of the already beleaguered group' of transgender and gender-diverse people; Amnesty had warned the government on 17 May 2023 not to adopt amendments violating human-rights standards.

The News, Pakistan (21 Oct 2025): analysis of the gap between law and reality — the 2018 Act affirmed self-perceived gender identity and the 2020 Rules introduced the neutral 'X' marker for administrative recognition, but trans Pakistanis still face bullet-riddled bodies on highways, street harassment, rejection by landlords, dismissal at hospitals and suspicion/ridicule at police stations.

Erasing 76crimes (3 Feb 2026, citing the Guardian): a wave of violence has left Pakistani transgender people afraid to go out — describes the Karachi night-time shooting at activists Zehrish Khanzadi and Bindiya Rana (three bullets fired through the door, narrowly escaped); also reports Senator Mushtaq Ahmad proposing a government 'gender re-assignment board' that would control trans people's official gender identity — an active retrograde legislative push.

Dawn analysis of the Federal Shariat Court verdict of 19 May 2023, delivered across 12 shairat petitions: the court ruled that sections 2(f), 3 and 7 of the Transgender Persons Act 2018, covering gender identity, the right to self-perceived gender identity and inheritance for transgender people, do not conform with the petitioners' reading of Islamic principles, and speculated that the Act could facilitate the rape and sexual assault of women by men disguised as transgender women.

The Diplomat (Jul 2025): Pakistan's 2018 Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act was hailed as a legislative turning point — granting right to self-identify and protection from discrimination in education, employment and healthcare — yet the piece documents citizens 'legally recognized, socially forsaken', i.e. statutory rights not matching lived status.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Pakistan: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised under Section 377; societal violence and discrimination; transgender persons (khwaja sira) have some legal recognition but face harassment and violence.

The 2018 Act's third-gender recognition (gutted by the religious court in 2023, under appeal) and the hijra community's legal recognition are resident-facing; the 267 documented violence cases and jirga case-closures describe residents' situation.

Third-gender recognition has existed since 2009, a dedicated ride-sharing service for trans safety operates in Lahore, and civil society is active — all resident-facing facts a visitor would not directly rely on.

PHL.name: Philippines
PHL.summary:
The Philippines is one of the most socially accepting destinations in the region for trans visitors, with deep cultural traditions of gender diversity, a vibrant Pride scene in the capital, and no criminalisation — trans identity has never been criminalised in this country.

However, there is a "near-complete absence of legal protections at the national level": no national legal gender recognition law at all (so identity documents cannot be corrected and retain the birth gender), the SOGIE Equality Bill — a national anti-discrimination law — has been stalled for 25 years, and there is no marriage equality. Documented violence includes the killing of an 18-year-old trans woman found in a river (June 2025), a foreign national arrested for raping a trans woman at a resort (May 2025), and a drag artist assaulted mid-performance. The national human-rights commission actively investigates discrimination cases but lacks enforcement power without a national law.

For a visitor: no border friction and genuinely warm social acceptance, but the legal-protection vacuum means limited recourse if discriminated against at a venue — documented incidents include bathroom, fitting-room, and resort denials; partner or marriage-based protections do not exist. The vacuum extends into custody: transgender women at the capital's main city jail are held by birth sex in the ordinary male dormitories — where mandatory head-shaving applies on arrival to the male dorm and safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than any gender-matched placement policy — while Davao City Jail answers abuse risk by relocating LGBT detainees to a separate annex; a trans visitor arrested in the Philippines has no documented path to identity-matched custody.
PHL.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (kidnapping risks in certain provinces, scams, typhoon risks) affects all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical treatment of identity documents at borders is not documented, and the sources do not detail how bathroom and fitting-room policies at venues are enforced.

Custody axis: no national rule on trans-prisoner placement — birth-sex vs identity housing, special units, or solitary/segregation practice — is documented; the male-dorm housing is documented at Manila City Jail and the annex segregation at Davao City Jail only, so practice appears to vary by jail; the head-shaving intake requirement applies to the male dormitory generally rather than to transgender detainees specifically, and the 2022-23 reports are the only custody sources in this record.

sources.summary: Outright/IGLHRC Philippines legal overview (fetched page): lawyers' Code of Professional Responsibility updated 2023 to bar SOGI-based discrimination of clients; openly gay/bisexual people allowed in armed forces since 2009 and transgender people since 2017 (uniform policy follows legal gender on birth certificate); Clerical Error Law RA 9048 (2001) blocks administrative birth-certificate sex change for trans people (judicial order required) and the 2008 Supreme Court ruling in Republic v. Jennifer Cagandahan bars legal-gender change even after gender-affirming surgery.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): two killings in days — 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol found dead in a Cagayan river on 23 June after being reported missing, and a trans woman former journalist/activist shot by an unidentified gunman inside a General Santos clinic the same day; Bahaghari says the cases are an urgent reminder to pass the SOGIESC Equality Bill, which has been stuck in Congress for 25 years — no national SOGI anti-discrimination law exists.
Manila Bulletin report (May 2025): a foreigner was arrested for raping a trans woman in Batangas.

Interaksyon (10 Apr 2024): drag artist Taylor Sheesh (Taylor Swift impersonator) was physically struck on stage by a man from the crowd at Bayambang, Pangasinan's Kalutan Concert on 6 April 2024 — she called the attack traumatic and urged passage of the SOGIE Equality Bill; the town mayor publicly apologised to the LGBTQ+ community.

Rolling Stone Philippines explainer (7 Feb 2025): 25 years of legislative inaction on the SOGIE Equality Bill; patchwork protections that do exist — SOGIE anti-discrimination ordinances in provinces (Albay, Agusan del Norte, Bataan, Batangas, Cavite, Dinagat Islands, Ilocos Sur, Iloilo) and 32 cities/municipalities; Magna Carta for Public Social Workers (SOGIE harassment: P20k-40k fine and/or up to 1 year); Magna Carta of Women and Safe Spaces Act punish transphobic/homophobic/misogynistic slurs and ridicule (fines P1k-10k, up to 30 days, sensitivity seminar).

Rappler: trans Filipinos' legal gender recognition bill would let applicants — including minors with consent — choose markers beyond male/female (X/nonbinary), addressing the lack of a recognition process that drafter Chase Go says drives social exclusion, privacy invasion and violence; the Commission on Human Rights has called the year's trans killings a 'disturbing pattern of transfemicide'; allies plan to endorse the bill to the 20th Congress (28 July).

WanderSafe LGBTQ+ travel guide (2026 data as of 18 Jun 2026): Manila 'Generally Safe' — LGBTQ+ 69, but Trans travellers only 62 ('Exercise Caution'), HIV+ 81; same-sex relations never criminalised, deep gender-diversity traditions (bakla/tomboy), vibrant Pride/nightlife scene and high media visibility, but SOGIE Bill (filed since 2000) stuck, no marriage equality, Catholic Church resistance; accessibility caveat: 80% of Metro Manila's 46 train stations lack step-free entrances, only 5 of 46 LRT-1 stations have elevators.

HRW report (21 Jun 2017), 'Just Let Us Be': documents bullying and discrimination against LGBT students across Philippine schools, with law short on remedies at the time — basis-level evidence of school-setting climate for gender-diverse youth; includes Tagalog summary and recommendations.

sources.title: Inside jails, gay men and trans women ‘wed’ fellow PDLs to escape abuse (Philippine Center for Investigative Journalism, by Aie Balagtas See)
sources.summary: Investigative feature on Manila City Jail: transgender women and gay men are held in the ordinary MALE dormitories (mandatory head-shaving on arrival for the male dorm), where they assume housekeeping/entertainer roles and informal same-sex “weddings” with male inmates are widely used by gangs as a survival/protection strategy against abuse. Documents that trans women in Philippine jails are housed by birth sex in male facilities with no gender-matched placement, and that safety comes from inmate hierarchies rather than policy.

sources.title: BJMP-Davao transfers LGBT inmates to annex facility for safety (SunStar Davao, by Ian Carl Espinosa)
sources.summary: Official practice documented: BJMP-Davao Community Relations chief Jail Senior Inspector Ellen Rose Saragena said LGBT detainees at Davao City Jail are relocated in batches to the City Jail Annex “to prevent abuse”, alongside persons with disabilities, the sick and senior citizens; three LGBT groupings live in the annex since its establishment. Shows the official Philippine response is administrative segregation of LGBT detainees into a separate annex for “safety”.

CHL.name: Chile
CHL.summary:
Chile's statutory framework for trans people is among the more developed in the region. Legal gender recognition has operated since 2019 on a self-determination basis, with no medical or surgical conditions attached. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and since 2012 the criminal code has treated sexual orientation and gender identity as aggravating circumstances in hate-motivated offences. Birth certificates also offer a third sex option for intersex children.

Detention carries specific protections. The national director of Gendarmería de Chile signed a protocol guaranteeing trans detainees the recognition of their assumed gender, including placement and segmented housing by gender identity, entry examinations, and rules on access for trans visitors; a standing committee with Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives monitors implementation.

The policy record has stalled. A Chilean advocacy group's annual assessment judged 2024 a year of regression for LGBTIQ+ rights, the first such reversal since the return of democracy in 1990, attributing the failure of equality and trans-rights bills to the rise of the ultra-right and to government inaction. Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report, published in 2025, describes a breakdown of social, political and institutional consensus around LGBTIQ+ rights, with non-discrimination law reform rejected by lawmakers.

Documented violence remains a live risk. In 2023 a young trans man, Ever, was murdered by an acquaintance and hidden for 24 hours; the case is treated as the country's benchmark anti-trans killing and was described in the national press as Chile's biggest hate crime. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour in a transphobic attack at a hotel in Santiago, during which the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Institutional hostility is also visible inside state employment. Isabella Panes, Chile's first trans police officer, sued Carabineros in 2025 alleging she was relegated to administrative duties, had her private life exposed without consent, and was denied support.
CHL.outOfScopeNotes:
The F&M Global Barometers profile is cited as a source of comparative indices, including a specific trans rights barometer, but no numerical scores or ranking positions were carried in the inventory; those values remain unverified here.

Movilh's 24th Annual Human Rights Report (2025) is identified by title and publisher, but its underlying incident counts, methodology and specific findings beyond the consensus-breakdown assessment were not extracted and are therefore unresolved.

Whether the hate-crime aggravating circumstance in force since 2012 has produced convictions or sentencing uplift in trans-specific cases is not sourced. Likewise, no evidence was available on how the Gendarmería protocol has performed in practice, on outcomes of the Panes litigation, or on whether the stalled non-discrimination reform will be reintroduced.

Policies on entry screening, passport gender markers for foreign visitors, and recognition of foreign documents in Chilean institutions were not covered by the inventory and remain unsourced.

COL.name: Colombia
COL.summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Colombia is among the most developed in Latin America. Since a rule change approved in June 2015, trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. The official Reyes, who defended the change, described those examinations as "profoundly invasive of privacy rights... rooted in unacceptable prejudice".

Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on the basis of self-recognition, without a surgical requirement. Marriage equality has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025.

The courts have also intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.

The gap between that framework and enforcement is severe. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025 alone. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected, and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

The sharpest risk sits where armed groups operate, including in territories under their control. In the department of Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyer campaigns targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots", and threatened a further wave. Trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work; Tatiana Cespedes, a trans salon owner, was forced to relocate twice after receiving death threats from armed men, and a friend of the trans woman Yesenia Rodríguez was killed. In the department of Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans".

Targeted killings of trans people continue in the country's ordinary, urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025. A 28-second video of the assault went viral from 5 April, showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned; her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation, and solidarity events were held in several cities. One report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.
COL.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the comprehensive trans law legislated in 2025 is unresolved in the source inventory: it is reported as being under consideration, but no source confirms enactment, its scope, or whether it is in force at the time of publication.

Full-year 2025 homicide totals for trans and LGBTI people are not sourced. Available figures are partial and differently defined, so they are not directly comparable: the Attorney General's Office counted 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, while a separate report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025, and a 2024 report counted more than 40 transgender women killed in 2023.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, the treatment of foreign trans documents at Colombian border and airport controls, whether screeners or officials may question a traveller's gender presentation, or whether the domestic notary-based marker procedure is available to non-residents or visitors.

Healthcare, asylum and hate-crime sentencing provisions for trans people are not sourced here. There is no inventory item on whether Colombia maintains trans-specific hate-crime aggravation in the criminal code, and none on access to gender-affirming care, insurance coverage, or waiting lists.

Facilities, such as access to gendered bathrooms, changing rooms and shelters on the basis of identity documents, are not covered by the inventory, and neither are detention conditions beyond the single court ruling on trans detainees, which is reported without its case number, date or court name.

Whether the notary-based ID change procedure operates consistently across the national territory is unresolved; the sources describe the rule change and its rationale but contain no implementation data.

Colombia's situation is distinctive for how much of the protection it extends comes from the judiciary and transitional justice rather than from the statute book alone. The 2015 notary-based marker change, the 1993 Constitutional Court recognition doctrine, and the 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment are all products of courts and peace-process bodies, and the Attorney General's Office is the institution recording LGBTI homicides while the courts recognise gender persecution.

Colombia's decades-long armed conflict is the structural context for the most severe documented risks. Kill-lists and "social cleansing" campaigns are attributed to armed groups, not to private individuals acting alone, and they intersect with the country's history of persecution of people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities in the context of conflict.

Within Latin America the country pairs one of the region's broadest document and family-law regimes with homicide figures of a scale that most other regional jurisdictions with comparable legal recognition do not report.

International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): strong legal protections - 1999 constitutional-court rulings restricting nonconsensual intersex surgeries; same-sex marriage since 2011 (refusals illegal since 2016); adoption since 2015; simplified legal gender recognition since 2015; a third legal gender classification for nonbinary people recognised March 2022; 2025 court order against a volleyball-league regulator for discrimination.

Legal news outlet (May 2025): a UN independent expert, concluding a fact-finding visit across this country, praised legal reforms but warned of a stark gap between institutional progress and lived reality - discrimination and violence persist, particularly against trans women and those facing intersecting marginalisation (migrants, indigenous people, youth, persons with disabilities).
Regional legal-news outlet: a court in this country protected the rights of a trans woman deprived of liberty - ruling on treatment of trans detainees.

Foreign news agency (Nov 2025): the national civil-registry authority announced that citizens will be able to record 'trans' and 'non-binary' in the sex field of identity documents - 'a key step' for recognising gender-diverse identification.

Foreign business daily (June 2015): this country allowed trans people to change name and sex on ID cards without physical or psychiatric examinations - a notarised declaration replaces the previous 'cumbersome' process that involved judges ordering bodily inspections; the justice minister approved the decree.
COL.blindLocalsOnly:
Trans residents change the sex marker on national identification documents by signing a document before a notary, without physical examinations or psychiatric assessments. The notary procedure replaced a judicial route under which judges ordered invasive examinations.

Legal gender recognition rests on self-recognition under Constitutional Court jurisprudence dating from 1993, with no surgical requirement. Identification documents carry "trans" and "non-binary" markers from November 2025. a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025, so some trans-specific entitlements still depend on court rulings rather than on a consolidated statute.

Same-sex marriage has been available since 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015.

a court has ruled on the treatment of trans women deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees and addressing how the prison system must handle trans prisoners.

Residents of armed-group-controlled state/province, including in one inland department and one coastal department, report flyer campaigns listing named LGBTQ people for violence, with trans women in those departments facing forced relocation and limited livelihood options beyond sex work. Trans women working in public-facing businesses have been driven out by armed men issuing death threats.

The Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging conflict-driven violence as gender persecution, which opens a formal channel for victims in the armed-conflict setting.
COL.blindTangential:
The state/province situation is distinctive for how much of the protection it extends comes from the judiciary and transitional justice rather than from the statute book alone. The 2015 notary-based marker change, the 1993 Constitutional Court recognition doctrine, and the 2023 Special Jurisdiction for Peace indictment are all products of courts and peace-process bodies, and the national top government lawyer's Office is the institution recording LGBTI homicides while the courts recognise gender persecution.

The national government has positioned itself as aligned with LGBTIQ+ equality, which is why the UN Independent Expert Reid found the reforms themselves credible even as he documented the violence. The political direction and the security outcome point in opposite directions, and the mismatch is documented by national and international human rights bodies rather than asserted by advocacy groups.

The state/province decades-long armed conflict is the structural context for the most severe documented risks. Kill-lists and "social cleansing" campaigns are attributed to armed groups, not to private individuals acting alone, and they intersect with the state/province history of persecution of people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities in the context of conflict.

Within the region the state/province pairs one of the broadest document and family-law regimes with homicide figures of a scale that most other regional jurisdictions with comparable legal recognition do not report.

NGA.name: Nigeria
NGA.summary:
Nigeria is among the most severe environments for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised nationally under the SSMPA (14 years, applies to all including tourists), and 12 northern states apply Sharia law with the death penalty for male same-sex conduct. A transgender TikToker known as "Abuja Area Mama" was found beaten and dead on a highway in Abuja; police misgendered her in death and, six months later, no one has been arrested. Police have beaten LGBTQ+ people for "looking gay" — the SSMPA has been described as a "weaponised" law — and dating-app "kito" gangs use Grindr to lure victims into assault and robbery. The UK Foreign Office has warned LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, and death-penalty risks.

A proposed cross-dressing ban (not yet passed) would criminalise gender expression in public. Trans identity is NOT explicitly criminalized nationally (the SSMPA targets same-sex conduct), and the violence concentrates against local communities rather than tourists. But the Sharia death penalty, the trans-specific killing with impunity, the police brutality, and the UK advisory make this an environment to avoid entirely.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through the country's only recorded trans-imprisonment case: Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman, pleaded guilty to four counts of Naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of a fine, and served the term in Kirikiri maximum-security prison, Lagos, released on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked 'which prison they will keep the crossdresser in', and the article does not record whether she was assigned to a male or female section — placement was discretionary — while an October 2024 investigative panel found the maximum-security placement itself unlawful for a first-time offender under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act. For a trans visitor, the SSMPA's 14-year exposure already applies to tourists; on top of that, detention would land in a prison system with a documented discretionary, unlawfully-assigned placement practice and no recorded housing standard for trans prisoners.
NGA.outOfScopeNotes:
Terrorism (Boko Haram in the northeast), kidnapping, and violent crime affect all travellers in many regions; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Prison axis: no Nigerian law, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) is documented in any source in this record; the Bobrisky biography does not record which section she was assigned to, the October 2024 panel finding concerns the lawfulness of a placement rather than a housing standard, and the Reuters report on the proposed cross-dressing ban could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 401), so that bill's status rests on its written summary.

sources.summary: BBC (Aug 2024): the beaten body of Abujan trans TikToker 'Abuja Area Mama', a 33-year-old transgender woman, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police said preliminary investigations showed 'a man fully dressed in female clothing' and the Abuja police chief ordered a 'thorough and discreet' investigation. For this record: a documented trans-specific killing with official misgendering of the victim.

The Dial (Feb 2025): six months after Abuja Area Mama's killing, no suspects had been charged despite the announced investigation; Nigeria has no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people and the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 reinforced colonial-era criminalisation. For this record: impunity is documented — police response to a trans victim's killing produced no arrests half a year on.

Sahara Reporters (Aug 2026), reporting the latest UK FCDO travel advice for Nigeria: LGBT+ travellers warned of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states. For this record: current (2026) official foreign-office warning aimed squarely at LGBT+ visitors.

TimesLIVE (Mar 2025): a 24-year-old man, Okafor, was stopped by Lagos police, struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and freed only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for 'looking gay'; the SSMPA is described by those affected as a 'weaponised' law creating a climate of hostility. For this record: police extortion and violence against perceived-gay people, with the specific bribe amount and injury.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Aug 2024), marking 10 years of the SSMPA: the 2014 law has fuelled violence, extortion and discrimination far beyond its scope, effectively sanctioning abuse; LGBTQ+ Nigerians report lost job prospects and attacks have increased since the law passed. For this record: a decade-outcome assessment of the national criminalisation law, not just its text.

Context/Thomson Reuters Foundation (Apr 2024): 'kito' gangs entrap LGBTQ+ Nigerians via Grindr and other apps — victims lured to meetings then beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing; community counters with exposure forums (one admin's alert page drawing 43,000 followers) and sting operations. For this record: documented app-based luring crime specifically targeting queer people, relevant to a visitor using dating apps.

UK Home Office CPIN on Nigeria (June 2025, updated April 2026): same-sex sex between men is criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment; Sharia law in all 12 northern states criminalises same-sex acts between men and women, with male sodomy carrying the death penalty under state Zina provisions. For this record: current official UK-government assessment of penalties, including the north/Sharia overlay.
Reuters (Sept 2022): transgender Nigerians report fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing.

HRW report (Oct 2016) 'Tell Me Where I Can Be Safe': the SSMPA reaches far beyond marriage — it bans cohabitation between same-sex partners, any 'public show of same sex amorous relationship', and gay organisations, with punishments of 10-14 years' prison; the report documents police torture and arbitrary arrests under it. For this record: the scope and severity of the national law visitors fall under.

KEN.name: Kenya
KEN.summary:
Kenya criminalises consensual sex between men under the colonial-era Penal Code, with imprisonment of up to 14 years, and the provision applies regardless of the nationality of those involved. There is no statute governing gender identity and no codified pathway for legal gender recognition, although intersex people are legally recognised as a third gender.

Police conduct is the most immediate risk for a trans visitor. Twenty-six trans and intersex interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi described routine detention on pretexts such as being drunk and disorderly, followed by on-the-spot extortion, including demands to "look for 5,000 shillings". Several of those interviewed use traditionally male names as pseudonyms to move through public space safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

Document access is obstructed in practice. Evidence placed before the High Court showed that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused corrections by civil registration offices, with some spending close to four years' wages on attempts that failed.

Violence against sexual and gender minorities is documented rather than alleged. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's Lives on the Line report, published in September 2025, covers October 2023 to September 2024, was built with more than 14 community organisations, and expressly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence.

The courts have moved in the opposite direction from the police. On 12 August 2025 the Eldoret High Court found that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender Kenyans and directed the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act; the petition was brought by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered gender determination while incarcerated. On 20 May 2026 the Milimani High Court in Nairobi, in a decision delivered by Justice Bahati Mwamuye in Petition 27 of 2020, ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition. The Mombasa Court of Appeal had held forced anal testing unconstitutional in 2018, with compensation awarded in 2024, and the Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration in 2023. A man was sentenced to 50 years' imprisonment in December 2024 for killing an LGBTQ activist.
KEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the Transgender Protection Rights Act directed by the Eldoret High Court on 12 August 2025 has been drafted, introduced or enacted is unresolved in the sources available here.

The operative remedy of the Milimani High Court decision of 20 May 2026 is not specified in the inventory: the sources confirm that the court ruled on the constitutional right to legal gender recognition but do not state what relief was granted or whether a statutory recognition process was ordered.

No sourced material in this inventory records prosecutions of the criminal provisions against foreign nationals or visitors, so the practical likelihood of charge rather than extortion cannot be assessed from these sources.

The outcome of the petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination is unresolved.

The US State Department human rights report used here covers the 2010 reporting year and describes conditions more than a decade old; it is retained only as evidence of the long-standing pattern of societal discrimination and of the registration status of LGBTQ organisations at that time.

The inventory does not state whether the 2019 High Court ruling in Petition 16/2019 has been appealed, varied or remains binding notwithstanding the Kenya Human Rights Commission's challenge to it.

sources.summary: UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity, Kenya (Feb 2025): same-sex consensual sex between men illegal with prison penalty; no laws on gender identity (no legal change pathway); intersex people legally recognised as third gender; LGBTI civil-society groups may operate but only in restrictive civic space.

CNN 'A Equals' interactive on trans and intersex Kenyans: 26 interviewees in Mombasa and Nairobi describe routine police harassment — detention on pretexts like 'drunk and disorderly', on-the-spot extortion ('look for 5,000 shillings...'), and using traditionally male names as pseudonyms to navigate society safely amid widespread anti-LGBTQ+ sentiment.

KHRC 'Lives on the Line' (Sep 2025): the first comprehensive documentation of human-rights violations against sexual and gender minorities in Kenya, covering Oct 2023–Sep 2024; explicitly challenges the 2019 High Court ruling (Petition 16/2019) that dismissed LGBTIQ+ violence claims for purported lack of evidence; built with 14+ community organisations.

KHRC press release: Eldoret High Court handed transgender Kenyans a historic victory on 12 Aug 2025, directing the state to enact a Transgender Protection Rights Act after finding prisons fail dignity and privacy protections — from a petition by a trans Kenyan subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and court-ordered 'gender determination' during incarceration.

GATE.ngo on Nairobi Milimani High Court decision delivered 20 May 2026 (Justice Bahati Mwamuye, Petition 27 of Jan 2020): follows evidence that 94% of trans and gender-diverse Kenyans were refused by civil registration offices, some spending nearly four years' wages on failed document corrections; Kenya has never had a codified legal framework for gender recognition.
Reuters (Dec 2024): a Kenyan man was sentenced to 50 years in jail for killing an LGBTQ activist.

OutRight International Kenya profile (updated 12 Mar 2026): a decade of court-driven progress — 2018 Mombasa Court of Appeal ruled forced anal testing unconstitutional (compensation awarded 2024); 2023 Supreme Court upheld freedom of association allowing LGBTQ organisation registration; petition filed against incitement to hatred and discrimination.

The Star (23 Sep 2025) on the KHRC 'Lives on the Line' report: purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision; quotes the finding that despite Constitution Article 28's dignity guarantee, the data 'paints a blunt picture' — active LGBTIQ+ organisations raise awareness and provide community spaces amid documented violence.

US State Department Human Rights Report for Kenya (2010 reporting year): LGBT advocacy organisations such as the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya (GALCK) were permitted to register and operate; societal discrimination based on sexual orientation was widespread, causing loss of employment and education; in Feb 2010 Mtwapa religious leaders demanded closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute.

KEN.tangentialFactors:
LGBTI civil-society groups may operate in Kenya, but only within a restrictive civic space, according to the UK Home Office country policy note of February 2025. The Kenya Human Rights Commission's data collection relied on purposive sampling of organisations active in advocacy, data and service provision, and those organisations continue to raise awareness and provide community spaces despite the documented violence.

Societal discrimination is long-standing and reaches beyond legal exposure. The US State Department human rights report for the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, and noted that in February 2010 religious leaders in Mtwapa demanded the closure of a KEMRI HIV research institute, a demand bearing on access to health services for men who have sex with men. The same report recorded that the Gay and Lesbian Coalition of Kenya was permitted to register and operate.

Kenya's trajectory over the past decade has been court-driven rather than legislative: judicial decisions have struck down forced anal testing and affirmed freedom of association, while the legislature has produced no framework for gender recognition. The Constitution's Article 27 and Article 28 guarantees of equality and dignity sit alongside a criminal statute that has not been repealed.
KEN.localsOnly:
Kenyan residents live under the same criminal provisions as visitors, and the absence of a codified legal framework for gender recognition applies to them directly: civil registration offices refuse marker corrections in the overwhelming majority of cases, and the courts have yet to see that practice translated into a statutory process.

The Eldoret High Court's 12 August 2025 judgment addresses conditions that fall on residents in state custody. The petition established that prisons fail dignity and privacy protections for transgender detainees, and that the petitioner had been subjected to nonconsensual medical procedures and a court-ordered gender determination during incarceration.

Community infrastructure exists and is documented. The Lives on the Line report was produced with more than 14 community organisations, and active LGBTIQ+ organisations provide both awareness work and physical community space. A petition against incitement to hatred and discrimination has been filed; its outcome is not recorded in the sources available here.

Intersex Kenyans hold a distinct legal position, recognised as a third gender, which does not extend to transgender or gender-diverse people seeking marker change.

Societal discrimination is long-standing and reaches beyond legal exposure. a national foreign ministry human rights report covering the 2010 reporting year recorded widespread discrimination based on sexual orientation causing loss of employment and education, and noted that in February 2010 religious leaders in one town demanded the closure of a national medical research institute's HIV research facility, a demand bearing on access to health services for men who have sex with men. The same report recorded that a national LGBTQ coalition was permitted to register and operate.

The state's trajectory over the past decade has been court-driven rather than legislative: judicial decisions have struck down forced anal testing and affirmed freedom of association, while the legislature has produced no framework for gender recognition. The constitutional guarantees of equality and dignity sit alongside a criminal statute that has not been repealed.

ROU.name: Romania
ROU.summary:
Romania is broadly workable with a conservative political climate and significant legal-protection gaps, but a landmark EU court ruling and active civil society provide some positive trajectory. The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that Romania must recognize gender-identity changes made in other EU member states (the Mirin case), and a Romanian court definitively confirmed this in March 2026. Bucharest Pride marked its 20th anniversary with tens of thousands of marchers.

However, domestic legal gender recognition is court-based, restrictive, and inconsistently implemented. The anti-discrimination law does not explicitly cover gender identity (it covers "sex" and "sexual orientation" only), and the hate-crime law's aggravating-circumstance provision has never been applied in SOGIESC cases. No same-sex marriage or civil unions are recognised (the Orthodox Church successfully opposed reform). Far-right influences rose during the 2024-2025 election cycle, with anti-LGBTI rhetoric "intensified and repeatedly instrumentalised for political mobilisation."

For a visitor: EU/Schengen, no trans-specific border friction, no criminalisation, bathrooms unrestricted. The ECJ ruling means EU-issued LGR documents must be recognised.
ROU.outOfScopeNotes: No trans-specific travel advisory; general urban crime is moderate.

sources.summary: Reuters (Oct 2024) reported the CJEU ruling that Romania infringed a transgender man's rights in the Mirzarafie-Ahi case, which concerns recognition of a UK gender recognition certificate in Romania.

ACCEPT Romania (31 Mar 2026): the Sector 6 Court of Bucharest ordered a new birth certificate for trans man Arian Mirzarafie-Ahi reflecting his UK-recognised identity, and the ruling became definitive after the Bucharest Tribunal rejected appeals filed by the Cluj civil-status directorates — building on the CJEU's 2024 ruling that member states must transcribe intra-EU legal gender recognition. Announced on Trans Day of Visibility; ACCEPT urges others who changed documents in another EU country to pursue transcription in Romania.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2026 (covering Jan–Dec 2025): anti-LGBTI rhetoric intensified during the 2025 presidential campaign — candidate Călin Georgescu declared himself 'against LGBTQ' in February and PM Ciolacu mocked gender-marker changes; the National Audiovisual Council issued a public warning to B1 TV in August over anti-Pride 'provocation' framing after an ACCEPT complaint; a Ploiești deputy mayor of AUR made further derogatory announcements.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023): the CNCD investigated printing houses that refused to print LGBT and gender-equality materials; the IPSOS PRIDE 2023 survey found 51% of Romanians agree same-sex families should enjoy legal recognition; March 2024 education-law drafts carried anti-discrimination provisions that drew 13 religious groups' protests and a 50+ organisation counter-response.

Outright International Romania overview (updated 12 Mar 2026): same-sex relations legal nationwide; GO 137/2000 covers sex and sexual orientation but institutional follow-through is limited; no marriage or civil unions (the 2018 constitution-ban referendum failed on low turnout; the Orthodox Church has opposed a civil-partnership bill since 2017); legal gender recognition possible; LGBTI organisations can register.

Council of Europe thematic review (Jan 2023): 'Hate Crimes and Other Hate Motivated Incidents Against LGBTI People in Romania' - national report on implementation of Recommendation CM/Rec(2010)5, covering legal/policy frameworks, applicable ECtHR case-law and international standards.

ILGA-Europe and partners' submission to the EU 2025 Rule of Law Report (2025), with ACCEPT Romania authoring the Romania chapter (p.29): of nine country submissions, eight reported smear campaigns, disinformation and hate speech against LGBTI people — the surge in anti-LGBTI narratives during the Romanian election period is cited as the clearest example of rights-impacting rule-of-law erosion.
AP (Jun 2025): 'Bucharest gay pride march turns 20 as LGBTQ+ Romanians face growing hostility' — tens of thousands march on the 20th anniversary amid rising right-wing hostility.

ROU.localsOnly: The court-based domestic LGR regime and its inconsistent implementation are resident-facing; the ECJ Mirin ruling directly benefits EU-recognised trans visitors' documents.

BGD.name: Bangladesh
BGD.summary:
Bangladesh is a high-risk destination for trans visitors. The protests that ousted Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina in August 2024, known as the Monsoon Revolution, mark the inflection point: hardline conservative Islamist groups gained ground afterwards, and trans people who were previously visible now live in hiding. A Washington Blade assessment of 5 August 2025, one year after the ouster, found Bangladesh's LGBTQ community increasingly vulnerable to violence amid Islamist mobilisation and threats.

The current national incident baseline is set by the advocacy group JMBF, whose annual report published in April 2026 documents 260 human-rights violations affecting at least 426 LGBTQI+ individuals across the country in 2025. JMBF describes this as a sharp increase continuing an upward trend recorded since 2022, and the violations include murder and attempted murder, assault, abduction, arbitrary arrest, fabricated charges and extortion.

Lethal violence against visible trans people is ongoing. Shila, a prominent trans advocate originally from Chattogram district and widely known for humanitarian work, was murdered in her home in Betbunia, Rangamati district on 3 February 2025. Five unidentified individuals were accused in the case.

Police extortion is a routine hazard for visibly trans people. After hijra refused to pay extortion money on 10 September 2025, at least twelve were injured in a retaliatory attack at Gomdondi Phultala. On 17 September 2025 police arrested twelve hijras in Narayanganj while they collected money from vehicles carrying expatriates, a traditional livelihood. In April 2024, five transgender and hijra women were arrested while begging near Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka and sentenced to about a month in custody, which places the country's main transit hub among the documented policing hotspots.

Legal exposure is governed by an ambiguous framework. The Penal Code 1860 criminalises intercourse against the order of nature with a penalty of up to life imprisonment; Outright International reports that the provision is rarely enforced as a prosecution but is used by police to harass people presumed to be LGBTIQ. The UK Home Office country policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity (September 2023, updated April 2026) states that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within Section 377. A UK Upper Tribunal decision of February 2019 (PA/07096/2017) reproduces Home Office country material recording Islamist groups calling for the prosecution of LGBT people under Section 377 and Sharia, threats against LGBT journalists, and a government that does not recognise LGBT issues.

Bangladesh has officially recognised third-gender identity since 2013, but that formal recognition has not prevented the rollback of safety in practice since 2024.
BGD.outOfScopeNotes:
The scope of Section 377 as applied to lesbianism is unresolved in the sources. The UK Home Office country policy note records that it remains unclear whether lesbianism falls within the provision, while ILGA's 2019 State-Sponsored Homophobia report read female-female activity as not criminal and elsewhere described the provision as relevant to all genders. No source in the inventory settles the question.

Whether the murder of Shila on 3 February 2025 was motivated by her trans advocacy is not established in the available material; five unidentified individuals stand accused and the sources do not record a motive or a conviction.

No source in the inventory addresses entry and visa screening of trans visitors, acceptance of passports with altered gender markers at Bangladeshi ports of entry, or access to gender-affirming care while visiting. Those points are not sourced here and should not be read as either permitted or prohibited on the basis of this record.

The 260 incidents and 426 affected individuals for 2025 are JMBF tallies rather than government figures, and no official Bangladeshi crime statistic for anti-trans offences appears in the inventory for comparison.

VNM.name: Vietnam
VNM.summary:
Vietnam is broadly workable — described as one of the most tolerant countries in the region toward sexual minorities. Same-sex conduct is not criminalised, and the 2015 Civil Code (Article 37) was a landmark recognising transgender people's right to change their legal gender. However, the implementing Gender Affirmation Law has been stalled for over eight years — the right exists on paper but not in practice. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

No trans-specific killing has been documented here. Conversion efforts (SOGICE) are documented, and healthcare discrimination is a significant barrier — trans people face stigma and "red tape" in accessing care, and trans-competent providers are scarce.

For a visitor: no trans-specific border friction, unrestricted bathroom access, and no criminalisation — but the stalled recognition means no practical gender-marker change on documents. This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies. If a visitor is detained, the documented custody picture is structural and thin: as of a January 2015 reform proposal — never enacted — the prison system had no housing wing matched to gender identity, so transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, and no enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.
VNM.outOfScopeNotes:
Political controls of one ruling party, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon or monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the stalled recognition law on border document checks is not documented in the sources.

Prison axis: the placement finding (solitary confinement or general population only, no identity-matched wing) dates from January 2015 and comes from a never-enacted reform proposal; two search rounds found no enacted outcome and no newer documented placement practice, so today's practice is unknown — and that unknown cannot be read as a protected standard in a state with no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.

sources.summary: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

Lighthouse Vietnam study (Oct 2024): 'Exploring the lived experiences of conversion efforts (SOGICE) among LGBTIQ people in Vietnam' - documents experiences and forms of SOGICE in the Vietnamese context, with comprehensive data needs analysis.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House 3 Mar 2021); multi-source treatment briefing covering society/authorities in Hanoi and HCMC across education, employment, housing, health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

sources.title: Social News 16/1 — Separate jails proposed for transgender, gay prisoners
sources.summary: VietnamNet (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by the Social, Economic and Environmental Institute to Vietnam's Ministry of Public Security to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general prison population, to protect them from sexual harassment. The institute cited US California statistics that 67% of homosexual and transgender prisoners had suffered sexual harassment, and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. It stated that under Vietnam's then-current prison infrastructure transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, meaning no housing wing matched to a prisoner's gender identity existed, and asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome has been documented.

The placement finding concerns resident prisoners: in 2015 the only housing options documented for transgender prisoners were solitary confinement or the general population, because no wing matched their gender identity, and a 2014 survey found most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — resident-facing conditions a visitor meets only through arrest and detention.

This country is under one-party authoritarian rule, where an international human-rights organisation finds that "rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice"; a UN development agency is actively engaged on trans-rights strategies. If a visitor is detained, the documented custody picture is structural and thin: as of a January 2015 reform proposal — never enacted — the prison system had no housing wing matched to gender identity, so transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population, and no enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.
VNM.blindOutOfScope:
Political controls of one ruling party, arbitrary detention of dissidents, and typhoon or monsoon risks affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: the practical effect of the stalled recognition law on border document checks is not documented in the sources.

Prison axis: the placement finding (solitary confinement or general population only, no identity-matched wing) dates from January 2015 and comes from a never-enacted reform proposal; two search rounds found no enacted outcome and no newer documented placement practice, so today's practice is unknown — and that unknown cannot be read as a protected standard in a country with no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity.
blindSourceSummaries: A foreign public broadcaster (late Sep/Oct 2025): the largest city abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — a regional human-rights official called it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against the country's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

An international LGBTIQ organisation's country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; the health ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

An international human-rights organisation's 2025 country report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague penal-code provisions used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; the country re-elected to a UN human-rights body until 2028.

A research-institute study (Oct 2024): exploration of the lived experiences of conversion efforts among LGBTIQ people — documents the experiences and forms of such efforts and includes a comprehensive data-needs analysis.

A UN country-team feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially for trans women in outlying provinces and ethnic minorities; framed as a case for accessible legal recognition.

A local news site (Jun 2023): a Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans residents describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

A foreign refugee-board information request (30 Jun 2022): no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds; a multi-source treatment briefing covering society and authorities in the largest cities across education, employment, housing and health care.

Government media (Nov 2018): the national assembly was expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per a rights organisation (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

A local news site (16 Jan 2015) reports a proposal by a research institute to the public-security ministry to house homosexual and transgender prisoners in jails separate from the general population to protect them from sexual harassment; the institute cited subnational statistics from another country that 67% of such prisoners had suffered sexual harassment and a 2014 survey finding that most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails. Under then-current prison infrastructure, transgender prisoners could only be held in solitary confinement or mixed with the general population — no housing wing matched to the prisoner's gender identity existed — and the institute asked that prisoners be allowed to determine their own gender identity. No enacted outcome or newer documented placement practice was found in two search rounds.

The placement finding concerns resident prisoners: in 2015 the only housing options documented for transgender prisoners were solitary confinement or the general population, because no wing matched their gender identity, and a 2014 survey found most transgender prisoners wanted separate jails — resident-facing conditions a visitor meets only through arrest and detention.
VNM.tangentialFactors:
No trans-specific killing has been documented here, in contrast to several neighbouring countries. The September 2025 cancellations of the flagship Pride march and other LGBTQ events in the largest city — a national-level policy signal that may colour a visit — are adjacent climate rather than a direct travel restriction.

UGA.name: Uganda
UGA.summary:
Uganda is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act imposes life imprisonment for same-sex conduct and the death penalty for "aggravated homosexuality," and the US State Department explicitly warns that "the law applies to both visitors and residents." Over 1,000 rights violations (arrests, torture, evictions) were documented in nine months. Mobs have gathered outside trans people's homes (one woman described being grabbed and shouted at that she needed to die); police use digital entrapment (obtaining evidence via dating apps); and the government has "spread misinformation and hatred against LGBT people." The law also criminalises the "promotion of homosexuality," meaning any advocacy or support is banned.

There are no laws regulating gender identity — the AHA targets same-sex conduct and promotion, not trans identity per se — but trans people are swept up in the broader anti-LGBT crackdown, mobs, and state violence. The Constitutional Court upheld the AHA in April 2024 (striking down only a few provisions on healthcare access and renting).

Uganda's death penalty is for "aggravated" same-sex (not all same-sex like Iran; not gender expression per se like Saudi), and no trans-specific visitor killing or border-targeting is documented — but the systematic state-led crackdown makes this a environment to avoid entirely.
UGA.outOfScopeNotes: Terrorism (ADF in border areas), violent crime (armed robbery, sexual assault), and civil unrest affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch report 'They're Putting Our Lives at Risk' (26 May 2025): Uganda's 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act — death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', lengthy prison terms for 'promotion of homosexuality' — unleashed arrests, shelter raids, evictions and public outings; many LGBT people in hiding, with a small group of Ugandan mothers speaking publicly for their LGBT children.

Human Rights Watch (4 Apr 2024): Uganda's Constitutional Court upheld the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act's core provisions — including the death penalty in certain circumstances and penalties up to 20 years — rejecting public-participation challenges; contrasted with the same court voiding a similar 2013 law on procedure.
Reuters (June 2024): rights violations against Uganda's LGBTQ community are escalating, according to a pressure group.

The Guardian (7 Jan 2024): fear across Kampala after the anti-gay laws — a transgender woman mobbed and beaten into a two-week coma after a false TikTok allegation, sheltering with 20 others at a Kampala safe house; notes the death penalty for 'aggravated homosexuality', international condemnation, and continued political support for the law in parts of Africa.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying US State Department travel advisory for Uganda includes LGBT-specific warnings under the 'Do Not Travel' advisory.

Access Now (15 May 2025): Uganda's anti-LGBTQ+ laws are used to entrap people online — digital entrapment is one of the main tactics authorities use against LGBTQ+ people via apps, while the companies behind popular apps do too little; shares 2025 case research and safety recommendations — directly relevant to visitor device/app risk under the AHA.

Amnesty International (23 Oct 2024) report 'Everybody Here Is Having Two Lives or Names': the devastating impact of criminalisation on digital spaces for LGBTQ people in Uganda — widespread technology-facilitated gender-based violence (doxxing, impersonation, hacking, disinformation); the AHA 2023 fostered a climate of impunity forcing people and organisations to alter how they present themselves online.

AP (Feb 2026): 'Ugandan police arrest two women for allegedly kissing in public' — two women detained in Arua after neighbours reported them; one of the first known arrests under the 2023 Anti-Homosexuality Act.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Uganda: the three most important problems included 'violence and discrimination against marginalized groups (women...; children...; persons with disabilities; and the lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender community)' - the era of the Anti-Homosexuality Bill debates.

UGA.tangentialFactors: The AHA's life imprisonment and "aggravated homosexuality" death penalty apply to visitors — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; dating-app entrapment is a direct app-user risk.

EGY.name: Egypt
EGY.summary:
Egypt presents a direct and documented entry risk to trans visitors. The Ministry of Interior holds broad powers under the immigration law to refuse entry to, or deport, anyone whose presence is said to disturb public order and morality, and those powers have been applied to travellers perceived as queer. The Cairo 52 study "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" (27 November 2023) analyses that law and the case law built on it alongside 12 documented incidents between 2018 and 2022. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights separately records the deportation of foreign nationals suspected of being gay or trans even where no charge is ever upheld. Removal therefore does not require any offence under Egyptian law.

Same-sex conduct is not expressly written into the penal statutes, but prosecutions are a routine outcome rather than a theoretical one. Economic Courts have moved from de facto to explicit criminalisation by reading Penal Code provisions together with Article 9(C) of the Anti-Sex Work Law 10/1961, and Court of Cassation interpretations dating from the 1970s had already stripped out the requirement of a financial exchange, so habitual conduct or multiple partners is enough to sustain a charge. The cybercrime legislation adds six months' imprisonment and a fine for content held to violate "social and family values". The penalties that follow arrest are custodial.

Arrests are manufactured by police work rather than generated by complaints. The BBC investigation into how Egyptian police hunt LGBT people on dating apps describes officers running entrapment operations online, with victims recounting blackmail and detention, and the EIPR documentation identifies fake accounts used to draw in individuals, transgender women especially, on LGBTQ dating apps and websites. A visitor using those same apps is exposed to the same tactic. People taken into custody are subjected to coerced anal examinations, recorded by Bedayaa and by Human Rights Watch in its reporting on the Queen Boat-era crackdown, and the EIPR material notes violations continuing inside police stations after arrest.

Document handling at the border and in administrative dealings is tightening. A Ministry of Interior directive issued to civil-registry heads nationwide in December 2024 closes the Civil Status Law 143/1994 loophole that had allowed transgender people to correct their gender markers through governorate committees, which means corrected documents are increasingly difficult to obtain and mismatches between presentation and papers are more likely to be flagged.

Healthcare carries the same exposure. TIMEP's submission for Egypt's fourth Universal Periodic Review cycle (6 January 2025) finds discriminatory laws, policies and practices that violate the right to health for transgender and intersex people, pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in health services, and barriers to equitable care that persist since the preceding cycle. Egypt rejected all UN recommendations on sexual orientation and gender identity at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review.
EGY.outOfScopeNotes:
This inventory contains no source addressing restroom or facility access, nor any source describing how consular or border officers treat identity documents during routine screening; those questions remain unresolved here rather than answered negatively.

The 12 incidents analysed in "Your Kind Is Not Welcome Here" are reported as a set without individual outcomes, so the length of detentions and the number of deportations actually carried out are not established. The app-entrapment cases in the BBC reporting are anonymised at the victims' request, which leaves convictions and sentences unverifiable from this material.

The Ministry of Interior directive closing the gender-marker loophole is reported through civil-society documentation; whether a formal instrument has been published, and its exact text, is not confirmed in this inventory. The specific UN recommendations Egypt rejected at its 2025 Universal Periodic Review are cited in summary form here without the underlying session record.

Barriers to equitable health services persist since the last UPR, with pervasive gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare.

Human Rights Watch, 'In a Time of Torture: The Assault on Justice in Egypt's Crackdown on Homosexual Conduct' (29 Feb 2004): documents the Queen Boat-era crackdown, including arbitrary arrests, dark cells and beatings over sexual orientation, with testimony from defendants.

EGY.tangentialFactors:
The enforcement pattern has a long documented history. Human Rights Watch's report In a Time of Torture (29 February 2004) set out arbitrary arrests, beatings and confinement in dark cells on suspicion of homosexual conduct during the Queen Boat-era crackdown, with testimony from defendants, and the EIPR material on continuing violations inside police stations shows the same treatment logic still present two decades later.

Outright's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, states the gap plainly: homosexuality is not explicitly criminalised, yet vague public-morality and debauchery provisions are used to secure prison sentences. Bedayaa's February 2023 briefing adds that authorities turn a blind eye to harassment while arresting the people being harassed, and that Egypt maintains no anti-discrimination policy or law covering sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or sex characteristics. The absence of any such statute removes the principal route to redress for a visitor who is stopped, searched or detained.

Residents face the same health system described in TIMEP's January 2025 UPR submission: discriminatory laws, policies and practices, and widespread gender-identity and sexual-orientation discrimination in healthcare that leaves transgender and intersex Egyptians without equitable access. Bedayaa's briefing documents rising arrests of homosexual and transgender people, deteriorating detention conditions, and the complete absence of anti-discrimination law or policy at national level.
