PER.name: Peru
PER.summary:
Peru is a country that demands real caution for trans visitors, with a nationally-legislated bathroom ban and documented police violence, but no criminalisation of trans identity. The national legislature approved (February–April 2025) a bathroom ban prohibiting trans people from using public bathrooms matching their gender — a nationally-legislated restriction comparable to bans passed in other countries. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed — trans women most affected. In one documented case, three police officers were sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of a trans woman (December 2025), an unprecedented conviction. An official decree briefly classified trans identity as a "mental disorder" (May 2024) before being walked back after mass protests.

For a visitor: no border friction or criminalisation, but the bathroom ban creates daily legal exposure whenever public facilities are used. Same-sex or partner recognition does not exist, so marriage-based protections cannot be assumed.
PER.outOfScopeNotes:
General crime (theft, robbery) and political instability affect all travellers; the score reflects trans-specific risk only.

Unresolved: how the bathroom ban is enforced in practice at public facilities and how it applies to visitors is not documented in the sources.

sources.summary: Infobae Peru (20 Feb 2025): Congress's committee approved unanimously (for plenary) the dictamen of bills 6506 and 8457 (presented by Jorge Montoya and Honor y Democracia party) that threatens trans people's rights by restricting their use of public bathrooms; the article also records community demands — HIV medication supply, scrapping outdated medical rules, recognition of diverse families, equal marriage, and LGBTIQ+ quotas in public office.

IDEHPUCP (PUCP human-rights institute) analysis: the bathroom-restriction article openly discriminates against trans and non-binary people by barring access to facilities matching their gender identity, implicitly framing trans people as harassment risks — the institute cites IACtHR Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and states must guarantee trans people's full rights; also quotes congressman Lizarzaburu's dehumanising comparisons.

Agencia Presentes (22 Jul 2024): report finds hate crimes rose in Peru with trans women most affected; co-author Gianna Camacho (trans human-rights defender/journalist) stresses recorded numbers are only a sub-registry; cites the 2012 Universidad Peruana Cayetano Heredia study that 70% of trans women in Lima and Callao work in sex work.

BBC News Mundo (19 Dec 2025): three police officers sentenced to 17 years in prison for torture and sexual abuse of Azul Rojas Marín, trans woman and LGBTI activist — Peru's first conviction in a sexual-discrimination-motivated case and, per the article, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history (case reached the Court via the CIDH).

Infobae Peru (15 Dec 2025): officers Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León sentenced to 17 years for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas, nearly 20 years after the attack. The judgment was issued after years of litigation.

HRW (19 May 2025): the April-2025 'Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents' mandates public-restroom entry be restricted by 'biological sex', barring trans people — including trans youth — from facilities matching their identity; vague child-protection articles (art.4 media/advertising ban, art.5) enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational content; obscenity-minimum sentence raised 3→4 years; HRW says child protection is a pretext for repression and trans scapegoating.

HRW dispatch (27 Jun 2024): Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as 'a step toward dignity' for trans patients in healthcare settings.

Outright International current Peru overview: public institutions themselves contribute to anti-LGBTIQ discrimination; July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional; April 2025's 'sexual integrity' law restricts restrooms by biological sex; April 2025 NGO foreign-funding law lets authorities revoke registrations on 'public order/security' grounds, risking weaponisation against queer organising; Pride marches held annually since 2002 (oldest recorded 1984).

Peru Support Group (Apr 2025): Congress approved bills 6505/2023-CR and 8457/2023-CR (Muñante/Montoya), banning bathroom use contrary to birth sex and inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'. Willax TV's Ana María Salcedo publicly harassed the first openly-lesbian congresswoman, Susel Paredes ('go use the men's room'). Congressional pressure continues against therapeutic abortion at INMP.

URY.name: Uruguay
URY.summary:
Uruguay is one of Latin America's safest and most progressive destinations for trans visitors. The Comprehensive Law for Trans People (Law 19,684, 2018) provides legal gender recognition by administrative self-declaration (no surgery or diagnosis required), a reparation pension for trans victims of institutional violence, and a state employment quota for trans people. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2013 (Latin America's first), and bathroom access is legally protected.

The country is consistently ranked among Latin America's safest (Global Peace Index), with a "strong democratic governance structure and positive record of upholding political rights and civil liberties" (Freedom House). However, a 29-year-old trans woman, Joana, was shot dead in her home in Montevideo in July 2025 (the assailant was sentenced to 7 years), and discrimination incidents have been documented at a hospital (San Carlos) and a bank (BROU). Freedom House notes "disparities in treatment" for transgender people despite legal equality.

For a visitor: no border friction, bathrooms protected, no criminalisation, and Montevideo is welcoming. Even the custody consequence axis is comparatively benign: at a 2023 parliamentary hearing the National Rehabilitation Institute's director stated that a trans person entering the prison system has the right to decide whether to go to a men's or women's prison, trans women are currently placed in women's prisons, and a dedicated trans sector was planned for a new Montevideo prison — though he conceded the gap: "the laws are very advanced in Uruguay, but the mentality and infrastructure are not in line."
URY.outOfScopeNotes: General crime is very low; no trans-specific travel advisory. Prison axis: the dedicated trans sector and Punta de Rieles accommodation were commitments announced in July 2023 (commissioner's estimate: ready within two years); nothing in the current sources documents whether delivery has occurred, and no source records special-unit or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners beyond the planned sector.

QAT.name: Qatar
QAT.summary:
Qatar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely, with the most severe documented police practice in the Gulf — its region. An international human-rights organisation interviewed four transgender women arrested by the security department between 2019 and 2022 based solely on their gender expression in public places. One was arrested for wearing makeup — officers made her wipe it off, used the stained wipes as evidence, photographed her, and shaved her head. Another was beaten until her lips and nose bled. All described sexual harassment in custody, forced phone-unlocking to identify other LGBT people, and mandatory conversion-therapy sessions as a condition of release. Detention was in an underground prison in the capital, Doha; one woman spent two months in solitary confinement, and physical detransition (forced breast-tissue removal) was reported.

No statute has been repealed: trans people are arrested for "impersonating the opposite gender" and "violating public morality" under community-protection laws allowing up to 6 months' detention without charge or trial. Same-sex conduct is also criminalised, so a partner travelling with you carries the same exposure. Arrests continued even as this country hosted the 2022 World Cup — a major international sporting event — under international scrutiny.
QAT.outOfScopeNotes:
Migrant-worker abuses and the sponsorship labour system, and general human-rights concerns, affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: how trans visitors are treated at border entry and document checks is not documented in the sources; the documented detentions begin after entry, in public places.

The reported physical detransition rests on a single documented account and could not be independently verified from the current sources.

Wikipedia LGBTQ rights in Qatar: same-sex acts illegal (up to 3 years for Muslims and non-Muslims; Sharia allows a capital sentence never imposed); documented beatings/torture and forced 'conversion therapy' by police; cultural norms view homosexuality and cross-dressing harshly. Baseline legal-persecution picture.

QAT.comparisons: Unlike Kuwait (statute repealed, courts awarding compensation) or Bahrain (rare enforcement), Qatar's targeting of gender expression is systematic, current, and unreformed — placing it below both despite their shared Gulf context.

KWT.name: Kuwait
KWT.summary:
Kuwait criminalised "imitating the opposite sex in any way" in 2007, when the National Assembly added Article 199 bis to Penal Code Article 198, punishable by up to one year in prison or a fine of 1,000 dinars (about US$3,500). Human Rights Watch reported that the only known targets of the provision were transgender people, who could neither change their legal documents nor find protection from such policing. Within two weeks of the law taking effect, at least 14 people were arrested at checkpoints, coffee shops and taxis; three were beaten, one into unconsciousness, and heads were shaved as punishment. HRW's 2012 report "They Hunt Us Down for Fun" documented police violence against trans women under the provision.

The 2007 amendment was proposed by MP Waleed Al-Tabtabaei and passed with overwhelming parliamentary support. In February 2022 the Constitutional Court struck it down as unconstitutional, after an individual targeted by police brought the challenge; the ruling is recorded by both Human Rights Watch and the Library of Congress. HRW urged the National Assembly to repeal the statute outright, observing that the judgment removed criminal exposure without ending the underlying dress-code policing practice. A cisgender woman arrested over a short haircut was later awarded 4,000 dinars in compensation, with the Court of Cassation finding that police had detained her "without justification." Being visibly trans is no longer a crime in Kuwait, and Kuwait is the only Gulf state to have repealed its cross-dressing statute.

Criminal exposure elsewhere in the penal code is unchanged. Article 193 still punishes consensual sexual relations between men by up to seven years, and adultery by up to five years. There is no route to changing gender markers on legal documents, so a visitor whose papers do not match their presentation has no domestic remedy for the mismatch.

Discrimination did not end with the ruling. Writing a year after the Constitutional Court decision, DAWN MENA reported that transgender people continue to face social and employment discrimination in practice, and that the judgment was not a first step toward recognition of transgender rights.

Regional conditions shape the risk. Gender segregation and enforced dress codes make trans people especially vulnerable across the area, according to Brian Whitaker's 2016 overview. Human Rights Watch's 2018 study of LGBT activism across 22 jurisdictions in the region, based on interviews with 34 activists, found that six interviewees from Bahrain, Kuwait, Iraq, Oman, Syria and Morocco had relocated to Europe for security reasons tied to their identity or their activism.
KWT.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the National Assembly has since enacted a replacement or amending statute after the Constitutional Court struck Article 198 is not resolved by the sources held here; HRW's February 2022 appeal for outright parliamentary repeal is the last word available on the legislative track.

Enforcement data after February 2022 is thin. The inventory contains no post-ruling arrest figures, so the frequency of dress-code stops, raids, or administrative harassment of transgender people since the ruling is not sourced and should be treated as unknown rather than as absent.

How Article 193 is applied in practice to transgender people, as distinct from cisgender men who have sex with men, is not documented in these sources; the seven-year penalty is stated for consensual relations between men without further specification.

The compensation award to the cisgender woman detained over a short haircut is carried from the existing record; the case number and the date of the Court of Cassation judgment are not verified against a primary source in this inventory.

Censorship narrows access to information. The communications regulator CITRA blocked LGBTQI+ material, including advocacy content and legal information, according to the US State Department's 2023 country report; censors also banned the film "The Danish Girl" in Kuwait alongside other regional states. A visitor researching rights or support networks before or during travel may find those resources unreachable on local networks.

Political visibility is effectively absent. No candidate in the National Assembly election openly acknowledged an LGBTQI+ orientation, a finding from the same State Department report. The Cairo 52 Legal Research Institute's July 2024 analysis sets out the steps it considers still necessary after the abolition of the 2007 provision, indicating that the repeal settled the criminal-law question without delivering a wider framework of protection.

Kuwait's position relative to its neighbours is unusual rather than protective: it retains the region's general criminalisation of consensual same-sex relations while having removed the cross-dressing offence that its neighbours still hold on the books.

BHR.name: Bahrain
BHR.summary:
Bahrain decriminalised same-sex sexual activity in 1976, repealing a British colonial-era statute, and is the only Gulf state that does not explicitly penalise same-sex intimacy. No statute criminalises transgender expression. A foreign government's official guidance records that arrests for homosexual behaviour are relatively rare.

Decriminalisation has not removed exposure. Authorities continue to arrest gender and sexual minorities under broadly-phrased indecency and debauchery provisions, which carry imprisonment, fines and deportation. Nine cross-dressers were arrested at a hotel discotheque party in Manama on New Year's Eve and charged with public debauchery. In February 2024 the Council of Representatives adopted further moral legislation, extending the framework under which such charges are brought.

Legal gender recognition is refused by the courts. In a May 2023 judgment a Bahraini lower court rejected a trans man's application for legal gender recognition and for gender-affirming healthcare, citing Islamic Sharia, and declined his request for a Ministry of Health medical-committee examination. The same pattern appears in the treatment of identity documents: a foreign trans woman arrested on drug charges was tried "as a man" despite carrying a passport marked female, indicating that corrected documents may not be respected by the judicial system.

For a visitor, the practical exposure sits in the morality provisions rather than in a dedicated statute, and in a court that has shown it will disregard a foreign passport's gender marker. Arrest risk is documented but infrequently reported; the consequences of an arrest, including deportation and public charges of this kind, are severe.
BHR.outOfScopeNotes:
Two source baselines conflict on the fundamental question of legality. The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada record BHR105575.E (August 2016) reports that "according to sources, homosexuality is illegal in Bahrain," citing Canadian government material of 14 July 2016 and Gulf News of 5 February 2011, while the Wikipedia infobox sourced to ILGA, Outright International and the 2023 US State Department report the 1976 decriminalisation. This conflict is unresolved and is not settled by the sources in hand; the 1976 reading is the more consistently sourced of the two.

Sourcing for this jurisdiction is thin and partly remote. Bahrain has denied entry to or impeded independent human-rights researchers for roughly a decade, including bodies of the United Nations and Amnesty International, so local media frequently serve as the only source of documentation, and many findings rest on second-hand reporting.

The scale of active enforcement is not established. The available material gives individual arrests and a general foreign-government statement that arrests are relatively rare, but no arrest totals, conviction rates or sentencing data for gender-based charges.

No sourced information was found on prison conditions for trans detainees, on access to legal representation, or on whether any administrative appeal lies against the May 2023 gender-recognition refusal.

OMN.name: Oman
OMN.summary:
Oman is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — it combines an explicit anti-trans statute with a documented trans-traveller abuse case. The 2018 Penal Code criminalises "imitating the opposite sex" with up to 3 years' imprisonment, a provision that extends to foreign nationals. Enforcement is documented: in January 2018 the national police force announced arrests of transgender women after private-party photos circulated on social media; an international human-rights organisation documented further arrests and convictions under the provision.

Most concretely for travellers: in February 2024 a foreign non-binary traveller arriving at the capital's airport on a tourist visa was pulled aside while friends cleared immigration, taken to a private room, forced to remove their shirt, touched inappropriately, and denied entry to the country. They warned publicly: "if you identify as someone from the community, do not go to these countries."

Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the same code, so partner travel carries the same exposure; consensual same-sex activity risks prosecution for foreign nationals too. The consequence axis of an arrest is documented rather than hypothetical: in September 2018 a Salalah court sentenced two men to four years' imprisonment and a fine of OMR 3,000 each for cross-dressing and publishing the photos, and two further men to three years with the same fine for featuring in the video — the judicial outcome of the January 2018 police arrests under the Penal Code's Article 22, which penalises appearing in female clothing or demeanour. A gender-nonconforming visitor detected on arrival can therefore be jailed, and nothing in the sources records where inside the prison system such prisoners are held.
OMN.outOfScopeNotes:
Political restrictions and labour conditions affect all residents; the score reflects trans-specific risk to visitors only.

Unresolved: the airport account rests on a single traveller's first-hand account and could not be independently verified from the current sources, and whether the anti-trans statute has been applied at border entry for other travellers is not documented beyond that reported incident.

Prison axis: no Omani rule, practice or case is documented on where trans or gender-nonconforming prisoners are housed — nothing on birth-sex vs identity placement, no special units, and no solitary or segregation practice. That absence cannot be read as a protected standard in a state that criminalises cross-dressing and has jailed people for it.

BGR.name: Bulgaria
BGR.summary:
Bulgaria is an EU member state that imposes no traveler-facing restrictions on gender expression. There is no criminalisation of gender identity or presentation, no law governing which public facilities a person may use on the basis of gender, and no document, entry, or border screening that turns on a visitor's gender marker. Same-sex relations have been decriminalised since 1968. Entry and visa rules are applied to foreign passports on ordinary terms, and a foreign visitor's recorded gender raises no separate question at the border.

The statutory baseline offers a partial shield. Anti-discrimination legislation in force since 2004 prohibits both direct and indirect discrimination in housing, education and medical treatment, and a 2015 amendment extended coverage to 'sex' as including 'sex change'. A visitor refused a room, a treatment or a service on that ground therefore has a named statutory ground to invoke, though the practical value of that hook depends on institutions that have shown little appetite for pursuing bias cases.

Recognition of a visitor's own documents is where Bulgaria is under active legal pressure. In September 2025 the Court of Justice of the European Union heard the opinion of Advocate General Richard de la Tour, who concluded that EU law precludes national legislation of the kind Bulgaria maintains refusing identity documents that match a trans person's presented gender; the court indicated agreement with the Advocate General's reasoning. The Shipov case remains pending a full judgment, and EU free-movement law supplies a backstop for anyone holding documents issued or recognised in another member state.

The Strasbourg court has already ruled against Bulgaria on the same question. In Y.T. v Bulgaria (2020) the European Court of Human Rights found a violation of Article 8 over the refusal of legal gender recognition, and it made clear in December 2024 that those obligations were unaffected by the registry revision adopted that year, consistent with P.H. v Bulgaria. Judge Šimáčková dissented, judging the revision decision over-formalistic. The Bulgarian Supreme Court of Cassation nonetheless ruled in 2023 that legal gender recognition is impossible, treating gender as an unchangeable biological factor.

The social environment is markedly harsher than the travel rules. Parliament passed a law in August 2024 banning 'propaganda' of non-traditional sexual orientation in schools, on the model of Russian legislation. The EU Agency for Fundamental Rights survey records that 75% of LGBTIQ people in Bulgaria avoid holding hands in public and 46% avoid certain locations for fear of assault. Organised hostility to visible LGBT events is documented: in June 2017 Human Rights Watch reported that a group calling itself the National Resistance rallied counter-demonstrators to 'cleanse Sofia from garbage' ahead of the Sofia Pride march on 10 June, prompting the organisation to call on authorities to protect the march.

Public LGBT events are policed rather than prohibited. The fourth annual Sofia Pride parade in June 2011 passed without incident under heavy police guard, drawing only a protest from a 'Family NGO', after far-right extremists marred the 2008 and 2010 editions. Amnesty International's 2015 'Missing the point' review found that authorities consistently fail to identify and adequately investigate hate crimes: bias attacks spiked in 2013 according to the Bulgarian Helsinki Committee, legislation exists but such attacks go unpursued, and the Sofia Prosecution opened only some cases. SVK.name: Slovakia
SVK.summary:
Slovakia is workable for trans visitors. There are no traveller-facing restrictions: no bathroom law, no border issues under the free-movement rules of the regional union this country belongs to, and legal gender recognition has existed for over 40 years (though medicalised and historically requiring sterilisation). Police protect Pride events.

The climate is the concern. In October 2022 a radicalised teenager murdered two people outside an LGBT bar in the capital — classified as the country's first modern terrorist attack. The national authorities responded seriously (terrorism charges, official condemnation), but anti-LGBT political rhetoric intensified afterwards rather than receding. In July 2022 teenagers beat two men perceived as gay in the capital.

For a visitor: no legal exposure and functioning institutions, but a real threat of street hostility and a political trajectory moving against transgender recognition. The sources document no marriage or partner-recognition protections, so partner-based expectations should not be assumed.
SVK.outOfScopeNotes:

BLR.name: Belarus
BLR.summary:
Belarus presents an acute and documented risk to transgender visitors, and travel there should be avoided. In April 2024 the authorities widened the legal definition of pornography to cover depictions of same-sex relationships and of transgender people, grouping these alongside necrophilia and paedophilia as "non-traditional relationships". Production and distribution carry up to four years' imprisonment, rising to thirteen years for material involving children. Human Rights Watch described the change as an explicit attack on LGBT dignity, and it hands prosecutors a charge that can attach to a trans person's visibility rather than to any conduct.

Enforcement followed quickly. In September 2024 the organisation TG House Belarus recorded more than fifteen LGBTQ+ people detained within a single month, at least eight of them transgender; most were charged with hooliganism and two with pornography. Detainees reported physical and psychological abuse in custody, several were beaten and pressured into statements circulated on pro-government channels, and some left the country rather than face further proceedings. Reporting by the Associated Press documents police beating LGBTQ+ people during arrest, laying coerced charges against them, and an expanding campaign of "LGBT propaganda" repression.

Official hostility is carried through state media and policy as well as through the courts. State television has equated LGBTI identities with paedophilia and called them a weapon in the hands of the West, and TG House recorded a rise in hate speech across state propaganda during 2024. The Prosecutor General's Office has announced plans for an administrative-penalty law against "LGBTI propaganda", which had not been tabled as of the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, and a new National Security Concept places "traditional values" at the centre of state policy. At least ten transgender people left Belarus within a year because of discrimination and repression.

Protection machinery is effectively absent. Belarus has not reported hate-crime data to the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights since 2015 and maintains no National Point of Contact, so the only 2024 incident reporting comes from civil-society monitors such as Human Constanta. The constitutional guarantee of equality in Article 22 is unenforced in practice: analyses of the legal climate record clampdowns on civil society, harassment of activists, arbitrary detentions, and retention of the death penalty.
BLR.outOfScopeNotes:
No official hate-crime statistics exist for Belarus after 2015, so the scale of violence against transgender people cannot be verified from state sources; every incident count in the sources held here derives from civil-society monitors and carries the sampling limits of that reporting.

The administrative-penalty law on "LGBTI propaganda" announced by the Prosecutor General's Office had not been tabled at the time of the ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025, and its current legislative status is unresolved in the sources held.

The sources do not address legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, entry or visa screening, border or airport questioning, bathroom and facility rules, access to hormone therapy or other healthcare, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or recognition of partners and marriages. Whether a transgender visitor's documents are checked against gender presentation at the border is not established by anything in the inventory.

The 1999 US State Department report is a historical baseline and does not describe current conditions. The UN Treaty Body case digest cited here is a general compilation; the specific decisions it treats as relevant to Belarus are not identified in the sources held.

The planned administrative-penalty law on "LGBTI propaganda" remains untabled, but state television already frames LGBTI people as paedophiles and as a tool of foreign influence, and a local monitor recorded increased hate speech in state/province propaganda during 2024.

Community organising carries direct risk. The September 2024 detentions reached at least eight transgender people, several arrested for subscribing to resources designated extremist, with physical and psychological abuse reported in custody. At least ten trans people left the country in a year. Civil-society groups, including a monitoring group and the local LGBTQ+ organisation, remain the only source of incident data, because the state reports nothing to international hate-crime mechanisms.
BLR.tangentialFactors:
The climate is not new, only newly aimed. A 1999 US State Department human rights report on Belarus already documented the legal and social treatment of homosexuality under the Lukashenka government, and the report "Are all equal before the law?" sets the constitutional equality guarantee of Article 22 against arbitrary detentions, harassment of activists, a clampdown on civil society and a retained death penalty. The 2024 measures extend that machinery to transgender identity specifically.

International litigation channels exist on paper. A 2024 ILGA World compilation of United Nations Treaty Body decisions covers 25 cases touching criminalisation, asylum, violence, expression, families and legal gender recognition, and the toolkit flags jurisprudence relevant to Belarus. Whether those routes reach people inside the country is a separate question from the domestic enforcement picture.

UKR.name: Ukraine
UKR.summary:
Ukraine is workable for trans visitors — with the caveat that this scores trans-specific risk, not the general risks of an active war zone. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; legal gender recognition exists (medicalised — a "transsexualism" diagnosis and psychiatric observation under the 2016 protocol); civil society, including two support NGOs and other groups such as Gender Stream and Insight, operates openly, and the capital Kyiv hosted a three-day Trans Forum in June 2026 even during the war.

For a visitor: a foreign passport is not subject to conscription rules, so border crossing follows standard wartime entry rules, but wartime document checks can out people, and civil-society groups report that since martial law began, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border. There is no SOGI-specific hate-crime law, societal attitudes lag the regional average, and the healthcare system is war-disrupted (hormone shortages, diagnostic corruption reported). No marriage- or partner-travel-specific rule for visitors is documented.
UKR.outOfScopeNotes:
General war risks (missile strikes, infrastructure, mobilisation) apply to all travelers and are out of scope for the trans-specific score; trans residents' draft exposure is context, not the visitor score.

One cited news piece (June 2022) was not retrievable at research time. No source directly documents visitor border-screening practice for trans foreigners, and no marriage- or partner-travel-specific consequences for visitors are recorded.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch essay (15 May 2024) 'When Laws Fail to Protect Trans People': Ukraine-trans war-displacement case work — cross-border networks became critical support for trans women in Ukraine, arranging assessments, diagnoses and the often-humiliating Military Medical Commission confirmation; a Ukrainian activist notes commission hours (8am-8pm) and gatekeeping ('if a doctor says I'm a woman, the state can shrug').
France24 (June 2022) reports on Ukraine's trans community caught in the crosshairs of war.

ZMINA (28 Jul 2026): trans women in Ukraine now find it harder to obtain a diagnosis — stereotypes, corruption and wartime barriers; Trans Forum 2026 (Kyiv, early June 2026) discussed the new draft Civil Code's effect on transition procedure and whether being trans grounds exemption from mobilisation — visitor-relevant documentary friction for trans Ukrainians and those crossing borders.

Gender Stream (Ukrainian NGO): consultations and support — advises and accompanies LGBTQI+ people and families evacuating from frontline regions to western Ukraine/EU, and helps with processing/reissuing documents for transgender people, including those planning to legally cross the border; documents that since martial law, holders of male gender markers were stopped at the border by the State Border Guard Service.

MDA.name: Moldova
MDA.summary:
Moldova is workable for trans visitors — the best-protected in its immediate neighbourhood. Since 2022, anti-LGBT hate speech and hate crimes are criminal offences covering SOGI explicitly, and the equality law was amended in 2023 to cover sexual orientation and gender identity; the capital Chisinau's Pride marches through the city centre under police protection, and police have deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters seeking to disrupt it.

Counterweights for a visitor: no accessible legal gender recognition exists for anyone (a medicalised process exists on paper but is reported not functional in practice); the predominant Orthodox Church and major politicians (including the capital's mayor) regularly issue homophobic statements that colour the climate; and the breakaway separatist region of Transnistria, controlled by the neighbouring power Russia, has its own anti-LGBT “propaganda” law — travelers should treat that region as a separate, much riskier jurisdiction.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented through a single contested case: a transgender man (registered female at birth in 1972, documents changed to male in 2007) served his sentence at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, where he says he was held alone in unsanitary cells — three years fully isolated from other detainees per a 2025 corroboration — including long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit, supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12 (the ward for detainees requiring protection) was refused and no special-unit option existed. He described staff humiliation (forced strip body searches, demeaning roll-call name-calling, bathroom-door intrusion) and said only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The penitentiary administration contested the account, replying that he was held alone at his own written request, that no rights were violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. For a visitor, the practical lesson is that a detained trans person in Moldova's system faced solitary-style isolation presented as protection, a refused protection-ward transfer, no special-unit option, and an administration that denies mistreatment — in a country that is otherwise the safest in its neighbourhood.
MDA.outOfScopeNotes:
The breakaway region of Transnistria is scored as part of Moldova de jure, but travelers should treat it separately: foreign-controlled, anti-LGBT “propaganda” law, no consular access. General poverty and corruption affect all travelers. No source addresses border-screening or document-practice for trans visitors, and no visitor-specific incident record exists to independently verify the assessment.

Prison axis: the placement finding rests on a single detainee's account that the prison administration disputes (it says the isolation was at his own written request and no rights were violated), so the disputed details are unadjudicated; no codified Moldovan rule on trans-prisoner housing, trans special units, or solitary/segregation placement is documented, and whether his planned court and European Court of Human Rights claims were filed is unverified in these sources.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), Moldova: a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the Equality Council confirmed discrimination, recommending preventive measures; hate speech remained serious with no meaningful state response (echoed in the European Commission country report); election-period political hate speech rose.

Amnesty International Moldova 2025: discrimination against LGBTI people remained commonplace and freedom of expression and assembly was arbitrarily restricted (impunity for past violations); in Russian-occupied Transnistria new legislation prohibits promotion of "non-traditional sexual relations".

GENDERDOC-M report (2023) citing the Equality Council study "Prejudices and Marginalization in Moldova 2022" (published January 2023): acceptance of LGBT+ people is extremely low. 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% would not accept them as work colleagues (social-distance 5.7), and marginalisation of LGBT+ people increased in 2022.

Attitude (2 February 2026) revisits Moldova Pride 2024: participants of all ages and backgrounds joined the festivities, in a country described as "slowly emerging from its past to carve a new queer identity". Public Pride proceeds openly.

ECOM legislative analysis on SOGI and HIV in Moldova (Tallinn, 2024): identifies legal barriers affecting LGBT people and people living with HIV — access to justice, hate-crime and discrimination provisions — based on a survey of local partners, benchmarked against international standards.

PinkNews (19 May 2018): police deployed tear gas against anti-LGBT protesters trying to disrupt the annual Moldova Pride solidarity march in Chisinau (19 May) as marchers carried foam hearts; activists feared a repeat of earlier violent scenes.

PinkNews (1 March 2013): the Balti Court of Appeals ruled on 28 February that the northern city’s "gay propaganda" ban was unconstitutional and violated human rights — local church-led bans struck down after protests against the EU-backed anti-discrimination law.

sources.title: Trăind de gardă/ Deținut transgender – dublu condamnat în închisoare de către „oamenii cu epoleți”
sources.summary: Ziarul de Gardă (15 June 2024) documents the four-year detention of Igor Brumarețchi, a transgender man registered female at birth in 1972 whose documents were changed to male in 2007. He served his sentence in Moldova's penitentiary system, mostly at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, held alone in unsanitary, rat-infested cells for long periods in the disciplinary isolation unit ('izolator disciplinar'), supposedly for his own safety, while his request for sector 12, the unit for detainees requiring protection, was refused. He describes forced strip body searches, 'go to the gynaecologist' calls over the intercom, staff opening his bathroom door, and being called 'Natașa' at roll-call, and says only self-harm and hunger strikes got him heard. The National Penitentiary Administration (ANP) replied that he was detained alone 'at his own written request' with no rights violated, and that the discrimination claims were unconfirmed. Brumarețchi says he will sue in Moldovan courts and the ECtHR, and ZdG has notified the Ombudsman and GENDERDOC-M. The case amounts to de facto placement of a trans detainee by birth sex in the men's system, prolonged solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, and no special-unit option.

sources.title: Deținuți ai prejudecăților în instituțiile de stat. Persoane LGBT+, la un pas de suicid. Povestea tragică a unui locuitor al satului Dubna
sources.summary: Observatorul de Nord (7 April 2025) corroborates the same case: Igor Brumarețchi from Dubna village (Soroca district) spent three years locked alone in a cell at Penitentiary No. 6 in Soroca, fully isolated from other detainees and humiliated by prison staff on grounds of sexual orientation, which brought him to the edge of suicide. The piece states the authorities admit homophobia still persists in state institutions and say they are training staff and preparing stricter penalties for discrimination and harassment; the full investigation appeared on anticoruptie.md. Confirms the solitary-style isolation placement practice for a trans detainee in Moldovan prison No. 6 as of 2025.

MDA.localsOnly:
The non-functional legal-gender-recognition process is resident-facing.

Resident data: an equality-body study found acceptance of LGBT+ people extremely low — 79% would not accept LGBT+ neighbours, 60% not as work colleagues (social-distance score 5.7) — and marginalisation increased in 2022; in 2024 a trans woman was denied bank service over a document/appearance mismatch and the equality body confirmed discrimination.

The documented custody case is resident-facing: the detainee is a national held in the national penitentiary system at Soroca, and the solitary-style isolation, refused protection-ward placement, staff conduct and administration denial described in the two investigations all fall on residents in state custody — a visitor meets the practice only through arrest and detention.

LUX.name: Luxembourg
LUX.summary:
Luxembourg is among the strongest jurisdictions in its region for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition rests on self-determination: the Act of 10 August 2018 replaced the previous long and costly judicial procedure with a declaration-based route, and the process is administered through the official government portal (Guichet.lu) as an application to change gender status and first name(s) in the civil register. The reform was presented in May 2017 by Justice Minister Félix Braz and approved by the Chamber of Deputies in July 2018. The procedure is open to foreign nationals as well as citizens.

Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited across employment, goods and services, education and health, with the CET equality body handling complaints. A national LGBTI action plan has operated since 2018, and in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, which LGBTIQ+ organisations criticised for omitting depathologisation and other key elements.

The protection machinery has a documented gap on hate crime. As of June 2019 reporting, Luxembourg law contained no LGBTphobic aggravating circumstance for assaults, victims under-reported, and the justice minister signalled that the law would evolve following the 2017 intervention by a Council of Europe monitoring body.

Entry raises no trans-specific issue: travel falls under the common border-free travel zone, and there are no bathroom or facilities laws targeting trans people. No pattern of anti-trans violence against visitors is documented in the sources.

Detention is handled protectively. Prison authorities place detainees who disclose or openly show an LGBT or trans identity so that they are shielded from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans situations assessed case by case on the information available; such placements are described as exceptional, requests by LGBT detainees to be moved to an ordinary section are generally granted, and no codified birth-sex rule or special custody unit applies.

Standing gaps are narrow but real: no nonbinary marker is available, gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly named in anti-discrimination law, and no measures exist on conversion practices or intersex interventions. None of these gaps has a documented visitor-specific impact in the sources.
LUX.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the aggravating-circumstances reform signalled by the justice minister in June 2019 has since been enacted is not confirmed by any source in the inventory.

Unresolved: the content, funding and implementation status of the July 2025 LGBTIQ+ Action Plan beyond its unveiling and the criticism it received are not sourced here.

Not sourced: no trans-specific violence statistics, conviction rates for LGBTphobic assaults, or visitor-incident data for Luxembourg appear in the inventory, so the absence of a documented violence pattern rests on the absence of reporting rather than on recorded low incidence.

Not sourced: the inventory does not state whether gender expression or sex characteristics are covered indirectly through other legal instruments, only that they are not explicitly named in the anti-discrimination framework.

Not sourced: the specific rankings or scores assigned to Luxembourg by either travel index are not reproduced in the inventory.

sources.summary: Official Luxembourg government portal (Guichet.lu) page on applying to change one's gender status and first name(s) in the civil register - the administrative procedure for legal gender recognition.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): marriage and adoption; self-determination-based gender markers (no nonbinary markers); discrimination banned on sexual orientation and gender identity but not gender expression or sex characteristics; no measures on conversion practices or intersex interventions; in July 2025 the government unveiled a comprehensive LGBTIQ+ Action Plan, criticised by organisations for missing depathologisation and other key elements.

Centre LGBTIQ+ Cigale UPR submission (April 2023) for Luxembourg: describes the organisation's services and Luxembourg's equality laws (employment, goods and services, education, health), the CET equality body and the national LGBTI action plan.

Asher Fergusson's LGBTQ+ Travel Safety Index (updated June 2023) ranks countries on laws affecting LGBTQ+ traveller safety and includes a companion Global Transgender Rights Index; both indexes cover Luxembourg.

Le Quotidien (June 2019, in French): 'Agressions LGBTphobes: un durcissement des sanctions attendu' - Luxembourg law lacks LGBTphobic aggravating circumstances; victims under-report; the justice minister signalled the law would evolve after ECRI's 2017 intervention.

sources.title: Prisons luxembourgeoises : Les détenus gays et transgenres sont protégés
sources.summary: L'essentiel (26 August 2015), reporting Justice Minister Félix Braz's parliamentary answer to LSAP MP Cécile Hemmen, documents that Luxembourg prisons place inmates who disclose or openly show LGBT/trans identity so they are sheltered from reprisals, threats or attacks by other prisoners, with trans-detainee situations handled case by case (the administration gathers all available information on the prisoner); such cases are described as 'exceptional'. Requests by LGBT detainees to be placed in an ordinary section are generally granted, and the minister warned against solutions that would stigmatise or isolate these detainees. A 1989 grand-ducal regulation requires staff to address detainees by surname, and penitentiary staff honour a detainee's chosen 'Monsieur'/'Madame' form of address. The Justice Ministry kept no statistics on LGBT prisoners (disclosure cannot be compelled without illegal privacy interference), and the planned Uerschterhaff prison (Sanem) was designed with multiple sections so detainees could be separated by sex, personality, grounds of detention and, among these, sexual orientation. Outcome: placement follows disclosed identity/need on a case-by-case basis with no codified birth-sex rule and no documented special custody unit or solitary/administrative-segregation practice for trans prisoners in Luxembourg.

LUX.blindSummary:

Standing gaps are narrow but real: no nonbinary marker is available, gender expression and sex characteristics are not explicitly named in anti-discrimination law, and no measures exist on conversion practices or intersex interventions. None of these gaps has a documented visitor-specific impact in the sources.

AND.name: Andorra
AND.summary:
Andorra's legal framework for trans people rests on the 2022 Law of the Person and Family, which introduced legal gender recognition provisions alongside unified civil marriage. The Ministry of Equality obliges companies operating in the country to maintain protocols against sexual and gender-based harassment.

Andorran police recorded an average of two to three bias-motivated incidents each month during 2025, according to ILGA-Europe's most recent annual review. DiversAnd, the country's principal LGBTI organisation, flagged incidents around the June Pride celebrations of that year and reported them publicly.

No formal system exists to register and classify bias-motivated violence. DiversAnd has called for one so that such incidents can be recognised as hate crime, which indicates that the generic hate-crime provisions of the Penal Code are not routinely applied to bias against trans people.

Entry and movement carry no documented trans-specific obstacle. Andorra sits between Spain and France with open land borders, and it lies outside the Schengen area, where no document-gender checks are applied to arriving visitors. No facility or bathroom law restricts where trans visitors may use restrooms.

The media climate is not uniformly benign. A transphobic opinion piece published in El Periòdic d'Andorra on 27 September was pulled from the website with a public apology after DiversAnd requested its removal, although the article had already run in print.

Practical tolerance remains high in a small, tourism-dependent country with a conservative Catholic history, and the Ministry of Equality implemented equality measures during 2025.
AND.outOfScopeNotes:
GayLawNet's Andorra page carries a 'limited information' marking, and its index entries on civil unions, discrimination, hate crimes, marriage, sodomy and trans legal status have not been verified against the underlying statutes in this pass.

Whether the Ministry of Health adopted the gender-affirming protocols DiversAnd requested, and on what timeline, is unresolved in the available sources. The inventory records the request, not the outcome.

The procedure, documentary requirements and waiting periods for legal gender recognition under the 2022 Law of the Person and Family are not sourced here. The existence of recognition provisions is established; the process a visitor or resident would follow is not.

The two-to-three monthly figure is a police recording average for 2025. Its breakdown by type of bias, and in particular how much of it concerns gender identity rather than sexual orientation, is not sourced.

The relationship between the generic hate-crime provisions of the Penal Code and the absence of a bias-incident registration system is presented here as reported by DiversAnd; no court or prosecutorial data on how such cases are actually charged is available in the inventory.

PinkNews (Sep 12, 2023): Andorra's head of government Xavier Espot Zamora, in office since 2019, came out as gay publicly saying 'I never hid it' — a societal-climate signal for a country where he remains the serving prime minister.

A serving head of government who is open about being gay is a direct signal about the standing of the country's political climate, though it says less about trans-specific attitudes than about LGB ones.

The evidence base for any assessment is thin because the population is very small. Absolute incident counts are low in a way that reflects scale as much as safety, and monthly averages of two to three recorded incidents are the more informative figure for a country of this size.

MCO.name: Monaco
MCO.summary:
Monaco is workable for trans visitors — safe in practice, thin in law. Hate crimes and hate speech based on sexual orientation are penalised, and discrimination on grounds including gender identity is banned. A visitor faces no legal exposure whatsoever: no bathroom laws, no border friction (a tiny tourist enclave embedded in the neighbouring country of France, entry under the common border-free travel zone), no documented anti-trans incidents, and street violence of any kind is rare in this heavily-policed, very low-crime destination.

The score reflects the gap between de facto safety (very high) and legal thinness: no functioning legal gender recognition process and limited explicit trans protections.
MCO.outOfScopeNotes: Family-law gaps (no marriage equality, cohabitation contracts only) are resident-facing concerns kept out of the visitor score, per the record's existing split. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. One source notes reported discrimination is described as rare, but no independent verification of current practice exists in the record.

LIE.name: Liechtenstein
LIE.summary:
Liechtenstein is workable for trans visitors: safe in practice, thin in law. Same-sex relations are legal and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation is prohibited, but gender identity, gender expression and sex characteristics are absent from every anti-discrimination statute in force, and no procedure exists for changing a legal gender marker. Those gaps bind residents, employers and public bodies; a visitor entering for a short stay faces no legal exposure from them.

Entry falls under the common border-free travel zone operated with Switzerland and Austria, and no source reports friction at that border for trans travellers. There is no statute restricting access to sex-segregated facilities, and no documented pattern of anti-trans violence. The jurisdiction is very small, has very low crime, and is closely integrated with both neighbouring states.

Social attitudes are conservative without being mobilised against trans people. VAT.name: Vatican City
VAT.summary:
Vatican City is workable for trans visitors — an unusual case: a tiny 0.49 km² tourist enclave with essentially no resident jurisdiction a traveler can fall afoul of. Nothing about being trans is criminalised; there are no bathroom inspections, no morality police, and the guards and gendarmerie do not police tourist gender expression. Millions of tourists of every presentation visit annually without incident; entry is via the neighbouring city of Rome with no border formality.

The doctrinal climate is hostile — the 2024 declaration "Infinite Dignity" condemned gender-affirming surgery and "gender theory" as violations of human dignity, and no legal recognition or protection of any kind exists — but this is a climate signal, not a traveler-facing mechanism: the realistic worst case for a visitor is being refused entry to the basilica over a dress-code dispute (shoulders/knees rules apply to everyone).

The custody axis completes the picture: the state operates no prison system — only a few cells used for pre-trial detention — and persons sentenced to imprisonment by the state serve their time in Italian prisons with costs covered by the state, so there is no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case in this jurisdiction; any custodial consequence for a visitor would be served in another nation's prison system, outside this record's scope.
VAT.outOfScopeNotes:
Doctrinal positions are climate signals, not enforcement mechanisms; the nation's employment and canon-law matters are resident-facing and excluded from the visitor score. Very small population — the evidence base is thin, and this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty. No source addresses document checks or screening for visitors beyond the recorded absence of border formality, and marriage/partner-travel questions for visitors are undocumented.

Custody axis: no trans-specific prisoner-placement policy, trans custody facility, or documented trans-prisoner placement case exists because the state has no domestic prison system — the sole prison-axis source is a general encyclopedia article on crime in the state, used as a last resort because no dedicated custody source exists; how the Italian system treats anyone serving a prison sentence there is outside this record's scope.

CYP.name: Cyprus
CYP.summary:
Cyprus is a workable destination for trans visitors. There is no legal restriction on gender presentation, no facility or bathroom law of the kind enacted elsewhere in the region, and no border obstacle beyond the standard entry rules that apply to any European Union member state. Tourist infrastructure is Western-standard and accustomed to international visitors.

The statutory framework contains explicit gender-identity protections in criminal law. Law 87(I)/2015 makes public incitement to violence or hatred on grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity a criminal offence; the underlying penal code amendment dates from October 2013 and carries up to three years' imprisonment and/or a fine of €5,000. Law 31(I)/2017 provides that prejudice-based motivation is an aggravating factor in sentencing for hate crimes. Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices.

Legal gender recognition remains the principal gap. A self-determination bill was approved by the Council of Ministers in September 2022 and received its first parliamentary reading in November 2022; it was still pending as of 2024. Until it is enacted, change of registered sex is governed by the 2002 Civil Registry Law and requires surgery, an arrangement that binds residents rather than visitors.

Gender identity is not yet an explicit ground in the country's equal-treatment framework, and no national anti-homophobia action plan exists. The country's division is relevant to routing: the northern part of Cyprus operates under a de facto Turkish-controlled administration with its own, separate arrangements and a weaker protection framework, so the statutory guarantees described above should not be assumed to apply there.
CYP.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the legal gender recognition bill advanced beyond its first parliamentary reading after early 2024 is unresolved in the available inventory; the most recent sourced status is pending as of 2024.

The dating of the hate-speech offence is not fully consistent across sources: one account places the penal code amendment in October 2013, while the UPR material attributes the offence to Law 87(I)/2015. The penalty figures of up to three years' imprisonment and a €5,000 fine come from the 2013 account and are not independently corroborated here.

No enforcement record is sourced: conviction numbers under the incitement offence, or sentencing practice under the 2017 aggravating-factor provision, are not documented in the inventory.

The two European Commission Network of Legal Experts country reports are cited for scope only; their detailed findings on how gender-identity aspects of European Union directives are transposed were not extracted and remain unverified here.

Conditions facing trans people under the northern administration are described only in general terms; the inventory contains no legal analysis of that administration's framework beyond the existence of its own recognition process.

sources.summary: UPR-info Cyprus advocacy sheet (2024): Law 87(I)/2015 criminalises public incitement to violence/hatred on SOGI grounds; Law 31(I)/2017 makes prejudice motivation an aggravating sentencing factor; Law 39(I)/2023 bans and criminalises conversion practices; the legal gender recognition bill was approved by the Council of Ministers Sept 2022 with first parliamentary reading Nov 2022 (still pending at 2024); gender identity remains absent from equal-treatment grounds and no anti-homophobia action plan exists; prison guards received 2-day LGBTI+ training (Apr 2023) after anti-LGBTI harassment complaints to the Ombudswoman.

The European Commission Network of Legal Experts country report on gender equality in Cyprus (2024, reporting period 2023) sets out how EU equality rules are transposed into Cypriot national law, including gender-identity-related aspects of the legal framework.

Queer Cyprus Association UPR presentation (Erman Dolmacı, 4th-cycle): confirms the same three Criminal Code amendments (87(I)/2015 incitement, 31(I)/2017 aggravating factor, 39(I)/2023 conversion-practices ban), frames 'ISSUE 1' as trans and gender-diverse rights with the Sept 2022 LGR bill as the outstanding implementation step, and lists the state response to prior UPR recommendations — i.e. hate-speech law delivered, gender-identity discrimination ground and trans legislation not yet delivered.

Queer Cyprus 'Diversity of Colours' LGR booklet: documents gender-recognition practice on the divided island — the record's framework is self-determination without psychiatric or surgical gatekeeping ('no psychiatric involvement'), and the northern part of Cyprus runs its own recognition process, explicitly including recognition of non-binary identities. Practical resource: Queer Cyprus runs a 7-days/week confidential psychosocial and legal support line covering identity, work, family, shelter, health and military-service issues.

ILGA 32nd UPR session report (29 Jan 2019): Cyprus received 8 SOGIESC recommendations and accepted all 8; national report stated new legislation for correcting registered sex (adults and minors) was in preparation requiring only a Registrar decision, no prior medical intervention or psychiatric reports; ECRI had urged gender identity as a prohibited discrimination ground; Cyprus joined the Equal Rights Coalition as 40th member (Aug 2018). Marks the reform promise the 2022 bill was meant to fulfil.

The European Commission legal experts' country report on non-discrimination in Cyprus (2020, reporting period 2019) covers transposition and implementation of the EU equality directives, including SOGI grounds in Cypriot law.

PinkNews (10 Oct 2013): Cyprus amended its penal code to criminalise incitement to violence or hatred based on sexual orientation or gender identity, punishable by up to 3 years' imprisonment and/or a €5,000 fine; workplace SOGI protections were added in 2004. It is the hate-speech offence the 2015 law extended.

Gender identity does not appear among the statutory equal-treatment grounds, so discrimination complaints outside the criminal and employment spheres rest on an incomplete basis. The European Commission of Racism and Intolerance has urged Cyprus to add gender identity to its prohibited discrimination grounds, and the state joined the Equal Rights Coalition as its 40th member in August 2018. Both facts point the same direction as the accepted UPR recommendations: external pressure is consistent, domestic implementation is partial.

Implementation capacity has been questioned at home. Complaints of anti-LGBTI harassment lodged with the Ombudswoman prompted a two-day training course for prison guards in April 2023, a short intervention that indicates the issue had reached custodial settings rather than remaining abstract.

The European Commission Network of Legal Experts has published country reports on non-discrimination (2020) and on gender equality (2024) covering how European Union equality directives are transposed into Cypriot law, including gender-identity-related aspects. These are the reference points against which the missing gender-identity ground is measured.

KHM.name: Cambodia
KHM.summary:
Cambodia has never criminalised same-sex sexual activity, dating from the French protectorate period through independence in 1953, and gender expression is not criminalised. The statutory framework nonetheless contains no SOGI non-discrimination provisions, and no legal gender recognition procedure is in force.

The state's posture toward sexual orientation and gender identity is formally cooperative. At its 2019 Universal Periodic Review Cambodia accepted recommendations to legalise same-sex marriage, and at the 2024 review it accepted all 12 SOGIESC recommendations, covering marriage equality, legal gender recognition based on self-defined identity, and anti-discrimination measures. Acceptance is a stated commitment; the inventory contains no evidence that implementing legislation has been enacted. Cambodia also hosted the visit of the UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose report identifies good practices, remaining challenges and recommendations to strengthen protection against violence and discrimination, and was circulated to national stakeholders in an unofficial Khmer translation.

The operative risks are street-level and detention-level rather than statutory. A Cambodian Centre for Human Rights study documents more than 135 cases of harassment and abuse against transgender women on city streets, describing the treatment as shocking, and records a police practice in Siem Reap in which transgender sex workers were targeted and forced to bathe in dirty, stagnant river water. Comparable abuse is reported across urban centres, including extortion attributed to police.

Violence also originates inside the household. A Rainbow Community Kampuchea study reported in 2019 found that 81% of queer women and transgender people under 35 had suffered emotional abuse from a family member, and that 35% of participants in that age group had considered suicide as a result of family rejection; one case involved a 27-year-old trans man sent by his mother to a rehabilitation facility to correct his gender.

Placement in detention is decided case by case rather than by published rule. In February 2025 the president of the Cambodian Human Rights Committee, Keo Remy, stated at a ceremony at Correctional Centre 2 in Prey Sar prison, Phnom Penh, that transgender offenders who have undergone sex-change surgery are transferred from the men's facility, Correctional Centre 1, to the women's facility, Correctional Centre 2. The remarks praised the centre and cited no statute or formal policy text. The same report notes that prison overcrowding has worsened amid arrests from a gang crackdown.

Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, the two principal cities, have visible trans communities and tourist infrastructure accustomed to diverse visitors, and international guidebooks carry dedicated sections for LGBT travellers. That infrastructure sits alongside the documented street and policing risks rather than displacing them.

The prison transfer practice described in February 2025 rests on a ministerial-level statement at an event, not on a published regulation. No statute or formal policy text is available to confirm its scope, its criteria or whether it binds the prison administration.

Hate-crime law, entry and visa rules for transgender travellers, document screening at ports of entry, and access to gender-affirming healthcare are not addressed by any source in this inventory and remain unsourced here.

The CCHR figures on street harassment and the Siem Reap policing practice are reported through press coverage of the study; the underlying report's methodology, sample and time period are not reproduced in the sources available for this pass.

NPL.name: Nepal
NPL.summary:
Nepal is workable for trans visitors — South Asia's most legally recognising country. The Supreme Court has protected gender identity since a landmark 2007 ruling; a third-gender category exists on documents by self-identification; and in 2024 the Supreme Court ruled that a trans woman must be recognised as female without medical verification. Nothing is criminalised, and Kathmandu, the capital, has an established activist scene.

The gap between doctrine and practice is large: an international observer, Human Rights Watch, documents that implementation is piecemeal and humiliating, and trans people in provinces face physical and sexual harassment in public spaces with little police protection. These burdens fall overwhelmingly on residents navigating citizenship documents — a visitor with a foreign passport faces none of the bureaucratic gauntlet.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, tolerant tourist areas, but expect stares and possible harassment if visibly trans outside the main tourist bubbles.
NPL.outOfScopeNotes: Documentation barriers are resident-facing; citizenship-law discrimination does not affect visitors. The citizenship-document process after the rulings is not independently verified in this record; the documented failures date from the 2024 observer report and the 2024 ruling account. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

sources.summary: HRW (Feb 2024): calls on Nepal's government to urgently create a clear, simple, rights-respecting procedure so transgender and third-gender people can obtain official documents — illustrating that despite progressive rulings, no straightforward document-change process exists (photo shows a Kathmandu trans woman holding her 2023 citizenship certificate listing female gender). For this record: official-observer statement on the documentary-recognition gap.

JURIST (Aug 2024): Nepal's Supreme Court ruled that trans law student Rukshana Kapali must be legally recognised as a woman on all documents without medical verification, after she filed 50+ lawsuits since 2021; changing markers to 'female'/'male' has usually required surgery abroad plus in-country medical evaluations including intrusive post-operative genital exams. For this record: the landmark ruling and the pre-ruling barrier path, dated.

The Diplomat (Feb 2024): Nepal's 2007 ruling allowing self-identified legal gender was novel at the time and later cases reinforced it, but government officials limited changes to people identifying as 'third gender' while male/female marker changes lagged — the country's progressive reputation outruns policy. For this record: documented doctrine-versus-implementation gap.

Kathmandu Post feature (Nov 2024) on trans life in Janakpur: trans people face discrimination in public spaces and in government institutions and are often subjected to physical and sexual harassment. For this record: ground-level conditions for visibly trans people in provincial cities, dated 2024.

APTN (Asia Pacific Transgender Network) publication (Oct 2021, in Nepali): 'Gender Identity Draft Bill 2078: Civil Society Proposal' - by Rukshana Kapali and Allan Bhandari with advocate Subin Mulmi, produced through the Amplifying Trans Advocacy Fellowship; a civil-society draft bill on legal gender recognition in Nepal.

The Record (Sept 25, 2020) by Queer Youth Group and Queer Rights Collective: argues that despite the Constitution awarding the right to self-determine name and gender markers (2007 case), 'an extensive overhaul of the law and the language of the law' is still needed to address inequalities faced by the trans and broader PoMSOGIESC community. For this record: local-activist assessment of the gap between constitutional right and statute.

SIT Study Abroad ISP (Spring 2015) by Sophia Greene: 'Gender and Sexuality in Nepal: The Experiences of Sexual and Gender Minorities in a Rapidly Changing Social Climate' - despite changing legislation, sexual and gender minorities face deeply rooted stigma and obstacles in virtually every arena of life amid the clash of patriarchal tradition and modernisation.

LKA.name: Sri Lanka
LKA.summary:
Sri Lanka is dangerous for trans visitors. Sections 365/365A of the 1883 Penal Code criminalise same-sex activity (up to 10 years, applying to men and women), and Human Dignity Trust lists Sri Lanka as criminalising the gender expression of trans people: police use vagrancy and “cheating by personation” provisions against trans people. The International Commission of Jurists identifies Sri Lanka Police as “the foremost perpetrators of human rights violations against LGBTI individuals” — harassment, arbitrary detention, and abuse are documented as systematic, though formal prosecutions remain limited.

There is no legal gender recognition (a 2016 recognition circular exists but is not law), no anti-discrimination protection, and no hate-crime statute. Colombo has a small organised community (EQUAL GROUND) and tourist areas are accustomed to foreigners, which moderates but does not remove risk: the realistic worst case is police harassment or detention under personation/vagrancy provisions rather than prosecution.

The consequence axis makes the danger concrete: as of October 2024 the Prisons Department has no dedicated transgender housing — its media spokesperson/Commissioner said current facilities make giving transgender prisoners their own space impossible, with separate accommodation only planned for prisons built in the future — and placement defaults to birth sex in the current male/female ward system, with a discretionary, medicalised exception route: trans detainees holding the recognised identity card (issued since the June 2016 gender-recognition-certificate circular) are accommodated per their preferred gender ‘where possible’, while those without it undergo a doctor’s assessment of whether they ‘can be considered a transgender’ before placement, with the inmate’s preference weighed. Officials also cite the fear of people accused of sex offences ‘identifying as transgender’ to enter female housing with born-male offenders as a stated reason for resisting gender-based placement. A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.
LKA.outOfScopeNotes:
Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; LGR circular limits are resident-facing.

Prison axis: the placement statements are a Prisons Department spokesperson’s remarks (October 2024), with no statutory placement rule and no written policy text; how ‘where possible’ actually operates is unquantified; separate accommodation exists only as a plan for facilities built in the future; and no trans special unit or solitary/segregation practice is documented for the current prison system.

Legal gender recognition is possible (via a certification process).

Outcome: placement by birth sex is the practical default in the current male/female ward system, with a medicalised, discretionary exception process and no statutory placement rule.

sources.title: Future prison constructions: Transgender inmates to receive separate accommodation

The piece also reports the Committee for Protecting Rights of Prisoners (CPRP) asking that future prisons give transgender and non-binary inmates a separate, chosen space (including possible space within prison hospitals), citing that 'developed countries have recognised transgender rights'. Confirms the absence of a codified placement policy and the official preference-assessment route as of Oct 2024.

A detained trans visitor — unlikely to hold the recognition card, in a country where police already use vagrancy and personation provisions against trans people — would default to birth-sex placement under a practice with no statutory rule and no dedicated housing.

MNG.name: Mongolia
MNG.summary:
Mongolia is a country workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 1993, discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity is prohibited, and identity grounds were added to the hate-crime provisions of the Criminal Code in 2015. There are no bathroom laws, no border/document friction for foreign passports, and no police targeting pattern; police guidance requires officers to address transgender detainees by their identified gender regardless of identification documents, a favourable enforcement practice.

The realistic risk for a visitor is street harassment if visibly trans, particularly at night and outside the capital's central districts, where social acceptance is low.
MNG.outOfScopeNotes: Comprehensive anti-discrimination gaps and medicalised LGR are resident-facing. The assault documentation and the training figures are from reporting sources and have not been independently re-verified in this record; the older scene account describes 2008 conditions. This record contains no border-screening or document-procedure information for visitors.

MMR.name: Myanmar
MMR.summary:
Myanmar is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Section 377 of the Penal Code criminalises same-sex intimacy, and police use “shadow laws” — notably Section 30(d) of the Rangoon Police Act, allowing detention of anyone who cannot “satisfactorily account” for themselves — to target trans and gender-nonconforming people. Since the February 2021 coup the situation has turned lethal: the National Unity Government documented 17 LGBT people killed by mid-2022, and rights groups document arrests, torture, and sexual abuse of LGBT people by junta authorities, with the 2024 Conscription Law falling brutally on queer people.

In 2025 the junta banned seven books for LGBTQ+ content as “obscene.” There is no legal gender recognition, no protection of any kind, and no institutional recourse — police and military are the primary predators. Resistance-controlled areas are nominally friendlier but are active war zones.

For a visitor: any visible gender nonconformity risks detention under police-act powers, with torture documented in custody; the general security collapse compounds everything.
MMR.outOfScopeNotes: General civil-war risks affect all travelers and are out of scope; the score reflects trans-specific persecution by the junta.

sources.summary: Outright International overview (updated March 2026): Section 377 used to detain people who cannot 'satisfactorily account' for their presence; after the 1 Feb 2021 coup risks intensified — torture/sexual violence in detention, Oct 2022 Organization Registration Law (prison terms for NGO non-compliance), compulsory military service announced Feb 2024, seven LGBTQ-themed books banned 2025. Verdict: avoid entirely.

DVB (Jan 2024): post-coup authorities commit attacks, arrest, torture and sexual abuse against LGBT people; the NUG recorded 17 LGBT killed and 2 critically injured since 1 Feb 2021; 'Rainbow Amid the Storm' found 50% of LGBT respondents have no confidence in the legal system and 68%+ fear repercussions from abusers.

Human Rights Myanmar submission (June 2024) to the UN Special Rapporteur on extrajudicial executions: killing of LGBTIQ+ persons in military-controlled Myanmar - 5 to 12 individuals dead since the coup; Section 377 enforcement intensified as an aggravating factor; militarised policing, arbitrary detention and vague public-decency laws endanger the right to life.

RFA (10 Jan 2025): junta banned seven named LGBTQ-themed books as 'obscene' with prosecutions announced for publishers; colonial-era law carries up to 10 years for gay sex; LGBTQ+ people hit hard since the Feb 2021 coup.

HuffPost (17 Oct 2015): colonial-era criminalisation; 2013 Mandalay arrests of trans women forced to strip and parade naked while photographed (police called it a 'public service'); nat kadaws (spirit mediums) are culturally visible transgender women — visibility coexisting with criminalisation.

MMR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Russia (0.12) and Belarus (0.13) only because Myanmar's persecution, while lethal, is part of generalised wartime violence rather than a codified anti-trans machine; below Uganda (0.17).
