CUB.name: Cuba
CUB.summary:
Cuba's legal framework for trans people rests on the 2019 Constitution, whose Article 42 names sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories, the first constitution to do so. The 2022 Family Code, approved by referendum on 25 September 2022 with 66.87% support, legalised same-sex marriage and adoption and permits legal gender change without surgery. Consensual same-sex relations were removed from the Penal Code in 1979.

Legal gender recognition is administrative rather than surgical or judicial. The July 2025 civil-registry reform removed the remaining bureaucratic hurdles to name changes, and the Family Code already established that surgery is not a precondition.

Employment protection is narrower than the constitutional text. The Labor Code (Law 116) bars discrimination on grounds that include sexual orientation, but its article 2(b) covers orientation and does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground. A 2013 parliamentary amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation passed after intense debate; Mariela Castro's proposal to extend the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, but only the sexual-orientation ban is confirmed as enacted.

Healthcare access has an explicit official basis. Resolution 126 (2008) brought trans healthcare into the public system, and CENESEX, the state sex-education centre, runs an official trans-care programme alongside a trans-rights campaign, working with the police and the supreme court on sexual-diversity education. In practice the economic crisis has degraded healthcare and hormone availability is reported as unreliable.

The equality settlement is contested rather than state-enforced. Opponents of the Family Code cited religious objections and feared that child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown, which produced more than 1,400 arrestees, and record emigration. The 25 September 2022 vote was only the fourth national election since 1959.

The counterweights are systemic rather than trans-specific. Cuba is a one-party state with no independent civil society, arbitrary-detention powers are broad, and police discretion is wide. There is no documented pattern of police targeting people for gender expression; the documented state hostility runs toward emigration and asylum claims rather than toward gender presentation.
CUB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether the gender-identity, disability and HIV-status extension to the 2013 employment amendment was ever enacted is not confirmed in the sources; only the sexual-orientation ban is confirmed as passed.

Not sourced: entry and visa rules, including whether passports or entry documents carry sex markers that do not match a visitor's presentation, and whether border or immigration screening can out a traveller. No information is available on airport or border practice.

Not sourced: rules on restroom and facility access, hate-crime penalties or their enforcement, recognition of a foreign spouse or partner, and how Article 42 has been applied by courts in individual cases.

Not sourced: any sub-national variation in enforcement, since the sources describe national law and Havana-based institutions only.

sources.summary: LegalClarity overview (30 May 2026): documents Cuba's arc from the UMAP forced-labour camps for gay men (1965-68, ~60 hrs/week cutting cane in Camagüey, electric-shock and injection 'curing' experiments) to today's progressive framework — 1979 Penal Code removal of consensual same-sex acts, Castro's public acceptance of blame (La Jornada, 2010), Resolution 126 (2008) trans healthcare in the public system, the 2019 Constitution (Art 42, first to name sexual orientation and gender identity as protected categories), and the 2022 Family Code (same-sex marriage/adoption, legal gender change without surgery). Notes the gap between law and daily life: Labor Code Law 116 bars SOGI discrimination but does not list gender identity as a separate protected ground, and the Labor Code's article 2(b) covers orientation, not identity.

Americas Quarterly (15 Sept 2022): previews Cuba's 25 Sept 2022 Family Code referendum — only the 4th national vote since 1959 — which would guarantee marriage equality, surrogacy, codified domestic-violence penalties and shared parental rights; opponents cite religious objections and fear child-welfare provisions could be used against dissidents, while some government opponents planned to vote No purely to deny the Díaz-Canel administration a win amid the post-July-2021 crackdown (1,400+ arrestees) and record emigration. Useful context for how contested (rather than state-enforced) the equality settlement is.

Links International Journal of Socialist Renewal (23 Dec 2011): sympathetic first-person account 'Rainbow Cuba' disputing claims of systematic state homophobia — documents the UMAP camps (conscripts paid seven pesos a day), the 1975 declaration-era turning point, and CENESEX's state-backed programme: a trans-rights campaign, work with the police and the supreme court, and sexual-diversity education. Historical baseline (pre-2019 constitution) showing official institutions campaigning for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s.

Washington Blade (21 Dec 2013): Cuban lawmakers approved a labor-law amendment banning employment discrimination on sexual orientation after intense parliamentary debate. Mariela Castro of CENESEX proposed extending the ban to gender identity, disability and HIV status; the trans-specific amendment drew support from some Christian and intellectual legislators, while passage of the sexual-orientation ban was the confirmed outcome. The measure predates the 2019 Constitution and the 2022 Family Code.

Washington Blade (26 May 2018): documents Cuba's use of 'treason'/'treason against the homeland' charges against LGBTI citizens who flee to seek asylum — Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to 8 years in prison if they returned after filing Dutch asylum claims (Jan 2018); a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained (19 May 2018), and LGBTI activists (incl. Nelson Gandulla, Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation) remained monitored. Relevant to visitors: Cuba's hostility toward emigration/asylum, not toward gender expression as such.

CUB.tangentialFactors:
The historical baseline is severe and well documented. Between 1965 and 1968 the UMAP forced-labour camps held gay men, who cut cane in Camagüey roughly 60 hours a week for seven pesos a day and were subjected to electric-shock and injection experiments presented as cures. Consensual same-sex acts left the Penal Code in 1979, and Fidel Castro publicly accepted blame for the UMAP era in 2010.

Official institutions have campaigned for LGBT acceptance since the late 2000s, with CENESEX running trans-rights work and engaging the police and the supreme court, a baseline that predates the 2019 Constitution.

Cuba's hostility toward departure is documented and distinct from its stance on gender expression. In January 2018 Victor Manuel Dueñas and Onasis Torres faced up to eight years in prison for treason against the homeland after filing asylum claims in the Netherlands, a woman deported from the Netherlands was detained on 19 May 2018, and LGBTI activists including Nelson Gandulla of the Cuban LGBTI Equality Foundation remained under monitoring. A trans visitor who sought asylum or fled could meet this machinery; a visitor who does not is unlikely to encounter it.

Compared with neighbouring jurisdictions, Cuba's constitutional and family-law settlement is among the most transformed in Latin America, though the employment-law gap on gender identity places it behind the standard its own constitution sets.
CUB.localsOnly:
Cuban workers are covered by Labor Code Law 116, which bars discrimination including on sexual orientation, but gender identity is not listed as a separate protected ground and article 2(b) addresses orientation only. Residents seeking redress therefore have a weaker statutory hook for identity-based workplace claims than for orientation-based ones.

Residents access trans healthcare through the public system under Resolution 126 (2008) and through CENESEX's official programme, which also conducts sexual-diversity education and works with police and courts. Supply-side reliability is constrained by the economic crisis.

The Family Code governs resident families directly, covering marriage, adoption, shared parental rights and codified domestic-violence penalties, and the July 2025 civil-registry reform governs name changes for people registered in Cuban civil records.

Citizens face the treason provisions if they leave to seek asylum, and independent LGBTI activists have been monitored. The absence of independent civil society means there is no organisation outside the state to which a resident can appeal.
CUB.comparisons: Pairwise: below Argentina (0.73 — democracy, independent NGOs, stronger recourse) and above Lithuania (0.66) and Vietnam (0.63 — Cuba's constitutional GI protection and official trans programme edge it).

ECU.name: Ecuador
ECU.summary:
Ecuador's legal framework on gender identity is among the strongest in the region. Legal gender recognition has been available since 2016, and the December 2023 reforms to the Organic Law on Identity Management and Civil Data, regulated by a decree issued by President Daniel Noboa on 11 June 2024, allow adults to change name and sex or gender marker directly at the civil registry, once, without surgery. Constitutional Court rulings in 2024 and 2025 extended document changes to trans adolescents and publicly rebuked the National Assembly for stalling implementation of trans-rights legislation; an April 2026 report describes the adolescent ruling as opening a path for others seeking legal recognition.

The constitutional footing is explicit. Article 11 of the 2008 Constitution binds the state to respect differences of ethnicity, nationality, social and generational standing and gender, and names sexual orientation and gender identity among the principles that underpin non-discrimination in a secular, multinational state.

Violence remains the dominant visitor-facing risk. A monitoring group documented 27 LGBTQ+ people murdered in 2023 with inadequate state response, and reporting from January 2024 recorded rising violence against LGBTQ Ecuadorians as the government's declared internal armed conflict against gangs got under way; two further LGBTQ people were killed in the conflict's first weeks. Quito and Guayaquil, the two largest cities, carry real street risk, and police capacity is absorbed by the security crisis, which weakens the practical value of the formal protection machinery.

Detention is a serious exposure. Ecuador's prisons are almost universally male, and trans detainees are placed according to birth sex or legal sex rather than gender identity, with protective placement applied unevenly. Trans women held in male pavilions have reported rape, torture directed at their gender identity, beatings, forced head-shaving and denial of medical care. A visitor who is arrested should expect placement in a male facility.

Family and partner recognition is partial. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 2019, but a constitutional ban bars same-sex couples from adoption. JAM.name: Jamaica
JAM.summary:
Jamaica criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. The Offences Against the Person Act punishes buggery with up to 10 years' hard labour, and the US State Department's 2023 country report confirms the provision remains in force. No law prohibits discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and individuals are not legally permitted to register a change of gender, so a trans visitor has no domestic legal recognition to rely on.

The defining case is Dwayne Jones, a gender-nonconforming 16-year-old beaten, stabbed and shot to death by a mob at a street party in 2013 after being outed. Police did not investigate the killing. The case is now before the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights as Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica, and an amicus brief filed in February 2024 argues that continued criminalisation and systemic discrimination leave transgender Jamaicans exposed to housing, educational and employment insecurity.

Police protection is unreliable. The US Department of Justice country packet records that LGBT victims do not report attacks because police leak incident details, fail to investigate violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks. The Inter-American Commission's 2012 report on Jamaica describes the violent persecution and fear to which gay and lesbian people are subject as deplorable. Human Rights Watch documented police harassment of gay men and of HIV/AIDS outreach workers alongside community and family violence carried out with impunity and official indifference. Amnesty International's 4 June 2006 urgent appeal reported police ill-treatment and torture of LGBT people as well as vigilante attacks.

Vigilante violence remains a live risk. Amnesty documented gay men and lesbians beaten, cut, burned, raped and shot once their orientation became known, and lesbians raped and driven into exile abroad. Community members report that beatings and stonings of trans people are common but rarely reported because reporting achieves nothing.

Detention carries a specific and documented danger. The State Department reports that prisoner-on-prisoner violence is common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for perceived LGBTQI+ identity, in facilities operating far beyond capacity; a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by other inmates accusing him of being gay. No gender-recognition framework exists to inform how a trans detainee would be housed.
JAM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not state whether the Inter-American Commission has decided Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica or what remedies, if any, it has ordered.

Unresolved: no source here gives conviction or enforcement figures for the buggery provision in recent years. The sources establish that the offence is on the books; how often it is applied is not sourced.

Unresolved: treatment of trans travellers at entry, including visa and border screening, acceptance of foreign documents bearing a changed gender marker, and any risk of being screened or questioned on gender identity, is not covered by this inventory.

Unresolved: whether conditions differ in tourist areas such as Montego Bay, Negril or Ocho Rios is not sourced in this inventory.

Currency caveat: the Amnesty appeal dates from 2006, the Human Rights Watch letter from 2004, the Inter-American Commission report from 2012 and the Department of Justice packet from 2013; whether each specific account still describes current practice is not verified here. The State Department report (2023) and the UNDP survey (March 2023) are the most recent sources.

Scope caveat: the prison study rests on 2018 fieldwork at a single facility, so its figures should not be read as a national prison-wide measurement.

sources.summary: Amicus brief in Dwayne Jones v. Jamaica before the Inter-American Commission (filed Feb 2024): argues Jamaica's continued criminalisation of LGBTQ persons and systemic discrimination make transgender persons especially vulnerable — sections document housing insecurity, educational and employment insecurity for transgender Jamaicans under the discrimination regime.

UNDP 'Being LGBT in Jamaica' National Survey (March 2023): national survey of LGBT Jamaicans with dedicated chapters on violence due to prejudice and discrimination and on transgender access to health care; quantifies lived experience of violence and service exclusion under the criminalisation backdrop.

US DOJ/EOIR Jamaica country packet (2013): Offences Against the Person Act makes 'buggery' punishable by up to 10 years' hard labour; LGBT victims are reluctant to report because police leak incident details, fail to investigate LGBT violence including murder, and do not intervene during attacks (documented via the CVC and local organisations).

IACHR Report on the Situation of Human Rights in Jamaica (10 Aug 2012): finds 'the violent persecution and fear to which gays and lesbians are subject in Jamaica to be deplorable'; covers citizen security, police killings including the May 2010 operation, and justice administration, with civil-society input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays (J-FLAG).

HRW letter (30 Nov 2004) citing its report 'Hated to Death: Homophobia, Violence, and Jamaica's HIV/AIDS Epidemic': documents police harassment of gay men and HIV/AIDS outreach workers, community and family violence carried out with impunity, and official indifference; five Jamaican human-rights organisations backed the report's 16 Nov 2004 Kingston launch.

sources.title: Gays ostracised in prison – study
sources.summary: Jamaica Gleaner reporting (5 Feb 2019) on UWI lecturer Carla Moore's 2018 study (Apr-Nov 2018, funded by the Inter-American Institute of Human Rights, the IBA and the UN Latin American Institute for the Prevention of Crime): Jamaicans perceived as gay, bisexual or transgender 'are isolated' in Jamaica's penal institutions and rehabilitation opportunities for them are 'basically non-existent'. Inmates' movement inside facilities is severely curtailed and access to resources often limited because of entrenched homophobia/transphobia - other prisoners refuse to touch objects or sit on seats used by gay prisoners. The study estimated that about 300 of the 1,800 prisoners at Tower Street Adult Correctional Centre belong to sexual or gender minorities and reported that lesbians face prevalent 'corrective rape'. Evidence that LGB/trans prisoners are socially ostracised and isolated rather than integrated, with no specialised housing policy documented.

sources.title: Jamaica 2023 Human Rights Report (US Department of State)
sources.summary: US State Dept country report: 'Prisoner-on-prisoner violence was common, including severe violence against prisoners targeted for their perceived lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, or intersex (LGBTQI+) identity'; correctional facilities were significantly overcrowded (Tower Street maximum-security cells at three times capacity), with harsh, life-threatening conditions, and a January 2023 video showed an inmate at a pretrial police lockup beaten and attacked with scalding liquid by inmates accusing him of being gay. The report also records that Jamaica barred legal gender registration ('Individuals were not legally allowed to register a change of gender'), that the buggery law (up to 10 years' hard labour) criminalised consensual same-sex conduct, and that no anti-discrimination law protected SOGI. Official-state confirmation that trans prisoners face identity-targeted violence in Jamaican prisons with no gender-recognition framework for accommodation decisions.

JAM.tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Commission's report of 10 August 2012 places LGBT persecution inside a wider pattern of citizen security failures in Jamaica, covering police killings including the May 2010 operation and the administration of justice, with input from Jamaicans for Justice and the Jamaica Forum for Lesbians, All-Sexuals and Gays.

Human Rights Watch's documentation was launched in Kingston on 16 November 2004 with the backing of five Jamaican human-rights organisations, and the Inter-American Commission likewise drew on local civil society, indicating an established domestic advocacy infrastructure that a visitor may encounter as a source of assistance.

Amnesty International's 2006 urgent appeal also raised concern that prominent Jamaican musicians promote homophobia, a cultural influence that operates alongside the legal regime rather than within it.

The UNDP national survey published in March 2023 supplies quantified baseline data on violence and service exclusion among LGBT Jamaicans, against which the older qualitative accounts can be read.
JAM.comparisons: Pairwise: above Malaysia (0.28 — adds Sharia caning statutes) and below Sri Lanka (0.33 — police-as-perpetrator but less mob-killing culture). Jamaica's mob-violence pattern plus failed investigation of the Dwayne Jones killing keeps it in High Risk.

TTO.name: Trinidad and Tobago
TTO.summary:
Trinidad and Tobago demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the colonial buggery laws (Jones v. AG, 2018, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still “beaten, stoned and chopped,” with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of Grindr ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including a Cocorite man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

The consequence axis of an arrest is acknowledged in official terms as unsafe: the 2018 ‘Justice through a Gender Lens’ Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers states plainly that ‘in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities’. The only mechanism is a judicial officer’s sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate’s physical safety, and the Protocol’s other directives — courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress — govern court process rather than custody placement. Placement for a detained trans visitor is therefore discretionary, with no dedicated facility, special unit or statutory placement standard on record; the documented official position is that the penal system cannot safely accommodate trans prisoners.
TTO.outOfScopeNotes:
Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

Prison axis: the Protocol is a judicial-officers’ standard, not a statute — no trans-prisoner placement rule, dedicated facility, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is on record; how prison authorities actually respond to sentencing recommendations is undocumented; and the Protocol dates from November 2018 with no implementation evidence in this record.

sources.summary: Trinidad and Tobago Newsday (July 2024): 'Long way yet for recognition, safe spaces' - TT Transgender Coalition director Rae Alibey says the trans community is the most marginalised and not even recognised in T&T; gender identity is not recognised separately from sexual orientation; gender-identity markers on institutional forms are absent; national discussions and attitudinal research needed.

Newsday (Nov 2024): police warning over cyber criminals - Grindr hook-ups ending in cars, cash and phones stolen; criminals create fake dating accounts to lure LGBT+ victims into meetings followed by armed robbery, beatings or sexual assault; two separate incidents reported in one week.

Newsday editorial (June 2024): 'Grind hate to a halt' - a spate of Grindr-related attacks (almost half a dozen in recent months); Supt Claire Guy-Alleyne points to gaps in the law: 'We don't have a specific hate crime category in legislation'; the editorial argues the gap must be closed.

CNC3 (23 Aug 2024): the PNM Constitution Review Committee rejected adding sexual-orientation protections to the national constitution (decision announced at a special convention); CAISO's Dr Angelique Nixon said the community has 'been waiting far too long for equal rights and protection'. Documents LGBTQ-rights exclusion from the 2024 constitutional-review process.

GlobalGayz (Aug 2012): travel/culture profile stating that although homosexuality is illegal the laws are mostly ignored in practice; describes the tourist-facing social scene and island context. The profile predates the 2018 decriminalisation ruling, so its statement of the law does not reflect current law.

PinkNews (21 Nov 2017): first-person appeal by activist Jason Jones during his High Court challenge to T&T's same-sex criminalisation, stating he faces up to 25 years' imprisonment for consensual sex with an adult male partner. Marks the constitutional challenge that put the criminal law in play.

Erasing 76 Crimes (23 Jun 2016): PM Keith Rowley told Parliament (17 Jun 2016) the state must protect all citizens 'regardless of whom they sleep with', while refusing to repeal the same-sex criminal laws; cites Newsday. Documents the reform-refusal gap in official rhetoric as of 2016.

sources.title: Protect transgender inmates'
sources.summary: Trinidad Express (Camille Hunte, 28 Nov 2018) on the official 'Justice through a Gender Lens' Gender Equality Protocol for Judicial Officers (launched Nov 2018 by the CCJ, CAJO, UN Women, JURIST Project, TTAWJ and the Judicial Institute of TT): the Protocol states plainly that 'in Trinidad and Tobago, there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities'. It directs judicial officers sentencing a person whose gender identity does not accord with their birth certificate to use recommendations to prison authorities to ensure provisions are in place for the inmate's physical safety, and instructs courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress. Official acknowledgment that housing placement for trans prisoners is discretionary, unsafe, and mediated only through sentencing recommendations - with no facility of its own.

TTO.tangentialFactors:
The Grindr ambush robbery pattern is a direct risk for trans visitors using apps.

Placement-framework context: the Protocol was a justice-sector initiative launched in November 2018 by the Caribbean Court of Justice, the CAJO, UN Women, the JURIST Project, the TT Association of Women Judges and the Judicial Institute of TT — institutional recognition of the custody gap rather than a visitor-facing protection.
TTO.localsOnly:
No LGR and no SOGI anti-discrimination protection — resident-facing; the “beaten, stoned and chopped” pattern describes residents.

The custody findings govern residents held in custody: the absence of special facilities for persons with non-traditional gender identities and the sentencing-recommendation mechanism are national prison/court practice — a visitor meets them only through arrest and detention.
TTO.comparisons: Pairwise: above Kenya (0.38 — TTO decriminalised via courts; Kenya retains criminalisation) and below Turkey (0.47).
TTO.blindSummary:
The nation demands real caution from trans visitors — legally improved, socially dangerous. The courts struck down the historic buggery laws (2018 legal challenge, upheld on appeal), removing criminalisation of same-sex intimacy; but there is no legal gender recognition, no SOGI anti-discrimination protection, and parliament has repeatedly rejected reforms (the ruling party's constitution review again refused SOGI protections in 2024).

Documented street risk is substantial: community advocates report trans people are still "beaten, stoned and chopped," with most incidents never reported; and police have publicly warned of a spate of dating-app ambush robberies — criminals using fake profiles to lure LGBT victims to meetings followed by armed robbery (multiple cases through 2023-2024, including one man beaten and robbed). This dating-app predation pattern is a direct traveler concern.

The consequence axis of an arrest is acknowledged in official terms as unsafe: the 2018 gender-equality protocol for judicial officers says plainly that "there are no special facilities in our penal system to safely accommodate persons with non-traditional gender identities". The only mechanism is a judicial officer's sentencing recommendation that prison authorities make provisions for the inmate's physical safety, and the Protocol's other directives — courts to refer to intersex/transgender persons by their chosen pronoun and permit court access irrespective of dress — govern court process rather than custody placement. Placement for a detained trans visitor is therefore discretionary, with no dedicated facility, special unit or statutory placement standard on record; the documented official position is that the penal system cannot safely accommodate trans prisoners.
TTO.blindOutOfScope:
Decriminalisation status and reform rejections are climate/legal context; no trans-specific statute exists.

Prison axis: the Protocol is a judicial-officers' standard, not a statute — no trans-prisoner placement rule, dedicated facility, special unit, or solitary/segregation practice is on record; how prison authorities actually respond to sentencing recommendations is undocumented; and the Protocol dates from November 2018 with no implementation evidence in this record.

GHA.name: Ghana
GHA.summary:
Trans visitors in Ghana face a legal framework that, in its current form, criminalises identity itself. The Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill passed by Ghana's Parliament on 29 May 2026 provides for up to three years' imprisonment for identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer, with total prison terms of three to ten years and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Presidential assent by President John Mahama was still outstanding at the time of the most recent reporting, and Mahama had previously signalled willingness to sign a reintroduced bill after the earlier version failed to reach him.

The 2026 bill adds a reporting obligation: it establishes a duty on persons who become aware of prohibited acts to report them to the police. For a visitor, that converts acquaintances, colleagues, landlords and hotel staff into potential informants, and it removes the discretion that previously shielded people from formal complaint.

The 2026 law is not an isolated event. Parliament unanimously passed the Promotion of Proper Human Sexual Rights and Ghanaian Family Values Bill in February 2024, carrying up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and up to five years for forming or funding LGBTQ+ groups. President Nana Akufo-Addo declined to assent while legal challenges were pending; the Supreme Court of Ghana unanimously dismissed two of those challenges, with Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson observing that until there is presidential assent there is no act and deferring review until signature. The bill then lapsed unsigned when the 8th Parliament dissolved before the 2024 election. Its unanimous passage, and its reintroduction, indicate the direction of travel rather than a stray piece of legislation.

Criminalisation predates both bills. Section 104(1)(b) of Ghana's Criminal Offences Act, a colonial-era provision on 'unnatural carnal knowledge', remains on the books, though Human Rights Watch reported in 2018 that it is rarely enforced through prosecution. That low formal enforcement rate did not make Ghana safe. Human Rights Watch documented mob violence against LGBT people, police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals, including victim interviews conducted in Kumasi and Tamale in 2017, and published a report titled 'No Choice but to Deny Who I Am: Violence and Discrimination against LGBT People in Ghana' in January 2018.

The new bill enumerates transgender people explicitly alongside lesbian, gay, bisexual and queer people. It therefore supplies the state pathway by which a trans person in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone, with no requirement of any act. The bill contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed, and there is no publicly documented policy in Ghana on the housing of trans prisoners, leaving placement to correctional discretion.

Community organisations describe the effect of the 2026 bill's passage in advance of assent. One Love Sisters Ghana reports panic among LGBT people, risk of eviction and widespread self-censorship. A 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland, conducted for a Diaconia University of Applied Sciences thesis, found that most respondents opposed decriminalisation or legalisation on religious and cultural grounds and concerns about effects on children, while most supported families loving and accepting LGBT relatives but not blessing their marriages. That diaspora sample is not representative of Ghana's population, but it is consistent with the political support the bill received.
GHA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether President John Mahama has assented to the 29 May 2026 bill is unresolved in the source inventory. The most recent reporting states that ratification was still required and that the bill was expected to be signed. The legal status of the bill at the time a visitor reads this record should be verified against Ghanaian official sources before travel.

Nothing in the inventory addresses gender-marker or identity-document rules for trans people in Ghana, the treatment of foreign passports bearing conflicting markers at ports of entry, asylum or non-refoulement claims, or access to gender-affirming healthcare. These are not sourced and remain unaddressed here rather than assumed either way.

The Reuters report of the February 2024 parliamentary passage returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read directly; the passage itself is corroborated by JURIST and Human Rights Watch.

The inventory does not document any instance of a trans person actually being prosecuted or imprisoned for identity under section 104(1)(b) of the Criminal Offences Act, nor any data on the current population of LGBT detainees in Ghanaian prisons. The claim that the 2026 bill creates a pathway to imprisonment for identity alone is a statement about the statute's terms, not about documented enforcement.

sources.title: Ghana parliament passes bill criminalising gay acts
sources.summary: BBC (30 May 2026): Ghana's parliament approved a new bill criminalising homosexuality and the promotion of LGBTQ+ activities. Identifying as lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender or queer carries up to three years' imprisonment, and the bill adds a duty to report prohibited acts to police. It was passed under pressure from religious leaders on President Mahama, whose ratification is still required. The bill establishes the state pathway by which trans people in Ghana can be imprisoned for identity alone and contains no provision on how such prisoners would be housed.

sources.title: People 'panicking' as Ghana passes sweeping law criminalising LGBTQ+ activity
sources.summary: The Guardian (1 Jun 2026): the Human Sexual Rights and Family Values Bill, passed by Ghana's parliament on 29 May 2026 and expected to be signed by President Mahama, mandates prison terms of three to 10 years, with up to three years for identifying as LGBTQ+ and longer terms for promotion or advocacy. Community groups such as One Love Sisters Ghana report panic, eviction risk and self-censorship. No publicly documented policy exists in Ghana on housing trans prisoners.

GHA.tangentialFactors:
Ghana illustrates how a legislative instrument can matter without ever being law. The 2024 bill passed unanimously and was defeated only by the absence of presidential assent and the dissolution of Parliament, not by court judgment or popular rejection. A visitor assessing Ghana should therefore treat the 2026 bill's pending status as a question of timing rather than of outcome, given the President's stated willingness to sign.

The Supreme Court's dismissal of the challenges to the 2024 bill did not clear the statute. Justice Avril Lovelace-Johnson's reasoning was procedural: there was no act to challenge because no assent had been given, and review was deferred until the President signed. The petitioners' lawyers said they would explore further options. This sequencing means that constitutional challenge in Ghana has so far operated at the threshold rather than on the merits of criminalisation.

The gap between the colonial-era offence and the new statutory scheme is a gap in evidence rather than in law. Section 104(1)(b) survived unchanged for decades with little reported prosecution, while the violence documented by Human Rights Watch in 2018 came largely from police and vigilante actors rather than from courts. The 2026 bill's reporting duty is designed to shift the enforcement burden toward third parties and formal complaint, which may change that pattern.

Human Rights Watch has been the principal external documentation of LGBT conditions in Ghana since its 2018 report, and has consistently urged the President to veto the 2024 bill and, by extension, opposes the 2026 legislation. Its reporting on Ghana forms part of its wider work on criminalisation in West Africa, though the source inventory for this record does not extend to comparative data on other states in the region.
GHA.comparisons: Pairwise: above Nigeria (0.19 — SSMPA in force with mob lynching culture) and below Kenya (0.38 — criminalisation but stronger courts). Ghana's near-passage of an identity-criminalising bill is what separates it from Elevated band: the legal floor is currently the old 3-year statute, but the demonstrated legislative intent is far harsher.

GHA.localsOnly:
Residents, not only visitors, are caught by the reporting duty introduced in the 2026 bill. Members of households, landlords, employers and community members who learn of prohibited acts become obliged to report them to the police, which places LGBT Ghanaians in conflict with their own families and neighbours rather than only with the state.

Organisations working with LGBT people have been operating in a climate of documented police and vigilante violence well before the 2026 bill. Human Rights Watch's 2018 report recorded police abuse and extortion of suspected LGBT individuals alongside mob attacks, and its endnotes document interviews conducted in Kumasi and Tamale in 2017. Residents of those areas have reported to such organisations that the principal threats come from vigilantes and from police, not from prosecution.

One Love Sisters Ghana reports that LGBT Ghanaians are experiencing panic, risk of eviction from housing and self-censorship following the 2026 bill's passage. Housing insecurity is a direct consequence where a landlord can report a tenant under the new duty to report.

Public opinion research touching on the Ghanaians' own attitudes is limited to a small 2017 survey of 113 Ghanaians living in Finland, which found majority opposition to decriminalisation but majority support for familial acceptance of LGBT relatives short of marriage. No national polling data on attitudes to transgender people is available in this record.

MAR.name: Morocco
MAR.summary:
Morocco is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 489 criminalises same-sex “indecent acts” (6 months–3 years), and Cairo 52 documents that trans people face de-facto criminalisation under Article 498 morality provisions — arrests based on gender-expression discrepancies and forced outing. The 2026 Cairo 52 report “A Web of Violence” describes a legal-medical-social system of erasure for trans people, including a de facto prohibition on transition care.

Visitor-relevant cases exist: in 2024, Brazilian influencer Liziane Gutierrez was arrested in Marrakesh, accused by police of being transgender, and alleges she was forced to show her genitals — she spent a month in jail. In 2019, Marrakesh police filmed and humiliated a cross-dressing man after a traffic accident, leaking the video online. There is no LGR framework and police have wide discretion; tourist areas (Marrakesh, Agadir) are more tolerant in practice but the legal exposure is constant.

The Gutierrez case demonstrates that even a cisgender visitor suspected of being trans can face genital inspection and jail.
MAR.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is a situational/climate factor; the 2024 Gutierrez arrest was officially for filming a policeman — the trans-suspicion genital inspection is her allegation, disputed by Morocco.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 report 'A Web of Violence: The Systemic Erasure of Transgender People in Morocco' (Jan 2026, by Hamzawya and Nora Noralla): based on interviews with 17 trans and non-binary Moroccans - documents an interlocking system of legal, medical, social and economic hostility; Morocco once pioneered gender-affirming surgery for foreigners but now enforces a de facto prohibition for its own citizens; Article 489 weaponised to arrest trans people based on gender expression; no legal gender recognition pathway.

Cairo 52 country review of Morocco: no specific provisions on transition, but de facto criminalisation under Article 498 (moral charges, gender-expression discrepancies, involuntary outing); no gender-affirming healthcare framework, leading some to self-medicate; a 2021 recognition process exists for intersex people only; the Grand Mufti opposes transition.
Hindustan Times (Nov 2024): an Instagram model alleges Moroccan police forced her to show her genitals over trans suspicions - reported police abuse of a trans woman based on appearance.

El País (Jan 2019): Moroccan police subjected a Marrakesh cross-dresser to online humiliation - after a minor traffic accident, Chafiq was handcuffed and filmed by bystanders and police officers, who also photographed his ID documents and posted them online; he sought asylum in Europe. Homosexuality is punishable in Morocco.

Outright International country overview (updated March 2026): Article 489 criminalises 'indecent acts' between persons of the same sex (6 months to 3 years) with wide police discretion and arbitrary arrests; 170 people charged with same-sex relations in 2018; HRW documented a 2020 campaign of online harassment of presumed gay and bisexual men; no legal gender recognition; public identification as LGBTIQ carries significant risk of violence and harassment; authorities block LGBTIQ organisations.

HRW report (April 2018) 'Audacity in Adversity': LGBT activism in the Middle East and North Africa - includes Morocco's Article 489 criminalisation and the annex of laws used to punish same-sex conduct and gender expression across MENA.
ILGA 'State-Sponsored Homophobia' (May 2008, Daniel Ottosson): world survey of laws prohibiting same-sex activity between consenting adults - country-by-country legal survey including Morocco.
Washington Blade (Sept 2014): the UN Human Rights Council adopted the SOGI resolution, establishing an international human-rights scrutiny framework applicable to Morocco.

DZA.name: Algeria
DZA.summary:
Algeria is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is criminalised under the Penal Code of 1966 (Ordinance 66-156 of 8 June 1966), which ILGA records as covering both male/male and female/female relations with 2 months' to 2 years' imprisonment and fines of 500-2000 Algerian dinars. The US State Department's 2023 country report gives the same range, 2 months' to 2 years' plus fines, for undefined "homosexual acts". The UK Home Office country-of-origin information report of 26 July 2026 confirms that this 1966 Penal Code remains the operative framework.

Gender transition is not addressed by a dedicated statute, but it is blocked in practice. TUN.name: Tunisia
TUN.summary:
Tunisia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — the country is in an active crackdown. Between 26 September 2024 and 31 January 2025, authorities arrested at least 84 people in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity — mostly gay men and transgender women, per Amnesty International. Penal Code Articles 226 bis (public indecency) and 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) are applied to effectively criminalise gender expression, and enforcement disproportionately targets transgender women.

In detention, trans women are processed under birth names and housed in men's prisons, where local NGO Intersection documents severe abuse. The courts have hardened: in April 2023 the Tunis Court of First Instance refused legal gender recognition to a trans man, dismissing gender dysphoria as “mental illness.” Since President Saied's 2021 power consolidation, the post-revolution space for LGBT organising (Shams, Damj) has been crushed — Shams was dissolved.
TUN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is statutory context; the 2024-25 wave explicitly targeted trans women on gender-identity grounds.

sources.summary: Amnesty International (11 Feb 2025): at least 84 people, mainly gay men and trans women, were arrested, arbitrarily detained and prosecuted in Tunis, Hammamet, Sousse and El Kef between 26 Sep 2024 and 31 Jan 2025 on public indecency and morality charges. A mass conviction on 31 Oct 2024 imposed prison terms of up to 4.5 years, upheld on appeal on 5 Feb 2025, with four people released after sentence reduction.

Cairo 52 country page: Penal Code Article 230 criminalises same-sex conduct with up to 3 years' imprisonment; records enforcement (e.g. Oct 2021 arrest of two transgender women under morality/debauchery provisions) and gaps in legal gender recognition. Primary-law summary for visitor risk.

Intersection Association (Nov 2024): transgender women in Tunisian prisons are processed under their former names and birth gender in detention records, arrest processes and court hearings — systemic identity refusal from detention onward, described as continuous suffering and discrimination inside the prison system. Direct trans-specific custodial-risk evidence.

Cairo 52 (30 Jan 2024): reports the Tunis Court of First Instance's Apr 2023 refusal of legal gender recognition to a transgender man; the court weighed contradictory lower-court judgements (incl. case No. 12304/2018) and found no consistent precedent, leaving recognition unsettled below the Court of Cassation. Shows LGR is court-by-court and often denied.

Human Rights Watch (29 Mar 2016): documents at least seven men prosecuted for consensual same-sex conduct in two cases over six months, all convicted under Penal Code art. 230 (up to 3 years); interviewed detainees reported beatings, forced anal examinations and humiliating treatment by police. Core enforcement-abuse evidence.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 Sep 2017): Tunisia pledged to the UN to stop forced anal testing in homosexuality cases, but kept the anti-gay law itself; Kapitalis warns the pledge does not decriminalise anything. Shows reform-by-commitment without legal change.

TUN.tangentialFactors: Article 230 (sodomy, up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners; the 2024-25 arrest wave explicitly included trans women on gender-identity grounds.
TUN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Egypt (0.22) and Algeria (0.22) on the strength of the current documented arrest wave explicitly including trans women; above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute and lynching culture Tunisia lacks). Tunisia's trajectory is among the world's worst right now.

CMR.name: Cameroon
CMR.summary:
Cameroon criminalises same-sex conduct under Article 347-1 of the penal code, which carries a sentence of up to five years' imprisonment. The 2016 penal code explicitly outlawed same-sex relations, and Cameroon is one of 31 African countries that criminalise them; reporting places Cameroon among the states in Africa with the highest prosecution rates. There is no legal gender recognition procedure and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protection covering gender identity or sexual orientation.

Appearance alone has served as the basis for prosecution. In November 2011 a Cameroonian court jailed Jonas Kimie and Franky Ndome for five years after they were seen wearing women's clothes and ordering Baileys, with the original judge citing their dress, speech and the drink as proof that they were gay. An appeals court acquitted both men on 9 January 2013. Defence lawyer Alice Nkom said the conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts, and Amnesty International welcomed the acquittal. Arrests made on grounds of effeminacy or appearance under the colonial-era sodomy law have carried sentences of six months to five years.

The February 2021 prosecution of the trans woman Shakiro (born 29 July 1997 in Douala, a YouTuber and activist with a substantial online following) is the clearest documentation of how the law reaches visibly gender-nonconforming people. She and her friend Patricia were arrested in a Douala restaurant for the clothes they were wearing and were convicted of attempted homosexuality, indecent dressing and identity-document irregularities. A Douala court sentenced each to five years, the maximum statutory term, plus a fine of 200,000 CFA francs (about $370), on 12 May 2021 reporting, with an appeal filed. Lawyers Alice Nkom and Richard Tamfu called the judgment a political decision made with no proof of any acts. Shakiro described five months of what she called hell in Douala's central prison, held initially in leg chains, before release pending appeal; she subsequently left Cameroon to claim asylum abroad, and has since been granted asylum in Belgium. Her case and exile form part of Cameroon's record of criminalisation prosecutions.

Human Rights Watch reported on 11 May 2022 that violence against LGBTI people had risen sharply: from 9 March 2022 onward, security forces arbitrarily arrested at least six people and detained eleven, all of them victims of group attacks, over alleged consensual same-sex conduct and gender nonconformity, and gendarmes beat two of them in detention. HRW senior researcher Ilaria Allegrozzi framed the pattern as a consequence of the statute itself, which lets both civilians and security forces abuse LGBTI people without consequence. Police violence and mob violence against perceived LGBT people are both documented, and beatings of gay and trans people in public are reported as common. US State Department reporting as far back as 2010 recorded discrimination against gays and lesbians among societal abuses alongside security-force killings, torture, harsh prison conditions and arbitrary arrests, describing the criminalisation context of Article 347.

For a visitor: visible trans expression in a public place is treated in practice as a prosecutable offence, arrests have been made on the strength of clothing, speech and drink orders rather than any observed act, and detention carries a real risk of beatings. No legal mechanism exists in Cameroon to recognise a trans person's gender, and no protection machinery covers anti-trans violence.
CMR.outOfScopeNotes:
Several points remain unresolved or unsourced. The outcome of the appeal against the Shakiro and Patricia sentence is not stated in the sources; only that an appeal was filed and Shakiro was released pending it. Her asylum grant in Belgium is not independently corroborated within this inventory beyond the record carried forward here.

Whether the at least six people arrested and eleven detained by security forces in the period Human Rights Watch described from 9 March 2022 were charged, convicted or released is not sourced. Nor is the number of prosecutions brought annually under Article 347-1: the claim that Cameroon has among Africa's highest prosecution rates is carried without a figure.

The exact current wording and full penalty range of Article 347-1 are not reproduced in the sources; only the five-year maximum is documented. The six-month-to-five-year range for arrests on effeminacy or appearance grounds comes from 2013 reporting and may reflect the colonial-era statute rather than the 2016 penal code. It is unresolved whether the 2013 acquittal established any binding precedent.

Nothing in this inventory addresses passport or visa screening of gender markers at Cameroonian entry points, availability of healthcare for trans visitors, or which specific facilities are accessible; these are not sourced and should not be inferred from the legal findings above.

Conviction rested on stereotypes with no observed acts. Establishes the pattern: arrests on appearance grounds under a historic-era sodomy law with six-month-to-five-year sentences.
CMR.blindTangential:
The prohibition is historic in origin: reporting on the 2013 acquittals describes the underlying statute as historic-era, and the 2016 penal code carried the ban forward in explicit statutory language rather than replacing it. The jurisdiction's position is comparable to that of the 30 other states that criminalise same-sex relations, though its prosecution rate is at the high end of that group.

Outcomes are not uniform. The 2013 appeals-court acquittal, welcomed by an international human rights organisation, shows that convictions resting on appearance and stereotype can be reversed, while the 2021 judgment shows the same evidence base producing the maximum statutory term. The involvement of defence counsel and of two international monitoring organisations indicates an active but narrow defence and monitoring presence.

The trans woman at the centre of the 2021 case had a public profile: she built a large social media and video-platform following discussing trans life before her arrest, and her subsequent exile is part of the same documented pattern. Adjacent official reporting from 2010 lists killings, torture, harsh prisons and arbitrary abuses by security forces alongside anti-gay discrimination, situating LGBTI mistreatment within a broader record of abuse rather than a distinct regime.

Nothing in the sources indicates that general street crime, transport, entry formalities or other travel logistics differ for trans visitors from what applies to any traveller; those are outside this assessment.
CMR.localsOnly:
Cameroonian residents live under the same Article 347-1 exposure as visitors, but with no exit route: gender-nonconforming residents have been arrested in their own neighbourhoods and restaurants, and the Shakiro judgment demonstrates that a residence in Douala offers no protection against a five-year term for how a person dresses.

Residents face abuse from both sides of the enforcement line. HRW documented that in the period from 9 March 2022 security forces arrested and detained LGBTI people who were themselves victims of group attacks, rather than investigating the attackers, and that gendarmes beat two detainees. The researcher's assessment is that the statute licenses civilians and security forces alike to act with impunity.

No procedure exists for a Cameroonian to change legal gender markers on national documents, and no anti-discrimination or hate-crime law protects residents on grounds of gender identity or sexual orientation. Detention itself is a documented hazard: held in Douala's central prison for five months, Shakiro was kept initially in leg chains and described the period as hell, conditions consistent with the harsh-prison and arbitrary-arrest findings in US State Department reporting from 2010. Residents convicted under the statute carry a criminal record that constrains them indefinitely, and those who fled, as Shakiro did, do so by claiming asylum abroad.

TZA.name: Tanzania
TZA.summary:
Tanzania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex activity with up to life imprisonment, and the political environment has been actively hostile since the Magufuli-era crackdowns (arrests, forced anal examinations documented by HRW in earlier years, de-registration of LGBT-serving organisations). The 2024 case of Mauzinde is emblematic: a transgender woman and activist found abandoned in a forest in Rahaleo, beaten, her ears cut off — an attack the UN Human Rights Office called “horrendous.”

OONI documented extensive targeted blocking of LGBTQ websites correlating with the escalating crackdown, and Amnesty's 2024 regional report notes Tanzanian pushes to further criminalise LGBT people. Zanzibar has its own, harsher penal code. There is no legal gender recognition and no protection infrastructure.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest under indecency provisions and mob violence; Zanzibar is worse than the mainland.
TZA.outOfScopeNotes: Life-imprisonment statute is same-sex (climate/situational); the Mauzinde attack is trans-specific.

sources.summary: JURIST (9 Jun 2024): UN Human Rights Office condemned as 'horrendous' the attack on Tanzanian transgender activist Mauzinde of Rahaleo — abducted by 12 men, found beaten in a forest with her ears cut — calling for 'bold action to combat discrimination against #LGBTIQ+ people'; the UN flagged possible violations of ICCPR Art. 20 and Tanzania's Constitution Art. 13 equality guarantees.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Tanzania's criminalisation of same-sex activity (life imprisonment possible).

OONI report 'Tanzania: Surge in online LGBTIQ censorship' (2024, PDF): documents the blocking of LGBTIQ websites and other targeted blocks in Tanzania based on OONI measurement data — including LGBTIQ social networks and rights sites — evidencing state-directed online filtering that constrains LGBT access to information.

Amnesty International report (Jan 2024, AFR 01/75/33/2024, 'We Are Facing Extinction'): documents escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment and the weaponisation of law against LGBTI people in Tanzania, with legislation on same-sex relations deferred after protests, in a documented climate of discrimination limiting rights enjoyment — national-level findings.

Interview (Rainer Ebert, 4 Sep 2020) with three pseudonymised Tanzanian LGBT activists: documents substantial prejudice, discrimination and violence against LGBT people in Tanzania and denial of basic rights, with homophobia and transphobia driving the urgency of rights advocacy; includes definitions of sexual orientation, gender identity and trans woman terms.

Zanzibar Penal Decree Act No. 6 of 2004 (full text, PDF): enacted by Zanzibar's House of Representatives; defines 'gross indecency' broadly as any sexual act falling short of intercourse, sets sexual-offence age thresholds (absolute under 12; under-18 and marriage distinctions) and penalties including imprisonment for three years — Zanzibar-specific criminal law applying to the semi-autonomous islands alongside mainland law.

US State Department 2013 Human Rights Report for Tanzania: the three most widespread problems were security-force excessive force, gender-based violence including FGM/C, and lack of access to justice; also 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' and societal violence against persons with albinism.

TZA.tangentialFactors: Same-sex activity criminalised with up to life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
TZA.comparisons: Pairwise: below Tunisia (0.19 — active arrest wave but no life-imprisonment statute) and above Uganda (0.17 — death-penalty statute, though Tanzania's mutilation attack and life-imprisonment law put it in the same tier).

ETH.name: Ethiopia
ETH.summary:
Same-sex conduct is a criminal offence in Ethiopia under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code, which covers conduct between men and between women. Enforcement is rare, but the provision underpins pervasive stigma, harassment and violence against LGBTIQ+ people. Stakeholder submissions to Ethiopia's Universal Periodic Review report penalties of up to one year, with harsher terms under aggravating provisions; a 2009 academic study of the same legal framework reports a maximum of three years for male homosexuality.

Ethiopia has no legal gender recognition, by either surgical or psychiatric pathway. A stakeholder submission to the 47th session of the UPR states the practical consequence directly: trans men are legally women and trans women are legally men. A trans visitor in a different-gender relationship can therefore be characterised as engaging in same-sex conduct under the criminal code.

The same UPR stakeholder material documents discrimination, violence, stigma in access to services and an absence of police protection for LGBTQ+ people, and identifies transgender people as particularly at risk within the criminalisation framework. The Advocates for Human Rights and House of Guramayle reached the same findings in their April 2024 submission on SOGIE in Ethiopia.

The US State Department's 2023 human rights report describes near-total concealment of identity as the practical result of criminalisation: individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+, activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, and harassment and violence increased toward the end of 2023. Societal discrimination is reported at high levels nationwide across education, employment and healthcare, and being outed carries a risk of physical violence and ostracism.

Enforcement and incitement have converged in documented episodes. In August 2023 security forces carried out a crackdown on 'homosexuality', while non-state actors ran an online incitement wave that ended in physical attacks. Christian and Muslim groups campaign publicly for harsher penalties, and the Orthodox Church declared its stance in June 2024.

There is no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covering gender identity, no protection from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity or expression, and no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protection including gender identity. LGBTI organisations cannot register, and Pride events are not allowed with participants unprotected. The Charities & Societies Proclamation, Article 69, blocks registration of LGBTI groups as contrary to public morality.

US State Department reports from 2008, 2010 and 2011 record the same criminalisation and societal stigma, indicating a legal regime that has persisted across the period covered by the sources. The F&M Global Barometers time series scores Ethiopia 'no' on every protection axis in every year from 2011 to 2024.
ETH.outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty for same-sex conduct is stated inconsistently across the sources: UPR stakeholder material gives up to one year with harsher terms under aggravating provisions, while the 2009 Lund University thesis gives up to three years for male homosexuality. The current operative figure under Article 629 of the 2004 Criminal Code is not resolved by the inventory.

No source in the inventory documents a prosecution of a trans person under the same-sex conduct provision on the basis of their birth-sex legal status, so the mechanism described in the UPR submission remains a legal-structure finding rather than a case-based one.

The inventory contains no material on entry or visa rules, border or airport screening, document checks at the point of entry, or whether gender markers on foreign passports are inspected. Nothing is sourced on how Ethiopian authorities treat a visitor whose passport marker differs from their presentation.

There is no source on access to gender-affirming care, medication continuity or health facilities for visitors, beyond the general finding of discrimination in healthcare. Nor is there sourced material on recognition of foreign marriages or partnerships.

Source dates range from 2008 to March 2026, and several key documents are stakeholder submissions rather than government statements; enforcement practice in the current period is described mainly through the 2023 report and the August 2023 crackdown, with no later enforcement data in the inventory.

ETH.tangentialFactors:
Documented trans-specific enforcement in Ethiopia is thinner than in jurisdictions where gender-identity offences are charged directly; the risk here is structural rather than case-based, arising from criminalisation combined with the absence of legal gender recognition rather than from a documented pattern of trans-targeted prosecutions.

The wider civil-society environment constrains any protection machinery a visitor might hope to reach. US State Department reports for 2010 and 2011 document restrictions on civil society under the Charities & Societies Proclamation, alongside anti-terrorism prosecutions, arrests of opposition figures, torture and harsh prison conditions; the 2023 report records activists describing surveillance and entrapment.

A 2009 Lund University thesis analysing Ethiopian discourse finds that media and elite actors construct homophobia, that the church campaigns effectively in that direction, and that female homosexuality is largely overlooked in public discussion. LBN.name: Lebanon
LBN.summary:
Lebanon is dangerous for trans visitors — the Arab world's most socially open country layered over one of its most explicitly anti-trans statutes. Article 521 of the Penal Code prescribes up to six years' imprisonment for “men disguising themselves as women” — a direct criminalisation of trans feminine expression. Article 534 (“intercourse contrary to the order of nature,” up to 1 year) remains in force though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations. Courts have granted legal gender recognition in some post-surgery cases since 1987, but inconsistently.

Beirut's queer scene is the region's most visible — bars, NGOs (Helem, Proud Lebanon), and a documented court history — but the climate deteriorated sharply since 2022: state-affiliated militia groups attacked queer venues after an anti-discrimination bill was introduced, and Cairo 52 documents rising prejudice and violence against trans people, particularly trans women, who face entrenched marginalisation and family/community violence.

For a visitor: Beirut is navigable with discretion; visible trans feminine expression carries real (statutory) arrest risk; the economic collapse has degraded police predictability in both directions.
LBN.outOfScopeNotes: LGR case law and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing; Art 521/534 are the traveler-relevant statutes.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country review: Lebanon employs both de facto and explicit criminalisation to penalise transgender expression, particularly targeting transgender women; a rise in prejudice and violence against trans and queer people is documented in Beirut, including incidents responding to a decriminalisation bill tabled in parliament; gradual legal-gender-recognition progress since 2015 when a judge approved a plaintiff's gender-marker change on identity documents.

EUAA Country Focus Lebanon, section 7.5, carries a dedicated section on LGBTIQ persons, including activists, in the country-of-origin report. LGBTIQ claims are treated as a distinct risk category with defined terms of reference and a stated source methodology.

HRW (8 Apr 2022, Nora Noralla), regional dispatch 'Tough Territory for Transgender People', documents trans people in Lebanon facing policing and documentation barriers, alongside Egypt and Tunisia, and calls on the three states to ensure access to legal gender recognition.

Manara Magazine (Mar 2022, Nora Noralla) reports that the Lebanese judiciary has a long history of reviewing trans plaintiffs' name and gender-marker changes, governed by the civil registry code of 1951, with an 1887-era precedent recorded as Lebanese Civil Decision 1987, and that medical and religious authorities hold heavy roles. It compares this reasoning with Egypt, Kuwait and the UAE.
Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026) records that same-sex relations for men and for women are not legal throughout the country, and that legal gender recognition is not possible.

HRW (18 May 2018): security forces arrested a prominent LGBT rights activist and pressured him to cancel Beirut Pride — nine days of LGBT-identity activities — in a crackdown HRW called a violation of freedom of assembly and a step backward for LGBT rights.

The Daily Beast (15 May 2018) profiles Georges Azzi, who co-founded Helem in 2004, the first LGBT advocacy group in the Arab world, and later led the Arab Foundation for Freedoms and Equality, campaigning for LGBT equality across hostile regional countries.

HRW (2 Feb 2017): 'Another Judge Questions Legal Basis of Prosecuting Homosexivity Under Lebanese Law' — a ruling pushed Lebanon closer to decriminalising same-sex conduct, following the 2009 precedent that consensual same-sex conduct is not a criminal offence.

LBN.tangentialFactors: Article 534 ("intercourse contrary to the order of nature," up to 1 year) — a situational risk for trans visitors with partners, though several courts have ruled it inapplicable to same-sex relations.
LBN.localsOnly: The case-by-case post-surgery LGR rulings and healthcare pathologisation are resident-facing.
LBN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Sri Lanka (0.33 — Lebanon's scene and partial judicial recognition edge it despite the Art 521 statute) and below Kenya (0.38).

JOR.name: Jordan
JOR.summary:
Jordan does not criminalise same-sex relations: the colonial-era ban was abolished in 1951, and no statute on the books criminalises gender expression as such. That baseline does not translate into safety. Human Rights Watch reported in June 2024 that authorities in Jordan, Egypt and Kuwait substitute public-morality and debauchery provisions for formal criminalisation, using them to harass LGBT people legally.

Legal gender recognition has no clear pathway. Intersex people can change official gender markers, transgender people cannot. The Court of Cassation's ruling in Case No. 2092/2014 allowed a plaintiff born in 1977 to change name and gender from male to female in official records after hormone therapy and surgery undertaken in Australia, since such procedures are unavailable domestically; the court justified the change by reclassifying the plaintiff as intersex rather than recognising a trans identity.

Gender-affirming surgery is permitted for intersex people and criminalised for transgender people under Article 8 of the Medical and Health Liability Law No. 25 of 2018, with penalties reaching ten years' imprisonment; providers face liability under the same medical-liability framework. Care that cannot be obtained at home must therefore be sought abroad.

The operating environment has tightened. A cybercrime law enacted in 2023 criminalises online speech on grounds of inciting immorality and undermines free speech and privacy, and Human Rights Watch's World Report 2024 records the arrest and harassment of peaceful dissidents and journalists under vague laws alongside intrusive digital surveillance. In December 2023 Human Rights Watch documented a coordinated crackdown in which authorities targeted LGBT rights activists, officials smeared activists online by sexual orientation, social-media users circulated their photographs with messages inciting violence, and directors of two LGBT organisations described official intimidation.

CAIRO 52's Jordan profile reports a notable rise in the targeting of transgender individuals and spaces by both security forces and civilians, working through Ottoman- and British-era morality provisions, and states that security forces coerced queer community spaces into complete cessation of activity, pushing transgender and queer people to leave. New legislation further curtails LGBTQ+ speech and digital access, and intersex people can change legal gender markers while transgender people cannot.
JOR.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory attributes a ten-year maximum penalty for sex reassignment to Jordanian legislation in the context of the 2014 case analysis, while the statutory citation supplied for the current ban is Article 8 of the 2018 Medical and Health Liability Law. Whether the ten-year figure derives from the earlier statute, from the 2018 law, or from both is unresolved in these sources.

OutRight International's profile, updated 12 March 2026, states that marker changes are allowed 'in some cases' without specifying the criteria, which sits uneasily with the intersex-only reading given by CAIRO 52. The scope of any exception beyond intersex classification is not sourced here.

Enforcement frequency is not established: the sources document a 2023 crackdown, coerced closures and a reported rise in targeting, but give no figures on arrests, prosecutions or convictions under morality provisions, and no data on violence against trans visitors specifically. Whether the 2014 Court of Cassation ruling binds lower courts as precedent is also not addressed.

IRQ.name: Iraq
IRQ.summary:
Iraq is among the most dangerous countries in the world for a trans visitor. On 27 April 2024 the Council of Representatives passed an amendment to the 1988 Law on Combatting Prostitution that explicitly criminalises consensual same-sex relations, gender-affirming healthcare and diverse gender expression; the President signed it on 29 June 2024 and it has been in force since 1 July 2024. The Library of Congress Global Legal Monitor and ILGA Asia both record it as the operative legal baseline.

The penalties are severe. Same-sex relations carry 10 to 15 years' imprisonment. Undergoing or performing gender-affirming procedures carries 1 to 3 years, which places transition itself beyond the law. The statute also penalises the 'promotion of homosexuality'. Human Rights Watch called for outright repeal on 20 May 2024; the BBC recorded that supporters framed the law as upholding religious values while rights groups condemned it.

State violence is not the only hazard. The US State Department's 2012 human rights report for Iraq documented sectarian violence, torture and impunity alongside what it called societal discrimination and violence against individuals based on perceived sexual orientation and gender identity. A BBC investigation found that dozens, possibly hundreds, of gay people have been killed in recent years while authorities turned a blind eye, and reported a UN assessment that state neglect makes Iraq a perpetrator of the violence rather than a protector of those targeted.

Targeted killings of visible figures have occurred. In October 2023 a prominent Iraqi TikToker was fatally shot in Baghdad amid a crackdown on the LGBTQ community, an attack that coincided with a hardening anti-LGBT climate. The UK Home Office's July 2025 country policy and information note assesses risk from both state and hybrid actors and from non-state actors as substantial enough to underpin LGBT+ asylum claims, including on internal relocation and certification grounds.
IRQ.outOfScopeNotes:
The exact passage date is recorded inconsistently across sources: Human Rights Watch gives 27 April 2024 and ILGA Asia gives 28 April 2024. Both agree on presidential signature on 29 June 2024.

The precise penalty attached to the 'promotion of homosexuality' offence is not stated in the available sources and remains unresolved here.

Whether the amended statute applies uniformly across the Kurdistan Region, and how regional authorities enforce it, is not sourced in this inventory and is unresolved.

Enforcement statistics for the 2024 offences are not available in these sources; the violence documented by the BBC and the US State Department predates the statute and is largely non-state in origin.

VEN.name: Venezuela
VEN.summary:
Venezuela demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing about gender expression is criminalised, but Venezuela has achieved no meaningful legal recognition for LGBTIQ+ people: no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, no hate-crime statute. Since the disputed July 2024 election, activists document unprecedented persecution of the LGBTQ community amid the broader repression wave, and arbitrary detention powers are used broadly against perceived dissidents.

The capital, Caracas, has a small visible scene, and trans women have historically been a visible part of urban life, but the economic collapse means healthcare (including HRT access) is severely degraded, police are predatory toward everyone, and there is no institutional recourse. The risk profile for a visitor is less about trans-specific targeting and more about the combination of zero legal protection, arbitrary state power, and high general violence.
VEN.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether arbitrary detention and the wider repression wave would touch a trans visitor in practice, since the documented persecution is tied to the political crisis rather than trans-specific enforcement; general humanitarian and repression context affects all travellers, and the assessment reflects the trans-specific protection vacuum. Unverified: the current sources record no documented incidents specifically involving trans visitors.

sources.summary: Washington Blade (10 Sep 2024): LGBTQ Venezuelans face unprecedented persecution after the disputed July 2024 election; the opposition presidential candidate fled the country on 7 Sep 2024 -- persecution of LGBTQ people tied to the political crisis, dated.

EUAA asylum country-focus (reference period through 2025): dedicated LGBTIQ+ profile of conditions in Venezuela used for international protection decisions -- the EU asylum agency's factual baseline on how LGBTIQ+ people are treated.
AFS/Vance Center published an LGBTQ guide covering Venezuela in Oct 2024.

Sydney Morning Herald (8 Aug 2015): Tamara Adrian, Venezuela's first transgender candidate, ran for the National Assembly -- landmark trans political candidacy under Venezuela's gender-recognition law context.

Cronica Uno poll (2-3 Mar 2023): a majority of Venezuelans agree the LGBTIQ population should have the same rights as other citizens; 82% know the LGBTIQ+ term (13% do not); 36% think gay/lesbian/bisexuality is innate -- dated public-opinion data.

Blog record (31 Jan 2014): an equal-marriage bill was set to be presented to Venezuela's National Assembly that week (per Aporrea) -- legislative push for same-sex marriage, historic milestone (no later enactment recorded).

El Mundo (13 Dec 2015): Amnesty International declared Rosmit Mantilla -- Voluntad Popular deputy and Venezuela's first openly gay parliamentarian -- a prisoner of conscience held in SEBIN custody; he turned 33 in his cell -- state persecution of an openly gay politician.

Resident-facing political facts: a 2023 poll recorded a majority of the public supporting equal rights for the LGBTIQ+ population, with most respondents familiar with the term; a transgender candidate ran for the national legislature in 2015; and an openly gay parliamentarian was declared a prisoner of conscience in 2015.
