BOL.name: Bolivia
BOL.summary:
Bolivia's 2016 Gender Identity Law grants legal recognition on the basis of self-declared identity through an administrative procedure, permitting a change of name and gender marker without surgery or a medical diagnosis. Gender identity is a protected ground in the country's anti-discrimination legislation.

The 2009 Constitution prohibits discrimination, and the US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report on Bolivia documented that constitutional guarantee alongside persistent societal discrimination against LGBT people.

The 2016 statute was enacted despite low public support for trans rights. Trans activists secured access to legislators of the ruling party, and heteronormative provisions were adopted in the same period because organised religion and LGBT organisations were both constituencies of the party in government. Contradictory laws therefore stand side by side, so a visitor who relies on the gender-identity statute may still encounter provisions built on a heterosexual, cisgender presumption.

Partner recognition followed later: the Inter-American Court of Human Rights issued an opinion in January 2018, and in December 2020 Bolivia's civil registry recognised free unions between same-sex couples.

Formal protection has not produced equal treatment in practice. Agencia Presentes reported in December 2024 that Bolivia's first virtual survey of LGBTI people documented what it called the great exclusion of LGBTI people in the country.

Official institutions show the same gap. Reporting from August 2014 described homosexuality as taboo in Bolivia's armed forces, with gay soldiers testifying anonymously to discrimination and sanctions.

The inventory contains no sourced material on entry or visa rules for trans travellers, on airport or border screening that could disclose gender history, on which gender markers Bolivian authorities accept in foreign passports, on bathroom or facility access rules, on hate-crime sentencing, or on access to legal and medical care while visiting. Those questions remain unresolved on this record.

Whether the administrative recognition process under the 2016 law is available to non-residents or holders of foreign documents is not stated in any source here.

Whether the discrimination documented in Bolivia's armed forces in 2014 persists in its 2014 form is not sourced by the inventory; the reporting is dated and its current status unresolved.

The December 2024 survey source does not give its sample size, method, or whether trans respondents were identified separately from LGBTI respondents as a whole, so the strength of that finding cannot be assessed from this inventory.

A Newsweek article of July 2017 counting 18 countries believed to fully legalise LGBT military service after the US trans military ban does not single out Bolivia and cannot be used to characterise Bolivian policy.

The US State Department's 2011 report also covers arbitrary deprivation of life, prison conditions and corruption; that material is outside the scope of trans visitor risk and has not been carried into the record.

PRY.name: Paraguay
PRY.summary:
Paraguay demands real caution from trans visitors — the most conservative country in its region. There is no legal gender recognition (ten lawsuits on trans name recognition remain pending, unresolved), no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and no hate-crime statute. AP documents that many LGBTQ+ people feel compelled to leave their hometowns due to discrimination, harassment, and gender-based violence; trans women face particular social rejection. Amnesty reports persistent structural discrimination and high gender-based violence.

Nothing criminalises being trans, the capital, Asunción, has a small organised community, and there is no documented police targeting pattern — the risk is social hostility and a total protection vacuum rather than state persecution. Tourist traffic is low and there are no documented trans-visitor incidents.
PRY.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: the pending gender-recognition lawsuits have produced no final rulings, a communication before the international human-rights committee remains pending, and the discrimination-law absence is resident-facing so its direct application to visitors is untested. Unverified: no documented trans-visitor incidents appear in the current sources — tourist traffic is low, and recorded hostility is social rather than institutional persecution.

sources.summary: AP (Sep 2025): 'For Paraguay's transgender women, survival often means leaving home' — discrimination, harassment and gender-based violence push trans women out of hometowns into migration and sex work.

Amnesty International Paraguay page (2025-26): trans people face obstacles to legal identity-document recognition - two trans migrants were denied identity documents; Asuncion's city council banned an event honouring a trans human-rights defender who died in March; plus 37 registered feminicides in 2025 and April's bill to merge the Ministry of Women into a Ministry of the Family.

ecoi / US State Dept reporting: judiciary had yet to issue final rulings on 10 lawsuits filed by trans people for legal name recognition - plaintiffs Yren Rotela and Mariana Sepulveda (suits since 2016) awaited a UN Human Rights Committee decision on their ICCPR Optional Protocol communications. Documented pace of recognition litigation.

PinkNews (20 Oct 2017): political climate report - ruling-party figure Horacio Cartes said he would 'shoot himself in the testicles' if his son married another man (later apologised to those offended); frames the report's account of a push to burn books not promoting 'traditional gender ideology'. Elite-level anti-LGBT rhetoric.

Tico Times (10 Jan 2018): on the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' advisory opinion that OAS signatories must allow same-sex marriage - notes Bolivia, Paraguay and Peru recognise neither same-sex marriage nor unions, i.e. the ruling binds Paraguay (OAS party) though local law lagged; ~300 Costa Ricans celebrated at the court. Inter-American framework applying to Paraguay.

ABC Color (30 May 2017): adoption analysis - Law 1136/97 does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or singles from adopting (prohibitions cover only infectious disease, mental disorders or child-abuse records), a legal gap allowing same-sex adoption as couples or as single men/women, amid a society that still closes doors. Adoption-law reality check.

Ultima Hora: post-IACtHR ruling analysis says people in Paraguay must overcome difficulties adapting the country's laws to extend the right to marriage to everyone - the domestic-law gap the inter-American opinion leaves for Paraguay to close.

Resident-facing facts: the adoption statute does not explicitly bar same-sex couples or single people from adopting; two trans migrants were denied identity documents; and dozens of registered feminicides were documented in 2025.

GTM.name: Guatemala
GTM.summary:
Guatemala demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans, but violence against LGBT people is severe and documented: Asociación Lambda's observatory recorded 147 cases of day-to-day violence and at least 29 murders of LGBTQIA+ people in 2022, with 35 victims saying they intended to flee the country. Guatemalan officials have explicitly excluded trans women from femicide-law protection on the grounds that they are not "biological women," an exclusion that Central American governments have long maintained and that underpins the documented violence context.

There is no legal gender recognition in Guatemalan law. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights' 2017 Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 urged Guatemala and neighbouring states to deliver gender recognition and marriage equality, but compliance remains uncertain; reporting in January 2018 recorded the region's states as urged rather than bound. The Arcus Foundation reported in May 2024 that an organised opposition defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash against recognition in Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras and Mexico.

No SOGI hate-crime statute protects trans people. A 2022 law instead increased penalties for "aggravated" LGBT visibility before being struck down, and Human Rights Watch warned in January 2022 that a bill before Congress threatened to erase gender-identity protections and restrict legal recognition of trans people. Congress has repeatedly advanced anti-LGBT initiatives, including Law 5276 and the 2022 "Life and Family Protection" bill, shelved after protests.

Detention carries documented physical danger. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that trans women held in Guatemala's men's prisons on the basis of birth sex are exposed to sexual assault; Bárbara Herrarte of Redmmutrans described being raped by cellmates at night. The report found no gender-identity-based placement policy, no trans-specific unit or segregation practice, and no court ruling on the custody of trans detainees.

The community is organised, with groups such as Asociación Lambda and Redmmutrans documenting violence and advocating for recognition.
GTM.outOfScopeNotes:
Compliance with Inter-American Court Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 in Guatemala is unresolved in the source material: the inventory records the 2018 urging of states to abide by it and a 2024 assessment that backlash persists, but does not establish whether Guatemala enacted a gender-recognition statute afterwards.

Whether Guatemala's prison authorities adopted a gender-identity placement policy, a trans unit or a segregation practice after the October 2020 Human Rights Watch report is not sourced here and should be treated as unresolved.

The fate of the January 2022 anti-trans bill documented by Human Rights Watch (whether enacted, amended or stalled) is not stated in the inventory; only that it was introduced and threatened gender-identity protections.

Arcus Foundation report (May 2024): the Inter-American Court's 2017 gender-identity opinion (Advisory Opinion OC-24/17) advanced legal gender recognition in El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, but a vociferous opposition movement defining gender in strictly binary terms is fomenting backlash in all four countries.

HND.name: Honduras
HND.summary:
Honduras is among the most dangerous countries in the Americas for trans women. Human Rights Watch finds that states in the region exclude transgender women from their femicide legal frameworks, and Vicky Hernández v. Honduras, heard by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case worldwide. The Court's 2021 judgment held the Honduran state responsible for the 2009 killing of trans activist Vicky Hernández and for failing to investigate it as a bias crime, and ordered reforms including legal gender recognition; Honduras has partially implemented them.

Nothing in Honduran law criminalises being trans, and a legal name-change process exists. Against that, Human Rights Watch's 2009 report "Not Worth a Penny" documents police rape, assault and extortion of trans people, and the US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human-rights problems.

The Lawg Education Fund places Honduras among the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, with trans women facing the sharpest obstacles to justice. Its conclusion is that institutions "fail to effectively investigate and prosecute" these crimes; it attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources and intentional mishandling of cases.

Detention is a specific and acute hazard. Human Rights Watch reports that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which exposes them to physical and sexual abuse. A Honduran judge told the organisation of a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, and said she had informed prosecutors, who did not investigate: "There's no way to protect trans women in men's prisons."

For a visitor, the practical position is that formal legality and formal protection coexist with near-total impunity and with documented abuse by security forces. Arrest, detention or police contact carries the risk of placement in the men's system and of extortion or violence by officers. Coverage of the country's legal framework records bans on same-sex marriage and adoption, so a partner carries no recognition in law.
HND.outOfScopeNotes:
The Reuters feature on Central America's LGBT people returned HTTP 401 at research time and could not be read; only its headline framing is available, and no claim in this record rests on its contents. Whether the trans candidate in the 26 November 2017 congressional election won the seat is not sourced here.

Compliance with the Inter-American Court's 2021 orders is described in the sources as partial; the specific outstanding obligations and their deadlines are unresolved in this inventory. The prison evidence is dated 2017 and 2020, so current conditions in the penitentiaries are not confirmed by these sources. The US State Department material cited is the 2021 edition, and no later edition was reviewed.

SLV.name: El Salvador
SLV.summary:
El Salvador demands real caution from trans visitors — in an unusual transition. Historically it was among the world's most dangerous places for trans women (documented life expectancy of 35 years, among the lowest anywhere; the Camila Díaz Córdova case — a trans woman deported from the US and killed — became the first hate-crime homicide prosecution of its kind). Since 2022, President Bukele's gang crackdown collapsed the national homicide rate by ~98% (107 to 1.9 per 100k), dramatically reducing the gang violence that drove much anti-trans predation.

The trade-off is a state of exception (an exceptional security regime) with mass arbitrary detention (tens of thousands imprisoned, over 75,000 reported, minimal due process) — a risk mechanism that falls on anyone police decide to target, including gender-nonconforming people, with no effective recourse. There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative name change only), no SOGI hate-crime statute, and no institutional protection infrastructure.

The consequence axis of an arrest is documented and grim: since the state of exception began (March 2022), trans women arbitrarily captured in the mass raids are held in the ordinary prison system with no gender-identity accommodation. The only documented custody case (2024 investigative reporting): a trans woman arrested in San Salvador in April 2022 was held at police lockups and then in prison, where custodians forcibly shaved her hair, singled her out with another trans woman for outdoor punishment drills (handcuffed, forced squatting in the sun), and denied her HIV clinic access; a judge freed her after about four months, finding the arrest unsupported, while the second trans woman remained imprisoned. The state-of-exception risk mechanism is therefore not hypothetical in custody: it is where the regime's arbitrary power meets identity-based mistreatment, with no special custody provision documented and release dependent on judicial review.
SLV.outOfScopeNotes: Unresolved: whether the exceptional security regime is applied to trans visitors in practice — its trans-specific application is a risk mechanism, not a documented pattern, and the regime affects all travellers. Unverified: the sources document no trans-visitor incidents, and the historic danger figures describe residents' experience before the recent crackdown. Prison axis: the custody documentation is a single 2024 investigation of one case — no Salvadoran statute, regulation or policy on trans-prisoner housing (birth-sex vs identity placement, special units, solitary/segregation) appears in this record, no special custody provision is documented for prisoners captured in the raids, and how widespread the documented mistreatment is across the mass-detention population is unverified.

CRI.name: Costa Rica
CRI.summary:
Costa Rica decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and, in 2020, became the first Central American country to adopt marriage equality. For a trans visitor this is the region's most permissive legal setting, backed by institutions that operate rather than merely exist.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. Executive Decree 41173-MP, in force since 2018, allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. The state health system funds gender-affirming care.

The UN Special Rapporteur on the right to health, reporting on her July 2023 visit (A/HRC/56/52/Add.2, April 2024), praised near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording her concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups. She recommended intersectional data collection as a basis for addressing it.

Policy headwinds are real. A conversion-therapy prohibition bill has been stalled in committee since its 2019 report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol, withdrawing two of the main preventive frameworks in schools.

Detention is the clearest gap between policy and practice. In June 2017 the Justice Ministry, then under Vice-Minister Marco Feoli, announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual could choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, with relocation decided case-by-case alongside prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module was under consideration, with Spain's model cited. Reporting in June 2019 found a trans woman, Stephanie, held at CAI Orosi de Cartago, a men's facility where staff said only men are held, and she described identity-targeted abuse including a rape with a broomstick-handle at La Reforma in Alajuela witnessed by a custodian. The Justice Ministry told the outlet there were 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time.

Official posture has generally been supportive and has drawn organised opposition. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, when President Óscar Arias and Health Minister María Luisa Avila directed public institutions to facilitate and support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. In May 2014 President Luis Guillermo Solís flew the rainbow flag at the Casa Presidencial on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May, prompting lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and other conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending.

Partner protections extend into social security: survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans (Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016, first individual survivor benefit approved 29 June 2018), with the teachers' separate budget excluded.
CRI.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the post-2018 document process also alters the sex marker on all identity documents, or only the name and photograph, is not resolved by the sources held here; Outright International states only that gender change on documents is possible without surgery or court order.

The practical implementation of the 2017 prison placement policy after 2019 is not sourced beyond the CRHoy reporting of that year, which documented a trans woman held in a men's facility. The 23 transgender prisoners cited by the Justice Ministry is a June 2019 figure and has not been refreshed.

The ILGA World Database entry for Costa Rica is held as a reference link but its individual indicators are not itemised in the inventory, so no claim here rests on it.

Enforcement of anti-discrimination law against trans people, and any screening of gender markers at ports of entry, are not documented in the sources supplied; the UN Special Rapporteur's discrimination findings are stated at the level of marginalised groups generally.

The current status of the stalled conversion-therapy bill beyond its 2019 committee report, and the legal instrument used to scrap the 2025 sex-education programme and anti-bullying protocol, remain unresolved.

CRI.tangentialFactors:
Opposition to LGBT equality is organised and parliamentary rather than street-level. Conservative lawmakers from PASE, National Restoration and allied parties attacked the presidential rainbow flag in 2014 as a provocation, and the conversion-therapy bill has been held in committee since 2019 — a legislature that contains a durable blocking bloc even where the executive and courts move ahead.

The 2025 repeal of the comprehensive sex-education programme and of the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol sits alongside the stalled conversion-therapy bill as the main indicators of rollback pressure. These affect school environments rather than visitors directly, but they signal the direction of domestic policy debate.

The UN Special Rapporteur's 2023 country visit placed Costa Rica among states praised for near-universal coverage, and her concern about discrimination was framed for marginalised groups generally rather than as a finding specific to trans people.

A 2000 Supreme Court ruling held IVF unconstitutional; GayLawNet records it in the context of partnership benefits rather than as a trans-specific rule.

The survivor's-pension extension for same-sex partners, announced in 2016 and applied from 2018, shows benefits machinery reaching same-sex couples, but the teachers' pension budget was excluded, so coverage is not uniform across public schemes.
CRI.localsOnly:
Residents can obtain a legal gender marker change on identity documents administratively under Executive Decree 41173-MP (2018), with no surgery and no court order required.

The state health system funds gender-affirming care for residents. The UN Special Rapporteur recommended that the authorities collect intersectional data to measure and address discrimination against LGBT and gender-diverse people in access to services.

The Justice Ministry's 2017 circular allows trans prisoners to request placement in a facility matching their gender identity, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists, and ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners; an exclusive trans module was under consideration, modelled on Spain's protocols for vulnerable prison populations developed with CEJIL since 2016.

Residents with same-sex partners are entitled to survivor's pensions under all national-budget pension plans, following the Ministry of Labor announcement of 25 June 2016 and approval of the first individual survivor benefit on 29 June 2018; the teachers' separate budget remains outside the scheme.

Since 2008 the state has officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia, with directions to public institutions to support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. The comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol were scrapped by authorities in 2025.
CRI.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Poland and Croatia (0.72 — very different profiles; Costa Rica's judicial trajectory is better, its social conservatism comparable), below Chile (0.74 — fuller LGR) and well above Panama (0.63) and the Dominican Republic (0.50).
CRI.blindSummary:
The state decriminalised same-sex conduct in 1971 and in 2020 became the first jurisdiction under the national framework to adopt marriage equality. For trans visitors it is the most permissive legal setting in the state/province, backed by institutions that operate rather than merely exist.

Legal gender recognition is administrative. an executive decree in force since 2018 allows a change of gender marker on identity documents without surgery and without a court order. The national health system funds gender-affirming care.

The national human rights mechanism's health mandate, reporting on a July 2023 country visit published in April 2024, praised near-universal health coverage and specific protective legislation while recording concern about discrimination affecting LGBT and gender-diverse people among other marginalised groups, and recommended intersectional data collection.

Policy headwinds are real. a conversion-therapy prohibition bill has been stalled in committee since its 2019 report. In 2025 authorities scrapped the comprehensive sex-education programme and the 2022 anti-LGBT bullying protocol.

Detention is the clearest gap between policy and practice. In June 2017 the national justice ministry announced that prisoners who self-identify as transsexual could choose whether to serve their sentence in a men's or a women's facility, decided case-by-case with prison social workers and psychologists; a circular ordered a census of self-identified trans prisoners and an exclusive module was under consideration. Reporting in June 2019 found a trans woman held in a men's facility, where staff said only men are held, and she described identity-targeted abuse including a rape witnessed by a custodian. The ministry told the outlet there were 23 transgender people in the national prison system at the time.

Official posture has generally been supportive and has drawn organised opposition. The government officially recognised the International Day Against Homophobia in 2008, with public institutions directed to support activities directed at the eradication of homophobia. In May 2014 the head of state/province flew the rainbow flag at the presidential residence on equal mast with the national flag for 17 May, prompting lawmakers from conservative parties to call it a provocation while a same-sex civil union bill was pending.

Partner protections extend into social security: survivor's pensions were extended to same-sex partners under all national-budget pension plans, announced in June 2016 and applied from June 2018, with the teachers' separate budget excluded.

PAN.name: Panama
PAN.summary:
Panama is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex activity was decriminalised in 2008 by presidential decree on constitutional nondiscrimination grounds. Legal gender recognition exists but requires surgery — a resident-facing barrier. There is no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and in March 2023 the Supreme Court ruled same-sex marriage is not a constitutional right, signaling judicial conservatism. Panama City has a visible, established trans community and hosts regional LGBT organising.

No traveler-facing restrictions exist: no bathroom laws, no border friction, no documented police targeting pattern. Social hostility is moderate — machista culture persists, and trans women face documented employment exclusion — but violent targeting is far below Northern Triangle levels.
PAN.outOfScopeNotes: Surgery requirement for LGR and marriage ruling are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International current Panama overview: amendment of the general anti-discrimination law to include SOGI grounds was blocked by the National Assembly in 2024 (claiming implicit coverage), no acts are formally recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgeries are not prohibited; at the 2025 UN UPR multiple states urged explicit anti-discrimination protections, gender-recognition reform and stronger violence safeguards — legal reforms remain stalled and Panama lags much of Latin America.

Equaldex data for Panama: homosexuality legal, marriage banned, gender change legal but requires surgery, no nonbinary recognition, no hate-crime protections, no employment/housing discrimination protections, blood donation banned (indefinite deferral), conversion therapy not banned. Only 12% approve of same-sex marriage (AmericasBarometer 2023, ranked #18 of 22).

Washington Blade (16 Feb 2018): Supreme Court Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega withdrew his October 2017 draft ruling against marriage rights — the draft had held the family code's same-sex marriage bars not unconstitutional while suggesting the Assembly consider civil unions; the Panama government signalled it would comply with the landmark 9 January 2018 Inter-American Court of Human Rights decision.

BBC features (14 Aug 2018): in Panama's Guna Yala indigenous territory a flourishing 'third gender' community (Omeggid) is accepted as completely normal, with powerful matriarchal figures elevating women's status — cultural context for how gender diversity is received in this part of the country.

Outright International's current Panama overview: the National Assembly blocked an anti-discrimination amendment in 2024, no acts are recognised as hate crimes, intersex infant surgery is unregulated, the 2025 UPR produced calls for SOGI protections and gender-recognition reform, and reforms remain stalled.

Washington Blade (22 Oct 2017): La Estrella reported Justice Luis Ramón Fábrega's draft ruling finding the family-code sections barring same-sex marriage 'not unconstitutional' while leaving the National Assembly to legislate civil unions ('equality must be constitutionally guaranteed via the law'); the two marriage lawsuits (a UK-marriage recognition suit and a direct family-code challenge) were combined after summer 2017 oral arguments, with amicus briefs from regional marriage-equality advocates and public support from the First Lady, while Catholic and evangelical groups spearheaded opposition.

PAN.tangentialFactors: The 2008 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2023 marriage ruling is a climate signal.
PAN.localsOnly: The surgery-required LGR process is resident-facing; the documented employment exclusion affects residents.
PAN.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Bolivia (0.63 — different profiles: Bolivia has self-declaration LGR, Panama has lower social hostility and better infrastructure) and Vietnam (0.63), below Costa Rica (0.72 — the regional outlier), above Cambodia (0.61).

DOM.name: Dominican Republic
DOM.summary:
The Dominican Republic does not criminalise same-sex relations. The Constitutional Court's 2024 review of the surviving sodomy-law articles resolved that the current criminal code contains no prohibition on same-sex conduct; those articles had reached only police officers and members of the armed forces, with no equivalent provision for heterosexual acts, and Human Rights Watch filed an amicus brief arguing that they violated equality and privacy. The outcome settles the criminal-law question but leaves the wider framework untouched: there is no anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, and no recognition of same-sex partnerships or marriage.

There is no legal gender recognition. A trans visitor has no route to have a chosen name or gender marker reflected in documents, and the Dominican authorities recognise no domestic process for it.

The Dominican Republic accepted recommendations at its Universal Periodic Review on discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and on the rights of intersex persons. The review record shows the commitments being accepted without any accompanying detail on domestic implementation, so no statute, regulation or complaint mechanism follows from them in the sources available.

Documented violence against trans women in the Dominican Republic is high and falls hardest on the most marginalised, in particular trans sex workers. The country's longest-standing trans-led organisation, the Community of Dominican Trans and Transvestite Sex Workers (COTRAVETD), co-founded in 2004, has recorded the community's conditions first-hand for two decades.

Tourist enclaves such as Punta Cana and Puerto Plata operate as insulated resort environments under international scrutiny, and Santo Domingo has a visible trans community and an annual Pride caravan. Beyond those settings, machista culture shapes daily life and police harassment of trans people is a documented feature of enforcement practice, so visibility carries risk that varies sharply by place and by who is present.
DOM.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the source inventory for this pass contains nothing on entry or visa screening, on document or marker rules applied to travellers at the border, on hate-crime sentencing enhancements, or on access to gender-affirming care. Absence here means not sourced, not that the position is permissive.

The UPR record shows accepted recommendations on intersex rights and SOGI discrimination with no domestic implementation detail attached; whether any implementing measure has since been drafted is unresolved in these sources.

The material on the Brewster ambassadorship and the 2017 Santo Domingo conference is LGB-focused. It is used here only as evidence of the hostility and polarisation a trans visitor would be entering, not as direct documentation of trans-specific incidents.

The 2024 constitutional review of the sodomy-law remnants is resolved: the current criminal code does not prohibit same-sex relations; still no anti-discrimination or marriage recognition.

UPR database (Sexual Rights Initiative): the Dominican Republic accepted recommendations on intersex persons' rights and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity — an accepted international-commitment record with no domestic implementation detail shown.

Washington Blade (1 Apr 2017): 300+ activists from Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT/intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo, where Dominican government officials spoke.

Washington Blade (27 Apr 2016): documents the backlash against openly gay US Ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster after his June 2015 presentation with his husband in Santo Domingo, including attacks on LGBT Dominicans and showing organised domestic opposition.

Washington Blade (3 Apr 2017): the openly gay US ambassador's departure left an advocacy void after two years of visible presence, including speaking at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 Jul 2016; his tenure exposed a polarised climate.

Santo Domingo supports an annual Pride caravan and a visible community infrastructure, and Dominican officials have appeared at regional LGBT conferences hosted in the capital. Access to that infrastructure is concentrated in the capital and does not extend to most of the country.

DOM.tangentialFactors:
Organised domestic opposition to LGBT visibility has been demonstrated at the highest levels of diplomatic contact. The June 2015 Santo Domingo appearance of the openly gay US ambassador James 'Wally' Brewster alongside his husband triggered a sustained backlash that included attacks on LGBT Dominicans, and his two-year tenure exposed a polarised climate. When he departed in early 2017, observers noted that his absence left an advocacy void; he had spoken at Santo Domingo Pride on 3 July 2016.

More than 300 activists from across Latin America and the Caribbean attended an LGBT and intersex political-engagement conference in Santo Domingo in April 2017, at which Dominican government officials spoke, and Brazilian authorities formally recommended anti-discrimination legislation to the Dominican Republic at the 2024 UPR. The pattern is one of official engagement coexisting with entrenched organised hostility rather than a consistent line from the state.

Regional comparisons: several neighbouring and peer Caribbean states retain criminal penalties for consensual same-sex conduct, which places the Dominican Republic's settled decriminalisation ahead of parts of its immediate neighbourhood while leaving it behind on protective legislation.

CAN.name: Canada
CAN.summary:
Canada is among the safest large destinations for trans visitors. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and Prince Edward Island's 2016 amendment to its Vital Statistics Act removed the prior surgery requirement, replacing it with a declaration supported by a letter from a doctor. Federally, identity documents can carry an X marker. Entry carries no trans-specific friction: Canadian authorities have neither issued nor received alerts concerning trans travellers.

Healthcare coverage is universal. Discrimination complaints have a defined route as well: the Ontario Human Rights Code expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission publishes guidance setting out how such complaints are handled under the Ontario Human Rights Code.

Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since Bill C-16, federal correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which lawyer Barbara findlay represented a trans prisoner challenging her placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

The counterweight is a rising hate-crime climate. Statistics Canada recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the year before; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from a 2023 peak of 889. Across the longer arc, police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and Egale Canada documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

Two provinces have moved against residents. Alberta and Saskatchewan have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.
CAN.outOfScopeNotes:
Egale Canada's 2024 hate-crime analysis report covering 2SLGBTQI people could not be retrieved for verification; its findings are unresolved here and no claim rests on them.

The federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan survey findings page could not be retrieved either; the content of those quick stats is unresolved.

The inventory provides no gender-identity or gender-expression hate-crime counts for 2024. Only the sexual-orientation category is quantified, so the trans-specific figure for that year is not sourced.

No source in the inventory gives processing times, fees or turnaround for legal gender recognition, for the federal X marker, or for updating passports and identity documents. Those practical timelines are unresolved.

Whether the federal correctional placement rule is applied uniformly across provincial institutions is not sourced; the correctional evidence here comes from one province's officers and from reporting, not from a national audit.

The specific scope, commencement and any litigation over the Alberta and Saskatchewan rollbacks are not detailed in the inventory; only the existence of the measures is carried forward.

sources.title: LGBTQ people in prison — Canada section (Wikipedia)
sources.summary: Placement policy: after Bill C-16 (2017) banned discrimination based on gender identity, transgender prisoners were to be placed in correctional facilities based on their gender identity, and Prime Minister Trudeau promised to review transgender prison assignment to ensure facilities match gender identity; transgender prisoners imprisoned for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security but with some concerns about risk to other prisoners; a 2022 CTV report alleged gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. No special-unit or solitary/segregation policy detail beyond the federal identity-based placement rule.

sources.title: Barbara findlay (Wikipedia) — Synthia Kavanagh case
sources.summary: Canadian lawyer Barbara findlay represented Synthia Kavanagh, a transgender prisoner, in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's correctional institution, showing that trans-prisoner placement and gender-affirming care have been contested in Canadian courts.

CAN.localsOnly:
Residents in Ontario can invoke the Ontario Human Rights Code, which expressly covers gender identity and gender expression, and the Ontario Human Rights Commission's published policy on sexual-orientation and gender-based discrimination sets out the legal context, case law and complaint route.

Document rules vary by province of residence. Prince Edward Island's Vital Statistics Act pathway, requiring a declaration of identified gender plus a doctor's letter with no surgery requirement, is one province's route; residents elsewhere depend on their own provincial statute.

Correctional conditions are documented and contested. A 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some officers raising concerns about risk to other prisoners. A 2022 CTV report alleged that gender-diverse prisoners face a pattern of abuse and discrimination in Canadian jails and are more likely to be victims of sexual assault. Federal policy places prisoners by gender identity and requires consideration of sex-reassignment surgery after 12 continuous months of imprisonment.

Residents are covered by universal healthcare, including gender-affirming care where provinces provide it, and the federal 2SLGBTQI+ Action Plan is the government's standing policy framework for 2SLGBTQI+ issues.
CAN.comparisons: Pairwise: above Australia (0.85 — comparable, but Canada's federal X marker and earlier statutory protection edge it), below Ireland (0.87) and Denmark (0.87).
CAN.blindSummary:

Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the national human rights statute and under the hate-motivation provisions of the national criminal code, both added by a 2017 bill that the upper chamber passed 67-11 in June of that year. Courts have applied those protections consistently, and no jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities.

Legal gender recognition operates largely on self-declaration. Most provinces allow the gender marker on official documents to be changed by declaring one's identified gender, and one province's 2016 amendment to its vital statistics statute removed the prior surgery requirement, replacing it with a declaration supported by a letter from a doctor. Detention is the weakest part of the framework. Since the 2017 bill, national correctional policy requires transgender prisoners to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery. Both placement and gender-affirming treatment have been contested in court, including litigation in which a lawyer represented a trans prisoner challenging her placement in a women's institution and the withholding of gender-affirming medical care.

The national statistics agency recorded 4,882 police-reported hate-crime incidents in 2024, up 1% after a 34% jump the year before; incidents targeting sexual orientation fell 26% to 658, ending three consecutive years of increases from a 2023 peak of 889. Across the longer arc, police-reported hate crime has risen for six consecutive years and is up 169% since 2018, with offences motivated by gender identity and gender expression among the fastest-growing categories, and a national equality organisation documents an increasingly organised anti-trans movement.

Two provinces have moved against residents. Two provinces have enacted policy rollbacks affecting trans people living there, including school-facing measures on names, pronouns and notification of parents. These rules govern residents rather than visitors, but they mark the direction of provincial politics running alongside the human-rights statutes.

AUS.name: Australia
AUS.summary:
Australia treats gender identity as a protected ground under the federal Sex Discrimination Act, in force since 2013. In August 2024 the Federal Court held in Tickle v Giggle that gender-identity discrimination protection extends to trans women as women, and awarded compensation against a female-only dating app that had excluded a trans woman member.

State law has moved the same way. Queensland strengthened discrimination and vilification protections for gender-diverse people in April 2024, and New South Wales passed the Equality Legislation Amendment (LGBTIQA+) Act 2024.

Visitors encounter none of the restrictive machinery found elsewhere: there are no laws confining bathrooms or changing facilities by gender identity, no border friction has been reported for trans travellers, and marriage equality has held since 2017, which matters to same-sex couples arriving together.

Counterweights are documented. The Tickle case itself grew out of organised exclusionary activism, and ANROWS research maps current and emerging threats to trans and gender diverse rights in Australia, naming organised exclusionary campaigns, disputes over access to facilities and to records, and pressure to roll back existing rights. The same body of research documents systemic discrimination and harassment experienced by trans people.

Detention carries the sharpest residual risk. Queensland's 2009 corrective services procedure on transgender prisoners was assessed as largely ineffective; oversight passed to the Inspector of Detention Services Act 2022, fully in force from 2023, and inspection standards issued in August 2023 for Queensland prisons and youth detention centres direct that transgender and intersex prisoners are generally admitted to facilities corresponding to their lived or experienced gender. Queensland placement is therefore identity-based, with a discretionary admission caveat and an exception tied to sexual reassignment surgery.
AUS.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sources in the inventory were not retrievable at research time: the Queensland Human Rights Commission page on strengthened protections for gender-diverse people returned HTTP 404, and the New South Wales Parliament bill document returned HTTP 400. The claims drawn from them rest on the inventory's own descriptions of the underlying items and remain unverified against the primary documents.

Entry and visa screening is not directly sourced. The absence of border friction for trans travellers rests on no contrary reporting in the inventory rather than on a rule or official statement, and the treatment of a foreign passport carrying a changed gender marker is unresolved here.

The wording of the Queensland surgery exception is ambiguous in the source: it states that only transgender people who have undergone sexual reassignment surgery are excluded from the identity-based admission process, and the direction of that exclusion is not resolved.

The assessment that Queensland's 2009 procedure was largely ineffective comes from a 2009 Queensland Law Student Review article rather than an official evaluation, and no source in the inventory reports on how the 2023 standards have been applied in practice.

The historical account of state-by-state decriminalisation of homosexual conduct was set aside as general LGB legal history with no trans-specific bearing. No source in the inventory addresses hate-crime statutes, public-accommodation rules outside the facilities disputes ANROWS maps, or healthcare access for visitors.

NZL.name: New Zealand
NZL.summary:
New Zealand is exceptionally safe for trans visitors. Legal gender recognition by self-declaration has been in force since 2023 (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act); the Law Commission reviewed Human Rights Act protections for trans, non-binary and intersex people in 2024; and takatāpui/rainbow communities have deep institutional recognition. There are no bathroom laws and no border friction.

The counterweights are documented and significant for the street climate: reports of gender-identity hate crimes jumped 42% between 2022 and 2023 (161 to 229 incidents), spiking around the Posie Parker visit (the visiting campaigner); the national survey (Counting Ourselves) found almost 1 in 5 trans and non-binary people were threatened with physical violence in four years, and 8% experienced it; and community advocates accuse police of failing rainbow communities amid far-right agitation (library events crashed, church arson threats).

For a visitor: full legal protection; moderate probability of harassment in charged spaces; functioning (if criticised) institutions.
NZL.outOfScopeNotes:
Counting Ourselves (resident-survey) data describes residents; healthcare gaps are resident-facing; marriage and partner-travel questions are not covered by the current sources (equal marriage has been legal in this nation since 2013, per the historical materials).

Unresolved: whether the documented 42% hate-incident increase translates into visitor-facing encounter rates; the community-archive source is context material with no risk finding for this record.

sources.summary: RNZ (17 Apr 2024), Official Information Act data: 229 gender-identity-motivated hate incidents reported to police in 2023 vs 161 in 2022 — a 42% rise — with police saying the figure likely understates true anti-trans hate, and a spike in the month anti-trans activist Posie Parker visited (March 2023). For this record: the quantified police dataset with the undercount caveat.

RNZ (27 Feb 2025), Counting Ourselves survey: almost one in five trans and non-binary New Zealanders were threatened with physical violence because of their gender identity in the past four years, and 8% experienced deliberate physical violence — the first clear population picture of violence against these communities. For this record: survey-based prevalence figures.

New Zealand Law Commission Issues Paper 53 'Ia Tangata' (June 2024): a review of the protections in the Human Rights Act 1993 for transgender people, non-binary people and people with innate variations of sex characteristics - official law-reform consultation document.

The Spinoff opinion (2 Jul 2024) by Jennifer Shields: after a spate of rainbow event cancellations and a 2023 Posie Parker protest, calls for more security for rainbow communities — noting statutory wins (Births, Deaths, Marriages and Relationships Registration Act 2021 easing ID correction; Conversion Practices Prohibition Act 2022) alongside a worsening street climate. For this record: community-safety assessment dated mid-2024 with the recent statutory wins named.

PrideNZ.com: archive of over 1,000 audio recordings of interviews and events from Aotearoa NZ's LGBTQIA+ communities, a rainbow timeline, over 18,000 GayNZ.com articles (2001-2017), and Homosexual Law Reform 40th-anniversary resources including Hansard transcripts of the parliamentary debates. For this record: a usable local community/archive resource base (context, not risk).

ALB.name: Albania
ALB.summary:
Albania does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct or gender expression. Homosexuality carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; the operative instrument since 2010 is an anti-discrimination law that covers sexual orientation but provides no basis for same-sex marriage. A National LGBTI Action Plan runs from 2021 to 2027, and observers record that implementation falls short of its commitments.

Nothing in the record indicates trans-specific screening at the border or on arrival, and no restriction on facilities or bathrooms is on record. Police targeting of trans visitors is not documented in any source here. The realistic exposure is social rather than legal: Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people in 2023, and hostility is sharper outside Tirana and in more conservative rural areas. Tirana hosts an annual Pride.

International scrutiny is unusually open for the region. Graeme Reid, the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, carried out a country visit from 1 to 12 July 2024, issued an end-of-mission statement on 12 July 2024, and presented report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 on 17 June 2025 assessing Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards. EU candidate status is the stated driver of slow alignment with those standards.

Protection machinery exists and has been used. An Anti-Discrimination Commissioner receives and mediates complaints, and has ruled against public figures who made hostile statements about LGBT people.
ALB.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no sourced information on legal gender recognition in Albania, on rules for changing name or sex markers on identity documents, or on whether such changes affect passport presentation at entry. This is unresolved here, not established either way.

No source addresses visa or border screening procedures that could disclose a visitor's trans status, nor any restriction or requirement affecting access to hormone therapy or other trans-specific healthcare while in the country.

Sentencing outcomes and enforcement results for the ten bias-motivated violence cases logged in 2023 are not stated, so the effectiveness of criminal-law responses to that violence cannot be assessed from these sources.

The two Koha Jonё items carry 2018 URLs but 2021 publication dates; the discrepancy is unresolved. Whether the implementation deficits identified in the National LGBTI Action Plan have been remedied following the July 2024 visit and the June 2025 report is likewise not sourced.

sources.summary: End-of-mission statement of the UN Independent Expert on violence and discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity after the country visit to Albania, 1-12 July 2024. It assesses good practices and challenges and offers recommendations to the State, and stands as the international-review baseline for Albanian SOGI conditions.

ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) Albania chapter: discrimination complaints filed over the film 'Strange World' screenings were mediated, with the Commissioner ruling in favour in one case; Rainbowphilia logged ten bias-motivated violence cases against trans people; groups ran support schemes including food packages for trans sex workers and people living with HIV.

UN report A/HRC/59/43/Add.1 (17 Jun 2025) by Independent Expert Graeme Reid on the Albania visit of 1-12 Jul 2024: evaluates Albania's adherence to national and international human-rights standards on sexual orientation and gender identity, drawing on information gathered before, during and after the visit.

PinkNews (Feb 5, 2010): Albania passed an anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation but without same-sex marriage; homosexuality had carried a ten-year prison sentence until 1995; Prime Minister Sali Berisha had voiced support for gay marriage in July 2009, framing the law as EU-integration driven.

Koha Jonё (Jul 30, 2021, Albanian): Democratic Party MP Luçiano Boçi attacked LGBT campaigning in high schools as extra-curricular groups with a 'suspicious, revolting agenda' — a record of parliamentary hostility toward LGBT education work under the Berisha-led opposition.

MKD.name: North Macedonia
MKD.summary:
North Macedonia is workable for trans visitors. Nothing is criminalised, and the capital, Skopje, hosts both Pride and an organised Trans March for Visibility (TransFormA, March 2024) — public trans organising that proceeds without serious incident. Anti-discrimination law covers sexual orientation and gender identity (2019 amendments). There are no same-sex or equal marriage rights (the 2014 marriage-definition motion, defining marriage as a union of one man and one woman) — a consideration for partners travelling as a couple — and the Law on Civil Registry’s legal gender recognition chapter was withdrawn.

Counterweights: hate speech and hate crimes remain common with no effective justice-system response (European Commission), social-media death threats are routine, and the legal gender recognition absence is documented.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; small but functioning community; standard regional street-hostility caution; no marriage recognition for same-sex visiting couples and no local document-change pathway; border and document-screening practice is not covered in the current sources.
MKD.outOfScopeNotes:
Justice-system non-response and legal-gender-recognition absence are resident-facing/climate signals; the sources do not address visitor document screening or border treatment of trans travellers.

Unverified: whether the 2014 marriage-definition motion is current law (the sources only record its submission), and whether reported community events continue to proceed without serious incident.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia: hate speech remained serious with countless reports and no meaningful state response (European Commission country report concurs); in September the Basic Criminal Court of Skopje sentenced a man to two years for assaulting an LGBTI activist with SOGI aggravating grounds of the Criminal Code; ECRI called for a ban on nonconsensual intersex surgeries.

Global Voices (30 March 2024): TransFormA’s March for Visibility of Trans People in Skopje marked Transgender Day of Visibility with the words "we march bravely". The report also notes a worrisome trend of mobilising religious institutions to scapegoat this small vulnerable group.

ILGA-Europe/ERA LGBTI Enlargement Review 2024 (covering 2023), North Macedonia chapter with the National Network against Homophobia and Transphobia: top priority is Legal Gender Recognition — the government withdrew the Draft Law on Civil Registry containing the LGR chapter a day before Parliamentary Committee review.
US State Department 2019 Human Rights Report for North Macedonia: official assessment including the SOGI section - anti-discrimination law, societal violence and discrimination against LGBT persons.

Washington Blade (13 October 2023): Serbian and North Macedonian LGBTI groups quantify how anti-LGBTQ discrimination harms the economies of Serbia and North Macedonia, casting discrimination as a measurable drag on growth and jobs.

Balkan Insight (February 2012): ILGA-Europe’s Rainbow Europe Index ranked Macedonia worst in the Balkans at −2 on the 17-to−7 scale — the only Balkan country in the "red zone" of gross human-rights violations and discrimination.

Balkan Insight (July 2014): the government submitted a constitutional motion defining marriage strictly as a union of one man and one woman — ruling out same-sex marriage and adoption — as an early act of the re-elected Gruevski government, needing two-thirds of MPs with the conservative DPA expected to supply the extra votes.

MNE.name: Montenegro
MNE.summary:
Montenegro is workable for trans visitors — the Western Balkans' most advanced legal framework. It has a same-sex partnership law (2020), anti-discrimination law covering gender identity, and SOGI-inclusive hate-crime provisions; Podgorica Pride proceeds annually. Counterweights documented by ILGA-Europe: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech in political rhetoric is a serious issue, and misdemeanour charges are overused in place of proper hate-crime prosecution (European Commission). There is no legal gender recognition law (administrative practice is inconsistent).

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning institutions, small tolerant coastal tourist scene; standard caution in the north.
MNE.outOfScopeNotes: LGR inconsistency and prosecution-practice gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2024 (covering 2023) chapter on Montenegro: anti-LGBT and misogynistic hate speech and political rhetoric continued; a psychologist wearing non-gender-conforming clothes on TV was targeted by hate comments, threats and several physical attacks (police response monitored); a groundbreaking study found only 28.1% of companies' anti-discrimination policies explicitly mention sexual orientation; a new Action Plan for the 2019-2023 LGBTI Strategy was adopted with €45,000; over 222 online hate-speech incidents reported.
Human Dignity Trust records Montenegro's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct in 1977, grouped with Croatia and Slovenia as a European cohort of that year (page updated 18 June 2026).

GlobalGayz (March 2012): decriminalised in 1977; small gay scene with deeply entrenched anti-gay opinion, discrimination and harassment when visible; the first Podgorica Pride was cancelled in May 2011 after two attacks on gay people in the capital. Dated but concrete on social climate.

Al Jazeera (Oct 2013): Montenegro's first Pride marched through Podgorica — roughly 150 marchers guarded by some 2,000 police, rock-throwing opponents stopped by tear gas; Queer Montenegro's Danijel Kalezic: 'From this day we are no longer invisible.' Shows both state protection and organised hostility.

PinkNews (2 Aug 2019): MPs blocked the same-sex partnership law on 31 July 2019 despite government backing — ERA's Western Balkans office: LGBT people 'forced to live as second-class citizens' (no hospital visitation or shared-benefit rights); a 2018 ERA study found 51% of LGBT+ Montenegrins were closeted.

CDM (Dec 2018): the Government adopted the Draft Law on Same-Sex Partnership granting couples near marriage-equivalent rights via registrar ceremony — explicitly excluding parenting, foster care and adoption; shows the reform trajectory before the 2019 parliamentary block.

MNE.tangentialFactors: The 2020 same-sex partnership law — relevant to trans visitors travelling with partners.
MNE.localsOnly: No LGR law (administrative practice inconsistent) — resident-facing; the misdemeanour-overuse practice affects resident victims.
MNE.comparisons: After the 2026-08 audit: the audit found Montenegro’s framework (partnership law + SOGI hate-crime provisions + protected Pride) objectively stronger than Hungary’s (propaganda law in force + LGR ban + German court’s extradition-refusal finding). MNE raised to 0.67, effectively tied with ROU; HUN sits at 0.68 by its own anchors; MNE at 0.67 reflects slightly thinner implementation.

BIH.name: Bosnia and Herzegovina
BIH.summary:
Bosnia and Herzegovina does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina removed it from its criminal code in 1996 and Republika Srpska followed in 1998, each through its own entity-level code, so a trans visitor carries no legal exposure on that basis.

Statutory protection at state level is explicit. The amended Anti-Discrimination Law, adopted in 2016 after public consultations in autumn 2015, covers sexual orientation and gender identity in the terminology used locally; the Sarajevo Open Centre presented the amendments together with the Agency for Gender Equality. Bias-motivated violence is treated as an aggravating circumstance in sentencing in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, where the hate-crime regulation names sexual orientation and gender identity directly.

Institutional practice has moved as well. Sarajevo Pride has proceeded annually since 2019 under heavy police protection, and most cantons have appointed prosecutors specifically for anti-LGBTI hate crimes.

The counterweight is documented hostility. The Sarajevo Open Centre's Pink Report 2024, the annual monitor of LGBTI human rights in the country, records a year in which a number of negative events had significant impact and concludes that the worsening trend visible for some time is becoming increasingly evident. Organised anti-LGBTI violence has occurred even where security was arranged in advance: in February 2014 attackers assaulted Sarajevo Pride organisers after the Sarajevo Open Centre had coordinated security with police roughly three weeks earlier, and Human Rights Watch called for the attackers to be prosecuted.

For a visitor the assessment is that there is no legal exposure, that Sarajevo and established tourist areas are workable, and that visible trans presentation carries elevated risk in Republika Srpska and in rural areas, where the monitoring trend is unfavourable and the protection machinery is thinner than in the capital.
BIH.outOfScopeNotes:
Marriage and partner recognition for trans visitors and residents is not addressed by the sources assembled for this record and remains unresolved here.

The content of Republika Srpska's separate hate-crime regime, as distinct from the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina's, is not sourced in this inventory; only the fact that the two regimes differ is established.

Whether the attackers who assaulted Sarajevo Pride organisers in February 2014 were prosecuted is not stated in the available material, despite Human Rights Watch's public demand that they be.

The Pink Report 2024 is cited here for its overall assessment of the year and the direction of the trend; the specific incidents it catalogues are not reproduced in this record.

For this record: the documentation pathway a trans person navigating the system faces — resident-facing, not a border issue.

For this record: entity-level legal baseline plus the pre-2016 gender-identity protection gap.

For this record: entity-level sentencing enhancement for bias attacks in FBiH (RS runs its own separate regime).

BIH.localsOnly:

The Council of Ministers' 2022 action plan conditions changes to identity documents on completed medical transition, and the constraints imposed through that pathway are described by local researchers as discriminatory and degrading.

Trans residents also face restricted access to healthcare and institutional suspicion when dealing with the authorities, a position the Balkan Diskurs reporting of October 2024 characterises as precarious. These are documentation and care-access problems that arise inside the system rather than at the border.

Residents bringing a bias-motivated incident forward can draw on the state Anti-Discrimination Law and, in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, on hate-crime aggravation at sentencing; most cantons have designated prosecutors for anti-LGBTI hate crimes, which affects how such complaints are handled locally.
BIH.comparisons: Pairwise: below North Macedonia (0.62 — MKD's anti-discrimination law is stronger) and above Cambodia (0.61, tie — different profiles).

GEO.name: Georgia
GEO.summary:
Georgia is dangerous for trans visitors, and the position has deteriorated sharply. In September 2024 the Parliament of Georgia adopted the law "On the Protection of Family Values and Minors", which bans legal gender recognition, transition-related healthcare, public LGBT assembly and the dissemination of "LGBT information". It is the harshest such legislative package in the region, and it removed the two routes by which a trans visitor or resident would ordinarily deal with documents and care.

One day after the law passed, Kesaria Abramidze, a trans model and influencer and one of Georgia's best-known transgender women, was stabbed to death in her apartment in Tbilisi. German foreign-affairs committee chair Michael Roth and EU foreign policy chief Josep Borrell condemned the law as further derailing Georgia's EU path. AP reported in October 2024 that the killing, together with Russia-style "gay propaganda" provisions, had raised fears of hate crimes against LGBT people in the conservative South Caucasus nation.

The refusal of protection by the security apparatus predates the 2024 law. In June 2019 the Interior Ministry declared the country's first-ever Tbilisi Pride "impossible" in the planned city-centre locations, citing safety risks; organisers reported a week of pressure from an unidentified government official to cancel the march, and far-right groups had vowed to thwart it. In 2021 the Pride office was ransacked by far-right mobs while police stood by, and investigators have documented police failure to protect demonstrators.

The machinery of protection is itself under strain. The foreign-agents law is choking local rights groups and LGBT organisations, which refuse to register as "foreign agents" and consequently face fines or bankruptcy. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that the anti-LGBTI law has eroded trust in institutions, that applications to LGBTI services have fallen as a result, that large numbers of LGBTI people are fleeing Georgia and seeking asylum documentation, and that misinformation demonising the LGBTI community is spreading.

Trans-specific legal barriers are older than the 2024 package. Legal activists told IWPR in May 2012 that the law needed changing to allow gender recognition, and that job applications become difficult when a person's gender identity does not match official paperwork. In August 2024 WISG and partner organisations reported to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers calling for urgent action: effective investigations into anti-LGBTI violence, withdrawal of the proposed anti-LGBTI legislation, improved hate-crime data collection, and protection of LGBTI assembly and expression. Those requests describe protections that are not currently in force.
GEO.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the killing of Kesaria Abramidze has resulted in arrests, charges or convictions is not sourced in the available inventory; the reporting establishes the death and its timing against the law, not the criminal outcome.

The quality and completeness of hate-crime data collection is not resolved here. The August 2024 report to the Council of Europe Committee of Ministers recommends improved collection, which implies gaps, but no figures on recorded anti-trans offences or prosecution rates are available in the inventory.

The enforcement posture of the 2024 law against visitors specifically is not documented. The inventory establishes the statutory bans and a documented pattern of police non-protection of demonstrators, but contains no reported case of a foreign visitor prosecuted under the package.

The status of the 2019 and 2021 incidents as to any legal liability of the Interior Ministry or of the mobs remains unresolved; no sourced outcome of investigations or litigation is available.

The 2012 employment-material is more than a decade old and predates both the 2024 statute and subsequent administrative changes, so its precise current application to residents is undated rather than confirmed.

The extent to which the foreign-agents law's registration requirements fall on a foreign visitor's own advocacy, as distinct on resident organisations, is not sourced and should be verified with a Georgian legal adviser before relying on it.

ARM.name: Armenia
ARM.summary:
Armenia carries no criminal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct; the provision was repealed in 2003, and the country has no statute of the restrictive type applied to LGBT people in neighbouring Azerbaijan. Trans visitors face no legal exposure for being trans, but the legal framework offers them little affirmative protection: there is no discrimination protection on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the anti-discrimination bill tabled in 2018 did not pass.

Legal gender recognition exists as an administrative practice and is medicalised. Equaldex records that a legal gender change has been available since 2006 but requires surgery, that gender-affirming care is restricted, and that no non-binary recognition is available. Hate-crime protection covering bias-motivated violence is characterised as ambiguous since 2022, and same-sex marriage is prohibited.

Pink Human Rights Defender NGO's annual report on the human rights situation of LGBT+ people in Armenia during 2024 documents discrimination, torture and inhuman or degrading treatment including sexual violence, domestic violence and extortion, violations of private and family life, and discrimination in education and work. It records hate speech as a persistent feature of public discourse and devotes a chapter to the pressure directed at a transgender individual who participated in a beauty pageant.

Trans people in positions of visibility have drawn extreme political hostility. In April 2019 Lilit Martirosyan, Armenia's first registered trans woman, received death threats after delivering a speech on LGBTI discrimination in the national assembly; members of parliament called for her to be burned alive.

Enforcement of violence against LGBT spaces is unreliable. In May 2012 a Molotov cocktail was thrown at the gay-friendly DIY bar in Yerevan and a fire set; police took twelve hours to respond, though two suspects were later detained through CCTV footage. Equaldex's public-opinion measure puts acceptance at 5 out of 100, indicating a social environment where visible trans presence draws hostility well beyond central Yerevan.

The capital has an organised community, with Pink Armenia and the trans-led organisation Right Side operating locally. Visibility outside those networks remains a source of risk rather than protection.
ARM.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current inventory addresses Armenian border control, visa issuance or document-screening practice as it affects trans travellers, including what happens if a passport gender marker does not match presentation. That question remains unresolved here.

The requirement that legal gender change be preceded by surgery is sourced to Equaldex, a comparison aggregator, rather than to the text of the Armenian legislation itself; the governing statute was not supplied for verification. The same applies to the characterisation of hate-crime protection as 'ambiguous since 2022' and to the restricted status of gender-affirming care.

The 5/100 public-acceptance figure comes from Equaldex's methodology and has not been corroborated against an Armenian polling source. The ILGA-Europe/COC mission report dates from 2009 and describes conditions at that time rather than the present.

AZE.name: Azerbaijan
AZE.summary:
Police conduct is the clearest documented danger. In September 2017, national police in the capital detained dozens of LGBT people on dubious charges and beatings were documented; at least 60 people were imprisoned or fined, and the raids formed part of a wave of arrests ahead of an international sporting event. In July 2023, officers raided a private birthday party at which queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

A trans woman was murdered in the capital in March 2024, and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. The response of the authorities is as significant as the violence itself: nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring a serious investigation.

In April 2024 the European Court of Human Rights issued a ruling on the September 2017 arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, a matter the Azerbaijani government had acknowledged in 2019. The judgment addresses state conduct that the authorities themselves conceded had occurred.

Hostile messaging originates in official and state-affiliated media. State-affiliated Real TV aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding access to trans healthcare. Media monitoring by QueeRadar found 77% of 428 analysed pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag from a cafe in Baku.

For a visitor, the practical reading is that contact with police carries a risk of mistreatment rather than an expectation of protection, and that visible signs of LGBTI affiliation can attract hostile attention from media and officials in both public and semi-public settings.
AZE.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources reviewed here do not address whether gender expression or gender identity is criminalised in Azerbaijan, what penalties might apply, or whether any statute regulates public order in ways used against trans people. That question is unresolved on this inventory.

Entry and visa rules, gender markers on passports and other travel documents, and border screening practices are not covered by these sources and remain unsourced.

The outcome of the investigation into the March 2024 murder of a trans woman is not stated in the material reviewed, and whether charges were brought is unresolved.

Access to healthcare, including hormone therapy or gender-affirming care, appears only as the subject of a Women's Day march demand; no source here describes the availability of such care to a visitor.

Hate-crime legislation and its application to anti-trans violence are not addressed in this inventory.

Profiles 'Durdana', 29, arrested, denied housing and employment, and dependent on community support after her trans-friendly employer shut down.

In July 2023, officers raided a private birthday party at which queer guests were subjected to forced medical examinations, physical and sexual harassment, and threats of being outed.

a trans woman was murdered in the capital in March 2024, and the police investigation into the killing was inadequate. The response of the authorities is as significant as the violence itself: nothing in the record indicates that the state treats the killing of a trans woman as a matter requiring a serious investigation.

In April 2024 a supranational human rights court issued a ruling on the September 2017 arrests and mistreatment of LGBTI people, a matter the national government had acknowledged in 2019. The judgment addresses state/province conduct that the authorities themselves conceded had occurred.

Hostile messaging originates in official and state/province-affiliated media. A state/province-affiliated television channel aired discriminatory hate speech against LGBTI people after a Women's Day march demanding access to trans healthcare. Media monitoring found 77% of 428 analysed pieces hateful or biased against LGBTIQ people, and an activist was told to remove a rainbow flag from a cafe in the capital.

For a visitor, the practical reading is that contact with police carries a risk of mistreatment rather than an expectation of protection, and that visible signs of LGBTI affiliation can attract hostile attention from media and officials in both public and semi-public settings.

The outcome of the investigation into the March 2024 murder of a trans woman is not stated in the material reviewed, and whether charges were brought is unresolved.

Hate-crime legislation and its application to anti-trans violence are not addressed in this inventory.
