KAZ.name: Kazakhstan
KAZ.summary:
Kazakhstan carries no direct legal exposure for a trans visitor. Consensual same-sex conduct is not criminalised, no statute restricts changing clothes according to gender presentation, no bathroom or facilities restriction applies, and no propaganda law is in force. Police conduct toward trans people is described as unhelpful rather than predatory, with no recorded pattern of police targeting.

A propaganda ban is nonetheless under active consideration. In June 2024 the Ministry of Culture and Information confirmed it was reviewing the petition 'We Are against Open and Hidden LGBT Propaganda in Kazakhstan!', filed by the Union of Parents, which met the threshold for government consideration. Human Rights Watch warned on 10 July 2024 that the proposed ban would violate rights nationwide. A visitor should treat the current absence of a propaganda statute as the state of the law today, not as a settled position.

Legal gender recognition exists but is heavily medicalised. Psychiatric board assessment and surgery requirements are applied in practice, so a visitor whose documents do not match presentation should expect no administrative route to reconcile them while in the country.

The documentation of bias violence is weak. The OSCE/ODIHR hate crime reporting summary for 2024 records that Kazakhstan has not reported hate-crime data since its 2018 report and has no nominated National Point of Contact for hate crimes, with victim-support and awareness measures identified as lacking. A visitor who experiences bias violence would encounter a reporting machinery with no designated entry point.

Recorded incidents remain real. An international monitoring body recorded 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents in Kazakhstan in 2024. The ILGA-Europe Annual Review covering January to December 2023 documents an LGBTQI activist almost run over in a bias-motivated attack that drew no investigation, and an LGBTQI+ education NGO refused registration of its employment site after listing its focus as its stated activity.

Trans-specific movement into the country is documented: ILGA-Europe records a wave of transgender people arriving from Russia since 2022, indicating cross-border entry by trans people without a legal barrier to arrival.

Social risk operates alongside a functioning legal remedy. Kazakhstan's Supreme Court ordered compensation in September 2019 from a Facebook user who posted a video of two women kissing and solicited homophobic comments, rejecting a 'moral foundations' defence in favour of privacy rights. The two women fled Kazakhstan for eight months fearing for their safety before the ruling, which measures the gap between what the courts will protect and what daily life imposes.

For a visitor the assessment is: no legal exposure, low visibility for anyone who does not disclose, main cities presenting no practical difficulty, and social hostility rather than the state as the operative risk.
KAZ.outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the Union of Parents propaganda petition after June 2024 is unresolved in the available sources; no source confirms whether it advanced to drafting, was shelved, or produced legislation.

Whether the 62 anti-LGBTI bias incidents recorded in 2024 are disaggregated for trans victims is not sourced, so the trans-specific share of that count cannot be stated.

Whether the psychiatric board and surgery requirements for legal gender recognition are codified in subordinate regulation or applied as administrative practice is not sourced here; the inventory supports 'applied in practice' only.

Whether Kazakhstan has since resumed hate-crime reporting to ODIHR or nominated a National Point of Contact after the 2024 summary is unresolved.

No source in this inventory documents a trans-specific physical assault with a named victim and a dated outcome, so the violence findings rest on the activist incident recorded for 2023 and the aggregate 2024 count.

Within its region Kazakhstan stands as the most liveable country in Central Asia for trans people, a relative statement that does not lift it to the standard of European jurisdictions. The comparison matters mainly for expectation-setting: the floor is low, and the ceiling here is not high.

The June 2024 propaganda petition is the principal source of legal turbulence. It has not produced legislation in the sources available, but it is a dated, documented and government-acknowledged attempt that would, if enacted, restrict public expression about LGBT people nationwide.

Regional displacement affects the picture. Transgender people have been arriving from Russia since 2022, and the presence of a documented inflow suggests Kazakhstan is being used as a destination by people leaving a worse regime, not as a transit hazard.

UZB.name: Uzbekistan
UZB.summary:
Uzbekistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Article 120 of the Criminal Code criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — and Human Dignity Trust notes transgender people may be targeted under it, since there is no legal gender recognition and trans people are legally their birth sex. There is substantial evidence of recent enforcement: frequent arrests, and extortion by threat of arrest, with police as the most common perpetrators of anti-LGBT violence; torture goes unpunished (HRW). Because of criminalisation, victims cannot report violence to authorities.

ECOM's 2024 national report documents continuing rights violations, and the Justice Ministry denies registration to independent human-rights groups — no community infrastructure can operate openly. There is no documented trans-visitor case, but the legal mechanism (birth-sex status + Art 120) means a trans visitor discovered in a same-sex-appearing relationship faces direct prosecution risk, and discovery itself invites extortion.
UZB.outOfScopeNotes: Art 120 formally applies to male same-sex conduct; its application to trans people is via birth-sex legal status — a direct mechanism, not merely climate.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust's country profile documents Uzbekistan's criminalisation of same-sex activity under Article 120 of the criminal code, which carries up to 3 years.

HRW World Report 2024 (events of 2023): same-sex conduct between men remains criminalised (up to 3 years); police target gay/bisexual men and trans women with arbitrary detention, prosecution and imprisonment; forced 'forced examinations' amount to torture per WHO; impunity for police ill-treatment persists.

ECOM's 2024 national report on violations of the rights of LGBT people in Uzbekistan examines legislation, anti-discrimination provisions, criminalisation of HIV transmission, legal gender recognition, access to human rights, and the right to health and to work.

UK Home Office COI note (Jul 2024): consensual same-sex conduct between men criminalised under Article 120 of the 1994 Criminal Code, up to 3 years; documented Article 120 cases 2009-2023; police intimidation/violence/exploitation of gay men and trans people routine; LGBTI orgs cannot register, operate unofficially; rural taboo drives discrimination.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report, Section 6, records torture and ill-treatment and arbitrary detention in custody, together with social stigma and violence against LGBT people under the criminalised framework.

US State Dept 2023 HRR: LGBTQI+ people arrested then released or threatened with arrest unless paying bribes; police coerced LGBTQI+ people to inform on others under threat of prison; websites and bloggers self-censored on LGBTQI+ issues; societal harassment continued.

HRW (23 Mar 2021): Article 120 punishes consensual sex between males up to 3 years; gay/bisexual men face discrimination, violence, blackmail and extortion from state and non-state actors with almost no protections; HRW urges decriminalisation (Uzbekistan then on UN rights council).

UZB.tangentialFactors: Article 120 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 3 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active; extortion-by-threat-of-arrest targets discovered trans people.
UZB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Egypt (0.22 — Egypt's entrapment machinery is more systematic; Uzbekistan's extortion pattern is comparable) and Algeria (0.22), below Morocco (0.25) and above Tunisia (0.19).

NIC.name: Nicaragua
NIC.summary: Nicaragua is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors. Nothing criminalises being trans — sodomy was decriminalised in 2008 — but NGOs document 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 alone and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years, and arbitrary detention is used broadly against perceived opponents. Since 2018 virtually all independent civil society has been shut down or exiled, so there is no domestic protection infrastructure and no recourse for a visitor facing harm.
NIC.outOfScopeNotes: The violence and murder totals are NGO-counted resident tallies; how far visitors appear in them is unresolved. Generalised repression is regime-wide, so detention risk is not trans-specific; conversely the trans-murder count is trans-specific and cannot be generalised to visitors.

sources.summary: No documented finding for this jurisdiction.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report on Nicaragua: documents a police/parapolice campaign of harassment, intimidation and violence against perceived regime enemies that authorities did not investigate or prosecute, and lists violence or threats against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer or intersex persons among significant violations. For this record: official US assessment that anti-LGBTI abuse occurs inside a climate of state impunity.

Amnesty International (May 2019): the post-April-2018 protest crackdown left at least 325 dead and more than 2,000 injured per the IACHR; journalist Miguel Mora describes being beaten by a pro-government mob and being targeted partly for being gay, illustrating the intersection of political repression and homophobia. For this record: documented violence context and homophobia within the repression, with the casualty figures.

PinkNews (Nov 2007): Nicaragua's new penal code, effective March 2008, repealed the 1992 sodomy law (1-3 years' imprisonment), whose vague wording had also been usable against LGBT-rights campaigning and sexual-health work. For this record: dated decriminalisation — same-sex conduct not criminalised since 2008.

NIC.localsOnly: The documented violence falls on residents: 108 cases of violence against the LGBTIQ+ community in 2024 and 10 murders of trans women in the last two and a half years. The civil-society shutdown affects resident organisations and the residents who depended on them.

GUY.name: Guyana
GUY.summary:
Guyana is one of five countries in the Western Hemisphere that still criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 352 to 354 of the Criminal Law Act create offences of gross indecency and attempted buggery, and buggery carries a maximum sentence of life imprisonment. Prosecutions are rare, but the provisions anchor stigma against LGBT people and give police a vocabulary of threat.

No legal gender recognition exists. The direct anti-cross-dressing offence, section 153(1)(xlvii) of the Summary Jurisdiction (Offences) Act, derived from an 1893 statute, was struck down by the Caribbean Court of Justice in November 2018 in McEwan v Attorney General, which held it unconstitutionally vague and a violation of freedom of expression. The challenge was filed in 2010 with SASOD after trans women were arrested in 2009 and held for three nights under the same provision.

Violence against trans women is documented and persistent. At the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights' 191st session in Washington in November 2024, a hearing requested by the Guyana Equality Forum heard testimony from Blossom Inc., SASOD and the Guyana Sex Work Coalition on the impact of gender-based violence on migrant women, sex workers and trans women; Commission chair Roberta Clarke called on Guyana to take urgent action. The record carries 69 documented cases of violence against trans women between 2018 and 2022.

The justice system has failed trans complainants directly. In January 2017 trans woman Petronella Trotman was stabbed in Georgetown with scissors, sustaining a neck wound, and pelted with glass bottles. Public attitudes have shifted measurably: a 2022 poll recorded 72% acceptance, with hostility 13 percentage points lower than in 2013. Five of six parties in the 2025 general election, including the ruling party, backed decriminalisation, though no repeal has followed. There is no anti-discrimination legislation; the UN Human Rights Committee called for such legislation in April 2024. SUR.name: Suriname
SUR.summary:
Suriname is a country that demands real caution from trans visitors — legally unremarkable, socially mixed. Same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's 'any other status' clause is read to cover SOGI discrimination, and the penal code has carried sexual-orientation discrimination and hate-speech provisions since March 2015. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-murder pattern, but the capital's small community reports routine harassment, and the interior has essentially no protection.

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest street risk in the capital; low tourist infrastructure generally.
SUR.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of any documented trans-murder pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Interior protection levels and the real-world operation of the 2022 labour act are unverified. Community harassment reports are anecdotal rather than systematically counted.

sources.summary: Country overview updated 12 Mar 2026: same-sex relations legal for men and women nationwide; legal gender recognition NOT possible; LGBTI organisations CAN register. Constitution Article 8.2's 'any other status' clause is read by the government as extending to sexual orientation and gender identity despite no explicit statutory protection.

Civil-society report of July 2024 (Projekta Foundation with VIDS and LGBT Platform): Constitution Article 8 covers SOGI only implicitly through 'any other status', and same-sex conduct has not been criminalised since 1869. The LGBT Platform Suriname, founded 29 August 2011, unites PAREA, New Monday Foundation, Suriname Men United, Women's Way and Trans in Action; the report urges a comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation, gender identity and disability.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Suriname records discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and intersex (LGBTI) persons and other minorities. The report also documents the Bouterse trial, police brutality and corruption.

Submission to the UN Human Rights Committee (115th session) from LGBT Platform Suriname, Heartland Alliance and Akahata: despite constitutional protection LGBTI persons still face daily discrimination, violence and stigmatization. It records that in March 2015 Penal Code Articles 175, 175a and 176 were revised to cover discrimination and hate speech on the basis of sexual orientation.

Human Rights Committee review of Suriname, July 2024: the State asserted its laws protect against discrimination including on sexual orientation, backed by monitoring bodies such as the National Inclusive Labour Market Commission, while experts pressed on implementing the Inter-American Court's judgment on transgender identity. The Committee welcomed abolition of the death penalty in the Penal Code (2015) and Military Code (2021).

UN UPR pre-session summary of March 2016 from the Suriname LGBT Platform: since the 2011 UPR the State revised the penal code to equalise the age of consent for same- and opposite-sex conduct and to add sexual-orientation discrimination provisions. The platform also reports it has been excluded from state consultative processes despite repeated requests.

SUR.localsOnly: No legal gender recognition — a resident-facing gap. The 2022 Equal Treatment Labour Act adds employment protections for workers, and the harassment reports concern residents' daily street experience; the community also reports continued daily discrimination despite the constitutional reading.
SUR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Ecuador (0.57 — far less violence) and below India (0.58, tie).

KGZ.name: Kyrgyzstan
KGZ.summary:
Kyrgyzstan presents a high-risk environment for trans visitors. Consensual same-sex conduct has been legal since 1998, with the age of consent equal at 16, but the legal machinery around gender has moved in the opposite direction: a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status removed the provision allowing trans people to change their legal gender markers, and ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records that since 2021 trans people cannot obtain legal recognition at all under amendments to the law on civil acts.

Legal gender recognition is now unavailable in practice. TGEU's Trans Rights Index Map 2024 places Kyrgyzstan alongside Hungary, Bulgaria and Russia as states that removed the right to legal gender recognition, and scores Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at only the bare minimum of not banning recognition, the floor of trans legal status in their wider grouping.

There is no relationship recognition to rely on: Kyrgyzstan has no same-sex marriage and no civil unions, and a 2016 constitutional amendment explicitly bans same-sex marriage.

Law enforcement is the sharpest day-to-day exposure. ECOM data cited by ILGA-Europe shows high levels of stigma and discrimination against trans people, particularly from police, and an extortion culture directed at LGBT people has been documented in the country.

An active anti-LGBT political campaign is running. ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 records legislative pushes against LGBT people accompanied by a media campaign of homophobic and transphobic statements from members of parliament, and two discriminatory laws targeting the LGBTI community and restricting LGBTI organisations were adopted in 2023-2024.

Organised public LGBT life in the capital has contracted to nothing. Reporting on the closure of Bishkek's only LGBT club, a car-wash venue at Asanbay, describes patrons entering furtively through a derelict yard and confirms that no other gay venue remained in the city; The Guardian's 19 October 2017 account of the same closure attributes the change to a ban on 'LGBT propaganda' and records patrons saying that all of them would be victims at some point.

Access to transition-related care is documented as a regional problem rather than a solved one: an ECOM study from 2024 examines trans people's access to medical services including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy across the eastern Europe and central Asia region, with country-level coordination covering Kyrgyzstan, and it includes information relevant to trans migrants.
KGZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Sources give two dates for the removal of legal gender recognition: OutRight International attributes it to a 2020 amendment to the Law on Civil Status, while ILGA-Europe's Annual Review 2025 states that trans people have been unable to obtain recognition since 2021 under amendments to the law on civil acts. Both are recorded here; the relationship between the two instruments is not resolved in the available material.

The Human Rights Watch World Report 2025 chapter on Kyrgyzstan contains no material on transgender prisoners or prison housing, so the placement and conditions of trans detainees remain unsourced rather than established as safe or unsafe. The 2020 World Report chapter yielded no usable finding on this jurisdiction.

The 'LGBT propaganda' ban is cited by The Guardian in its account of the Bishkek club closure but its statutory basis, scope and enforcement record are not set out in the available sources.

No sourced material covers entry or visa rules, document screening at the border, hate-crime protection and its enforcement, or official protection machinery for LGBT people beyond the organisational restrictions recorded in the 2023-2024 laws.

Discrimination from law enforcement is a documented feature of daily life for trans residents. Data cited in the 2025 review identifies law enforcement as a particular source of stigma and discrimination, and extortion of LGBT people by police has been documented.

Two laws adopted in 2023-2024 restrict LGBTI organisations and target the LGBTI community, narrowing the operating space for resident advocacy and support services.

Practical information on medical access exists at regional level: a 2024 study covers access to services including HIV prevention and hormone replacement therapy, with country coordination for this state/province, and carries material addressed to trans migrants as well as residents.

On the overall index it sits with Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan at the bare-minimum tier, the lowest scored band available to states that have not affirmatively banned recognition.

The contraction of public LGBT venues in Bishkek is a turbulence indicator rather than a legal rule: the capital had been regarded as comparatively open within its wider region until organised nightlife was shut down, and the disappearance of the last venue removed the semi-private spaces where visitors and residents previously met.

Statements from legislators are part of the risk picture in their own right. The homophobic and transphobic rhetoric recorded by ILGA-Europe came from sitting members of parliament during the passage of the 2023-2024 laws, which means hostility is voiced at the level of lawmaking rather than confined to informal prejudice.

TJK.name: Tajikistan
TJK.summary:
Tajikistan is dangerous for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal, but police conducted a series of raids against LGBTIQ people in several cities in 2022-2023, and documentation in the country shows systematic patterns: discrimination in all spheres, police abuse, arbitrary detention, and forced disclosure. There is no transparent legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection, and authorities have previously maintained informal registries of LGBT citizens.

For a visitor: no expression statute, but police raids, registry practices, and zero recourse make discovery dangerous.
TJK.outOfScopeNotes: Whether the on-paper medicalised registration route is ever granted in practice is unverified. Registry practices are maintained informally, so their current status is opaque. The 2022 anti-discrimination law is on the books but assessed as failing to address discrimination — a gap between statute and practice.

TKM.name: Turkmenistan
TKM.summary:
Turkmenistan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 2 years under Article 135) and, more fundamentally, Turkmenistan is one of the world's most closed states: the state exerts strict media control and heavy internet monitoring, no independent research on LGBTI issues has been possible since 2019, and asylum is the community's most urgent need (ILGA-Europe). Amnesty has documented systematic abuses. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, no recourse, and no visibility — the only safe strategy is total concealment.

For a visitor: any discoverable online presence or visible nonconformity is dangerous in a state that monitors communications pervasively.
TKM.outOfScopeNotes: Absence of documentation is itself evidence of severity: data collection is impossible because it is unsafe.

sources.summary: ILGA-Europe Annual Review 2025 (covering 2024): the April 2022 Criminal Code retained the 'sodomy' provisions and increased both the severity and scope of punishments. Torture and inhumane treatment remain present throughout the country, with relatives reporting LGBTI people subjected to them.

US State Dept 2021 Human Rights Report, Turkmenistan: lists among significant human-rights issues laws criminalizing consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults, alongside officials in security services committing abuses and engaging in corruption with impunity.

EHPV mid-term UPR stakeholder submission (2020): LGBT persons and people living with HIV in Turkmenistan 'have no effective legislative means of enjoying their fundamental human rights'; identifies article 135 of the Criminal Code criminalising consensual same-sex acts between adult men as the core foundation of profound systemic discrimination, and notes increasing flight abroad.

ECOM legislative analysis, 'Legislative analysis related to LGBT rights and HIV in Turkmenistan' (Tallinn, 2019, 11pp, with Turkmen.news): sets out the statutory provisions and barriers facing LGBT people and PLHIV, compiled for use by NGOs, community activists and government in planning advocacy.

Columbia Law School (May 1, 2007): the Sexuality and Gender Law Clinic secured US asylum (DHS) for an anonymous Turkmen woman persecuted because she is a lesbian and for her political opinions — believed to be the first-ever asylum granted to a lesbian from Turkmenistan; documents persecution grounds cited by people fleeing the country.

Goldberg Kohn (Sept 2019): attorneys secured asylum for a lesbian couple from Turkmenistan who feared persecution including imprisonment and torture; homosexuality is punishable by up to 2 years; suspects face interrogation, torture and confinement to mental hospitals; women are vulnerable to sexual violence and 'honor killings'.

TKM.tangentialFactors: Article 135 criminalises male same-sex conduct (up to 2 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
TKM.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Qatar (0.12 — different profiles: TKM's opacity prevents even documenting abuse; QAT's abuse is documented), below Uzbekistan (0.22 — UZB has enforcement data and some civil society) and Russia (0.12, tie).

SYR.name: Syria
SYR.summary:
Syria is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Articles 520/517 of the Penal Code criminalise “sexual acts against nature” and public indecency; there is no legal gender recognition. Since the fall of the Assad regime (December 2024), the situation has worsened: the Guardians of Equality Movement documented “waves of violence” against Syrian transgender women in the first two months of 2025, implicating both non-state armed groups and security forces in multiple cities, and February 2025 videos showed authorities arresting trans women. Digital targeting (entrapment via apps, extortion) is documented across the conflict period.

For a visitor: active conflict, trans-targeted violence waves, no recourse whatsoever.
SYR.outOfScopeNotes: General conflict risk affects all; the 2025 trans-women violence waves are trans-specific.

sources.summary: GEM (Guardians of the Gem) report of April 2025 on LGBTQIA individuals in Syria after the fall: working through an on-the-ground reporter network, the organisation investigated and found inaccurate a report claiming LGBTQIA+ individuals were being hunted and targeted in Homs, debunking it to avoid stirring incitement against the community.
No usable finding recorded for Syria.

Country overview updated 12 March 2026: Syria's legal landscape remains highly restrictive - Penal Code Articles 520 ('acts against nature') and 517 (public indecency) criminalise same-sex conduct for both men and women; legal gender recognition impossible; LGBTI organisations cannot register.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' of 16 April 2018 (updated 30 August 2021): documents LGBT activism across the Middle East and North Africa including Syria, with tallies that ISIS claimed at least 16 killings in Syria for alleged sodomy as of June 2016 (23 in Iraq, 3 in Libya). Activists worked to draw attention to the killings including at the UN Security Council.

Syria Direct feature of 11 October 2020 (Will Christou, Alicia Medina): LGBT Syrians describe life at home and abroad - in Damascus homosexuality and 'public decency' offences are illegal, and a 36-year-old (Amira al-Tabbaa) describes living 'only in whispers' when meeting friends in gay-friendly cafes.

Newsweek, 2015: two gay refugees from Syria and Iraq testified at the first-ever meeting on LGBT rights at the UN Security Council - a closed session co-sponsored by the US and Chile - about the constant fear of violence and death under authoritarian governments, militant groups and ISIS.

PinkNews, 23 June 2010: Syrian authorities raided several private gay parties over preceding weeks, arresting more than 25 men in the latest swoop - most charged with 'homosexual acts', others with dealing or buying drugs, per gaymiddleeast.com.

SYR.tangentialFactors: Articles 520/517 criminalise “sexual acts against nature” — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SYR.comparisons: Pairwise: above Saudi Arabia (0.05 — SYR's chaos vs SAU's systematic state machinery) and below Iraq (0.08 — IRQ now has a codified anti-trans statute; SYR has codified indecency + active violence waves).

LBY.name: Libya
LBY.summary:
Libya's Penal Code criminalises "illicit sexual intercourse" and "indecent acts", with the indecent-acts provisions carrying up to five years' imprisonment; same-sex relations are not legal for men or women, and where no specific statute reaches conduct, other provisions are used instead. The Guardian's regional guide lists Libya among states where imprisonment is the penalty for homosexuality, with terms varying by country.

Cairo 52's country review finds de-facto criminalisation of gender nonconformity and of the transition process itself, whether social, medical or surgical, enforced through those same indecent-acts and illicit-intercourse provisions. Recent religious rulings have designated gender-affirming medical steps as impermissible, which narrows the ground on which a trans person can seek care or be seen in public.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable: official identity documents cannot be changed. Same-sex relationships carry no legal recognition, there are no legal protections against discrimination on sexual orientation or gender identity, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.

Extrajudicial violence is documented where armed groups hold territory. In Derna, Islamist extremists executed three young men accused of homosexual acts in April 2015, and a young man there was targeted by local Islamists from November 2014 for effeminate dress and "contemporary" clothing. In November 2012, twelve men accused of being gay were tortured and threatened with death by a Libyan militia. D+C reported in June 2015 that information in Derna flows only through the mosque and that the situation for LGBT people was worsening as militias controlled territory.

For a visitor, the modal bad outcome is detention by one of several armed authorities rather than a court process, with torture and threatened killing documented in militia custody.
LBY.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not resolve whether gender nonconformity or transition attracts a penalty distinct from the five-year maximum attached to the indecent-acts provisions; Cairo 52 documents de-facto criminalisation through those provisions but does not state a separate statutory term.

Enforcement frequency, arrest statistics and the identity of the authorities currently holding territory are not sourced in this inventory, so the relative weight of militia detention versus state prosecution remains unresolved.

Consular access for foreign nationals detained outside the capital is not addressed by any source here and should be verified independently before travel.

Descriptions of the religious rulings vary in scope: the sourced claim concerns gender-affirming medical steps, and any broader prohibition on the use of the term "gender" in media or institutions is not established by these sources.

YEM.name: Yemen
YEM.summary:
Yemen is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. The legal framework criminalises same-sex conduct (up to death under some interpretations of the Penal Code; 100 lashes/1 year otherwise), but Cairo 52 emphasises the operative mechanism: the erosion of the rule of law and the power of militias has facilitated a surge in attacks targeting transgender individuals — de facto criminalisation operating outside any judicial system. Houthi-controlled areas impose their own moral-policing regime; the south has its own militia authorities.

For a visitor: no safe authority to appeal to anywhere in the country.
YEM.outOfScopeNotes: War risk affects all; the documented surge in trans-targeted attacks is trans-specific.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 country review of Yemen: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by territory.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018, MENA): Yemen is one of 14 covered countries where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

HRW World Report 2026, Yemen chapter (events of 2025): its Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section states Yemen's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside world's-worst humanitarian crisis (19.5M needing aid) and Houthi/government factional control affecting where law applies.

BTN.name: Bhutan
BTN.summary:
Bhutan decriminalised consensual same-sex intimacy in 2021. Penal Code Sections 213 and 214, the 'unnatural sex' provisions carrying one month to one year of imprisonment, were voted down by the lower house 43-1 in June 2019; the upper house reinserted the ban, and a December 2020 joint sitting resolved that homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex. The Penal Code Amendment Act entered into force on 17 February 2021, and no reversal has followed. The provisions had gone unenforced for at least 15 years before repeal.

The repeal did not create a protective framework. Bhutan has no stand-alone anti-discrimination law and no explicit protections on the grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity or expression, and sex characteristics. Discrimination and stigma persist, with health-care access singled out as a domain where trans and LGBTIQ people are turned away or poorly served.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable. Administrative changes to gender markers on identity documents are suspended because standardised guidelines do not exist, leaving trans people with documents that do not match their presentation.

That document mismatch has direct consequences for reporting crime. Trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault. A 49-year-old trans woman interviewed by Bhutan Broadcasting Service in November 2024 described having nowhere to report violence: police dismiss her cases on the reasoning that her identity card reads male, so 'both parties are men'. Families pressure victims to accept what has happened as fate, and assistance routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee is slow. The result is practical impunity for anti-trans violence despite formal decriminalisation.

LGBTIQ organisations may register and operate legally, including Rainbow Bhutan, though activists describe the registration process as lengthy and burdensome.

Official engagement exists at institutional level. UNFPA Bhutan's 2024 Free & Equal campaign trained the Royal Court of Justice, the Attorney General's Office and the Cabinet Secretariat, and secured the first direct dialogue between Bhutan's LGBTIQ+ community and parliamentarians. Two consultation workshops brought community members together with UN representatives and the National Commission for Women and Children.

Public trans visibility remains exceptional. Dechen, described as one of only two trans women living publicly in Bhutan, fought at 16 to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. The LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, started around 2013-2014, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population. LGBTIQ Bhutanese otherwise report near-total social invisibility rather than overt persecution: there is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised.
BTN.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources give two different start dates for the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, one around 2014 and one in 2013; the discrepancy is unresolved in the inventory.

Whether the suspension of administrative gender-marker changes has a stated review date, or which ministry holds the file, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory records police guidance, training or disciplinary outcomes addressing the refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so the practical impunity finding rests on victim testimony rather than on documented institutional response.

Whether the 2024 Free & Equal training produced any change in Royal Court of Justice or Attorney General's Office practice is not stated in the sources.

The claim that trans people are more than four times as likely to experience assault is reported without a stated methodology or baseline population in the inventory.

Entry, visa and document requirements for visitors are not covered by any source in this inventory.

Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten: 'This is our first journey towards equality.'

Erasing 76 Crimes (11 Mar 2021): the Penal Code Amendment Act came into force 17 Feb 2021. After the upper house reinserted the ban, a December 2020 joint sitting clarified that 'homosexuality between adults shall not be considered unnatural sex', completing decriminalisation and lowering the global criminalising-state tally from 72 to 71. No post-2021 reversal has occurred.

Bhutan Broadcasting Service feature 'Black and White and the Colours of the Rainbow': the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page (from c.2014) produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population. The feature profiles Dechen, one of only two trans women living publicly, who at 16 fought to wear the female school uniform kira, a first in Bhutanese society. Public trans visibility exists but remains exceptional.

The Daily Beast (28 Oct 2015): Bhutan's LGBT people report very little persecution or violence but near-total social invisibility. 'Growing up gay in Bhutan was a very alienating experience'; there is no shared language for gay or trans identities, and lesbianism is under-recognised. Karma Dupchen, one of the most public LGBT figures, founded the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page in 2013.

BTN.tangentialFactors:
Bhutan's repeal lowered the global tally of states criminalising consensual same-sex conduct from 72 to 71 in March 2021, placing it among a small group of jurisdictions that have legislated out of criminalisation rather than been compelled to by a court.

The legislative path was contested rather than smooth: the upper house moved to restore the ban after the lower house vote, and the final position was settled by a joint sitting clarification rather than a clean amendment. The trajectory since has been stable, with no post-2021 reversal recorded in the sources.

The gap between institutional engagement and street-level outcomes is the defining pattern. Training of justice-sector bodies and first parliamentary dialogue coexist with police refusal to take reports from trans complainants, so formal decriminalisation has not yet translated into enforceable protection.

Social conditions lean toward invisibility rather than confrontation. Reporting describes little persecution or violence in everyday life alongside near-total lack of public recognition, no shared vocabulary for trans and gay identities, and under-recognised lesbianism. Public figures such as Dechen and activists including Rainbow Bhutan director Tashi Tsheten are exceptions that mark how narrow the space for open visibility remains.

Reporting anti-trans violence is obstructed at the first step. Police decline cases where the complainant's identity card records a male sex marker, reasoning that both parties are men. Where a case is accepted and routed through the national LGBTQIA+ committee, response is slow, and families commonly press the victim to accept the assault as fate.

Health-care access is the domain where discrimination and stigma are most consistently reported, and no anti-discrimination statute gives a remedy when a facility refuses service.

Community organising has a documented history: the LGBT Bhutan Facebook page, founded by Karma Dupchen in 2013, produced the country's first public affirmation of a gay population, and the first direct dialogue between LGBTIQ+ community members and parliamentarians took place in 2024.

LAO.name: Laos
LAO.summary:
Laos does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. The penal code, modelled on the French system after independence in the 1950s, contains no sodomy offence, distinguishing the country from neighbours that retained colonial-era prohibitions.

Trans visitors nonetheless have no legal footing. There is no legal gender recognition, no anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no documented recourse when officials withhold documents or services; the one-party political system leaves no independent civil society to appeal to.

Social visibility is real. Trans-feminine people are a recognised presence, and the LGBT scene is small, discreet and social rather than public or institutional. Tourist cities are accustomed to visitors, so the dominant risk is administrative — an opaque system in which a passport that does not match presentation can stall a traveller — rather than violent.
LAO.outOfScopeNotes:
The registration status of 'Proud to be us Laos' is unresolved. Al Jazeera names it as the country's only LGBT advocacy group, while the record treats no LGBT organisation as registered in Laos; the sources do not settle which is correct.

No source in the inventory documents a procedure, timeline or refusal rate for legal gender recognition, and none records a trans traveller denied entry, detained, or refused a document. Absence of such reports is not evidence that these events do not occur.

Two inventory sources, the UNAIDS joint analysis and the Asian Development Bank legal-status review, yielded no usable finding for Laos. Hate-crime protection, partner recognition and access to gender-affirming care therefore remain not sourced in this record.

The description of the social scene rests on a single first-person account from 2000 and may not reflect present conditions.

TLS.name: Timor-Leste
TLS.summary:
Timor-Leste is workable for trans visitors — a country where same-sex conduct is legal, the constitution's equality provisions have been read inclusively, and the capital hosts an annual Pride march with government participation, remarkable for a young, Catholic-majority nation. There is no legal gender recognition and services are thin, but no pattern of police targeting or anti-trans violence is documented, and the small community operates openly.

For a visitor: no documented risk pattern; the constraint is thin services and the absence of legal gender recognition rather than active hostility.
TLS.outOfScopeNotes: The absence of a documented police-targeting or anti-trans-violence pattern is an absence-of-evidence finding, not proof of safety. Service thinness is unquantified. Participation and endorsement claims rest on news reporting. The Catholic-majority character is a social qualifier, not a legal fact.

sources.summary: Australian Volunteers Program Pride Guide, Timor-Leste: country snapshot for volunteers — same-sex sexual acts decriminalised in 1975; the UN Human Rights Council joint statement on SOGI was adopted in 2011; Timor-Leste voted in favour of the 2013 UN resolution on vulnerability/disability... sets out the legal and policy context for living openly as a volunteer.

New Naratif (June 2018): Timor-Leste's first-ever Pride parade in 2017 drew international attention and a televised endorsement from the Prime Minister. The report also records day-to-day rejection, including messages sent to the organiser's family.

VOA (July 2018): East Timor held its second annual LGBT pride parade in Dili on July 20, evidence of a regional leadership role and an open environment for visitors while neighbours Indonesia and Malaysia turn hostile.

Star Observer (July 2019): an estimated 3,000 people joined the 'Marsa Diversidade' Pride March in Dili on July 12, six times the turnout of the 2017 first parade. President Francisco Guterres publicly backed the event, stating 'I am a President for all people'.

PNG.name: Papua New Guinea
PNG.summary:
Papua New Guinea is dangerous for trans visitors. Male same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 14 years), and PNG has extreme levels of gender-based violence generally — among the world's highest documented rates. Port Moresby and Lae are dangerous cities for everyone; tribal-justice dynamics and police brutality affect marginalised people severely. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and sorcery-accusation violence shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in the Pacific.
PNG.outOfScopeNotes: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.

sources.summary: The ADB publication 'Assessment of the Legal Status of Sexual and Gender Minorities in 17 Countries in Asia and the Pacific', content dated 17 May 2024, lists Papua New Guinea among the 17 assessed countries. Its keywords include decriminalization and SOGIESC inclusion.

HRW commentary (27 Jan 2009): PNG violence-accountability climate — a mob stripped, beat with hot iron rods and burned a woman accused of sorcery within yards of a police station; provincial commanders recorded 50+ sorcery-related killings in two highlands provinces in 2008 with perpetrators rarely brought to justice; sorcery accusations (linked to HIV deaths) used to hide murders and mitigate sentences; police routinely take no action.

ABC News (8 Oct 2014): Hanuabada village on Port Moresby's outskirts is a safe haven for PNG's gay and transgender community — residents live openly, transgender people wear women's clothes in the street without retaliation, while in Port Moresby gay/trans people are commonly raped or beaten, sometimes by police (documentary maker Vlad Sokhin, who found the village while travelling).

The Guardian (13 Jan 2017) on HRW's annual world-report assessment of PNG: the government of Peter O'Neill has failed to protect women and children and to respond to corruption and police violence — 'police abuse, including of children, continues to be reported with little accountability even for fatalities or egregious physical abuse'.

Guardian Nigeria (reprint): describes Hanuabada ('big village', built over the sea) as a pocket of tolerance where the gay community is accepted — set against PNG where sex between men is illegal and stigma/violence widespread (a 24-year-old gay man recounts being pelted with stones and bottles); campaigners say attitudes shift with exposure to the LGBT community.

PNG.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
PNG.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Cameroon (0.21 — both pair criminalisation with extreme ambient violence), above Nigeria (0.19) and below Egypt (0.22).
PNG.blindSummary:

Its two largest cities are dangerous for everyone; customary community-justice dynamics and police brutality hit marginalised people hard. There is no legal gender recognition, no LGBT organisation operating openly at national level, and violence driven by accusations of harmful spiritual practices shares the same social mechanics as anti-trans violence.

For a visitor: the trans-specific risk is inseparable from the general security situation, which is among the worst in its world region.
PNG.blindOutOfScope: General security conditions affect all travelers severely; criminalisation is the trans-relevant mechanism.
blindSourceSummaries: A country page on an international legal-status database: documents this country's legal status — same-sex conduct criminalised under historic law with sentences of up to 14 years.
A regional development bank's publication on the legal status of sexual and gender minorities across this country's world region - comparative overview including this country.

International human-rights organisation (Jan 2009): report on a country where violence against women is rampant - documents widespread gender-based violence in this country, the context of impunity that also affects sexual and gender minorities.

A foreign public broadcaster (Oct 2014): a coastal village on the outskirts of this country's largest city (notably the home of roughly half of the national team) is a safe haven for gay and trans people in a country where homosexuality is illegal.

Foreign broadsheet (Jan 2017): a rights group said this country had failed to act on corruption and police violence or protect women and children - a scathing assessment that also covers a wealthy neighbour's offshore immigration detention run here.

Foreign women's-interest publication (Nov 2018): feature on a village in this country that serves as a refuge for its LGBT community - an openly gay 24-year-old remembers thugs pelting him with abuse, stones and bottles; the coastal settlement offers refuge where gay sex is illegal and stigma and violence are widespread.

BWA.name: Botswana
BWA.summary:
Botswana decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct through its own courts. The High Court struck down the colonial-era "carnal knowledge" offence on 11 June 2019 in Letsweletse Motshidiemang v Attorney General, and the Court of Appeal upheld that judgment on 29 November 2021.

Penal Code Section 167, which addresses same-sex conduct between women, was not removed by that litigation. In the Universal Periodic Review of May 2023 (43rd session), Botswana declined Canada's recommendation to repeal Section 167.

Legal gender recognition has been won case by case rather than granted by statute. In 2017 the High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male on dignity and humanity grounds (ND v Attorney General), and the same year Tshepo Ricki Kgositau obtained a female identity card after a four-year legal battle, the first court-ordered recognition of a trans woman's gender in Botswana. No general legal gender recognition statute exists, and at the 2023 Universal Periodic Review Botswana did not accept a recommendation to introduce an administrative process for it; the review records that a clear administrative process was yet to be introduced.

Community infrastructure is legally protected. The Court of Appeal ordered the state to register LEGABIBO in 2016 on freedom of association, expression and assembly grounds, and the organisation now runs advocacy, awareness, sexual-health and HIV programming together with coming-out, legal and support resources.

A draft constitutional amendment considered in 2024 would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities. In June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct, and civic groups criticise the wider review process.

Implementation lags the judgments. Southern African Litigation Centre reported on 20 May 2024 that compliance with these precedent rulings "has not been satisfactory so far".

For a visitor: conduct decriminalised, courts functioning and willing to order the state, identity documents obtainable through litigation rather than administration, and continuing societal discrimination documented in official reporting.
BWA.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether Penal Code Section 167 has been used in prosecutions since the 2019 and 2021 rulings is not sourced in this inventory; the inventory establishes only that it was not repealed and that Botswana declined the repeal recommendation in 2023.

Unresolved: whether the draft 2024 constitutional amendment was enacted is not sourced here; the inventory covers the proposal and the June 2024 deliberations only.

Unresolved: Southern African Litigation Centre's finding that implementation "has not been satisfactory" is not broken down in this inventory by which specific orders went unimplemented, and it covers Namibia as well as Botswana.

Not sourced: there are no statistics or dated case records on physical violence against trans people in Botswana in this inventory. The 2011 US State Department report records societal discrimination but predates decriminalisation and should not be read as current.

sources.summary: SALC, Digashu & Mmolai-Chalmers (20 May 2024): Botswana's precedent wins — 2016 Court of Appeal ordered registration of LEGABIBO (freedom of association, expression, assembly), a 2017 High Court ordered the state to change a trans man's identity documents from female to male (dignity and humanity), and the 2021 Court of Appeal decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct — yet implementation across Botswana and Namibia 'has not been satisfactory so far'.

Alta Advisory (18 Jun 2024): Botswana's draft constitutional amendment would add discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities; in June 2024 deliberations the Minister of Labour and Home Affairs told legislators to keep 'intersex' and 'same-sex' distinct. Civic groups criticise the wider review process, but the intersex provision signals momentum toward broader LGBTQI+ protection.

UN UPR outcome, 43rd session (May 2023): Botswana did not accept Canada's recommendations to repeal Penal Code Section 167 (same-sex conduct between women) and to introduce an administrative process for legal gender recognition — 'a clear administrative process... was yet to be introduced' (para 570); abortion-decriminalisation recommendation also declined.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana: the LGBT section documents that same-sex conduct was then criminalised and records societal discrimination against LGBT people. The report's wider assessment covers violence against women, prison conditions and San discrimination.

LEGABIBO official site: Botswana's principal LGBTIQ+ organisation running advocacy, awareness campaigns and sexual-health/HIV work (e.g., World AIDS Day 2017 commemoration in Bobonong), with Coming Out, Law & Constitution and Help & Support resources — a functioning, legally registered community infrastructure (registration won in the 2016 Court of Appeal order).

The Independent (19 Dec 2017): Botswana's High Court ordered the government to legally recognise a trans woman's gender for the first time — Tshepo Ricki Kgositau won a female identity card after a four-year legal battle (gender confirmation surgery December 2016), dedicating the victory to 'every single trans diverse person in Botswana'. A landmark for legal gender recognition in the country.

Human Rights Watch (24 Jan 2018): previewed the Botswana constitutional challenge to the colonial-era 'carnal knowledge' law, with the hearing set for March 2018. The law was struck down on 11 Jun 2019 and the judgment upheld on appeal on 29 Nov 2021; the trans legal-gender right was confirmed 2017-22.

BWA.tangentialFactors:
Botswana's judicial record on sexual-orientation and gender-identity cases is the strongest on the continent after South Africa, and the courts have repeatedly been the route by which rights were obtained rather than the legislature.

Human Rights Watch previewed the constitutional challenge to the "carnal knowledge" law on 24 January 2018 with the hearing set for March 2018, placing the 2019 and 2021 rulings in a multi-year litigation sequence that also confirmed the trans legal-gender right between 2017 and 2022.

The US State Department's 2011 Human Rights Report for Botswana documented same-sex conduct as then criminalised and recorded societal discrimination against LGBT people; that report predates the decriminalisation rulings and describes the earlier legal position.

Official caution persists alongside the case law. The Minister of Labour and Home Affairs' instruction to legislators in June 2024 to keep "intersex" and "same-sex" distinct indicates that protection is being extended in segments rather than as a single package, and civic groups criticise the constitutional review process itself.

At the same Universal Periodic Review session Botswana also declined a recommendation to decriminalise abortion, an adjacent marker of how the government handled rights recommendations in 2023.
BWA.localsOnly:
Residents have no administrative route to change gender markers on identity documents. Recognition is obtained by going to court, as in ND v Attorney General (2017) and Tshepo Ricki Kgositau's 2017 victory, and the 2023 Universal Periodic Review confirms that a clear administrative process was yet to be introduced.

Penal Code Section 167, covering same-sex conduct between women, remains unrepealed by statute; the 2019 decriminalisation ruling concerned the "carnal knowledge" provision, and the government declined to accept a recommendation to repeal Section 167 in 2023.

LEGABIBO is the principal national LGBTIQ+ organisation, registered under the 2016 Court of Appeal order, and provides advocacy, awareness campaigns, sexual-health and HIV work including World AIDS Day commemorations such as the 2017 event in Bobonong, alongside coming-out, law and constitution, and help and support resources.

The draft constitutional amendment would write discrimination protection for intersex persons and people with disabilities into the constitution, and its treatment in the 2024 legislative deliberations is being contested by civic groups.

Southern African Litigation Centre's assessment of May 2024 is that compliance with the landmark rulings has not been satisfactory, so a right confirmed in court may not be delivered consistently by the administration.
BWA.comparisons: Pairwise: just below South Africa (0.66 — SA has constitutional protection and fuller infrastructure; BWA's recent jurisprudence is comparable but its implementation record is weaker) and above Serbia (0.64).

NAM.name: Namibia
NAM.summary:
Namibia demands real caution from trans visitors. Courts have delivered important rulings (the 2023 Digashu recognition of foreign same-sex marriages; earlier document-change wins for trans people), but same-sex conduct between men technically remains criminalised under the common law (the 2024 High Court declined to strike it, and parliament passed hostile marriage bills), and implementation of pro-LGBT rulings is documented as unsatisfactory (SALC). Windhoek has a small organised community (Equal Namibia); police are unhelpful rather than predatory.

For a visitor: enforcement of the old law is essentially nil, but the legal floor is hostile and the politics are deteriorating.
NAM.outOfScopeNotes: Common-law criminalisation is unenforced but real; implementation gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Washington Blade op-ed (22 May 2024) by Daniel Digashu and Anna Mmolai-Chalmers of the Southern Africa Litigation Centre: Namibia's Supreme Court in May 2023 ordered the government to recognise same-sex marriages concluded abroad under the Immigration Act, but compliance has failed — immigration officials tell litigant Digashu himself that the ruling covers only case couples (he receives a visitor's visa on every exit), and gender-recognition orders are applied only to named applicants rather than 'all persons'. A hostile parliamentary marriage-bill response and misleading media amplified the non-implementation. Documents the enforcement gap between pro-equality rulings and administrative practice.

UNDP report (Dec 2024) 'African Commission Resolution 275: Ten Years of Advancing LGBT+ Rights in Africa' - regional framework document; Namibia's courts have decriminalised same-sex conduct (2024) and recognised same-sex partners' residency rights, though implementation remains contested.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Namibia' (2017): constitutional analysis - Article 10 omits gender identity/sexual orientation but 'other status' should include them per the UN Human Rights Committee; section 7B of the Births, Marriages and Deaths Registration Act 81 of 1963 allows gender-marker changes on medical evidence, handled case-by-case and 'not problematic' per the Legal Assistance Centre (2015).

Mambaonline (28 May 2018): Out-Right Namibia opened Namibia's first dedicated LGBT drop-in centre, Outreach Health, on 17 May (IDAHOT) at 30 Lister St, Windhoek West — HIV testing and counselling, PrEP, mental and sexual/reproductive health services, with plans for legal assistance and screening for intimate-partner violence, gender-based violence and human-rights violations. ORN director Friedel Dausab: 'It is a first.' The article notes the colonial-era sodomy law is on the books but not believed used since independence in 1990, and recalls 2016 UN Human Rights Committee recommendations urging SOGI non-discrimination legislation.

Mambaonline (12 December 2018): dozens marched in Windhoek and Swakopmund on 8 December for LGBTI+ Pride — described as the 'biggest pride event' to date in Namibia. Dated evidence of a visible, tolerated public community presence.

Daily Maverick (26 June 2014): a Namibian version of South Africa's Economic Freedom Fighters was launched with identical branding (T-shirts, berets) but an explicitly anti-gay stance, unlike the South African original. Documents organised political hostility to LGBT rights in the record's political environment.

NAM.tangentialFactors: Male same-sex conduct technically remains criminalised under the common law (unenforced) — a formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the 2024 legislative backlash signals trajectory.
NAM.localsOnly: The earlier document-change court wins are per-case resident litigation; implementation gaps documented by SALC are resident-facing.
NAM.comparisons: Pairwise: below Botswana (0.65 — BWA decriminalised; NAM retains the common-law crime and legislative backlash) and above Brazil (0.55, tie).

MUS.name: Mauritius
MUS.summary:
Mauritius is workable for trans visitors — the Indian Ocean's most liveable jurisdiction. The Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct; the Equal Opportunities Act covers discrimination; and in 2024 Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan competed as the first trans woman in Miss Universe Mauritius — a public milestone met with national discussion rather than violence. There is no legal gender recognition law (a barrier highlighted by AfricLaw), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence and recognition gaps are resident-facing.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: the Supreme Court repealed Section 250 in 2023, decriminalising same-sex conduct — advances noted for lesbian, gay and bisexual people with 'less evident' progress for trans or intersex people. No same-sex marriage or civil unions recognised; Equal Opportunities Act 2008 and Workers' Rights Act 2019 protect against sexual-orientation discrimination; intersex newborns may be registered 'undetermined' under the 2021 Civil Status Act but nonconsensual intersex procedures are not banned; legal gender recognition not possible and LGBTI organisations cannot register. Pride held since 2005 with counter-protesters; during the 2024 national elections a parliamentary candidate branded sexual and gender diversity a 'Western deviation' and others used anti-LGBTIQ hate speech.

AfricLaw (23 August 2024, Lakshita Kanhiya): analyses the historic participation of Jeanny Michelle Karla Fanfan — the first transgender woman in Miss Universe Mauritius 2024 — against the country's legal obstacles: the Civil Status Act of 1981 and Central Population Database as the framework denying recognition, plus pervasive stigmatisation, with activism by the Young Queer Alliance and Association VISA-G. Concludes legal recognition and protection for trans Mauritians remain inadequate despite the visibility milestone.

US State Department 2016 Country Report — Mauritius: Section 250 almost never reached same-sex couples in court, since sodomy references arose overwhelmingly in heterosexual divorce cases as an aggravating factor. The report documents societal discrimination, with LGBTI victims of family verbal abuse or violence reporting to local NGOs including Collectif Arc-en-Ciel and Young Queer Alliance, and harassment of a transgender person for wearing women's clothing.

Young Queer Alliance policy brief (July 2021): 'Administrative recognition of Trans People in Mauritius' - argues for legal gender recognition; notes the WHO's ICD-11 removed trans categories from mental disorders (2019) and calls on Mauritius to join countries recognising gender identity in law.

MUS.tangentialFactors: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
MUS.localsOnly: No LGR law — resident-facing gap highlighted by AfricLaw.
MUS.comparisons: Pairwise: below Seychelles-region comparators and level with Latvia (0.69)/Israel (0.69) — above Hungary (0.68).

There is no legal gender recognition law (a gap highlighted by a regional legal-aid organisation), and social conservatism persists, but tourist infrastructure is extensive and accustomed to diverse visitors, and there is no documented police targeting pattern.

For a visitor: no legal exposure, functioning courts, low street risk in tourist areas.
MUS.blindOutOfScope: The absence of legal gender recognition and related documentation gaps are resident-facing.

MUS.blindTangential: The 2023 decriminalisation ruling removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

SYC.name: Seychelles
SYC.summary: Seychelles is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent archipelago with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
SYC.outOfScopeNotes: LGR absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.

sources.summary: Cornell Law gender-justice page: under the Penal Code (Amendment) Act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) Section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences. The Constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Art 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Art 27).

PinkNews, 18 May 2016: Seychelles repealed colonial-era Penal Code Section 151, which had allowed up to 14 years' imprisonment for male same-sex sex - framed as the popular holiday destination 'opening its arms to LGBT people'.

Travel guide: the 2016 decriminalisation of same-sex acts is recorded as a significant victory for the islands, with residents and visitors advised to stay informed about current legal and social conditions.

Erasing 76 Crimes, 27 September 2024: a newly revised law calls for increased prison sentences for violent crimes motivated by hostility toward victims' sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics, race, religion or disability - per the Human Dignity Trust, after South Africa Seychelles is only the second African country to protect against all forms of hate-based victimisation. Before 2016 the penal code punished male same-sex intimacy with up to 14 years.

SYC.tangentialFactors: The 2016 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
SYC.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Poland/Croatia/Costa Rica (0.72 — different profiles; Seychelles lacks their legal infrastructure but has lower hostility), above Mauritius (0.70 — MUS has the Equal Opportunities Act and 2023 decriminalisation ruling; SYC edges it on ambient safety) and below Chile (0.74).
SYC.blindSummary: This country is workable for trans visitors. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised in 2016; the constitution guarantees equal protection; and the country is a small, tourism-dependent state/province with extremely low violent crime and long exposure to international visitors. There is no legal gender recognition and no documented trans-specific infrastructure, but also no documented pattern of anti-trans violence or police hostility.
SYC.blindOutOfScope: Legal gender recognition absence is resident-facing; evidence is thin given the tiny population.
blindSourceSummaries: Legal-information institute's gender-justice page on this country: under the penal code amendment act 2024 (Act 13 of 2024) section 5, protected characteristics now include sexual orientation, gender identity, sex characteristics and HIV/AIDS status, giving an enhanced-protection basis for hate-motivated offences; the constitution separately guarantees freedom from torture (Article 16) and equal protection with non-discrimination on grounds including sex (Article 27).

SEN.name: Senegal
SEN.summary:
Senegal is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “unnatural acts” (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 for “false news” after accusing the Prime Minister of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — Dakar's scene is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
SEN.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Senegal criminalises same-sex sexual activity under Article 319 of the 1965 Penal Code, with a maximum of five years' imprisonment.

76crimes (16 Jul 2024) reports that anti-LGBT forces in Senegal are pushing for 15-year prison sentences for gay sex, up from the current maximum of five years. The debate has run since 2020, and abuses against LGBT+ people are commonplace in the West African nation.

BBC News: two men were jailed in Senegal for criticising opposition leader Ousmane Sonko — months and fined 100,000 CFA francs ($165, £130) each. They had been angered that Mr Sonko had allowed a visiting French politician to express his support for same-sex marriages. Homosexual acts are banned in the mainly Muslim West African country and are punishable by up to five years in prison. The political activist and the preacher were arrested two weeks ago after posting a video attacking Mr Sonko for giving a platform t

The US State Department's 2012 Human Rights Report for Senegal documents preelectoral violence, torture, and violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender persons among the major human-rights problems.

76crimes (24 Sep 2018) reports that four LGBT people, two women and two men, were detained in Dakar for 'acts against the order of nature'. The detentions came amid a wave of politically motivated arrests ahead of the 2019 elections, triggered after videos circulated.

Metro (Nov 2023) reports that a man's body was dug up and burned in the street in Senegal after it was revealed he was gay. Four men have been arrested in connection with the incident, though images from the scene show a crowd of hundreds gathering around the fire. The 31-year-old man, named locally as Cheikh Fall, had been buried in Léona Niassene cemetery.

SEN.tangentialFactors: “Unnatural acts” criminalised (up to 5 years, both sexes) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SEN.comparisons: Pairwise: below Malaysia (0.28 — comparable criminalisation-plus-mob climate) and above Pakistan (0.26) and Côte d'Ivoire (0.34 — CIV decriminalised but has the 2024 hunt-down violence wave; SEN has statutory criminalisation but no equivalent mob-hunt wave; net SEN slightly worse).
SEN.blindSummary:
Trans visitors face significant risk here. The penal code criminalises "unnatural acts" (up to 5 years, applied to both men and women), enforcement is active (periodic arrest waves), and anti-LGBT forces are pushing to raise sentences to 15 years. Mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented, and even public discussion is policed: two men were jailed in 2024 on "false news" charges after accusing the head of government of tolerating homosexuality. There is no legal gender recognition and no visible community infrastructure — queer life in the capital is deeply underground.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest and mob violence.
SEN.blindOutOfScope: Same-sex criminalisation is the statutory vehicle; mob violence is documented climate.
blindSourceSummaries: International legal-aid trust country profile: this country criminalises same-sex sexual activity (a provision of the 1965 penal code, up to 5 years' imprisonment).

Foreign public broadcaster (June 2024): two men jailed in this country for 'spreading false news' after accusing the head of government of tolerating homosexuality - an activist and a prominent religious leader received three months and fines; the head of government had said homosexuality was 'not accepted, but tolerated' after a foreign politician expressed support for same-sex marriage at a student forum in the capital.

A foreign government's 2012 human-rights report on this country: documents preelectoral violence, torture, and 'violence and discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons' among major human-rights problems.

CIV.name: Côte d'Ivoire
CIV.summary:
Côte d'Ivoire does not criminalise same-sex conduct. The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices states that same-sex relations are not an offence, so a trans visitor carries no statutory exposure on that ground. The sources assembled here do not cover entry, visa or identity-document screening rules specific to transgender travellers.

Non-state violence against LGBTQ people is documented and has been lethal. The 2023 report records three deaths within the community during that year. Police responses to violence committed by non-state actors were described as sometimes slow and ineffective and often blaming the victim, although authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

Gender-nonconforming people face the sharper risk. A transgender man was beaten in Abobo, a district of Abidjan, while walking with another man. Peer-reviewed research on Ivoirian travestis reports harsher stigmatisation and violence than is experienced by sexual minorities whose gender presentation avoids drawing attention.
CIV.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no source in this inventory addresses entry, visa or identity-document screening rules for transgender travellers to Côte d'Ivoire, including whether gender markers on foreign passports attract scrutiny at border control.

Unresolved: Human Rights Watch publishes no document, case or report on the housing of transgender prisoners in Côte d'Ivoire. Where trans detainees are placed (birth sex versus identity), whether dedicated units exist, and whether solitary confinement or segregation is used are not covered in any listed publication; on the HRW country page, 'LGBT Rights' appears only as a topic-facet link.

Unresolved: the Côte d'Ivoire country overview in the UNDP report of December 2024 was not read into this record, so its assessments of prosecution rates, access to justice and civic space remain unverified here.

Unresolved: the New York Times article of October 2024 could not be retrieved (HTTP 403) and contributes no findings.

sources.summary: A New York Times article dated October 2024 addresses the situation of LGBTQ people in Côte d'Ivoire. The article page could not be retrieved at research time (HTTP 403).

Authorities were handling complaints somewhat better than in previous years.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Côte d'Ivoire: post-electoral-crisis context (3,000 deaths, sexual violence, displacement) - general human-rights baseline with limited LGBT-specific content.

Critical African Studies (2015), Thomann & Corey-Boulet, 'Violence, Exclusion and Resilience among Ivoirian Travestis': travestis (born anatomically male, living as women) face harsher stigmatization and violence than sexual minorities whose gender normativity avoids attention, and have been underserved by Ivoirian rights groups that distanced themselves from them; examines isolation after the 2010-11 post-election violence.

Thomann and Corey-Boulet (2015) document violence and social exclusion experienced by travestis in Côte d'Ivoire, together with their resilience. The article is available via the PMC canonical URL, where it is retained as the canonical copy.
