MLI.name: Mali
MLI.summary:
Mali is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. In October-November 2024 the Transitional National Council adopted a new penal code criminalising homosexuality for the first time — with the Justice Minister declaring that anyone “engaging in, promoting or apologising for” same-sex relations will be prosecuted; vague drafting suggests broad application, and prior “public indecency” provisions (Art 225) were already used against gender-nonconforming people. The junta context means no independent judiciary, no civil society space, and active conflict in much of the country.

For a visitor: a brand-new criminalisation statute under a junta with no recourse, plus conflict conditions.
MLI.outOfScopeNotes: The 2024 penal code application to trans expression is via indecency provisions; drafting vagueness noted by HDT.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch (6 November 2024): Mali’s new penal code criminalises same-sex conduct with harsh penalties; previously legal but vague "public indecency" provisions (Article 225) were used against LGBT people and gender-nonconforming expressions, and the new law bans the undefined "promotion" of homosexuality, greatly expanding who can be prosecuted.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 403); the underlying Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Mali's new criminalisation of same-sex conduct.

The Conversation (15 January 2025), interview with anthropologist Christophe Broqua: Mali's new penal code, announced October 2024 and in force 13 December 2024, criminalises homosexuality and any citizen seen to encourage it. The escalation comes under the military junta, alongside clampdowns on opposition and media.
US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Mali: official assessment - same-sex conduct not criminalised but significant societal stigma; violence and instability from armed groups.
US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Mali: documents gender inequality, FGM, corruption, and 'discrimination based on sexual orientation' among other human-rights problems.

The HRW World Report 2025 Mali chapter (Events of 2024) covers the junta's rule, counterterrorism sweeps (arbitrary arrest of 25 people in Ouro Fero village, Nara region) and an ICC arrest warrant, but contains no transgender-specific content and no information on prison placement, special units, or solitary/segregation practice for trans prisoners.

MLI.tangentialFactors: The 2024 penal code criminalises homosexuality; its application to trans expression runs through the indecency provisions (Art 225) and the code's vague drafting.
MLI.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Nigeria (0.19)/Cameroon (0.21) — below Tunisia (0.19, comparable) and above Uganda (0.17).

BFA.name: Burkina Faso
BFA.summary:
On 1 September 2025 the Transitional Legislative Assembly of Burkina Faso passed a law making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence, carrying two to five years' imprisonment and fines. The law was passed unanimously by the military junta that has held power since September 2022. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala stated that the penalty range of two to five years' imprisonment, together with fines, applies to perpetrators of "homosexual or similar practices".

The criminal prohibition is carried by a revised Personal and Family Code (CPF) approved by the junta's council in July 2024 as part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law. Homosexuality had never before been outlawed in Burkina Faso; the ban took effect as criminal-code law on 1 September 2025.

Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala has stated that foreigners will be deported under the law. A trans visitor therefore faces not only imprisonment and fines but removal from the country under a statute whose drafting and application in relation to trans people are not further specified in the available reporting.

The law was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space. It was passed by a transitional legislature rather than an elected parliament, and the sources provide no indication of judicial review, complaint mechanism or other institutional recourse available to a person charged under it.
BFA.outOfScopeNotes:
Enforcement practice since the law took effect on 1 September 2025 is unresolved. The available sources report the passage, the penalties and the deportation provision, but no arrests, prosecutions, sentence lengths or documented police conduct under the new offence.

The reach of the phrase "homosexual or similar practices" as used by Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala is unresolved. Whether the provision captures gender identity, gender expression or trans people specifically is not stated in the sources, and no trans-specific case or guidance is sourced here.

The sources do not address whether Burkina Faso has any legal framework for recognition or change of gender markers on identity or travel documents, and no entry, visa or border-screening rule specific to trans travellers is sourced. The existing position on legal gender recognition before 1 September 2025 is likewise not sourced.

Whether the Transitional Legislative Assembly's proceedings, or any court, offered an avenue to challenge the law is not sourced beyond the fact of unanimous passage. Reported detail stops at the enactment date.

sources.summary: BBC (11 July 2024): Burkina Faso's military junta announced a ban on homosexual acts. Homosexivity had never before been outlawed in the socially conservative West African state. The ban formed part of a junta-led overhaul of marriage and family law and entered into force as criminal-code law on 1 September 2025.

Africanews (11 July 2024, updated 13 August 2024): the junta's council approved a decree for a new Personal and Family Code (CPF) that enshrines the ban on homosexuality, per a presidency statement, joining the roughly 22 of 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations. The code entered into force on 1 September 2025 and is the instrument that carries the criminalisation.

Human Rights Watch (3 September 2025): the Transitional Legislative Assembly passed the law on 1 September 2025 making consensual same-sex relations a criminal offence, carrying two to five years' imprisonment plus fines. It was enacted amid a junta crackdown on opposition, media and civil space.

LGBTQ Nation (September 2025): the junta unanimously passed the law. Justice Minister Edasso Rodrigue Bayala states prison terms 'between two and five years as well as fines' for perpetrators of 'homosexual or similar practices', and that foreigners will be deported under the law. Junta rule dates from September 2022.

BFA.tangentialFactors:
Burkina Faso joins roughly 22 of the 54 African states that disallow same-sex relations, placing it within a substantial regional pattern of criminalisation rather than outside it.

The prohibition did not arrive as a standalone statute on sexual conduct. It was folded into a broad rewrite of marriage and family law, so the Personal and Family Code is the operative instrument and the criminal penalty sits inside a wider package of family-law reform approved by the junta's council in July 2024.

Passage was unanimous in the transitional legislature, and the measure was announced by the presidency and defended publicly by the Justice Minister. The official framing presents the ban as deliberate government policy rather than an incidental consequence of the family-code revision.
BFA.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Egypt/Algeria/Uzbekistan (0.22), above Mali (0.20 — MLI's code is harsher and more explicitly enforced) and below Ghana (0.24).

MOZ.name: Mozambique
MOZ.summary:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. RWA.name: Rwanda
RWA.summary:
Rwanda demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex intimacy is not criminalised, and the government formally tolerates a small LGBT presence — but a 2025 Human Rights First Rwanda Association submission to the UN Human Rights Committee documents ongoing law-enforcement abuses against transgender persons, including arbitrary arrests and detentions (framed as “vagrancy” or “deviance” round-ups in Kigali's periodic street-cleaning operations).

For a visitor: no statutory exposure, but Kigali's sweep operations can net gender-nonconforming people, and recourse is nil. There is no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination protection, and the constitution recognises only civil monogamous marriage between a man and a woman — a partner-travel consideration for a trans visitor.
RWA.outOfScopeNotes: Sweep detentions are documented against trans persons specifically (2025 HRF submission). No source in this record covers visa or border document screening for trans visitors, and implementation practice of the 2024 NGO law is unverified. The 2016 presidential statement is dated and may not reflect current policy.

AGO.name: Angola
AGO.summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and freedom of expression sit across Title II. Sexual-orientation discrimination is therefore addressed in the Penal Code rather than anchored in the equality article, and gender identity does not appear as a protected ground in either place.

Formal international-review channels are active. A shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter was submitted for the African Commission's 81st session in Banjul in October and November 2024 by Angolan organisations including Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina, with support from ILGA and Synergia; it documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. Separately, Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations lodged a submission with the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights ahead of the Committee's 74th pre-session review of the state, foregrounding discrimination and health-access issues for lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

Trans visibility in Angolan public life has a documented history. In April 2012 the kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, became a mainstream star at 25, in a Catholic country where the article records homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. The trajectory from that period to the 2021 reform is one of open presence preceding and outlasting the legal change.
AGO.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved on this inventory: whether Angola provides legal gender recognition, and on what documentary or medical terms. None of the six sources addresses a recognition procedure, so no statement about changing gender markers on identity documents can be sourced here.

Unresolved: entry and visa screening practice, including any questioning of trans travellers at border or airport, and the gender-affirming care available to a visitor. The CESCR submission raises health access in a resident context; no source describes care access for non-residents.

Unresolved: enforcement data for the sexual-orientation discrimination offence, including whether any conviction has been recorded since the 2021 commencement, and any recorded case of violence against a trans person with date and outcome. The sources establish the existence of the provision and of documented violations generally, not case-level results.

Unresolved: how trans detainees or prisoners are housed, the constitutional standing of gender identity as such, and whether the anti-discrimination provision is read as covering gender identity rather than sexual orientation alone. The SALC chapter maps the Article 23 gap but the inventory carries no litigation outcome on the point.

Angola's reform is regularly cited comparatively as an outlier on the continent: a 2019 overview framed its drafting strategy, removing the colonial offence while adding an anti-discrimination penalty in one statute, as the most advanced of the African reforms of that cycle. COD.name: DR Congo
COD.summary:
The Democratic Republic of Congo does not criminalise same-sex conduct. Same-sex activity has never been outlawed, including under Belgian colonial rule, and the age of consent is equal for all partners. A stakeholder submission to the country's 5th-cycle Universal Periodic Review (Savie asbl and co-signatories, March 2024) states that the state neither protects nor promotes LGBTIQ+ rights, leaving the absence of a ban without any accompanying legal safeguard.

Public same-sex affection can be prosecuted under Article 176 of the Penal Code, which punishes anyone who publicly outrages morals by actions, and local ordinances are also applied against LGBTQ people. Queer In The World reports that LGBT expression is censored and can carry exposure to imprisonment. Enforcement is discretionary rather than statutory, which means the exposure arises from police and administrative action rather than a specific offence of identity or orientation.

There is no legal gender recognition and no procedure for legal gender change, so a trans visitor's documents will stand as issued and cannot be aligned locally. Same-sex marriage has been constitutionally banned since 2006, and no other relationship recognition exists, so a visitor's partner has no legal standing in the country.

Violence against LGBT people is documented as involving the police, the security forces and the armed forces, including reports of harassment and torture. Armed groups in the provinces have committed extreme violence against LGBTQ people with near-total impunity, and the collapse of state authority in parts of the country makes formal legal protections theoretical in practice. Human Rights Watch (4 December 2017), drawing on more than 120 interviews including nine Congolese security-force officers, UN officials and 21 M23 fighters, documented security forces recruiting ex-M23 fighters from Uganda and Rwanda between October and December 2016 and deploying them with orders to use lethal force against protesters in Kinshasa, Goma and Lubumbashi; the impunity for that violence bears directly on what a visitor can expect from the protection machinery.

Church groups inside the country actively promote the position that homosexuality is immoral, which shapes the social environment a trans visitor enters. Queer In The World advises visitors to keep a low profile and exercise discretion; given the combination of an unenforceable legal position, documented state violence and militia violence, that advice reflects the operative risk rather than a formality.
COD.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses entry or visa rules for trans visitors, the acceptance of passport gender markers at Congolese border posts, or airport and immigration screening that could result in outing. Those questions remain unresolved here and should not be read as cleared.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, availability of hormones, and the treatment of trans travellers in detention are not sourced in this inventory and are unresolved.

The frequency with which Article 176 is actually used against individuals, and whether prosecutions have resulted in imprisonment, is not established by these sources; the claim is limited to the provision being available and reported as applied. The status of any sub-national ordinance specifically targeting LGBTQ people is likewise not detailed.

Human Rights Watch material cited here concerns the 2016 recruitment of ex-M23 fighters and force against protesters; it does not document a trans-specific killing or assault with a named victim and date, so no such incident is asserted.

A trans visitor who is outed or who draws police attention enters that apparatus, where procedural protection is weak regardless of the underlying charge.

The legal position in the Democratic Republic of Congo differs from that of neighbouring jurisdictions that maintain explicit sodomy statutes: there is no offence to fall back on, which removes one category of statutory risk while leaving the discretionary exposure under Article 176 and local ordinances intact. The absence of criminalisation should not be read as an absence of enforcement risk, since the provisions used against LGBTQ people are general morality and decency clauses rather than identity-specific ones.

Religious messaging against homosexuality is a domestic current rather than a state policy, but it compounds the practical environment alongside militia activity and the weakness of state authority in the provinces.

Residents have no route to legal gender recognition or legal gender change, and no mechanism for recognition of a same-sex partnership, since the constitutional ban on same-sex marriage has stood since 2006.

Same-sex conduct carries no criminal penalty and the age of consent is equal, but LGBT organisations operate under constraint. Savie asbl, based in Bukavu, has used the Universal Periodic Review process to document systematic violations, indicating that formal human-rights channels are the available avenue for residents rather than domestic courts or police complaint procedures.

ZMB.name: Zambia
ZMB.summary:
Zambia is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.
ZMB.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; trans people are captured via birth-sex status and indecency provisions.

sources.summary: Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024), 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional, 36, had served three years by Nov 2024 for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; illustrates the persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.

ZMB.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years, active enforcement) — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
ZMB.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Ghana (0.24 — both criminalisation-plus-mobilised-hostility), above Zimbabwe (0.27, actually below — ZMB's documented 15-year serving sentence and current campaign edge it below ZWE) and below Morocco (0.25).

ZWE.name: Zimbabwe
ZWE.summary:
Zimbabwe is dangerous for trans visitors. The 2006 Criminal Law Act criminalises sodomy (up to 1 year — a lighter formal penalty than neighbours, though indecency provisions add exposure), and Amnesty's 2024 report documents shrinking civic space threatening LGBT organising (GALZ operates under pressure; its offices have been raided historically). There is no legal gender recognition, political rhetoric is hostile, and mob violence is documented — but prosecution under the sodomy law is rarer than in Zambia, and a small organised community persists openly enough to litigate.

For a visitor: statutory exposure exists but enforcement is sporadic; social hostility is the main risk.
ZWE.outOfScopeNotes: Same-sex criminalisation is the vehicle; enforcement pattern is sporadic.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Zimbabwe criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, covering sodomy and acts involving contact between males that would be regarded by a reasonable person as indecent.

Amnesty International report, 9 January 2024, index AFR 01/7533/2024: 'We are facing extinction — escalating anti-LGBTI sentiment, the weaponisation of law and their human rights implications in select African countries'. The report examines anti-LGBTI sentiment and the use of law against LGBTI people in select African countries.

New Zimbabwe, 9 July 2018: the health ministry released a 68-page training handbook for all health practitioners on serving gays, sex workers and transgender/non-gender-conforming people in public health institutions. The manual states care for these groups is legal and every provider's duty ('nowhere in policy or law states it is illegal to provide healthcare services to members of key population groups'), issued because patients had avoided clinics fearing mistreatment or police tip-offs by staff. For a trans visitor: formal policy guarantees health-service access including transition-relevant care at public facilities, though day-to-day treatment depends on staff trained under a 2018 handbook.

Mabvurira et al., 'The politics of sexual identities in Zimbabwe: A Social Work perspective?' (Int'l Journal of Humanities and Social Science, July 2012): homosexuals live secluded lives due to prejudice; argues homosexuality is 'as African as the baobab tree and as Zimbabwean as the Great Zimbabwe Ruins', tracing same-sex relations in pre-colonial and post-colonial Zimbabwe; social workers should promote social justice for the gay community.
Taylor & Francis (Journal of Homosexuality): academic article on homosexuality in Zimbabwe.

GALZ (Gays and Lesbians of Zimbabwe) official site: voluntary membership organisation established 1990, now 4,000+ community members, 35 years of advocacy, 10 affinity groups, 4 resource centres. Services include legal support (explicitly including for 'sodomy' arrests), counselling, hospital-fee assistance and empowerment programmes for LGBTI Zimbabweans. For the record: documented local support infrastructure — legal aid and counselling reachable despite criminalisation, useful for an LGBTI traveller needing assistance.

ZWE.tangentialFactors: Sodomy criminalised (up to 1 year, sporadic enforcement) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.
ZWE.comparisons: Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZWE's formal penalty is lighter and enforcement rarer) and below Senegal (0.27, tie).

MWI.name: Malawi
MWI.summary: Malawi is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) AND Human Dignity Trust lists Malawi as criminalising the gender expression of trans people. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the Constitutional Court upheld the ban — a case brought partly by a local trans woman and her Dutch partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. Discrimination and violence are regular despite the moratorium.
MWI.outOfScopeNotes: Prosecution moratorium is informal and revocable; the 2024 ruling keeps the statute fully alive.

sources.summary: Human Rights Watch dispatch, 11 July 2024: Malawi's Constitutional Court on 28 June 2024 rejected the challenge to Penal Code sections 153, 154 and 156. A three-member panel dismissed the application brought by Dutch national Jan Willen Akster and Jana Gonani, a trans woman who received an eight-year sentence in a men's prison in December 2021. The sections carry up to 14 years' imprisonment. Faith-based groups filed briefs and religious leaders led nationwide protests claiming the case sought to legalise same-sex marriage. The court left any reform to parliament. HRW called it a 'dark day' and warned of heightened arbitrary-arrest and violence risks.

US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Malawi: documents the July 2011 protest killings (20 dead), harsh prisons, and 'discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) persons'.

Human Rights Watch (26 October 2018), releasing the 61-page report 'Let Posterity Judge' based on interviews with 45 LGBT people in Lilongwe and Blantyre plus lawyers, activists and officials: police arbitrarily arrested and detained transgender people, sometimes assaulting them, and medical staff denied services on gender-expression grounds (a trans man beaten then refused treatment; nurses mocked people presenting for HIV tests). Men face up to 14 years and women five years under sections 153/156; the 2012 justice-minister moratorium on arrests was reaffirmed in December 2015 but suspended by the Mzuzu High Court in 2016 after religious leaders' litigation, leaving its legality contested. People whose gender expression differs from expectations are 'most likely to be targeted'.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 December 2015): two men arrested in Malawi on 7 December on homosexuality charges suffered house ransacking and assault by neighbours, threats of being burned alive, attempted extortion and humiliation by community police — forced stripping, forced medical and HIV/STD examinations, and photos distributed on social media. CEDEP's Gift Trapence contrasts the arrests with government Global Fund money for LGBTI HIV services. Documents the arrest-and-abuse pattern under the penal code.

Erasing 76 Crimes (27 April 2018): police arrested Limbani Sibande, 24, in Mzuzu for suspected homosexuality and charged him under section 156 ('indecent practices between males') rather than section 153 — apparently to circumvent the six-year moratorium on anti-gay arrests while both laws faced a constitutional challenge. Police spokespersons confirmed the custody. Evidence of law-enforcement attempts to elude the moratorium.

MWI.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 14 years, moratorium since 2014) — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners; the moratorium is informal and revocable.
MWI.comparisons: Pairwise: above Zambia (0.24 — ZMB has an active 15-year serving case; MWI's moratorium holds) and below Zimbabwe (0.27, comparable). The gender-expression criminalisation listing is what places MWI in the mid-0.2s rather than higher.

The penal code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years), and an international legal-aid trust lists this country as criminalising the gender expression of trans people as well. A moratorium on prosecutions has held since 2014, but in June 2024 the constitutional court upheld the ban — a case brought in part by a local trans woman and her foreign partner — and religious leaders led nationwide anti-LGBT marches in 2023. SDN.name: Sudan
SDN.summary:
Sudan is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely. Article 152 of the Penal Code criminalises gender nonconformity directly; sodomy carries life imprisonment (capital/corporal punishment removed in 2020 reforms); and Cairo 52 documents state violence against LGBTQIA+ people including extrajudicial killings. Since April 2023 the country has been in a catastrophic civil war (SAF vs RSF) with documented mass atrocities — the conflict intensifies every risk and eliminates any recourse. There is no LGR and no community infrastructure.

For a visitor: statutory criminalisation of gender nonconformity plus one of the world's worst active conflicts.
SDN.outOfScopeNotes: War conditions affect all; Art 152 is trans-specific.

sources.summary: Cairo 52 Sudan profile: penal code Article 152 criminalises wearing clothing of the opposite sex (cross-dressing provisions); no arrest statistics for trans people but documented state violence including extrajudicial killings against LGBTQIA+ individuals; no legal gender recognition, gender-affirming healthcare legally constrained, the ongoing conflict further restricts access, and state reliance on Sunni fatwas blocks transition. Gender-nonconformity framing for visitor risk.

Human Dignity Trust country profile: Sudan criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with sentences including a maximum of life imprisonment and, historically, the death penalty for a third offence.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Sudan: its LGBT section notes criminalisation under Article 148, with flogging and death penalty provisions. The report also documents extrajudicial killings, torture and abuses of the Bashir regime.

Berkouwer, Sultan & Yehia (2014): 'Homosexuality in Sudan and Egypt: Stories of the Struggle for Survival', produced with activists of Bedayaa, the LGBTQI organisation for the Nile Valley. The work records daily struggles, discrimination and violence rooted in societal gender and sexual norms.

Rainbow Sudan — Sudan's community magazine: runs sections on LGBTI rights in Sudan, including history and analysis, and profiles Sudanese LGBTI organisations, documenting an organised local community presence.

76crimes (15 Jul 2020): Sudan's Sovereign Council removed the death penalty for homosexuality — maximum now life imprisonment for a third offence — abolished the 100 lashes for same-sex intimacy, and set up to five years' imprisonment for a first offence in the criminal-code amendment.

SDN.tangentialFactors: Sodomy carries life imprisonment — a direct risk for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SDN.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Iraq (0.08 — IRQ has a codified anti-trans statute; SDN has Art 152 + active civil war) and above Syria/Yemen (0.06 — SDN's legal system, though hostile, nominally exists where SAF controls territory).

SOM.name: Somalia
SOM.summary:
Somalia is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous countries for any LGBT person. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 3 years), but the operative reality is worse: Al-Shabaab controls significant territory and applies its interpretation of sharia, under which homosexuality and gender transgression are capital offences — executions are documented. Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in Somalia.
SOM.outOfScopeNotes: Fragmented authority means enforcement varies; Al-Shabaab areas apply capital punishment.

sources.summary: The Human Dignity Trust country profile documents Somalia's criminalisation of same-sex sexual activity: up to life imprisonment under the 1964 penal code, and the death penalty under Sharia in some regions.

US State Department 2021 Human Rights Report for Somalia: official assessment - same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years); al-Shabaab enforces strict Sharia with death as possible punishment; pervasive violence and statelessness.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Somalia: criminalizes 'carnal intercourse with a person of the same sex', 3 months' to 3 years' imprisonment, no official reports of enforcement available; under local interpretations of sharia, homosexuality is punishable by death; no known state-conducted executions of that sort reported. Impunity generally remained the norm.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Somalia (archived): documents the conflict, al-Shabaab abuses, and the LGBT section noting criminalisation and the death penalty under Islamic law in areas under insurgent control.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Feb 2016) on Benjamin Christman's 'Report on the Treatment of Gay Persons in Somalia' (published 2 Feb 2016): evidence that gay persons should not be returned to Somalia due to persecution risk, supporting refugee-status claims and forming a non-refoulement basis for LGBT asylum seekers.

Al Jazeera (Jul 2013) 'Gay Somali refugees face death threats': refugees in Kenya face threats and racist discrimination; Al-Shabaab publicised intent to 'enforce harsh punishments' against homosexuality, and senior figures claimed a 'death chamber' for gay and lesbians if returned, while UN officials nevertheless pushed return. The account records persecution driving displacement.

SOM.tangentialFactors: Same-sex conduct criminalised (up to 3 years) and capital under Al-Shabaab's sharia — a catastrophic exposure for trans visitors with partners or perceived as same-sex-active.
SOM.comparisons: Pairwise: above Afghanistan (0.02 — AFG's Taliban control is more total and systematic; SOM's is fragmented between a weak government and Al-Shabaab) and below Syria (0.06).

Even in government areas, mob violence and clan-justice dynamics make any gender nonconformity lethal-risk. There is no legal gender recognition, no community, and no recourse of any kind.

For a visitor: there is no safe way to be visibly trans anywhere in the country.

ERI.name: Eritrea
ERI.summary:
Article 310(1) of Eritrea's 2015 Penal Code criminalises "homosexual conduct" and carries up to seven years' imprisonment. The provision descends from the 1957 Ethiopian penal code, which Eritrea retained after independence with a longer sentence. The UK Foreign Office records same-sex activity as a crime and confirms that no anti-discrimination legislation protects lesbian, gay, bisexual or transgender people.

Exposure is not limited to prosecution. The US State Department's 2023 reporting states that openly LGBTQI+ persons risk imprisonment and for that reason did not participate in the political process, and that societal discrimination against them continues. A 2011 State Department report relayed by Asmarino records societal abuse and discrimination against gay men and lesbians, and documents the government labelling disloyal individuals as "gay, traitors, rapists, pedophiles" — a state practice that makes the accusation itself a tool of official pressure.

The 2010 State Department report combines the criminalisation and stigma findings with torture, arbitrary detention and indefinite national service, which define what detention in Eritrea would mean for a person suspected of same-sex conduct. The UK raised these concerns with Eritrea bilaterally and through the EU; the US, UK and Outright International all maintain current reporting on the situation.

Nothing in the sources addresses trans people specifically. No data exists on how gender non-conformity is treated, whether identity documents can be changed, or what screening a traveller would undergo. The informational closure recorded in the reporting — no independent media and no civil society to document conditions — is itself the reason the risk for a trans visitor cannot be bounded.

No source in the inventory addresses these.

ATG.name: Antigua and Barbuda
ATG.summary:
Antigua and Barbuda requires real caution. In July 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court struck down Sections 12 and 15 of the Sexual Offences Act 1995, decriminalising sodomy and gross indecency between adults, and read the constitutional prohibition on sex discrimination to cover sexual orientation and gender identity as well.

That ruling does not amount to a statutory protection regime. No explicit anti-discrimination protection on the grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in Antiguan and Barbudan law, and same-sex unions are not recognised. A visitor who is refused service, housing or transport on these grounds has no statute to invoke, only the constitutional argument the court opened in 2022.

There is no mechanism to change a legal gender marker. Only name changes are available, and Outright International records that transgender people are particularly vulnerable in Antigua and Barbuda precisely because no legal gender recognition process exists. A visitor whose passport marker does not match their presentation should expect that mismatch to be visible at every point where documents are checked.

Social hostility remains a live factor. Orden David, the Antiguan activist who brought the challenge that produced the 2022 judgment, was bullied and physically attacked before his case succeeded, including being struck in the head and knocked out in daylight. Tourist resort areas are comparatively insulated, but that insulation is a matter of circumstance rather than legal protection.

The protection machinery is unfinished. A January 2025 submission from The Advocates for Human Rights to the UN Human Rights Committee, filed ahead of its review of Antigua and Barbuda, sets out the SOGI-protection questions the state still faces after decriminalisation, indicating that the post-2022 legal position remains under international scrutiny rather than settled.
ATG.outOfScopeNotes:
The consequence axis of an arrest is undocumented. The Outright International country profile (page states 'Last Update: March 12, 2026') contains no data on trans-prisoner housing placement: no birth-sex versus identity rule, no trans-specific units, no solitary or segregation practice. In a jurisdiction with no legal gender recognition and no anti-discrimination statute, a detained trans visitor would enter a prison system whose treatment of them is not described in any source held here.

Entry and visa screening are not covered by this inventory. Whether immigration or security screening asks about gender marker, sex or transition status, and what happens on a mismatch between a passport marker and presentation at the border, is unresolved and not sourced.

Facility access rules, including restroom and changing-room use in hotels, airports and public buildings, are not sourced. Nor is access to gender-affirming healthcare, its availability locally, or whether a visitor could obtain it.

It is also unresolved whether the 2022 constitutional reading of 'sex' has been applied in any decided case since the judgment, or how a court would handle a discrimination claim brought by a transgender complainant specifically rather than a sexual-orientation claim.

ATG.tangentialFactors:
Antigua and Barbuda sits inside a wider regional pattern rather than standing apart from it. Six Caribbean countries still criminalise same-sex conduct, and the 2022 judgment came out of a coordinated legal strategy: in December 2019 the Eastern Caribbean Alliance for Diversity and Equality (ECADE) announced court challenges to buggery and indecency laws in Barbados, St Kitts-Nevis, Antigua and Barbuda, Grenada and Saint Lucia, arguing that those laws stigmatise and legitimise hate speech, discrimination and violence against LGBT people.

The direction of travel across the Eastern Caribbean is therefore toward decriminalisation, but the pace is uneven and the accompanying protections have not followed the penalties out of the statute book. Comparable states that retain the offences provide a reference point for what a reversal would look like, and litigation of this kind remains subject to appeal and to legislative change.

BRB.name: Barbados
BRB.summary:
Barbados decriminalised same-sex conduct in December 2022, on the strength of a constitutional challenge filed in June 2018 with trans activist Alexa Hoffmann as claimant, supported by the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network and the University of Toronto's international human-rights program. The Human Dignity Trust records the Barbados case as one of a series of constitutional challenges to colonial-era anti-gay statutes across the Eastern Caribbean.

Impunity for anti-trans violence is documented and recent enough to matter. In April 2019 a Barbadian court imposed no jail time for the violent meat-cleaver attack on Alexa Hoffmann, an outcome reported through Maurice Tomlinson and the Canadian HIV/AIDS Legal Network. A visibly trans visitor who is assaulted should not expect a custodial sentence against the attacker.

Trans people on the island are visible and exposed at once. A second Trans Day of Remembrance vigil was held in Barbados in November 2018, organised with a national women's organisation, a local ally and veteran trans advocates, and Hoffmann has given first-person accounts of what visibility and danger look like there in daily life.

Employment offers no shield. Trans Barbadians are reported to be frequently fired or refused work for dressing in a way employers object to, and the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill does not cover them, according to an August 2020 commentary on the island's labour rules.

The Welcome Stamp remote-work visa is marketed to outsiders on a promise of openness, while the employment regime that trans residents face gives them no protection against dismissal. Entry on that visa says nothing about how a trans worker or visitor will be treated once on the ground.
BRB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved in this inventory: whether Barbados provides legal gender recognition or allows a trans person to amend gender markers on passport, birth certificate or national ID. No source here addresses it, and the summary makes no claim either way.

Not sourced in this material: hate-crime or aggravated-offence provisions covering anti-trans violence, rules on access to sex-segregated facilities, recognition of trans marriages or partners, and any entry or immigration screening that could disclose a traveller's trans status. Each would need separate verification.

The status of the Employment (Protection from Discrimination) Bill is unresolved here: the inventory reports what the bill excludes, not whether it was enacted or amended after 2020, so current statutory coverage for trans workers is unconfirmed.

The account of frequent dismissals of trans workers comes from an August 2020 commentary rather than official or survey data, and no enforcement record for employment complaints is available in this inventory.

The December 2022 decriminalisation is documented through the Human Dignity Trust's case page rather than through the text of the court judgment or the state's response to it; the precise scope of the ruling is not set out here.

The gap between the 2022 decriminalisation and the 2019 impunity outcome in the attack shows that a liberalised statute and a protective enforcement record are separate questions; the legal reform did not itself establish sentencing practice for anti-trans violence.

KNA.name: Saint Kitts and Nevis
KNA.summary:
Saint Kitts and Nevis no longer criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. In 2022 the Eastern Caribbean Supreme Court, in Jamal Jeffers v The Attorney General, struck section 56 (buggery) and section 57 (indecent assault against a man) of the Offences Against the Person Act as contrary to the rights to privacy and expression. Consensual same-sex conduct has been lawful throughout the country since that ruling.

Legal gender recognition is not possible in Saint Kitts and Nevis. A person cannot obtain official recognition of a changed gender marker, and the sources document no administrative route, court process or statute that would allow it.

No provision of the penal code or of any other statute prohibits discrimination or harassment on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity. Discrimination in the workplace, in education and in accommodation remains lawful, as does hate speech, and no anti-discrimination statute has been enacted in the years since decriminalisation.

Relationship recognition is absent in full. Same-sex unions are not recognised in any form, whether marriage or partnership, and same-sex households receive none of the rights granted to opposite-sex married couples.

The protection machinery that does exist sits in policy rather than law. LGBTQ+ citizens are included in the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027, but a 2025 joint presentation to the Universal Periodic Review by the Saint Kitts and Nevis Alliance and ECADE records a lack of tangible steps by the State to implement that inclusion.

Relations with the authorities are a separate matter from the statute book. The same 2025 submission states that LGBTQ+ people avoid law enforcement, which bears directly on whether a visitor can expect assistance if a bias-motivated incident occurs. LGBTI organisations are permitted to register, and civil society used the courts rather than the legislature to obtain decriminalisation.

The practical position for a trans visitor is therefore lawful private conduct without protective scaffolding: conduct between adults is not an offence, but there is no anti-discrimination law, no recognised gender marker, no recognised relationship, and no sourced evidence of state remedies being used after a bias incident.
KNA.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory records incidents of violence against trans people in Saint Kitts and Nevis, their frequency, dates, police response or judicial outcome. Absence of documented cases should be read as unsourced rather than as evidence that no such violence occurs.

Entry and border screening are not addressed by any source here: whether immigration officers question travellers whose passports carry amended gender markers, or require supporting documentation, remains unresolved from this material.

Hate-crime enhancement for bias-motivated assaults is not covered by the inventory. The sources establish that anti-discrimination and hate-speech conduct are not unlawful, which is not the same finding as whether a court would treat gender identity as an aggravating factor in sentencing.

Whether the Offences Against the Person Act or any other statute retains gendered or sex-based provisions that could reach a trans person in specific circumstances, such as public order or indecency offences, is not sourced and cannot be stated either way from this material.

The implementation record of the National Gender Equality Policy 2022-2027 is characterised in the 2025 Universal Periodic Review submission only as lacking tangible steps; no government response or subsequent evaluation was available to weigh against that assessment.

KNA.tangentialFactors:

Outlets tracking these statutes report ongoing lawsuits against several Caribbean nations over anti-gay laws and frame courts as the principal mechanism for expanding LGBTQ rights in the Caribbean, which indicates that the current legal position rests on a judicial ruling that a future legislature or court could in principle revisit.

Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, records the same three findings as the domestic submissions: consensual same-sex conduct legal since 2022, legal gender recognition not available, and LGBTI organisations free to register. DMA.name: Dominica
DMA.summary:
Dominica's High Court of Justice in Roseau struck sections 14 and 16 of the Sexual Offences Act on 23 April 2024, holding unconstitutional the provisions that criminalised consensual same-sex activity. The case was brought by a gay man living in Dominica (BBC, 23 Apr 2024; Human Rights Watch, 24 Apr 2024).

As a result of the ruling, consensual same-sex conduct between adults is no longer an offence under Dominica's Sexual Offences Act. The repeal came through judicial review of the statute rather than through an act of parliament: the High Court determined that the sections were unconstitutional.

The provisions had been under constitutional challenge before the 2024 ruling. MiRiDom founder Daryl Phillip announced a High Court challenge to Dominica's buggery and sexual-activity provisions at a news conference on 20 July 2019, five years before the provisions were struck down (Dominica News Online).

Dominica's documented diplomatic record includes signature of the 2011 Human Rights Council joint statement on ending acts of violence and related human rights violations based on sexual orientation and gender identity, whose signatory list includes 85 countries (US Mission Geneva, 22 Mar 2011). This is a dated commitment on the international record; it is not itself a domestic legal protection.

Local religious authority has publicly opposed criminalisation. Catholic Bishop Gabriel Malzaire of Dominica called in May 2013 for eliminating criminal penalties for homosexuality and for all forms of violence against LGBT people, citing the Holy See's position (Erasing 76 Crimes, 24 May 2013).

Regional context matters for planning: Human Rights Watch's April 2024 dispatch calls on all Caribbean nations to repeal comparable criminal laws, indicating that criminalising statutes remain in force elsewhere in the region. A visitor should not assume that the regime in Dominica is the regional norm.

Trans visitors face significant uncertainty. The sourced record addresses sexual-orientation criminalisation only. It does not document legal gender recognition rules, name or marker change procedures, anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections covering gender identity, access to trans-specific healthcare, or any documented pattern of anti-trans violence in Dominica.
DMA.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Dominica's law provides legal gender recognition for trans people is unresolved. No source in the inventory addresses marker or name change procedures, or any process for updating birth certificates or identity documents to reflect a trans person's gender.

Whether Dominica's anti-discrimination provisions extend to gender identity, and whether its criminal law recognises offences motivated by gender identity as hate crimes, is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No source in the inventory reports incidents of anti-trans violence in Dominica, and none addresses trans-specific healthcare access or the treatment of trans people in institutional settings. The absence of such reporting in the reviewed sources is not evidence that these risks are absent on the ground.

No source in the inventory documents how the former Sexual Offences Act provisions affected trans or gender-nonconforming people, including whether they could be used to compel psychiatric or medical intervention. This remains unverified.

A 2011 US State Department press statement relating to Dominica is cited in the inventory without its substance being reproduced; whether that statement addresses LGBT rights or other topics is unresolved.

LCA.name: Saint Lucia
LCA.summary:
Saint Lucia's High Court decriminalised same-sex conduct in July 2025, holding the criminal provision unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. The ruling, reported by Human Rights Watch on 31 July 2025 and by the Associated Press, arose from strategic constitutional litigation brought across the Eastern Caribbean rather than from a legislative amendment, and it struck down the colonial-era statute that had governed same-sex conduct.

For a visitor, the practical effect is that consensual same-sex conduct between adults no longer carries criminal exposure in Saint Lucia. Before the judgment, the statutory prohibition applied to everyone present on the island, residents and visitors alike; that specific criminal risk ended with the court's declaration of unconstitutionality.

The judgment addressed criminal liability only. The inventory before this pass contains no source establishing legal gender recognition, partner or marriage recognition, or statutory protection against discrimination in Saint Lucia, so a trans visitor should not assume the ruling carries those consequences.

Saint Lucia has an organised domestic rights community. United and Strong, a Saint Lucian organisation, and ECADE, a regional network of which Saint Lucian groups are part, have worked publicly on LGBTI issues for a decade or more; both figures in documented regional advocacy, including a 2017 protest by Caribbean activists, including United and Strong and ECADE, against an external publication's framing of regional sexuality issues under the slogan 'Nothing about us without us'.

Official-facing practice has been shaped by targeted training. On 19 May 2015 in Castries, United and Strong held human-rights sensitisation training for officers of the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and the Bordelais Correctional Facility, delivered with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson, extending sensitisation work begun in 2014. That history indicates sustained engagement with the very agencies a visitor may encounter at ports of entry or in custody, though the inventory does not evidence any comparable training after 2015.

VCT.name: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines
VCT.summary: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines demands real caution — the Eastern Caribbean outlier: its High Court UPHELD the buggery laws in 2024 (unlike its neighbours), so criminalisation (10 years) remains formally in force. Enforcement is rare, but the legal floor and judicial hostility distinguish it from the decriminalised neighbours.
VCT.outOfScopeNotes: 2024 ruling upheld criminalisation — opposite trajectory from neighbours.

PinkNews (17 Feb 2024): the High Court ruled on 16 Feb 2024 to uphold the ban on gay sex (sections 146/148 of the criminal code), dismissing a constitutional challenge -- same-sex conduct stays criminal in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

GRD.name: Grenada
GRD.summary:
Grenada criminalises consensual same-sex conduct. Section 430 of the Criminal Code addresses "grossly indecent acts" between men and Section 431 addresses "unnatural crime"; both provisions remain in force. The United States Department of State reported in its 2023 human rights report that these laws are not enforced in practice.

No legal gender recognition is available, so a trans visitor's documents will reflect the sex marker assigned at birth or by another jurisdiction, with no domestic route to amend them.

No statutory anti-discrimination protections cover sexual orientation or gender identity. LGBTIQ people in Grenada face discrimination in housing, education, employment and access to public services.

Fear of prosecution under Sections 430 and 431 inhibits LGBTIQ people from reporting crimes to the police, which weakens the practical value of police protection even where officers do not pursue prosecutions.

The 2023 United States Department of State report records no arbitrary killings, torture or forced disappearances in Grenada.

GrenCHAP has provided services to marginalised groups for more than fifteen years, working with LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth; it is the principal documented point of support for a visitor seeking community-based assistance.

An October 2024 stakeholder report by The Advocates for Human Rights, Khaleem Ali and GrenCHAP, submitted for the Universal Periodic Review, documents the legal and social situation of LGBTIQ+ people in Grenada, including the Sections 430 and 431 provisions.

Grenada is a small island society in which social visibility is high; the sources describe sustained social discrimination alongside formal non-enforcement of the criminal provisions.
GRD.outOfScopeNotes:
The current sources state the text of Sections 430 and 431 but do not set out the penalties those sections carry, so the sentence exposure attached to a conviction is not sourced here.

No source in this inventory addresses marriage or partner recognition for same-sex couples in Grenada; that question is unresolved rather than answered in the negative.

No source records whether any prosecution under Sections 430 or 431 has ever been brought, so the statement that the provisions are unenforced rests on the United States Department of State's 2023 assessment rather than on a prosecution-by-prosecution record.

Nothing in the inventory addresses border screening, entry refusal on the basis of gender identity or expression, or treatment at port of entry; those visitor-facing questions are not sourced.

Information on the availability of gender-affirming healthcare, including whether access is restricted by law, is not covered by these sources.

Outright International profile (updated Mar 2026): same-sex conduct criminalised under Sections 430 ('grossly indecent act') and 431 ('unnatural crime'); no legal gender recognition; no anti-discrimination protections; LGBTIQ people face discrimination in housing, education, employment and public services, and fear of prosecution inhibits reporting to police.

US State Dept 2023 report on Grenada: significant human-rights issues include laws criminalising consensual sexual conduct between men, though not enforced; no arbitrary killings, torture or disappearances reported.

GRD.tangentialFactors:

The gap between the statute book and enforcement is the defining feature of the country's position: conduct criminalised on paper is not prosecuted, but the existence of the offence shapes how LGBTIQ people interact with police and public institutions.

Community infrastructure is comparatively durable for a small jurisdiction, with GrenCHAP sustaining services to LGBT+ people, people living with HIV, sex workers and vulnerable youth across more than fifteen years.

BHS.name: Bahamas
BHS.summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct, and no pattern of police targeting is documented.

Transgender and intersex residents and visitors hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United stated this absence plainly when it launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016, and the organisation has campaigned against the dismissal of trans and intersex workers from their jobs. The gap is statutory, not merely administrative: no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources.

An official statement points the other way. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, the prison service and the police do not discriminate. That declaration is a ministerial assurance rather than a codified right, and a visitor cannot rely on it as a legal remedy.

Violence against visitors has been documented. On 8 May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and resident in the United States, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival; he said he wanted charges laid. The assault took place at a major tourist event in front of crowds, which indicates that a visitor whose appearance or manner is read as gender-nonconforming faces real risk of targeted violence in public, particularly during large festive gatherings, with no protective statute to fall back on.

The overall picture for a trans visitor is therefore one of legal exposure without legal cover: no criminalisation, but no legal gender recognition framework documented, no anti-discrimination statute, and hostility that has produced physical violence at a tourist venue.
BHS.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: whether charges were ever laid over the 8 May 2017 attack on Adrian Brown is not stated in the sources, and the outcome of his complaint is unknown.

Unresolved: the legal force of Frank Watson's May 1998 non-discrimination announcement is not established. The sources give the statement but not any implementing instrument, and whether it binds the police, prison service and military in practice is not sourced here.

Not sourced in this inventory: rules on legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, passport or visa presentation, entry screening that could out a traveller, access to gender-affirming care, facilities and bathroom rules, hate-crime provisions, and recognition of partners or marriages. No finding should be read either way on any of these points.

Not sourced: whether the 1991 Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act contains any provision reaching gender identity or public-order offences that could be used against a visibly transgender visitor.

BHS.tangentialFactors:
The 1998 non-discrimination assurance from Frank Watson and the 2016 findings of Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United describe the same country from opposite directions. One is a statement of intent from a cabinet minister; the other is an inventory of what the statute actually contains. Where the two conflict, the statute governs.

The 2017 assault on Adrian Brown concerned a gay man rather than a trans visitor, so it is an adjacent indicator rather than a trans-specific case. It nonetheless bears on trans visitors because the attack turned on how the victim was perceived in public, which is the same mechanism that exposes gender-nonconforming travellers.

The Bahamas runs a tourism-dependent economy with extensive international exposure, and the assault occurred at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, an event built for visitors. Incidents of this kind surface in the international press quickly, which shapes how the destination is perceived but does not alter the legal position on the ground.

Organised advocacy has existed since at least 2016, when Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United began the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign. Advocacy activity is evidence of an unprotected population, not evidence of protection.

Residents are covered by the 1991 decriminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, and by the May 1998 assurance from National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson that the military, the prison service and the police do not discriminate.

BLZ.name: Belize
BLZ.summary:
Belize decriminalised same-sex conduct through the courts. On 10 August 2016 the Supreme Court, under Chief Justice Kenneth Benjamin, struck down the colonial-era Section 53 sodomy law as unconstitutional in Orozco v Attorney General, the challenge filed in 2010 by LGBT advocate Caleb Orozco and heard in Belize City in 2013. The Human Dignity Trust carries the case among its documentation of constitutional challenges to anti-sodomy statutes, and Belize was the first former British Caribbean territory to overturn such a law.

Before the ruling the statute was rarely enforced, yet the expat reporting at hand argues it had fostered intolerance; a 1998 protest against a gay cruise docking is cited as evidence of residual public hostility. The same reporting holds that gay travellers have long found Belize friendly, and the country has an organised advocacy organisation in UNIBAM, which brought the Orozco litigation.

Belize accepted 15 of 17 sexual-orientation and gender-identity recommendations in its 2018 UN Universal Periodic Review, the first CARICOM state to accept that many. The accepted pledges cover legal reform, explicit anti-discrimination legislation, police training and the collection of SOGI data. Two rights-equality recommendations were 'noted' rather than accepted.

The detention axis is undocumented for Belize. The one prison-focused source in the inventory, a survey of LGBTQ prisoners worldwide, mentions Belize only through a navigation-box link and records no birth-sex-versus-identity housing rule, no trans housing units, and no solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Where a detained trans visitor would be placed is therefore unknown, and the absence of any recorded standard cannot be read as a protective one.
BLZ.outOfScopeNotes:
Prison placement for trans detainees in Belize is unresolved: no source here states a housing rule, a segregation practice or a trans-specific unit, so the question cannot be answered from this inventory.

Legal gender recognition is not addressed by any source in this inventory. Whether a trans visitor or resident can amend a birth certificate, passport or other marker, and on what conditions, is not sourced here.

Discrimination protection on grounds of gender identity in employment is not carried by any source in this inventory, despite the UPR pledge to legislate explicit anti-discrimination measures.

No post-2016 enforcement data, arrest statistics or police guidance on the treatment of trans people is available in this inventory; the practical operation of the Orozco ruling for a trans person is unverified.

Whether the accepted UPR recommendations have been implemented, in whole or in part, is not sourced here.

For residents, the accepted UPR commitments translate into promised police training, promised SOGI data collection, promised legal reform and promised explicit anti-discrimination legislation. HTI.name: Haiti
HTI.summary:
Haiti does not criminalise same-sex conduct; the prohibition has been off the books since 1791. There is no legal mechanism for gender recognition, no statutory anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity, and no hate-crime enhancement. The judiciary does not operate as a protection avenue in practice.

The legislature has twice moved to tighten the regime. In August 2017 the Senate passed a bill banning same-sex marriage and public LGBT advocacy, carrying up to three years' imprisonment and a fine of about US$8,000 for the parties. A June 2017 Senate bill would allow denial of the Certificat de Bonne Vie et Moeurs, the good-conduct certificate that employers and universities require, on grounds of homosexuality. Both measures awaited a vote in the Chamber of Deputies as of November 2017.

Generalised state collapse drives the practical risk. Gangs control most of Port-au-Prince, the police are outgunned, and mob violence against perceived LGBT people is documented; no protection machinery functions. Outing in gang-controlled areas can be lethal for a visitor.

The US State Department's 2018 report recorded attitudes in Haiti as hostile toward LGBTI individuals who were public and visible about their sexual orientation or gender identity and expression, particularly in Port-au-Prince. Human Rights Watch's 2018 world report found that LGBT persons in Haiti continued to face high levels of discrimination.

Visible advocacy carries a documented risk. Charlot Jeudy, president of Kouraj, the national LGBTQ advocacy organisation, was found dead at his home in Port-au-Prince on 25 November 2019; press reports attributing the death to poisoning were never confirmed. ILGALAC, the regional LGBTI body, issued a mourning statement.

Trans people have additionally faced targeted harassment in the post-earthquake displacement camps, where they were identifiable to other residents and to camp authorities.
HTI.outOfScopeNotes:

FJI.name: Fiji
FJI.summary:
Fiji decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct under the Crimes Act 2010, in force from 1 February 2010, repealing a colonial-era offence that had carried up to fourteen years' imprisonment. Arrests had already ceased in 2006, when the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex would no longer be arrested.

The 2013 Constitution prohibits discrimination on the basis of gender identity and expression alongside sexual orientation. The Asia Pacific Alliance describes that pairing as unique worldwide, and its 2023 policy brief treats it as the central legal fact for trans people in Fiji. Fiji was, with South Africa, one of the first two countries to enshrine sexual-orientation non-discrimination in a constitution, in 1997; the 2013 text reinstated and expanded that protection.

The constitutional guarantee has no implementing machinery for trans people. Legislative and policy frameworks permit no change of gender marker and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities, and the Asia Pacific Alliance records the resulting marginalisation and discrimination as documented. The traditional third-gender role known as vaka sa lewa lewa holds cultural recognition only, with no legal standing.

There is no route to recognition of a same-sex partner: the Marriage Act 2002 defines marriage as one man and one woman, and no civil union exists. Health professionals are barred from attempting to change a person's sexual orientation, while intersex bodily autonomy is unprotected in law.
FJI.outOfScopeNotes:
Outright International's overview carries an "at a glance" flag marking same-sex relations as illegal, which contradicts the same overview's account of decriminalisation under the Crimes Act 2010. The inventory does not explain the flag; the inconsistency is unresolved, and the 2010 repeal is corroborated by the other sources listed here.

The GlobalGayz country page is undated and pre-dates the 2013 constitution. Its statement that sexual-orientation and gender-identity discrimination is not banned describes the earlier legal position, not current law.

No source in the inventory quantifies violence or harassment against trans people in Fiji, and none reports a decided case testing the 2013 constitution's gender-identity and expression clause. Enforcement of that protection is not documented here.

The report that LGBT organisations cannot register rests on a summary flag in one overview, without detail on the registration regime or which organisations are affected.

Traditional third-gender vaka sa lewa lewa recognised culturally but no legal gender recognition route; no same-sex marriage/civil unions (Marriage Act 2002: one man, one woman); intersex bodily autonomy unprotected. At a glance: same-sex relations illegal per overview flag, LGR No, orgs cannot register.

Asia Pacific Alliance policy brief and case study, 'Legal Gender Recognition in Fiji' (2023): the 2013 Constitution's discrimination protection on gender identity and expression is described as unique worldwide, yet legislative/policy frameworks permit NO gender-marker change and do not recognise traditional third-gender identities — headline constitutional protection with zero implementation for trans people, resulting in documented marginalisation and discrimination.

Human Rights Watch (11 Apr 2005): two men (one an Australian tourist) received two-year prison sentences under colonial-era Penal Code Art 175 (up to 14 years) for consensual sex; HRW urged charges dropped and release, citing Fiji's 1997 constitutional ban on SO discrimination (Fiji one of first two countries worldwide, with South Africa); the judge called the acts 'so disgusting... any decent person vomit'. Documents the enforcement era before the 2006 no-arrest policy and 2010 decriminalisation.

PinkNews (10 Jul 2006): the Fijian High Commissioner confirmed an official policy that men engaging in consensual gay sex will no longer be arrested — the practical end of enforcement two years before the Crimes Act 2010 decriminalisation; NZ AIDS Foundation (Exec Dir Rachael Le Mesurier) linked criminalisation to undergrounding of sex and HIV spread.

Legacy-era overview — its claim that SOGI discrimination was not banned predates the 2013 Constitution.

Sydney Morning Herald (14 Apr 2005): PM Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, calling homosexuality a sin in 'the conservative Christian nation', days after an Australian tourist and a Fijian man received two-year sentences — the political/religious climate context behind the sodomy-law enforcement that HRW protested.

FJI.tangentialFactors:
The enforcement history is recent and well documented. In April 2005 two men, one of them an Australian tourist, received two-year prison sentences under Penal Code Article 175; the sentencing judge called the acts "so disgusting ... any decent person vomit". Human Rights Watch demanded that the charges be dropped and the men released, citing the 1997 constitutional ban on sexual-orientation discrimination.

Days after those sentences, Prime Minister Laisenia Qarase rejected international pressure to legalise gay sex, describing homosexuality as a sin in "the conservative Christian nation". That political and religious climate persisted through the 2006 no-arrest policy and the 2009 abolition of the constitution, before decriminalisation in 2010.

Criminalisation was also linked to public-health harm: an executive of the NZ AIDS Foundation argued in 2006 that the offence drove sex underground and fed HIV transmission.

Fiji's constitutional sequence is unusual. Sexual-orientation protection entered the 1997 constitution, workplace protection followed in 2007, that constitution was abolished in 2009, decriminalisation came in 2010, and the 2013 constitution added gender identity and expression to the protected grounds.

The traditional third-gender role of vaka sa lewa lewa is recognised in Fijian culture but confers no legal status, and legislative frameworks do not recognise third-gender identities for any official purpose.

WSM.name: Samoa
WSM.summary:
Samoa is workable for trans visitors — anchored by one of the world's most institutionalized third-gender traditions. Fa'afafine (and fa'atama) are culturally embedded: recognized as heirs to customary land and eligible for matai (chiefly) titles within fa'a Sāmoa, organized nationally through the Samoa Fa'afafine Association (a formal UN UPR stakeholder since 1987), and visible through a famous pageant culture. Samoa repealed its colonial-era “female impersonation” crime in 2013, so no law touches gender expression itself.

The remaining negatives are modest for a visitor: no anti-discrimination law and no legal gender recognition (both resident-facing); documented discrimination, cyberbullying and gender-based violence against fa'afafine (APTN peer-led study — primarily resident/domestic contexts); isolated police-harassment reports (2 respondents, no convictions); and village fono councils that enforce conservative dress and behaviour norms. The unenforced sodomy statute is a situational risk for a fraction of visitors, not a trans-universal one.
WSM.outOfScopeNotes: Fa’afafine cultural embedding is informal protection; criminalisation unenforced.

sources.summary: APTN (9 May 2024): Nadi, Fiji convening gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua, PNG — documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum (fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue, etc.) as living community infrastructure Samoa participates in.
Samoa's Crimes Act 2013 criminalises same-sex activity, with penalties of up to 5 years, as documented in the Human Dignity Trust country profile.

Samoa Fa'afafine Association (SFA) stakeholder report for Samoa's UPR (39th session, 2021): 'The Protection of the Rights of Fa'afafine/Fa'atama/LGBTIQ/SOGIESC persons in Samoa' - describes the culturally unique third-gender identities fa'afafine and fa'atama and documents lived experiences and struggles, with the aim of establishing grounds for non-discriminatory policy and legislation.
NOTE: Not retrievable at research time (HTTP 401); the underlying Reuters feature covers Samoa's third gender (fa'afafine) delicately balancing sex and religion.
APTN's Samoa socio-economic study is an image-based PDF with no extractable text.

RNZ Pacific (3 May 2013): Samoa's new Crimes Act, in force that week, scrapped the crime of impersonating a woman — Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief; interview also confirms the community was not then agitating to repeal sodomy provisions, i.e. decriminalisation outcome on that front remained unchanged.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fa'afafine of Samoa (with American Samoa and Tokelau) among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

It sits level with Greece — its lack of EU-style institutional recourse (a resident-weighted factor) is the only axis where European comparators hold an edge, and Estonia (0.77) keeps a 0.02 edge on that basis alone.

TON.name: Tonga
TON.summary: Tonga demands real caution from trans visitors. The Criminal Offences Act criminalises sodomy (10 years, plus corporal punishment on paper — unenforced in recent years) and also criminalises males “impersonating a female” while soliciting — a direct trans-expression statute on the books. Against that: Tonga has a visible leiti (trans-feminine) community with the famous Miss Galaxy pageant (documented by the Washington Post in 2024), family and church networks that are devout but not systematically violent, and no documented recent prosecutions.
TON.outOfScopeNotes: The male-impersonation statute is on the books but unenforced.

A Washington Post piece from Aug 2024 covers Tonga's trans pageant and LGBT rights.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Tonga: domestic violence, discrimination against women and corruption were the most prevalent problems; no reports of government abuses; the LGBT section notes the criminalisation of sodomy but rare enforcement.

Washington Blade (Feb 2018): Cyclone Gita 'tore off' part of the roof of Tonga's LGBTI drop-in center and shelter on Tongatapu (Nuku'alofa) with winds over 120 mph, damaging bathrooms and bedrooms used by LGBTI Tongans — documents the fragility of the country's only community shelter infrastructure.
No usable finding.
