KIR.name: Kiribati
KIR.summary:
Consensual sex between men is a criminal offence in Kiribati, carrying five to fourteen years' imprisonment depending on the offence charged. A 2015 US State Department human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the provision. The same report listed Kiribati, alongside Sri Lanka, among the states still maintaining anti-homosexuality laws in 2016, in the context of the UN General Assembly's 84–77 rejection of an amendment that would have defunded the Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity.

The Constitution of Kiribati bars discrimination by race, national origin and colour. It does not extend that guarantee to sexual orientation or gender identity, and no such non-discrimination statute was in force at the time of reporting. Gender-based discrimination is prohibited only in the field of employment, and the State Department observed that this narrow protection is poorly enforced.

Land ownership is restricted to I-Kiribati, a constitutional limitation affecting property rights rather than entry, but relevant to any longer stay.

At the 21st session of the Universal Periodic Review, France, Slovenia and Chile urged Kiribati to decriminalise homosexuality. The Kiribati delegation made no response to those recommendations, while stating that it was considering Uruguay's advice to adopt legislation prohibiting discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual identity and sexual orientation. Whether that legislation was enacted is not established by the sources.

Male same-sex conduct criminalised (14 years, unenforced); no LGR; very small, tight-knit, church-centred society; no specifically documented anti-trans violence (population ~11,000). Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

VUT.name: Vanuatu
VUT.summary:
Vanuatu demands real caution from trans visitors. Same-sex conduct is legal (never criminalised) with no legal gender recognition; there is a small VPride community in Port Vila, and kastom and church conservatism — but no documented anti-trans violence pattern.

Direct risk signals for visitors: in November 2024 the government moved to develop a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion, framed as contrary to constitutional and Christian values, and the Marriage Act was amended to define marriage as the union of a male and a female, so same-sex marriages cannot be registered — a partner-travel consideration.
VUT.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data: only three usable sources, no freshness re-check of the 2024 policy developments, and no source covers visa or border document handling for trans visitors. The drafted policy's scope, timeline and enforcement are unverified.

sources.summary: Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

NRU.name: Nauru
NRU.summary: Nauru demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2016; tiny population (~12,000); no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; the asylum-detention legacy shaped its international image but not its LGBT law. Caveat: very small population — the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

sources.summary: US Mission Geneva (Mar 2011): publishes the full text of the Joint statement on ending acts of violence based on sexual orientation & gender identity, delivered by Colombia on behalf of 84 countries — Nauru is among the signatories (with Fiji, Marshall Islands, Micronesia and others). For this record: dated evidence of Nauru's diplomatic position supporting SOGI rights.

Human Truth Foundation 'LGBT Rights Across the World' (Vexen Crabtree, 2025): the Vexen LGBT Equality Index ranks Nauru 101st at -0.10, far below top-ranked Germany/Spain at 4.88 and below most Pacific neighbours. For this record: a comparative-index placement for Nauru.

The Guardian, 29 May 2016, headline: 'Nauru decriminalises homosexuality and suicide'. The 1899 Queensland-derived criminal code provisions were repealed, including the attempted-suicide provisions. For this record: the dated decriminalisation event.

Kaleidoscope Trust Nauru country page: Nauru decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct in 2016 but same-sex marriages and unions remain illegal; intersex and transgender people have no explicit legal recognition or protection, and no employment-discrimination protection for LBTI people; Nauru supported the 2011 UN HRC Joint Statement, and its last CEDAW state report (2016) contained no LBTI-specific information. For this record: the current legal-status snapshot for trans/intersex people specifically.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Nauru (Wikipedia) — Nauru Regional Processing Centre Rules 2014 gender-identity non-discrimination clause
sources.summary: Wikipedia's LGBTQ rights in Nauru article documents the only detention-related gender-identity provision found for Nauru: the Nauru Regional Processing Centre (RPC) Rules 2014, made under the Asylum Seekers (Regional Processing Centre) Act 2012, ban discrimination against any person based on sex or gender, sexual preference or gender identity within the RPC immigration-detention facility. This covers immigration detention, not Nauru's criminal-justice prison system, and concerns non-discrimination rather than placement by birth sex vs identity, special units, or solitary-confinement practice. No documented data was found on where transgender prisoners are housed in Nauru's corrections system, nor any trans-prisoner case or ruling.

FSM.name: Micronesia (FSM)
FSM.summary:
The Federated States of Micronesia carries no documented legal penalty for consensual same-sex conduct. US State Department human rights reporting in 2010 and again in 2015 recorded no laws criminalising homosexuality in the country, and current legal overviews likewise describe no criminalisation. Earlier provisions of this kind existed in some constituent states, but none remain in force.

Discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been illegal since a 2018 constitutional equality reform, adopted by the national Congress. The archived US State Department reports from 2010 and 2015 predate that reform and describe only limited protection against such discrimination, so they should not be read as the current position.

No legal gender recognition procedure is documented for the Federated States of Micronesia, and no source in the current record describes the availability of marker or document amendment for transgender visitors or residents. Equally, nothing in the record establishes entry or visa screening that could expose a visitor's trans status, nor any provision governing single-sex facilities, transition-related healthcare, or hate-crime treatment of anti-trans violence.

The evidence base is thin in exactly the direction that matters for transgender visitors. Absence of criminalisation is documented; absence of anti-trans discrimination, violence, or official hostility is not. Where the record is silent, the map treats that as unresolved rather than as reassurance.
FSM.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the current record addresses entry, visa, or customs screening procedures for transgender travellers to the Federated States of Micronesia, including whether document markers are inspected or questioned. This is unresolved and should be verified with the FSM Immigration Office before travel.

The availability of transition-related healthcare, of doctors willing to prescribe hormones, and of competent, non-discriminatory medical care is not sourced. It should be checked with the FSM Department of Health and Social Services or a clinician in Pohnpei directly.

There is no documented hate-crime statute covering gender identity or expression, and no documented guidance for law enforcement or the FSM National Police on handling anti-transgender incidents. Whether the 2018 equality amendment has been interpreted to cover gender identity, and by which court or authority, is unresolved on the present evidence.

No sources address single-sex facilities, public-order laws affecting gender presentation, or the treatment of transgender people in detention or police custody. Claims about violence risk, partner recognition, or official protection cannot be supported from the inventory and remain unverified.

MHL.name: Marshall Islands
MHL.summary:
The Marshall Islands demands real caution — from thin evidence rather than documented risk. Same-sex conduct is legal (decriminalised in the 2000s), there is no legal gender recognition, and no anti-trans pattern is documented; no LGBT-specific abuses were reported in the 2015 official human-rights report.

Caveat: the population is very small and the evidence base is thin, so this assessment carries greater-than-usual uncertainty.

US State Department 2015 Human Rights Report for Marshall Islands: significant problems were prison conditions, corruption and domestic violence; no reports of torture, arbitrary killings or disappearances - no LGBT-specific abuses reported.

BEN.name: Benin
BEN.summary:
Benin does not criminalise same-sex relations anywhere in the country. Outright International's country overview records that, alongside this legality, SOGIESC discrimination is not prohibited by law, legal gender recognition is impossible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register. The statutory position is therefore legal but entirely unshielded: there is no recognition pathway and no statutory protection to invoke.

The US State Department's 2023 country report on human rights practices found that Benin's law does not explicitly prohibit discrimination on the basis of SOGIESC, and that LGBTQI+ couples and families are not recognised. The report describes hostility toward the community that is most pronounced outside major urban areas, and records LGBTQI+ persons being routinely refused medical care, including hormone treatment, as well as social services. A trans visitor needing routine or hormone-related care should expect refusal, particularly outside Cotonou and Porto-Novo.

Social violence is the sharper risk. Erasing 76 Crimes reported in April 2024 that anti-gay lynchings are commonplace in Benin. The same report describes the Hirondelles Club at the Rehoboth Friendship Centre, which has housed LGBT+ youth since about 2020: a 20-place temporary accommodation centre through which almost 380 young people from Benin and the sub-region have passed. Its existence indicates both that displacement and family violence are common enough to require such a shelter and that survivor-support infrastructure remains very small relative to need.
BEN.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced in this inventory: whether Benin's passport or identity-card authorities will amend a gender marker for trans citizens, and whether entry screening or immigration interview questions ask about gender history. No source addresses bathroom or facilities access, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, or whether gender-based rather than sexuality-based violence is recorded separately by Benin's police.

The claim that lynchings are commonplace rests on a single outlet's April 2024 framing rather than on police or court statistics, and no case-level incidents with dates and outcomes are available here. Whether the Hirondelles Club currently has capacity, and whether comparable shelters operate in other cities, is likewise not established. Any trans-specific violence figures distinct from anti-LGBT violence generally remain not sourced.

For this record: current social-violence risk (lynchings) plus the existence of small survivor-support infrastructure.

For this record: historical baseline supporting the localsOnly framing that today's statutory legality sits on pre-colonial practice, not recent liberalisation.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure, so Beninese trans people have no domestic route to align official documents with their gender, and no anti-discrimination law to which they can appeal in employment, housing, health care or education.

TGO.name: Togo
TGO.summary: Togo is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises “immodest or unnatural acts” (3 years); limited recent enforcement evidence but documented discrimination and violence; no LGR.

sources.summary: Human Dignity Trust country profile: Togo criminalises same-sex sexual activity between men and between women, with a maximum penalty of three years' imprisonment plus a fine.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Togo: the law prohibits 'acts against nature committed with an individual of one's sex' (widely understood as same-sex conduct) and also the 'promotion of same-sex conduct', reaching advocacy and gender identity expression. The law was enforced, and violence or threats targeting LGBTTQI persons were listed among significant human-rights issues.

Washington Blade (Aug 31, 2015): interviews with LGBT Catholics in Ghana, Togo, Benin and Nigeria (conducted 14-31 March 2015) include a Togo section. US State Department 2011 Human Rights Report for Togo: documents security-force torture, impunity, and 'official and societal discrimination... against members of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community'.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for Togo: listed among significant human-rights issues were 'crimes involving violence or threats of violence targeting lesbian, gay, bisexual...' persons. The report also cites cruel treatment, harsh prison conditions, arbitrary detention and criminal libel enforcement.

NER.name: Niger
NER.summary:
Niger is dangerous for trans visitors — and newly criminalising: in March 2025 the junta's Charter of Refoundation explicitly outlawed “LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior” for the first time (Article 25). Junta rule, jihadist insurgency, no recourse.

The criminalisation is now codified: a February 2026 revision of the penal code criminalises 'indecent, unnatural, and LGBTQIA+ acts' (penal code article 390; 5–10 years' imprisonment and fines), same-sex marriage (article 391; 10–20 years), and LGBTQIA+ associations (article 392); article 390 also covers anyone who 'artificially change[s their] sex at birth'. The drafting is broad and confused enough that asexuality has been read as included among sanctionable conducts, per reporting on the law. Junta-state enforcement followed: from July 2026 the junta began arresting LGBTQIA+ people under the new provisions, with dozens of arrests reported within days.
NER.outOfScopeNotes: March 2025 criminalisation is brand new; enforcement undocumented.

sources.summary: Outright International country overview, last updated 12 March 2026: in March 2025 Niger explicitly outlawed same-sex acts for the first time — Article 25 of the junta's Charter of Refoundation bans 'LGBTQIA+ practices or any other unnatural behavior' during the five-year transition following the July 2023 coup. No specific penalties are set yet, but a 2023 draft penal code proposes up to five years for same-sex conduct, 20 years for conducting/officiating/witnessing a same-sex marriage and five years for participating in or financing 'homosexual' organisations. Earlier in 2023 two women were prosecuted for alleged same-sex intimacy under public-indecency Article 276 (up to three years) and the trial judge was reassigned to an administrative post after acquitting them; the code fixes age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts versus 13 for different-sex acts.

BBC News (December 2022): Niger's lawmakers backed a motion to criminalise same-sex relationships, moved by MP Nana Djibou Harouna of the southern Maradi region, weeks after a Maradi court acquitted two young women of lesbianism charges because no legislation criminalised same-sex relationships.

The Guardian (1 July 2026): at least 40 people have been arrested for homosexuality and 16 men, including high-ranking military officials, imprisoned across Niger following the introduction of a new penal code earlier in 2026. Campaigners describe a 'witch-hunt' in a 'toxic' climate, and sources fear an HIV/AIDS resurgence as access to PrEP drugs collapses.
Agence Nigérienne de Presse (1 Jun 2026) reports that Niger criminalises LGBTQIA+ practice in the country under the criminalisation provisions adopted in the 2026 penal code revision.

TCD.name: Chad
TCD.summary:
Chad is dangerous for trans visitors — a high-risk verdict reached on thin data, not in spite of it. Consensual same-sex conduct between adults has been criminalised since 2017 as a misdemeanour carrying up to two years' imprisonment, so a trans visitor stands under formal criminal exposure — including one travelling with a partner. There is no legal gender recognition, no recourse, no protective or community infrastructure documented, and the state operates under junta-adjacent governance.

Enforcement of the criminalisation is not documented in either direction. That gap denotes an unknown, not safety: in a state that criminalises, denies recognition, offers no recourse and no documented protective or community infrastructure, the structural signals resolve toward danger, and the law remains usable against a visibly trans visitor at any time — arrest, prosecution and imprisonment of up to two years are live possibilities.
TCD.outOfScopeNotes: Very thin data: enforcement of the 2017 criminalisation in either direction is undocumented; no community or protective infrastructure is documented since criminalisation; the resident-side record rests on the pre-criminalisation baseline.

sources.summary: US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report, Chad: criminalisation section states the law criminalised consensual same-sex sexual conduct between adults with punishments ranging from three months to two years' imprisonment — official current-law baseline for visitor exposure; report also covers societal abuses.

US State Dept 2010 Human Rights Report, Chad (pre-criminalisation baseline): law prohibited but did not define 'unnatural acts' with no evidence it was used against LGBT persons that year; no known LGBT organisations and few reports of violence, most persons discreet due to social strictures — documents the pre-2017 legal climate.

US State Department 2006 Human Rights Report for Chad documents Deby regime abuses including extrajudicial killings, torture and the MINURCAT withdrawal. General country conditions with no trans-specific finding.

HuffPost/GroundTruth Project analysis: while further criminalisation attempts failed in Ethiopia and Rwanda, they succeeded in Chad and Nigeria — situates Chad's criminalisation drive within the broader wave of conservative anti-LGBT advocacy, relevant context for how the law's trajectory developed.

GAB.name: Gabon
GAB.summary:
Gabon has no law criminalising same-sex intimacy. The same conduct was nonetheless prohibited between July 2019 and July 2020, and that episode is the best guide to how quickly the position can move. Gabon gained independence in 1960 with no inherited colonial-era sodomy statute, and same-sex conduct was not an offence until the new penal code, Law 042/2018, entered into force on 5 July 2019.

The 2019 code did not name homosexuality. Article 402 listed "les relations sexuelles entre personnes de même sexe" within "atteintes aux mœurs", exposing those convicted to up to six months' imprisonment and a fine of five million CFA francs, roughly US$8,500. The National Assembly overturned the ban in July 2020, restoring the pre-2019 position in which same-sex relations between men and women were lawful nationwide. The reversal divided public opinion sharply, and Gabon's current decriminalised status rests on ordinary legislation rather than an entrenched constitutional settlement.

That settlement arrived at referendum on 16 November 2024, when the constitution adopted by the military government that took power in the August 2023 coup ending 56 years of Bongo-family rule was approved by more than 90% of voters on turnout of about 55%. Civil society had demanded the re-criminalisation of homosexuality during the drafting; that demand lost. The adopted text instead protects privacy under Article 18 in terms read as protective of LGBTI people. Article 16, however, defines marriage in a way that excludes same-sex couples, so the constitution blocks criminalisation while also blocking marriage equality.

A visitor presenting documents in a gender inconsistent with the marker on their passport should expect no domestic legal remedy for discrepancies, and there is no registered community machinery that would receive or advise a trans traveller. Conservative social attitudes remain widely held, and discrimination is documented rather than hypothetical. Discretion in public life remains prudent, and the constitutional privacy protection is a legal guarantee, not a guarantee of social tolerance.

COG.name: Republic of the Congo
COG.summary:
The Republic of the Congo does not criminalise consensual same-sex conduct between adults. A systematic review of the country's legislation carried out for the EUAA's May 2024 COI Query Response found no law that prohibits such conduct, and the US State Department's 2022 and 2023 human rights reports record no prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the ambiguity surrounding that conduct.

Penal Code Article 331 sets the age of consent at 21 for same-sex acts, against 18 for different-sex acts. The same provision criminalises 'shameless acts or acts against nature' with a person of the same sex under the age of 21, punishable by six months to three years' imprisonment and a fine. The EUAA review describes the provision's scope as applied to same-sex conduct as ambiguous, and reports that sources treat it as a basis for discriminatory treatment.

The provision is not a dormant text. The State Department's 2022 reporting states that police cite it to extract bribes from gay men, and its 2023 reporting confirms that the 'act against nature' law continued to be used as a pretext for soliciting payments from men. No arrests or prosecutions of LGBTQI+ persons under the provision were known during 2023.

For a trans visitor, the practical exposure lies less in a prosecution risk than in routine contact with police. Document checks, identity controls and any interaction that reveals or is assumed to reveal a person's gender history can bring a person into contact with the same officers who use the provision for extortion. The reported pattern is that the ambiguity is operationalised as leverage.

Reported violence against LGBTQI+ persons comes from both state and nonstate actors. Local NGOs told the State Department that LGBTQI+ people in the Republic of the Congo face psychological and physical harassment, violence and financial extortion, and that this pattern continued through 2023. The law offers no protection against any of it: the country has no anti-discrimination protections covering sexual orientation or gender identity.
COG.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory does not address trans-specific matters: legal gender recognition, requirements for changing sex markers on identity or travel documents, entry and visa screening procedures applied to transgender travellers, or whether immigration officers consult gender history in the course of border control. These are unresolved here, not absent from the jurisdiction's practice.

Access to gender-affirming healthcare, the legal status of facilities arrangements (bathrooms, detention, shelters), and any hate-crime or hate-speech provisions touching gender identity are not covered by the sources assessed, and no finding is made on them.

Whether the EUAA or State Department reporting captures the situation outside the capital, or the treatment of trans persons distinct from gay men, is not established in the inventory. The documented policing practice is described in terms of gay men specifically.

BDI.name: Burundi
BDI.summary:
Burundi criminalises same-sex conduct. The prohibition dates from the 2009 penal code, and US State Department human rights reports covering 2009, 2010, 2012 and 2015 document discrimination against gays and lesbians under that framework, together with arrests and harassment of LGBT people. No source in this inventory identifies any protection, exemption or decriminalisation measure.

The risk posture escalated in December 2023, when President Évariste Ndayishimiye publicly called for homosexuals to be "stoned", adding "that's what they deserve". Human Rights Watch, reporting in January 2024, condemned the remarks as stoking fear among LGBT people and urged the ruling party to renounce persecution. The Iteka League, the Burundian LGBTQ rights organisation operating in exile, characterised the speech as "a call for the lynching of LGBTQ people".

Burundians living under the criminalisation regime reported terror in the weeks that followed. SOS Médias Burundi, writing in January 2024, quoted members of two LGBTQ associations speaking anonymously, who described the presidential remarks as "a real license to kill (us)". The same reporting restates that same-sex relations are criminalised in Burundi.
BDI.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses legal gender recognition, identity-document markers, visa or entry screening that could disclose a person's status, hate-crime sentencing enhancement, same-sex partnership or marriage recognition, restroom or facility access rules, or restrictions on gender-affirming care. Whether any of these exist, and in what form, remains unresolved on the available material.

The inventory does not state the specific article or penalty range of the 2009 penal code provision criminalising same-sex conduct, nor does it record a prosecution, conviction or acquittal under that provision with a date and outcome. It also does not establish whether the presidential remarks of December 2023 were followed by any formal enforcement directive or arrests.

Following the December 2023 speech, LGBTQ residents described themselves as living in fear. Two association members, quoted anonymously in January 2024, said the remarks amounted to a licence to kill them. The exiled LGBTQ rights organisation urged recognition of the speech as a call for lynching, while a human rights organisation called on the governing party to renounce persecution.

CAF.name: Central African Republic
CAF.summary:
The Central African Republic is dangerous for trans visitors.

Nothing in national law protects a trans or gender-nonconforming visitor. The constitution defines marriage as a union between one man and one woman and same-sex marriage is banned, so a visitor travelling with a partner has no recognition of that relationship, and affection between same-sex partners in public can be prosecuted under the public-morals provisions.

Consensual same-sex relations between adults are not explicitly criminalised in the penal code. Article 85 instead criminalises attacks on public morals, and same-sex conduct in public draws harsher penalties than other offences covered by the same moral-offence provisions. The practical effect for a visitor is that any visible same-sex or gender-nonconforming conduct in public exposes them to arrest on morals grounds.

The United States State Department's 2023 human rights report states that same-sex activity in public is criminalised in practice and that this treatment has pushed the affected community underground. The same report records that there were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights in the country, so a visitor who faces trouble has no established local support network to turn to.

Legal gender recognition is not permitted in the Central African Republic. A visitor whose passport or identity marker does not match their presentation has no local legal route to align those documents, and should expect identity screening to proceed on the marker as issued.

Detention carries serious physical risk. Documentation from 2012 recorded extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and by Seleka rebels, together with harsh prison conditions. That reporting is more than a decade old and contains little trans-specific material, but it describes the conditions a visitor would enter if arrested on public-morals grounds.

The social climate compounds the legal exposure. Attitudes toward sexual orientation and gender identity issues are treated as taboo and characterised as imported from Europe or contrary to African values, which raises the likelihood of hostility from the public as well as from officials.
CAF.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the criminalisation question and this is unresolved. The 2019 overview states that same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, relying on Article 85's public-morals offence, whereas the 2023 United States State Department report describes same-sex activity in public as criminalised. The distinction between a specific offence and enforcement through the morals provision is not settled by the available material.

No source in the inventory documents arrests, prosecutions or sentences under Article 85, so the frequency and severity of enforcement are not sourced. Likewise there is no sourced information on hate-crime sentencing, on access to healthcare for trans visitors, or on airport and border screening practices directed at gender-nonconforming travellers.

The 2012 documentation of killings, torture, rape and prison conditions derives from a period of armed conflict and is not trans-specific; its current applicability to detention of a trans visitor is not verified. The 2024 Universal Periodic Review stakeholder submissions and the two earlier recommendations are recorded as inputs to the review process only, with no sourced outcome as to implementation.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for the Central African Republic: documents extrajudicial killings, torture and rape by security forces and Seleka rebels, and harsh prison conditions, with limited LGBT-specific content.

Erasing 76 Crimes / ILGA overview (20 May 2019): in the Central African Republic same-sex relations between consenting adults are not explicitly criminalised, but Article 85 of the criminal code criminalises 'attacks on public morals' — public same-sex acts carry harsher penalties than other moral offences. SOGI issues remain taboo and seen as 'imported from Europe'/'contrary to African values'; CAR received two UPR recommendations (SOGI non-discrimination, improving the situation of sexual minorities).

CAF.comparisons: Pairwise: level with Malawi (0.26), above Zambia (0.24), below Senegal (0.27).

It received two Universal Periodic Review recommendations concerning non-discrimination on the grounds of sexual orientation and gender identity and improving the situation of sexual minorities, and the January 2024 United Nations Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights summary of stakeholder submissions for the country's 45th-session review again contains SOGI-related recommendations. Whether any of these recommendations have been implemented is not sourced here.

The Central African Republic appears in ILGA World's 2023 survey of laws criminalising LGBT people, but the underlying national position is narrower than that inclusion suggests: consensual same-sex relations are not expressly prohibited, while exposure arises from the public-morals offence rather than a specific sodomy statute.

The 2012 human rights reporting that documents state violence also covers armed-group violence during the Seleka period, an environment of general instability in which a visibly gender-nonconforming foreigner has no special status or protection.

Residents have no statutory protection against discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity; the United States State Department's 2023 report confirms the absence of legal anti-discrimination provisions for LGBTQI+ persons.

LGBTQI+ persons cannot serve openly in the Central African Republic's armed forces.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so residents have no administrative procedure to change the sex marker on identity documents.

There were no known organisations promoting LGBTQI+ human rights operating in the country as of the 2023 reporting, and the affected community is described as having been driven underground by enforcement of the public-morals offence.

Residents seeking change must work through the Universal Periodic Review process, where two earlier recommendations on SOGI non-discrimination and the situation of sexual minorities, and further stakeholder recommendations in the January 2024 submissions, form the documented record of external pressure.

GIN.name: Guinea
GIN.summary:
Guinea is a high-risk destination for transgender visitors. Article 274 of the 2016 Penal Code punishes consensual same-sex conduct with six months to three years' imprisonment, a fine of GNF 500,000 to 1,000,000, or both; the US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report records the same criminalisation under the code's indecency provisions and documents violence and discrimination against LGBT persons alongside police harassment.

Enforcement is not confined to conduct. Arrests are made on the basis of clothing and appearance, and the statute operates as a basis for extortion, with releases commonly secured through payment to police. The Advocates for Human Rights and Khaleem Ali's joint stakeholder report to the Universal Periodic Review in October 2024 records arbitrary arrest, harassment and extortion by police, deepening stigma and fear among LGBT people.

The same 2024 reporting describes an environment that is hostile and at times lethal, with threats of physical violence and discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression. Widespread stigmatisation deters victims from reporting violence, so documented incidents understate the actual level of harm.

There is no legal gender recognition procedure in Guinea. A visitor whose passport or other documents do not match their presentation has no domestic mechanism to align them, which leaves identity checks, including at entry and in any contact with police, as a point of exposure.

Detention carries additional risk. US State Department reporting has documented torture and abuse by security forces and mistreatment in prisons, conditions that apply to anyone arrested under the criminalising provisions. Governance has been under military rule since the 2021 coup, and the 2024 stakeholder submissions address both state and non-state actors as sources of violence and discrimination.
GIN.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not resolve whether Article 274 or the indecency provisions have been applied against foreign nationals or visitors, or whether entry and visa processing includes any screening of transgender documents. No sourced material addresses access to healthcare, hormone treatment or HIV services for trans people in Guinea, nor any hate-crime enhancement, anti-discrimination statute, or recognition of partners or marriages.

Rules on restroom or facility access, and any guidance issued to accommodation providers or tour operators, are not covered by these sources. The scope of the military government's directives on LGBT matters since 2021 is likewise not established here beyond the fact of junta rule. The 2011 State Department material is more than a decade old and its specific findings on prison conditions should be treated as historical context rather than current measurement.

LBR.name: Liberia
LBR.summary: Liberia is dangerous for trans visitors. Sodomy is criminalised (1 year, both sexes — a domestic-origin law, never colonised); a legislator is seeking support for a harsh 2024 anti-homosexuality bill (so far unsuccessful); mob violence is documented; no LGR.
LBR.outOfScopeNotes: Active hostile bill (2024) not yet passed.

NPR (9 Apr 2012, 'Liberian LGBT Rights Under Spotlight'): anti-gay sentiment growing since the US announced plans to promote LGBT rights overseas; new legislation proposed longer jail time for homosexuality and a group distributed fliers targeting gay-rights supporters.

MDG.name: Madagascar
MDG.summary:
Madagascar's trans visitors get legality without protection. Same-sex conduct between adults is legal from age 21 under the Penal Code, but the age of consent is unequal: same-sex acts involving someone under 21 remain offences, with Penal Code Article 331 attaching an indecent-assault band of five to ten years' imprisonment. There is no anti-discrimination law, no legal gender recognition, and no recognition of same-sex marriage or civil unions, so a trans traveller — alone or with a partner — holds no local status and no named protection.

Practical safety is the dominant concern: LGBT people must hide their lives to keep jobs and live in peace, and there is no visible community outside the capital, Antananarivo. No police targeting pattern is documented, and the government has rejected UN recommendations to combat anti-LGBT violence and hate speech, so no protection is in prospect.
MDG.outOfScopeNotes: Thin data; legal but closeted profile. No source addresses border-screening, document handling, or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no police targeting pattern is documented either way — the absence of a documented pattern is not proof of safety. The legal baseline rests on a 2020 decriminalisation overview, a December 2023 guide, and a 2011 human-rights report describing a post-coup period.

COM.name: Comoros
COM.summary:
Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity under its penal code, and the provision has been used against people whose conduct became known to authorities. Reported penalties differ between sources: Outright International gives Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs (US$240 to 720), the Human Dignity Trust states a maximum of three years, and a December 2024 Washington Blade report cites Article 318 carrying up to five years.

Enforcement is documented. Two women were arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them, and on 12 December 2024 a Comorian court sentenced them to five and six months respectively for homosexuality before releasing them with the terms served. It was the first conviction of this kind, and the Human Dignity Trust called it a human-rights violation. The first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy followed a leaked video in 2022.

Application is uneven rather than absent. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. The statute itself remains in force, and the government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise.

No non-discrimination law protects LGBTQI+ persons. Police reported that they do not incite or tolerate violence against them and no such violence was reported in 2023, yet widespread impunity is listed among the country's major human-rights problems.

Detention carries additional exposure: the State Department's 2010 report records poor prison conditions, alongside restrictions on movement, press and religion and discrimination against women.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a trans visitor arriving with documents in a retained name or marker has no domestic route to a matching record. No hate-crime provision or partner recognition for same-sex couples is recorded in these sources.
COM.outOfScopeNotes:
The applicable penalty is unresolved in these sources: three years, two years plus a fine, and five years are each reported, and the discrepancy is not reconciled by any source in the inventory.

The enforcement position after the December 2024 conviction is not sourced. The inventory contains no reporting on arrests, prosecutions or police practice in 2025 or 2026, so the current enforcement posture beyond that date is not established here.

No source in the inventory addresses entry or visa screening of transgender documents, airport or border treatment, access to healthcare, restroom or facility rules, hate-crime charging, or recognition of same-sex partners. These are not sourced rather than confirmed absent.

The 2010 prison-conditions findings are more than a decade old and have not been refreshed in the inventory.

sources.summary: The Human Dignity Trust country profile documents that Comoros criminalises same-sex sexual activity, with up to 3 years' imprisonment under the penal code.
A Reuters report (Dec 2024) covers a couple in Comoros released after a same-sex sentencing verdict.

US State Dept 2023 Human Rights Report (Comoros): same-sex conduct is criminalised under the penal code, but authorities reported no arrests or prosecutions during 2023 and did not actively enforce the law. No non-discrimination law exists. Police reported not to incite or tolerate violence against LGBTQI+ persons, and none was reported that year. Widespread impunity is listed among major human-rights problems.

US State Department 2010 Human Rights Report for Comoros records poor prison conditions, restrictions on movement, press and religion, and discrimination against women, with limited content on LGBT issues.

Outright International (updated 12 Mar 2026): Art. 300 of the 2020 penal code punishes same-sex acts with 6 months–2 years plus a 100,000–300,000 franc (US$240–720) fine; no discrimination protections, no legal gender-marker change, no known LGBTIQ organisations (Art. 5 of Law 86-006/AF chills registration); enforcement documented — first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy after a leaked video (2022), first same-sex arrests of two women June 2024, conviction Dec 2024 with time served; government repeatedly refused UN decriminalisation recommendations.

Washington Blade (23 Dec 2024): Comoros court on 12 Dec 2024 sentenced two lesbian women to five and six months for homosexuality and released them with time served — the couple had been arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them; first conviction of this kind, called a human-rights violation by Human Dignity Trust; article cites Art. 318 (up to five years) as the provision.

COM.tangentialFactors:
Source reporting on the penalty does not converge, which matters when a visitor weighs the consequence of a charge. The Human Dignity Trust profile states up to three years, Outright International specifies six months to two years plus a fine under Article 300 of the 2020 code, and the Washington Blade report on the December 2024 sentencing cites Article 318 with a five-year maximum.

The enforcement picture shifts across reporting years. The 2010 State Department report offers little on LGBT issues while documenting poor prison conditions and general restrictions; the 2023 report describes non-enforcement; the 2022 leaked-video imprisonment, the June 2024 arrests and the December 2024 conviction show that prosecutions do occur when cases surface.

Police posture reported in 2023, namely no incitement or toleration of violence and no reported incidents, sits alongside the State Department's finding of widespread impunity, so the absence of recorded violence does not establish a protective framework.
COM.blindSummary:
The state criminalises same-sex sexual activity under its national penal code, and the provision has been used against people whose conduct became known to authorities. Reported penalties differ between sources: one international rights organisation gives Article 300 of the 2020 penal code as six months to two years' imprisonment plus a fine of 100,000 to 300,000 francs, a legal charity states a maximum of three years, and a December 2024 press report cites Article 318 carrying up to five years.

Enforcement is documented. Two women were arrested in June 2024 after asking an imam to marry them, and on 12 December 2024 a court in the state sentenced them to five and six months respectively for homosexuality before releasing them with the terms served. It was the first conviction of this kind, and the legal charity called it a human-rights violation. The first imprisonment for same-sex intimacy followed a leaked video in 2022.

Application is uneven rather than absent. The national 2023 human rights report records no arrests or prosecutions during that year and states that authorities did not actively enforce the law. The statute itself remains in force, and the government has repeatedly refused United Nations recommendations to decriminalise.

No non-discrimination law protects LGBTQI+ persons. Police reported that they do not incite or tolerate violence against them and no such violence was reported in 2023, yet widespread impunity is listed among the state's major human-rights problems.

Detention carries additional exposure: the 2010 national report records poor prison conditions, alongside restrictions on movement, press and religion and discrimination against women.

Legal gender recognition is unavailable, so a trans visitor arriving with documents in a retained name or marker has no domestic route to a matching record. No hate-crime provision or partner recognition for same-sex couples is recorded in these sources.

DJI.name: Djibouti
DJI.summary:
Djibouti does not explicitly criminalise consensual same-sex conduct. Articles 353 and 354 of the penal code refer vaguely to "good morals" and to obscene or public-morality offences without naming same-sex relations, and no statute states the position either way. Authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these provisions, and the country's at-a-glance legal assessment marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the territory. The practical result is that same-sex conduct is treated as de facto illegal even though no explicit offence exists on the books.

Public-morality and "obscene acts" provisions are used against people, so a trans visitor who is visible or who engages in any same-sex conduct in public faces exposure to prosecution on that basis. There is no reported case law defining the limits of these articles, and no guarantee of how they are applied to a foreign national.

No legal gender recognition procedure exists. A trans visitor cannot obtain or amend an identity document reflecting their gender under Djibouti law, and there is no statutory route by which a passport or other document issued by another country would be recognised as consistent with a presented gender marker.

LGBTI organisations cannot register in Djibouti. There is consequently no community infrastructure, no support or outreach services, and no organisation to contact in an emergency. The absence of any such body also means there is no domestic monitoring of how the public-morality provisions are enforced.

No legal prohibition of discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity exists in general law. The only protection reported is in the employment field, and it is not accompanied by any wider equality framework, hate-crime provision, or anti-violence mechanism.

Societal conditions are hostile. Sexual orientation and gender identity are treated as taboo, public societal discussion of homosexuality is not tolerated, and social and religious intolerance is pervasive. People fear family and community shunning if they are disclosed, which makes reporting to authorities unlikely and self-concealment the ordinary strategy.

The state does operate a complaint route: allegations can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH). No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable in the reporting period, which reflects the absence of documentation rather than a demonstrated record of protection.
DJI.outOfScopeNotes:
Two sourced statements on discrimination protection do not align: one describes protection as existing in employment only, while the United States State Department's 2023 report states that there is no legal prohibition of discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity. Whether an employment-level protection exists in practice, and whether it covers gender identity, is unresolved on this inventory.

No cases of official violence against LGBTI people are citable from the available reporting, and the inventory contains no documented instance of the public-morality provisions being applied to a trans person specifically. Whether articles 353 and 354 have been used against trans individuals, and with what outcome, is not sourced here.

The most recent detailed human-rights reporting in this inventory is from 2023. Whether the penal code articles have been amended, whether any registration decision on LGBTI organisations has changed, and whether any gender-recognition procedure has been introduced since then is unresolved.

Documentation of the treatment of sexual minorities in Djibouti has been scarce across independent research sources for well over a decade, so the absence of adverse findings should not be read as evidence of safety.

DJI.tangentialFactors:
Djibouti's wider political environment shapes how any legal provision would be enforced. Reporting on the country documents suppression of the opposition and harsh prison conditions, alongside other serious rights concerns including female genital mutilation and trafficking. A state that treats political dissent this way offers no realistic expectation that a marginalised foreign national would obtain discretionary protection.

The evidence base for the country's treatment of sexual minorities has been thin for a long period. A Canadian Immigration and Refugee Board research response covering 2009 to March 2012 found documentation scarce across all consulted sources and relied on the 2010 United States country report as its principal reference, indicating how little legal, protective or support framework existed at that time. The 2015 United States State Department report contained only limited LGBT-specific content and served mainly as a historical baseline. The 2023 United States State Department report is the most recent detailed account available here.

Compared with jurisdictions that have explicit decriminalising statutes, a constitutional equality clause, or a functioning gender-recognition process, Djibouti offers none of these. The ambiguity of the penal code is itself a risk factor: conduct that is not named in law can still be prosecuted under a morality provision, and the visitor has no advance way to know where the line sits.

MRT.name: Mauritania
MRT.summary: Mauritania is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely — one of the world's most dangerous legal environments. The 1983 Penal Code criminalises “acts against nature” with death by stoning (de facto moratorium on executions, but the statute is live); and Cairo 52 documents that gender nonconformity is effectively criminalised through debauchery, heresy, and Islamic-morality provisions — trans people can be apprehended solely for their gender expression. There is no LGR, no healthcare, no community, and sharia courts operate alongside the civil system.

Cairo 52 country review: transgender people are effectively criminalised through 'debauchery' provisions. Penal Code Art. 264 carries 1 month to 2 years' jail and 5,000-150,000 ouguiya fines for public indecency and debauchery offences applied to gender nonconformity. Official data on the trans community is gravely lacking.

US State Department 2023 Human Rights Report (Mauritania): consensual same-sex conduct criminalised but penalties not enforced; reports of violence and threats against LGBT people; civil society objected to scant indictments and officials sometimes acted with impunity.

Erasing 76 Crimes (16 Jan 2026, from Outright): the Penal Code keeps a maximum sentence of death by stoning for men; the government confirmed a de facto death-penalty moratorium in 2021; arrests and detentions under the provisions continue in recent years; low visibility drives stigma; since 2008 the country has served as refuge for Senegulese LGBTIQ people.

Liberals Mauritania (organisation website, c)2026): openly campaigns from within Mauritania on freethinker and LGBT-adjacent causes — titles include 'When the Law Deprives Rights and Freedoms' and 'The First Trans Woman to Speak Out in Mauritania's Media' — evidence of a minimal but real public advocacy space.

GNB.name: Guinea-Bissau
GNB.summary:
Same-sex conduct is legal in Guinea-Bissau. The 1993 penal code decree (4/93) omits same-sex offences entirely, and the country has never criminalised them. The Law on Prevention, Protection and Combating Domestic Violence (6/2014), Article 5, extends protection to victims regardless of sexual orientation. Guinea-Bissau signed the 2008 UN statement on sexual orientation and gender identity.

No legal gender recognition exists. There is no trans framework of any kind, no partnership or marriage recognition for same-sex couples, and no anti-discrimination law covering gender identity or sexual orientation in employment, services or public life. Nothing in the sourced record documents a document-amendment or border-screening pathway for trans travellers, and none can be assumed.

The dominant visitor risk is state capacity and enforcement rather than a specific statute. US State Department reporting for 2012 records a coup that year, arbitrary killings, torture, drug-trafficking-linked corruption and entrenched impunity within the security apparatus; the 2011 reporting records security-force torture and further impunity. These findings describe conditions a trans traveller would encounter regardless of the absence of anti-LGBT law.

Societal hostility is documented. The 2011 US State Department report notes stigma against LGBT people; the country guide records isolated violence cases in 2018 and no visible LGBT scene to orient visitors. The travel-safety assessment stands at 34/100, categorised Caution.
GNB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the inventory does not address legal gender recognition procedure, document amendment, or border and airport screening as they would affect a trans traveller. No source either confirms or excludes such a pathway, and the absence of a trans framework in law does not by itself establish what happens at a border post.

Unresolved: no source covers hate-crime provisions, sentencing enhancement for bias-motivated violence, or police handling of complaints from trans victims. Impunity for security-force abuse is documented, but its specific bearing on anti-trans violence is not.

Unresolved: entry and visa requirements, and any medical or HIV-related entry screening, are not sourced here.

Unresolved: adoption and general living-conditions material appears in one overview source as a general statement of legal challenge without supporting detail, and is not corroborated elsewhere in the inventory.

Unresolved: the 34/100 travel-safety score and the 2018 violence cases are drawn from a single country guide; neither is corroborated by an official or human-rights monitoring source in this inventory.

Domestic violence victims are protected under Article 5 of Law 6/2014 irrespective of sexual orientation, which gives LGBT residents a statutory basis for complaints in a domestic setting. The inventory does not show how that provision is applied in practice.

There is no anti-discrimination statute, so employment, healthcare and service denials based on gender identity or sexual orientation have no statutory remedy in the sourced record.

Social stigma is documented, no visible LGBT scene exists, and isolated violence against LGBT people was recorded as recently as 2018.

GNQ.name: Equatorial Guinea
GNQ.summary:
Equatorial Guinea is high risk for trans visitors. The 2022 penal code does not explicitly criminalise same-sex intimacy or gender diversity, but that gap in the statute does not translate into safety: authorities continue to apply the 1954 Law on Vagrants and Criminals, which classifies homosexuality as an illness and normalises conversion practices, and a 2020 Draft Law titled 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' would move conduct squarely into the criminal code if enacted; its current status is unclear.

Detention of LGBT people is documented. A Synergía IHR report on lesbophobia and police raids records police and military intervention in the assembly, expression and residential spaces of lesbian women, and in Bata the collective detention of women identified as lesbians on the stated grounds that 'lesbians are members of a sect', including collective punishment where a single individual is sought. The same reporting documents twelve women imprisoned between January and August 2024 in raids led by the Armed Forces and State Security, with detention used to extract bribes and sentences imposed indefinitely.

Three further instruments institutionalise discrimination against LGBT personnel and residents: the Military Justice Code, a ministerial order concerning 'immoral' activities, and a provincial regulation. The United States State Department's 2021 country report found no legal anti-discrimination protections and pervasive societal stigma toward LGBT persons. LGBT advocacy itself operates under the general repression of the country's government, one of the longest-ruling in Africa, which constrains freedom of expression, digital rights and journalist safety and leaves victims without meaningful recourse.
GNQ.outOfScopeNotes:
Several matters relevant to trans visitors could not be resolved from the available sources. Whether the 2020 Draft Law 'Regulating Prostitution and the Rights of Homosexuals' has advanced beyond draft status is unclear in the inventory. The sources do not address legal gender recognition, name or marker changes on identity and travel documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose gender history, or access to gender-affirming care; the current position on each of these is unsourced here.

No source in this inventory records a hate-crime statute, a complaint mechanism, or judicial remedy available to an LGBT victim of violence in Equatorial Guinea, and none records a documented case involving a trans foreign visitor specifically. The IRB-CISR country information record returned no usable finding for this pass.

SWZ.name: Eswatini
SWZ.summary: Eswatini is dangerous for trans visitors. Common law criminalises same-sex intimacy; trans people have no access to LGR and limited healthcare; the absolute monarchy punishes dissent harshly (sedition laws; activists assassinated, per BTI 2024); LGBT people face documented discrimination. Eswatini Pride has proceeded annually since 2018 under heavy conditions — a small space of visibility.
SWZ.outOfScopeNotes: Monarchy repression is general; Pride proceeds annually.

sources.summary: As of 12 March 2026, same-sex relations are illegal for men and women throughout Eswatini. Legal gender recognition is not possible, and LGBTI organisations cannot register.
Freedom in the World 2024: Eswatini rated Not Free with an overall score of 17/100 (Political Rights 1/40, Civil Liberties 16/60) - an absolute monarchy with severely restricted civic space.

BTI 2024 country report: the government denies LGBTQ+ groups the ability to register as organisations, within a wider pattern of restricted political formations, meetings and recruitment under an oppressive environment ('Mswati must fall' having become a common protest slogan).

US State Department 2021 report on Eswatini: some traditional, religious and government officials criticised same-sex sexual conduct as neither morally Swati nor Christian. In June, LGBTQI+ persons conducted a virtual Pride celebration without incident.
Swazi Media Commentary of December 2018: a church in Swaziland welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened - religious-space inclusion documented alongside 'no let-up on discrimination in the kingdom'.

MambaOnline, July 2018: the first eSwatini Pride was declared a 'perfect success' - the inaugural Pride in the kingdom, marking public LGBT visibility in a state where same-sex conduct remains illegal.
MambaOnline, July 2019: Eswatini's registrar of companies refused to register an LGBTI group - the documented administrative blocking of organisational recognition in the kingdom.

SWZ.tangentialFactors: Common-law criminalisation of same-sex intimacy — formal exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

blindSourceSummaries: International LGBT-rights organisation country overview (updated March 2026): common law criminalises consensual same-sex intimacy; no legal gender recognition and limited gender-affirming healthcare; intersex people lack safeguards; in April 2022 the high court rejected an LGBT organisation's bid for registration, but in June 2023 the supreme court declared the registrar's decision void; the commerce ministry still refuses registration, claiming the organisation's name and objectives 'seek to offend against customary principles'.

Freedom-watchdog annual assessment (2024): this country is rated 'not free' (17/100) - an absolute monarchy; political dissent harshly punished; discrimination against women and LGBT+ people among the human-rights problems.

Governance-index country report (2024) by a political foundation: the last absolute monarchy in its world region - the king and queen mother hold veto powers over all branches of government; governance and human-rights context.
A foreign government's 2021 human-rights report on this country: official assessment - sodomy laws (common law) remain; significant societal stigma; no legal protections for LGBT persons.

Media commentary site (Dec 2018): a church welcoming LGBTIQ people reopened in a residential area outside the capital; an activist at an LGBT advocacy organisation welcomed it while noting religious hate speech; a regional gender-rights report described a meeting where 20+ pastors called LGBTI behaviour 'demonic' and refused to let gay people 'flaunt' themselves.

LSO.name: Lesotho
LSO.summary: Lesotho demands real caution. Same-sex conduct is legal (sodomy common-law crime struck down in 2012); the Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho documents failures to prevent violence, harassment and discrimination by state and non-state actors (2024 UPR submission); no LGR; small organised community inside South Africa's geographic envelope.

sources.summary: Joint stakeholder UPR report (Oct 2024) by The Advocates for Human Rights, the Master of Healing Foundation and Rainbow Alliance of Lesotho on LGBTQ+ rights in Lesotho: documents discrimination, rape and assaults against LGBT people, barriers to health and education services, and community-level SOGIESC discrimination; same-sex conduct is not criminalised but no protections exist.

ICJ UPR submission (Nov 2024) on Lesotho: highlights LGBTIQ+ persons' rights to equality and non-discrimination among three key concerns (alongside inclusive education for children with disabilities and revocation of NGO lawyers' practising certificates).

SALC + People's Matrix Association + WLSA briefing (Oct 2020): 'Legal Gender Recognition in Lesotho' - analysis of law and policy against international best practice; Matrix is the only known LGBTI organisation in Lesotho; researched by Prof Alex Müller with community consultations.

US State Department 2016 Human Rights Report for Lesotho: documents the LDF mutiny arrests, torture of detainees, the killing of Lt-Gen Mahao, and the LGBT section noting no criminalisation but societal stigma.

SALC 'Transgender Rights in Lesotho' (2017): constitutional analysis - section 4(1) 'sex' and 'other status' should include gender identity per the UN Human Rights Committee; no law allows gender-marker changes; a trans person using a non-matching passport could be charged; the Labour Code's non-discrimination clause omits gender and sexual orientation.

Lesotho Labour Act 2024 (full text, ILO NATLEX): the new labour law - unfair discrimination, unfair labour practice, freedom of association, forced and child labour prohibitions - the current statutory framework for workplace rights.

LSO.tangentialFactors: The 2012 decriminalisation removed same-sex-conduct exposure for visitors travelling with partners.

CPV.name: Cabo Verde
CPV.summary:
Same-sex relations are not criminalised in Cabo Verde, and the country's employment discrimination prohibition covers sexual orientation. The protection does not extend to gender identity, leaving trans visitors and residents without an explicit statutory basis for workplace complaints (Outright International, updated 12 March 2026).

No legal gender recognition framework is on record. As of 2016 civil law blocked Tchinda Andrade, the first publicly self-outed trans woman in Cabo Verde, from changing her legal name to a female one; the source inventory contains no later statute or administrative route for legal gender change.

Same-sex unions are not recognised. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva stated on 11 July 2017 that same-sex marriage was not on the government's agenda, following LGBT community demands for civil unions and marriage.

Public visibility is high by regional standards. Cabo Verde held its first public Pride in 2013, the second African country to do so. The 2018 Pride Week in Praia combined a parade with campaigns by the Associação Gay de Cabo Verde, the Associação LGBTI de Praia and the Associação Arco Iris, which petitioned the National Assembly for same-sex marriage and an anti-discrimination law; the gender-equality institute ICIEG and UN Women took part. Polling in 2019–21 found 82% would accept a 'homosexual' neighbour.

Trans-specific violence is documented at individual level rather than as a recorded pattern. Tchinda Andrade, who came out in 1997 at age 19, described Cabo Verde as markedly free for LGBT people compared with other African countries and São Vicente as relaxed, but reported verbal violence and two physical attacks against her. The inventory contains no case series, prosecution record or official count of anti-trans violence.
CPV.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether any administrative practice permits a gender or name marker change on identity documents is unresolved. The only sourced statement is Tchinda Andrade's 2016 account that civil law blocked her name change; no later legal or administrative status is in the inventory.

Enforcement of the employment discrimination protection is not sourced. The inventory states the prohibition exists and that it covers sexual orientation, but records no complaint outcomes, labour-inspectorate practice or court decisions.

Hate-crime or aggravated-penalty provisions covering anti-trans motivation are not sourced either way. The absence of such a provision in the inventory is not evidence that none exists.

The scale of anti-trans violence beyond Tchinda Andrade's reported verbal abuse and two physical attacks is not sourced. No police statistics, NGO incident counts or court records are available here, so the assessment of low documented risk rests on a single first-person account plus the absence of a recorded pattern.

Entry, visa and border-screening rules for trans travellers, including how gender markers on passports are treated at arrival, are not covered by any source in this inventory.

STP.name: São Tomé and Príncipe
STP.summary: São Tomé and Príncipe demands real caution. Same-sex conduct decriminalised in 2012; small, peaceful, tourism-growing islands; no LGR; no documented anti-trans violence; thin community.

sources.summary: Same-sex conduct has been legal since 2012. The age of consent has been equal at 18 since 2021 under Law 15/2021, previously 16. There is no relationship recognition and no adoption. Labour Code 2019 Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination based on sexual orientation. There is no gender-identity recognition.

Under the Penal Code in force since November 2012 same-sex conduct is legal with an equal age of consent of 16 regardless of sexual orientation or gender identity. Labour Code (2019) Article 16.2 bans workplace discrimination on sexual orientation, and Penal Code Article 130(2)(d) allows enhanced sentencing for crimes motivated by sexual-orientation hatred. No same-sex marriages, civil unions or partnerships are recognised; a 2016 poll found 46% of Sao Tomeans would not mind an LGBTQ neighbour.

Same-sex conduct has been legal since the November 2012 Penal Code, with an equal age of consent of 16. Same-sex marriage, civil unions and domestic partnerships are not recognised. There is no general anti-discrimination protection beyond the 2019 Labour Code ban on sexual-orientation discrimination in employment. The country is listed among UN Joint Statement signatories on sexual orientation and gender identity.

MDV.name: Maldives
MDV.summary:
Maldives is dangerous for trans visitors — a sharp resort/local split. Under the Penal Code and sharia framework, same-sex conduct is criminalised (up to 8 years, with 100 lashes available), and gender-nonconforming Maldivians face prosecution and social erasure; activists operate from exile (a 2024 HRC shadow report documents ICCPR violations). BUT: the tourist resort islands operate as a legally distinct world — no LGBT tourist is documented as prosecuted on a resort; the risk concentrates in Malé and local islands.

A resort-only visit is lower-risk than the score suggests; any local-island contact raises it.

PRK.name: North Korea
PRK.summary: North Korea is a place trans visitors should avoid entirely: same-sex conduct is not named in the Criminal Code, but Article 193 prohibits “decadent culture,” and broad obscene-activities provisions give the authorities unlimited discretion, and reported incidents of criminalisation and even execution for homosexuality exist. Gender identity does not exist in public life, visitors travel under constant escort and surveillance in the world's most totalitarian system, and any nonconforming presentation or discovered digital material risks detention, with no recorded protection or recognition of gender identity to offset that exposure.
PRK.outOfScopeNotes: No source in this record covers visa or border-document screening of foreign trans visitors, and no marriage or partner-travel recognition fact for trans visitors is recorded anywhere in the sources — the criminal-code and surveillance profile is the entire documented visitor picture. One source records no documented violence against LGBTIQ people, by the government or by other actors, which sits in tension with the reported criminalisation and even execution incidents in the current summary; neither side is independently verified. Data scarcity reflects totalitarian control, and traveler surveillance is universal.

sources.summary: Outright International country page (updated 12 Mar 2026): DPRK Criminal Code (1950, rev. 2009) appears to contain no penalty for consensual same-sex acts, but Art. 193 bans import/keeping/distribution of 'decadent culture' incl. sexual recordings and Art. 262 bans collective 'obscene activities'; 2014 KCNA denied homosexuality's existence; an openly gay defector published an autobiography in 2017; no documented state or non-state violence against LGBTIQ people; no registration route for LGBTI orgs.

Legal Clarity overview: sex-marker change on birth certificate/citizen card technically possible under 'unavoidable circumstances' - application to People's Security Agency plus state forensic medical evaluation, in practice requiring surgical intervention; no law explicitly bans gender-affirming care but the under-resourced health system makes hormones/surgery effectively inaccessible.

BBC Korean feature (10 Oct 2024), 'Does homosexuality exist in North Korea too?': 10 years after the UN COI report, new laws (Pyongyang Cultural Protection Act etc.) tighten control; profiles Jang Young-jin, a novelist who defected in the late 1990s and was forcibly outed, as the first publicly known gay defector; documents how a collective-over-individual regime forces DPRK sexual minorities into silent self-suppression and frames LGBT life as human-rights abuse.

US State Department 2022 Human Rights Report for North Korea: official assessment - the totalitarian regime's pervasive abuses; the report notes no specific law criminalising same-sex conduct but the regime's total control leaves no space for LGBT life.

PSE.name: Palestinian Territories
PSE.summary:
Trans visitors face grave danger here, with a hard internal split: in the West Bank, same-sex conduct is not criminalised (Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual-private-sex offences, carried into the 1960 penal code applied there), but there are no protections, family/clan hostility is severe, and the Palestinian Authority has not legislated or signed key treaties. In the other part, Gaza, a 1936 British Mandate code technically allows up to 10 years for consensual same-sex acts, Hamas has executed people for alleged homosexuality, and the area is in a catastrophic war.

Trans identities are nowhere explicitly criminalised, but public-morality provisions can catch trans people, gender-affirming healthcare is essentially destroyed or unavailable, police action against a queer organisation drew rights-group condemnation, and periodic transphobic threats and attacks are reported.
PSE.outOfScopeNotes: The two parts — West Bank and Gaza — are scored as one de jure unit, yet Gaza is far worse in practice because of the war and Hamas, the group controlling the area. No source covers border screening, document handling or passport-marker practice for trans visitors, and no marriage or partner-travel recognition fact for trans visitors is recorded anywhere in the sources. Reported Hamas executions for alleged homosexuality and the police clampdown are documented claims, not independently verified elsewhere.

The page advances a pinkwashing critique: the occupation marginalises queer and trans Palestinians alongside everyone else, documenting de facto oppression.

West Bank criminal law derives from the Jordanian Penal Code No. 16 of 1960. Jordan's 1951 revision dropped consensual private-sex offences and the 1960 code carried that forward. Social and family persecution makes the practical reality harsher than the formal law.

Wikipedia LGBT rights in Palestine: patchwork decriminalisation (British Mandate code in Jordan until 1951; Jordanian Penal Code no prohibition of same-sex acts applied to the West Bank; Israel stopped using the code in 1977); PA has not legislated; no explicit prohibition on trans identity; periodic transphobic threats/attacks; PA a non-signatory to key treaties.

Regional movement context for Palestinian LGBT life.

Times of Israel: rights groups slammed Palestinian police for banning LGBTQ activity - after the police action against al-Qaws, the foundation received a wave of hate messages which activists said 'pose a serious threat' to the gay community.

Times of Israel: Israel to allow LGBT Palestinians granted temporary asylum to work - some 90 LGBT Palestinians have received temporary permits to seek refuge in Israel after fleeing violence in the territories.

A human-rights monitoring organisation and a local legal-aid centre interviewed 12 Palestinian women identifying as lesbian, bisexual or queer and documented widespread discrimination and abuse in public and family settings; the regional activist movement — personal stories, cross-border alliances and national campaigns — is resident life, not visitor guidance.

SLE.name: Sierra Leone
SLE.summary: Sierra Leone is dangerous for trans visitors. The 1861 Offences Against the Person Act criminalises buggery with up to life imprisonment (men only) — enforcement is limited but discrimination and violence are regular; no LGR; a small community organises quietly.

Amnesty International Sierra Leone 2025 country report (LGBTI section): consensual sexual relations between women are not explicitly outlawed, but lesbian women face significant social, cultural and economic barriers to living freely — stigma, harassment, and limited acceptance from families and communities; no non-discrimination protection for SOGI is documented.

Joint ICCPR shadow report (March 2014) to the UN Human Rights Committee: 'Breaking the Silence on Human Rights Violations in Sierra Leone' - discrimination and violence based on SOGI; covers civil-war sexual violence, discrimination in health and education, hate speech by religious institutions, and hate crimes against LGBTI human-rights defenders.

US State Department 2012 Human Rights Report for Sierra Leone: documents police killings, corruption, FGM/C, and 'official and societal discrimination against lesbian, gay, bisexual, and transgender (LGBT) individuals'.

XKX.name: Kosovo
XKX.summary: Kosovo is workable for trans visitors — the Balkans' strongest legal framework on paper. The constitution (Art 24) bans discrimination based on sexual orientation; the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covers gender identity; legal gender recognition is possible (medicalised); and the government attempted same-sex unions in 2024 as part of Council of Europe accession. Counterweights: implementation is inconsistent, political hate speech is common (2022 CSGD report: year marked by intolerance), and Pristina Pride proceeds under protection.
XKX.outOfScopeNotes: De jure unit: scored separately from Serbia per boundaries. Implementation gaps are resident-facing.
