GIB.name: Gibraltar
GIB.summary:
Gibraltar is a self-governing territory whose own legislature and Supreme Court govern its civil and criminal law. Measures enacted by the United Kingdom do not apply here of their own force: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued in 2025 bind Gibraltar only if extended by Order in Council. No such extension is on record in the sourced material.

The principal legal gap for a trans visitor is gender recognition. No route exists in Gibraltar to change legal gender. A trans visitor therefore expects to travel on a document whose gender marker cannot be altered by any local process, and to be read in public under that marker.

Discrimination protection covering sexual orientation and gender reassignment has been in force since 2007. The sourced material does not set out what that protection covers in practice: whether it reaches service counters, single-sex facilities, health care, or employment in the visitor's own terms is not stated.

Same-sex activity has been legal since 1993, with an equal age of consent since 2012. Civil partnerships have existed since 2014, and same-sex marriage was passed unanimously in December 2016. A Supreme Court ruling in 2013 established a right of adoption by same-sex partners.

The 2016 marriage bill followed a public consultation opened in December 2015, which returned 3,490 replies from an electorate of 24,117. Reporting at the time described the population as divided over the change, while noting that an inter-ministerial committee chaired by a government minister had weighed the arguments and that the main parties supported the amendment; a draft bill amending the Civil Marriage Act was placed before Parliament in August 2016.

Official language on hostility has been directed at anti-gay abuse rather than at transgender persons. In July 2021 the Ministry for Justice and Equality said it would 'urgently' consider legislation to tackle 'disgusting lurking homophobia' following an incident of anti-gay abuse. That statement evidences an enforcement intent against homophobic abuse; it does not establish trans-specific protection.
GIB.outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: the substantive scope of the 2007 protection for gender reassignment. The sourced material records that the term appears in the discrimination law but does not state what it covers in practice, including access to health care, single-sex facilities, or employment records.

Not sourced: whether any procedure, including a deed poll or statutory declaration, permits a Gibraltarian resident to obtain a corrected gender marker on a United Kingdom travel document, and whether United Kingdom gender recognition law applies to persons resident in Gibraltar. This is an open research question rather than a negative finding.

Not sourced: the existence, wording or enforcement of any hate-crime provision denigrating transgender persons, and any recorded incident of violence against a trans person in Gibraltar with a date and legal outcome.

Unresolved: whether the Ministry for Justice and Equality statement of July 2021, made in response to anti-gay abuse, resulted in enacted legislation, and whether any such legislation addresses abuse of transgender persons. The statement is the only enforcement-intent evidence on record here and it concerns homophobia.

BMU.name: Bermuda
BMU.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Bermuda; local legislation governs, and the United Kingdom measures could be applied only by Order in Council.

Bermuda decriminalised consensual sex between adult men in 1994, when the House of Assembly voted 22–16 to strike two sections of the Criminal Code. In July 2013 the Senate passed the Human Rights Amendment Act, which outlawed discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and, in the same instrument, on grounds of age; same-sex marriage was not permitted at that time.

Same-sex couples married in Bermuda in 2017 lost that route the following year. The Governor gave assent to the Domestic Partnership Act in February 2018, replacing same-sex marriage with domestic partnerships available to same-sex and opposite-sex couples alike, which made Bermuda the first jurisdiction anywhere to revoke marriage equality. In March 2022 the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council upheld that restoration of the opposite-sex definition of marriage, so a partnership rather than a marriage is the status available to same-sex couples.

For a transgender visitor the decisive fact is the protection gap. Bermuda has no legal recognition of transgender people and no gender-recognition framework, so there is no route to amend a gender marker on local documents and no recognition machinery a visitor could rely on at the border or in dealings with local authorities. The 2013 amendment's protected ground as enacted is sexual orientation; the inventory does not record gender identity as a protected ground, and no hate-crime provision covering gender identity is sourced here.

Whether gender identity functions as a protected ground under Bermuda's human-rights legislation, whether any local gender-recognition statute exists, and whether hate-crime provisions reach conduct motivated by gender identity are all unresolved on the present inventory; none of these points is sourced here.

The enforcement record of the 2013 discrimination protections, including complaint volumes and outcomes, is not sourced. Whether the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 or its 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been proposed for extension to Bermuda by Order in Council is likewise unresolved.

CYM.name: Cayman Islands
CYM.summary:
Same-sex intimacy was decriminalised in the Cayman Islands in 2001 by an Order in Council imposed from London after the local legislature declined to act, and the reform left an unequal age of consent in its wake.

London–local friction over the scope of protections is documented from 2009, when the United Kingdom's Foreign Affairs Committee criticised the draft Cayman Islands constitution for deliberately excluding gay rights, calling the omission deplorable and warning that the drafting could leave the territory's courts affording less protection than Article 14 of the European Convention on Human Rights requires. The Foreign and Commonwealth Office answered that the draft's list of discrimination grounds was open-ended.

The judiciary outran the legislature on relationship status. In March 2019 Grand Court Chief Justice Anthony Smellie struck down the prohibition on same-sex marriage; the Court of Appeal reversed that ruling in August 2019, so no same-sex marriages can be performed locally. In December 2020 the immigration authorities recognised the overseas same-sex marriage of Paul Pearson and Randall Pinder, who had married in Ireland, with the Court of Appeal holding that refusing recognition would treat persons unequally on sexual-orientation grounds. The practical position for a visitor is therefore recognition of an existing foreign marriage for immigration effects, without any locally conferred marital status.

Public visibility carries official backing. The territory's first Pride parade, held on 7 August 2021 and organised by the Cayman LGBTQ Foundation, drew around 600 participants including the premier, the governor, ministers and members of the Legislative Assembly. Participants were asked by organisers to refrain from excessive displays of affection, a condition reflecting sensitivities about public space rather than a legal prohibition.
CYM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the unequal age of consent identified after the 2001 decriminalisation has since been amended by the Legislative Assembly is unresolved in the available sources; no later legislative text is provided.

The scope of the December 2020 recognition beyond immigration effects is unresolved. Whether a foreign same-sex marriage is given general legal effect in the Cayman Islands, for purposes such as property, succession or next-of-kin status, is not sourced here.

No source in the inventory addresses whether the territory has enacted a civil partnership, domestic partnership or equivalent status scheme, or whether any such bill is pending.

Nothing in the inventory covers hate-crime provisions, their wording or their enforcement, or recorded incidents of violence against trans people in the Cayman Islands. Those questions remain unsourced rather than answered negatively.

Whether the Court of Appeal's equality reasoning in the recognition case has been applied to other areas of law, and whether any further appeal or legislative response followed, is not established by the available material.

VGB.name: British Virgin Islands
VGB.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to British Virgin Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Same-sex intimacy in the British Virgin Islands was decriminalised in January 2001 by order of the United Kingdom's Privy Council, after the local legislature refused to act — a local legislator's 'there is nothing we can do about it' captured the resentment with which the reform landed. Family status remains contested rather than settled: in 2022 the Court of Appeal refused the local churches council's attempt to appeal a judgment in favour of two women, married in the UK, who were seeking recognition of their marriage and a declaration that the prohibition is unconstitutional — the court finding the proposed appeal had no realistic prospect of success.

Visitors encounter a tolerant-but-quiet society: travel surveys rate these twin islands among the more gay-welcoming in the Caribbean while noting resistance beneath the surface, with most local hostility 'silent and invisible' and most visitors hardly noticing either way. Discretion, not danger, is the operative norm.
VGB.outOfScopeNotes:

No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans visitors, and no source documents legal gender recognition or trans-specific statutes — the assessment rests on the same-sex record and the general social climate. The marriage case's final resolution is unrecorded: the 2022 appeal refusal concerned case-management orders, and no ruling on the validity of a marriage performed abroad appears in the current sources.

AIA.name: Anguilla
AIA.summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands — acting unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories. A first-person account published in June 2023 dates the change to 2000 rather than January 2001.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguilla law. A commercial destination-wedding service states that plainly while marketing the island's venues to same-sex couples, which means a ceremony performed there carries symbolic status only.

Public LGBT life on the island is close to invisible: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, and only a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers. Anguilla's roughly 15,000 residents and 35 square miles are given as reasons the scene stays small, and the muted, not 'out and proud' atmosphere is attributed to the imposed colonial legacy rather than to local choice. A queer family visiting in June 2023 described the trip as uneventful.
AIA.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not contain the text of the instrument by which decriminalisation took effect in Anguilla, so the precise statutory mechanism and its current wording are unresolved here.

Sources disagree on the date of the change: a 2023 travel account gives 2000, while the contemporaneous Associated Press report of the Privy Council order is dated 5 January 2001. Both are reported as sourced; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been the subject of an Order in Council extending it to Anguilla is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

MSR.name: Montserrat
MSR.summary:
Same-sex activity is legal in Montserrat: its prohibitions were swept away in January 2001 by the same Order in Council that overrode the region's reluctant legislatures. What public LGBT life existed was effectively extinguished twice by disaster: the 1989 hurricane and the 1995 volcanic eruptions that buried the southern half of the island and depopulated it, leaving a scatter of survivors in the north and a gay presence described as 'decimated', only partially recovered.

Local religious leaders called the 2001 reform 'totally unacceptable,' and the territory appeared resigned to following London's order. Visitors today find a tiny, dispersed, private society where neither hostility nor community is much visible.

The description of the social scene rests on a dated 2012 country report, and no newer survey data is recorded. Whether the scene has recovered since the disasters is not measurable from the available sources. No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans travelers at entry, no trans-specific incident data is recorded, and no source addresses marriage or partner recognition for same-sex couples.

TCA.name: Turks and Caicos Islands
TCA.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Turks and Caicos Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Turks and Caicos decriminalised same-sex activity in 2001 through the UK-imposed Caribbean reform, and its constitution now bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation. The live frontier has been recognition rather than criminal law: the Court of Appeal ordered a residence permit for the same-sex spouse lawfully married abroad, holding that 'spouse' in the immigration ordinance must include same-sex spouses and declaring violations of the equality, non-discrimination and private-and-family-life guarantees — while declining to touch the constitution's male-female marriage definition, which it treated as controlling.

the United Kingdom's passport guidance maintains a standing profile of the territory's rules on marriage, civil partnerships, adoption and gender recognition. Socially, a resident's account described 'virtually nothing' documented about gay life — in a territory where around two-thirds of inhabitants are themselves not native-born — so visitor experience runs on privacy and the resort economy rather than any visible scene.
TCA.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

The 2025 passport-office profile establishes the document framework but no source verifies that local border practice matches it; whether a trans traveler's documents are accepted at entry without friction is unverified. The appellate ruling has no later confirmation recorded in this record. The 'virtually nothing' social read rests on a single 2009 resident account, no newer survey data exists here, and no trans-specific incident data is recorded.

Directly relevant: same-sex partners of visitors/residents get residence recognition.
Same-sex sexual activity has been legal in the Turks and Caicos Islands since 2001, and discrimination on sexual-orientation grounds is constitutionally prohibited.

FLK.name: Falkland Islands
FLK.summary:
The Falkland Islands, a British Overseas Territory with its own Legislative Assembly, legislate locally. Same-sex activity has been legal since 1989 and the age of consent has been equal since 2005. Same-sex marriage and civil partnerships have been available since 29 April 2017; the bill passed the Legislative Assembly in March 2017 by 7 votes to 1, and the registrar general subsequently confirmed that it is law. Civil partnerships are open to opposite-sex couples as well as same-sex couples.

The Constitution Order 2008 bans discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation at Article 16. The provision covers sexual orientation only; the sources do not identify a gender-identity ground in the Constitution.

UK frameworks do not reach the Islands. The UK Equality Act 2010 and the Gender Recognition Act 2004 do not extend to the Falkland Islands, and the territory's own ordinances govern instead. These include the Crimes Ordinance 2014, which makes sexual-orientation hate-stirring an offence; the Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014, which provides sexual orientation as an aggravating factor in sentencing and recognises acquired gender under a UK Gender Recognition Certificate; and the Prisons Ordinance 2017.

The Crime and Public Order (Equality) Ordinance 2014 has permitted legal gender change since 2014. Gender recognition is not available on a self-identification basis, and no non-binary status is recognised.

The registrar general also confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands, a separate dependency for which the UK is responsible; the equality reform applies to the Falkland Islands themselves.
FLK.outOfScopeNotes:
The sources state that the Crimes Ordinance 2014 criminalises sexual-orientation hate-stirring but do not give the penalty ranges, the elements of the offence, or any reported prosecution. Enforcement of the constitutional non-discrimination guarantee and the sentencing aggravating factor is likewise unsourced here; whether either has been invoked in a decided case is unresolved.

No source in this inventory addresses facilities or bathroom access, healthcare provision for trans residents or visitors, immigration or security screening, name and gender markers on travel documents presented at entry, or documented incidents of violence against trans people. Those points should be treated as not sourced rather than as absent risk.

The exact commencement procedure for the 2017 marriage legislation is not detailed: the bill passed in March 2017 and marriage has been available from 29 April 2017, with the registrar general's reply confirming the law in June 2017. Whether gender recognition under the 2014 ordinance is available to persons who are not settled residents is not covered by the sources.

[1] Rob Salerno blog (22 Jun 2017): the Falklands registrar general confirmed by reply that the same-sex marriage and civil partnership bill passed in March is law, resolving the outstanding question of its assent; the same registrar confirmed that same-sex marriage is not legal in the South Georgia and South Sandwich Islands dependency.

SHN.name: Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha
SHN.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Saint Helena, Ascension and Tristan da Cunha; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

A scattered South Atlantic territory of three island groups that legislated equality island by island: the 2009 constitutional order imposed by the United Kingdom bans discrimination on grounds including sexual orientation across all three, and equal age of consent sits at 16. Marriage equality arrived in staggered fashion — the first dependency's council approved the ordinance 5-0 in May 2016 and it commenced January 2017, the most remote island followed in August 2017, and the principal island itself completed the set on 20 December 2017 — with adoption law following the same year.

The rollout ran fast and orderly across very small councils. Survey data on social attitudes is entirely absent; remoteness, not resistance, is what the record characterises.

PCN.name: Pitcairn Islands
PCN.summary:
the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to Pitcairn Islands; local law governs, with the United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

Pitcairn's roughly fifty inhabitants govern family law themselves, and on paper they have adopted the most complete equality package in this group of territories: activity legal since 2001, a 2010 constitution that bans sexual-orientation discrimination, and a 2015 Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance — marriage defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, orientation or gender identity, foreign civil partnerships recognised, and adoption open to married, unmarried and single people alike.

No islander is known to be in a same-sex relationship — on an island this size, invisibility is arithmetic rather than atmosphere. Defence and external affairs are the United Kingdom's responsibility; family law is set locally as above.
PCN.outOfScopeNotes:
A British Overseas Territory; local law deviates from the UK's where noted.

The practicality of the on-paper equality package is unverified: no source records any same-sex couple or trans resident, no venues or organisations exist, and practical visitation is negligible. No source in this record addresses border-screening or document practice for trans travelers at entry, and the everyday enforcement of the legal protections is not documented here.

sources.summary: Same-sex activity has been legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001. The 2010 Constitution bans discrimination on sexual orientation, with protections in place since 2010. Same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015 and adoption since 2015. None of the roughly 50 residents is known to be in a same-sex relationship. Military service falls under UK responsibility.

The 2010 Pitcairn Constitution Order bans discrimination on sexual orientation. Marriage is defined as the union of two people regardless of sex, sexual orientation or gender identity, and same-sex marriage has been legal since 14 May 2015. The Same Sex Marriage and Civil Partnerships Ordinance 2015 also recognises civil partnerships performed outside Pitcairn. Adoption is open to married, unmarried and single people.

Full Wikipedia republication: same-sex sexual activity legal in the Pitcairn Islands since 2001; anti-discrimination constitutional protection from the 2010 Constitution Order; same-sex marriage legal 14 May 2015 — ordinance unanimously approved by the Island Council 1 Apr 2015, signed by Governor Jonathan Sinclair 5 May, published 13 May 2015; adoption legal since 2015; page also indexes the territory within UK LGBT-rights timelines.

GGY.name: Guernsey
GGY.summary:
Guernsey is a self-governing Crown Dependency with its own parliament, the States of Guernsey, and its own statute book. The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and the single-sex-services code issued under it in 2025 do not apply here automatically. Local law governs, and United Kingdom measures reach Guernsey only by Order in Council.

On 10 December 2015 the States approved same-sex marriage by 37 votes to 7. Two alternatives were put and rejected as insufficient: a civil-partnership-only scheme, and a single secular status called Union Civile that would have applied to all couples alike. The enabling legislation was left to a separate bill, which commenced in 2018.

Family recognition moved earlier the same year. A review of the Adoption Law recorded at page 1170 of the States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 ended a fifty-year bar on unmarried couples adopting. The States agreed that same-sex couples may adopt, that civil partnerships are recognised for that purpose, and that both partners hold equal parental responsibility.

No source establishes legal gender recognition or trans-specific protection in force in Guernsey.
GGY.outOfScopeNotes:
No source establishes a legal gender-recognition mechanism in Guernsey, and none establishes trans-specific anti-discrimination protection in force. Whether local equality law covers gender identity on the same footing as sexual orientation is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

The material reviewed on Les Nicolles contains no rule for housing trans prisoners by birth sex or identified gender, no trans-specific unit, and no stated solitary or segregation practice for trans prisoners. Nothing on the prison-housing axis can be verified from it.

No Order in Council extending the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 to Guernsey appears in the sources reviewed, so the Act and its 2025 single-sex-services code are treated as not applying. Confirming the absence of such an order is a research task still outstanding.

sources.summary: States of Guernsey Billet d'État of 24 June 2015 records the review of Adoption Law at p.1170, which led to adoption rights for same-sex couples.

BBC (10 Dec 2015): States of Guernsey approved same-sex marriage 37-7, rejecting both civil-partnership-only and single 'Union Civile' alternatives; implementing legislation separate and not expected before 2017. Charity Liberate: 'historic day'; debate described as 'extremely positive'.

BBC (24 Jun 2015): Guernsey repealed its 50-year Adoption Law's ban on unmarried couples adopting — States agreed same-sex couples may adopt, with civil partnerships recognised and equal parental responsibility for both partners (Jersey had approved the same change two days earlier).

BBC (23 Sep 2011): Guernsey adopted the UK's relaxed blood-donor rules — gay/bisexual men eligible after 12-month deferral, targeted ~7 Nov 2011 to match the UK change, ending the local 1980s HIV-era ban; other donation restrictions unchanged.

IMN.name: Isle of Man
IMN.summary:
The United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the Isle of Man. Local law governs, with United Kingdom measures extendable only by Order in Council.

The Isle of Man is a self-legislating Crown Dependency whose parliament, Tynwald, frames these questions through its own bills. The Legislative Council's proceedings of 26 April 2016 record the Third Reading of the Marriage and Civil Partnership (Amendment) Bill 2016 alongside consideration of the Equality Bill 2016, which is the primary legislative record of the island's marriage-equality debate.

Employment protection preceded that debate by a decade. On 30 November 2005 the House of Keys adopted an amendment to the Employment Bill, tabled by Onchan MHK Peter Karran, barring dismissal of gay and lesbian employees on sexual-orientation grounds and aligning the island's employment law with United Kingdom human-rights law.

Political commitment at the top of the Manx government followed. On 9 June 2015 Chief Minister Allan Bell publicly backed same-sex marriage and said he would formulate a bill to repeal the island's marriage prohibition.

The Marriage and Civil Partnership Act received Royal Assent and same-sex marriage took effect on the island in July 2016. The first conversion of a civil partnership to a marriage was completed within days of entry into force. Civil partnerships have been legal on the island since 2011 and are convertible to marriage without a second ceremony, and the registration process has run as a routine administrative matter.
IMN.outOfScopeNotes:
The outcome of the Equality Bill 2016 beyond its appearance on the Legislative Council's agenda of 26 April 2016 is not sourced in this inventory, and its final provisions remain unresolved here.

No source in this inventory addresses prison housing for trans detainees. The island's only functioning prison, the Isle of Man Prison at Jurby, operates remand, convicted, female, young-offender, vulnerable-prisoner and segregation units, but no birth-sex-versus-identity placement rule, trans-specific unit, or trans-specific segregation practice is documented; the point is unresolved rather than established either way.

Entry and visa screening that could disclose gender history, gender-marker rules on Manx documents, hate-crime protection, criminalisation, access to gender-affirming care, and facilities law are not covered by the sources assembled here and should be verified independently.

GUF.name: French Guiana
GUF.summary:
French Guiana stands under France's national framework as an overseas department: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as they do in metropolitan France.

Legal gender recognition has been available on a simplified administrative basis since 2017, by declaration, with no requirement of surgery, sterilisation or psychiatric diagnosis. Anti-discrimination protection covering gender identity has been in force since 2012, and hate-crime sentence enhancement provisions were added in 2017. Nothing in French law criminalises trans status or gender expression.

Same-sex relations and same-sex marriage are legal under French law. Pride events are held, the scene is small and anchored in Cayenne, and a travel guide rates the territory "Very Safe for LGBTQ+".

The sharpest documented state machinery is custodial. Trans women incarcerated in France on the basis of their legal gender occupy a legal gray area, and that practice reaches French Guiana as a jurisdiction applying French prison law. The CGLPL, France's national preventive mechanism, reported on 25 May 2021 that serious violations in the treatment of transgender persons persist across French places of deprivation of liberty; its findings apply to detention facilities here.

The friction a trans visitor meets is practical rather than legal. Specialised gender-affirming healthcare is thin, remoteness pushes residents into metropolitan France for care, and local reporting describes transphobia and cultural taboos that discourage visibility and reporting of incidents.
GUF.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the inventory documents an incident involving a trans visitor to French Guiana; the assessment rests on the general French legal framework and on national detention findings.

Whether French Guiana's detention facilities have received a CGLPL visit, and what was found there specifically, is unresolved in these sources.

The account of prison placement practice for trans women dates from January 2018; whether that practice has since changed is unresolved.

Entry and visa screening with respect to gender markers on travel documents is not sourced here, and neither is the enforcement record of the 2017 hate-crime provisions in French Guiana.

One country guide in the inventory returned no usable finding on the safety of trans visitors.

GLP.name: Guadeloupe
GLP.summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex marriage is available, gender-identity discrimination is prohibited, and legal gender recognition follows the simplified French procedure. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice, assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism, the CGLPL, issued an opinion of 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, reporting serious violations of fundamental rights across French detention facilities and drawing on some forty referrals received since 2010.

Support infrastructure has expanded. Guadeloupe's first dedicated LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and guidance for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities; it was driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations. During the opening, the minister responsible for family affairs and diversity, Aurore Bergé, announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted to overseas territories.

Community organisation is visible and growing. A September 2023 interview with organisers of Secret's Out described community members increasingly reconciling their lives with their orientation, with activism advancing after Martinique, alongside the work of Amalgame Humani's. In 2025, Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe. A 2023 local mapping of anti-LGBT violence exists, and organisers describe a gap between legal protection and lived experience.

MTQ.name: Martinique
MTQ.summary:
Martinique stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

As a full overseas department, the island carries the entire metropolitan framework: same-sex marriage and full anti-discrimination protection (constitutional provisions extending state law here are explicit in the rights record), decriminalised for two centuries, with simplified judicial gender-marker change available under the state's 2016-17 reforms. Nothing criminalises being trans, and case law and state protection capacity track the metropolitan norm.

Community infrastructure is real but modest: the island's lesbian, gay, bisexual and trans network organises private parties and garden socials and provides information and meeting services, supported by gay-friendly allies — there is no large commercial scene in the capital. The trans-relevant state mechanism documented across the framework is custodial: the national detention-places watchdog's findings of serious persistent violations against transgender prisoners apply to the island's prisons as to the metropole.

Territory of France; local deviations noted in summary.

No visitor border-screening or document-handling practice is documented beyond the national framework, and the custodial findings rest on inspections and referrals at sites elsewhere in the country rather than local prisons.

sources.summary: BuzzFeed News feature (12 Jan 2018): trans women in France are held in prisons matching the gender marker on their identity documents (Article D248 of the French criminal procedure code) — most end up in all-male facilities where other detainees threaten them ('we don't want any women here'), placement following the ID marker rather than anatomy. The French prison framework applies to the department's establishments as French law.

Opinion of the CGLPL, France's detention-places watchdog (25 May 2021): finds 'the persistence of serious violations' of the fundamental rights of transgender detainees across ALL French places of deprivation of liberty, based on referrals since 2010 concerning some forty transgender persons plus on-site inspections (eight trans women and one trans man interviewed at Fleury-Mérogis, Caen, Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse sites). Covers placement, isolation, safety and staff-training recommendations. Binds the department's prisons as French establishments.

Rights in Exile (AsyLex) Martinique resource page: same-sex acts decriminalised in 1815; Article 73 of the Constitution applies French law to the department; 2013 marriage-equality law applies; discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation prohibited in goods/services since Law No. 2001-1066 (Penal Code arts. 225-1/225-2) and in employment since Labour Code art. L1132-1 (2008); gender-identity discrimination prohibited since Article 4 of the 2012 sexual-harassment law, with 'sexual identity' replaced by 'gender identity' in 2016. Also lists local support organisations, case law and country-of-origin experts.

JM Concept 972 is a Martinique lesbian, gay, bi and trans network that provides information, meetings and services to the island's LGBT community and runs private parties and garden parties, with 2025 events listed for 4 July, 15 August and 5 September, supported by gay-friendly heterosexual supporters. Its active, dated operation evidences local community infrastructure on the island.

MYT.name: Mayotte
MYT.summary:
Mayotte stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

On paper the fullest of regional frameworks: French civil and criminal law applies — same-sex marriage (a genuine rarity in this part of the world), gender-identity anti-discrimination protection, and legal gender change by simplified procedure following the national reforms. No law criminalises being trans or being in a same-sex relationship.

The gap between book and life is the documented story. A 2023 report on a binational couple describes a 'long and complicated' path even to marry on this predominantly Muslim island; a legal-access directory shows no openly LGBT-friendly lawyer resident in the department (metropolitan counsel take cases); and the framework's prison findings — the state detention watchdog's report of serious violations against transgender prisoners — apply to the local jails. Social environment is conservative in a way the audited sources show through practice, not statute. For visitors, legal protection exists and enforcement of rights is slow; visibility invites social pressure more than police action.

Evidence of thin local legal-access infrastructure for anyone needing counsel on the island.

PYF.name: French Polynesia
PYF.summary:
Full France metropolitan law does not extend to French Polynesia unchanged; the territory legislates locally on many matters, with France responsible for documents and justice.

French equality law applies in full — gender-identity anti-discrimination protections since 2012, hate-crime provisions since 2017, a conversion-practice ban since 2022, and legal gender recognition without medical prerequisites — and it lands on genuinely entrenched indigenous ground: the mahuu third-gender role predates colonisation, rae-rae identities are visible in daily life across the archipelago, the territory hosted its first international LGBTQIA+ rights colloquium in 2023 with government and church participation, and travel literature calls the openness cultural rather than legal.

The undertow is real but social, not statutory: the rights overview records varying stigma, employment discrimination, and episodic transphobic violence that has pushed some rae-rae into sex work, while healthcare depth thins sharply outside the main island. For a visitor the combination is among the region's strongest — law, culture, and visibility aligned — with the standard framework caveat that the state's prison-system findings apply here too, and small-island anonymity cuts both ways.

WLF.name: Wallis and Futuna
WLF.summary:
The French civil and criminal framework applies: gender-identity anti-discrimination protection since 2012 and judicial gender-marker change under the 2016-17 reforms without surgery or diagnosis requirements; same-sex relations are lawful; non-binary recognition does not exist. No law criminalises trans presence.

Exposure here is shaped by scale and mores rather than statutes. The rights overview describes an isolated community of roughly eleven thousand where Catholic and Polynesian social norms create practical barriers to visibility, a traditional third-gender presence (fakafafine) coexists with stigma, there are no local gender specialists — residents travel out for any care — and anonymity in village life is close to zero. No hostile state action is documented; the only state-level adverse mechanism in evidence is the framework's own prison findings (the national detention watchdog's report). Visitors should expect personal identifiability, warm discretion, and effectively absent local institutional support.

BLM.name: Saint Barthélemy
BLM.summary:
Saint Barthélemy stands under France's national law as in the metropole: identity documents, criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute and the marriage regime apply here as in France proper.

Under the metropolitan civil law that governs this collectivity: same-sex marriage since 2013, gender-identity anti-discrimination protections, surgery-free legal gender change, gender-affirming care available for decades, and the state's 2023 conversion-practice ban — no legal restriction touches trans or same-sex visitors, and a rights-rating page scores the territory among the region's strongest frameworks with the caveat that non-binary recognition is absent and healthcare capacity is tiny.

Visitor-facing evidence is unusually direct: verified 2026 destination guides describe a discreet luxury culture — full legal protections, 'a cosmopolitan crowd that genuinely doesn't care', no organised scene but complete safety for same-sex couples — and the rights overview reports the island attracts trans residents from less accepting neighbours. A current-status review tempers that surface: local acceptance runs lower than the visitor economy implies, though no legal regression exists. The only documented adverse mechanism remains the framework-wide prison findings. Read: protected and comfortable, shallow community depth, care requires travel.
BLM.outOfScopeNotes: Collectivity of France; local deviations noted in the summary. The framework-wide prison findings concern detention conditions and are unresolved for visitor-facing practice; whether local acceptance figures track the visitor-economy picture is not independently measured.

Dossier on BLM trans rights: the French framework applies — legal gender-marker change without surgery or sterilisation, hormone therapy and surgery available since 1975, anti-discrimination coverage; non-binary recognition limited.

ABW.name: Aruba
ABW.summary:
Aruba stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

On 8 September 2016 the Staten of Aruba passed a civil-code amendment opening registered unions to same-sex couples by 11 votes to 5, with four abstentions. The amendment extends the marriage articles of the civil code to those registered unions and grants spousal pension succession and emergency medical decision-making rights. Aruba's own news service reported the vote as making the island the first in the Caribbean to act.

Marriages performed in the Netherlands were already recognised throughout the Kingdom, and the bill's sponsor had used exactly that route. The Associated Press reported that religious and cultural opposition to the measure was strong, and that neither Sint Maarten nor Curaçao allowed such unions at the time.

GlobalGayz records that the Aruban government initially declared same-sex unions illegal until it was challenged by a lesbian couple legally married in the Netherlands.

These remain not sourced rather than absent.

The safety claims on the tourism board page are self-description by the destination's marketer and are not independent verification of conditions on the ground. GlobalGayz is a cultural report rather than a legal source, and its statements on adoption and on the earlier government declaration were not corroborated against primary legal texts in this inventory.

CUW.name: Curaçao
CUW.summary:
Curaçao stands under the Netherlands's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here. It is an autonomous constituent country of the Kingdom of the Netherlands, holding full autonomy except in defence, foreign affairs and matters reserved to the Supreme Court of the Netherlands.

In April 2015 representatives of all Kingdom governments agreed that LGBT people on Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten should receive equal rights without delay, and a package of rights requests was delivered to ministers in The Hague. Curaçao's commissioner Marvelyne Wiels of Pueblo Soberano publicly endorsed equal rights for everyone.

That endorsement ran against organised opposition from within her own party. Winifred Raveneau's fierce resistance had already forced Curaçao's 2013 Gay Pride to relocate to a hotel after a last-minute, exceptionally strict permit requirement, and parliamentary opposition to equal-rights measures continued even as the island's own government publicly backed the community.

Community infrastructure exists but is small. An LGBT centre, the Pink House, opened in Curaçao in 2010, and reporting from GlobalGayz (updated January 2017) treats Curaçao, Aruba and Bonaire as quietly gay-friendly places within the Kingdom while crediting Curaçao, with Sint Maarten and Aruba, as a driver of equal-rights moves across the Kingdom. Curaçao Gay Pride's Frank Holtslag cites an IGLTA award naming the island the most gay-welcoming in the region.

For a trans visitor the composite reads as low legal risk with thin trans-specific infrastructure: no documented state hostility toward trans people, an active but negotiating community, and no sourced local gender-recognition pathway or trans-specific care capacity.
CUW.outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses a gender-recognition pathway for trans people in Curaçao: whether a legal procedure exists, what it requires, or which authority decides is unresolved here.

Entry, visa and border-screening practices that could expose a visitor's trans status are not sourced, nor are document or marker rules for passports and identity papers issued in Curaçao or by the Netherlands.

Hate-crime or hate-speech protection covering gender identity, and any enforcement record under it, is not sourced. Nor is trans-specific healthcare capacity, its availability to visitors, or any exclusion of trans-related care.

Whether the Pride permit friction documented in 2013 recurred after that year, and whether the 2015 Kingdom equal-rights agreement has been implemented in Curaçao legislation, both remain unresolved on this inventory.

No sub-national variation within Curaçao is sourced; the island is treated as a single unit throughout.

BES.name: Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba)
BES.summary:
Caribbean Netherlands (Bonaire, Sint Eustatius, Saba) consists of three special municipalities within the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Dutch national law governs civil status, marriage and anti-discrimination, and the same statutory framework that applies in the European Netherlands operates on the islands.

Same-sex unions have been registrable in the islands since 2012. On 4 December 2012 the Census Office in Saba registered the first such union in the Caribbean Netherlands, between Cedeno Xiomar Gonzalez, an Aruban national aged 26, and Israel Ernesto Ruiz Pinto, a Venezuelan national aged 27. FRO.name: Faroe Islands
FRO.summary:
Faroe Islands stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

The Faroe Islands are a self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark. Domestic equality and family law are set locally, beneath a Danish human-rights framework. Same-sex marriage arrived only in 2017, late for the Nordics, after friction between church and state.

In 2006 LGBT activists gathered around 20,000 online signatures in a population of about 47,000, demanding an end to discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation and a registered-partnership law aligned with the rest of the Nordics. The territory had neither at that date. Surveys of the period found violence and discrimination against openly gay people not uncommon and legally unaddressed.

Religiously motivated opposition sits openly in Faroese politics. On 7 September 2010 Centre Party leader Jenis av Rana refused to attend a state banquet for visiting Icelandic prime minister Johanna Sigurdardóttir and her partner, citing his religion. The refusal concerned the presence of an openly gay head of government at an official table.

Opposition to public visibility continued. In July 2015, when av Rana demanded that Pride be banned from its position two days before the national holiday, singer Eivor Pálsdóttir publicly urged people to ignore him. His party remains formally opposed to homosexuality.

For a trans visitor the recorded hostility is political and rhetorical rather than physical. The named targets are openly gay public figures and a Pride event, and the actions on record are a refusal to sit at a banquet and a call for a ban. Violence risk appears low on the sourced material.

GRL.name: Greenland
GRL.summary:
Greenland stands under Denmark's national criminal law and document rules as they apply here.

A self-governing territory within the Realm of Denmark, with its own parliament and courts for domestic law. Its LGBT record is quiet and consensual: partnership law came from the Danish model in 1996 with virtually no debate; marriage equality was adopted from Danish legislation in 2016, passed unanimously by the local parliament with the established church's bishop supportive; and in 2016 the territory took a self-declaration approach to gender recognition, ahead of the metropole's own practice.

For a visitor the picture is low-friction: gay life is described as 'almost a non-event' — integrated, non-violent, modest, with a small Pride since 2010 and a national equality association (Qaamaneq, 2014). The counterweight is capacity, not hostility: some 56,000 people across remote settlements means thin institutional reach, and anonymity comes from isolation rather than crowds.
GRL.outOfScopeNotes: Self-governing territory of the Kingdom of Denmark; local deviations noted in the summary. The dossier's reporting dates to 2014-2016; whether the self-declaration practice and service levels persist is not confirmed by later evidence, and the population figure derives from the travel reporting rather than official statistics.

PRI.name: Puerto Rico
PRI.summary:
Puerto Rico stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

A US territory: the federal anti-trans turn of 2025–26 (document/marker rules, TSA screening friction) applies in full — and unlike some territories, local law compounds rather than softens it. In July 2025 Puerto Rico's governor signed the most severe ban on gender-affirming care in the United States, criminalising provision of hormones or surgery to anyone under 21 even with parental consent — up to 15 years' imprisonment, $50,000 fines, loss of medical licences, with parents potentially exposed; civil-rights groups announced court challenges, and the signatory had campaigned presenting as LGBTQ-friendly.

Local politics have swung both ways: the island's marriage ban was dismantled in the federal courts after local couples sued (2014), while religious-freedom and conversion-therapy bills advanced in 2019 before the governor withdrew them under organised pressure. For a trans visitor today: federal paperwork friction, the country's harshest local care-crime regime, and a visible advocacy community pushing back in court.
PRI.outOfScopeNotes: Unincorporated US territory; local deviations noted in the summary. Court challenges to the care ban were announced but their outcomes are unresolved, and how the deliberately vague provisions will be enforced in practice is unverified; the 2014 marriage ruling and the 2019 bill episodes are history, not current law.

Road to marriage equality in PR ran through federal court.

GUM.name: Guam
GUM.summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated US territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows federal Transport Security Administration procedure. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers; travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit cannot be assumed.

In February 2025 the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sports, a rule that applies to arrivals here.

Guam recognises same-sex marriage. Chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down the territory's prohibition on 5 June 2015, following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero after they were denied a licence; the ruling took effect at 8am on 9 June 2015 and made Guam the first US territory to recognise such marriages.
GUM.outOfScopeNotes:
Two listed sources, a University of Hawaiʻi Pacific sexual identity guide and a Transgender Law Center Guam documents page, yield no usable finding for this record, so no claim rests on them.

Whether Guam's own territory-level statutes prohibit discrimination based on gender identity in employment, housing or public accommodations is unresolved in this inventory; no Guam statute or local case is cited here.

The scope of the February 2025 visa-denial announcement is stated for athletes entering to compete in women's sports; its bearing on other visitor categories is unresolved and not sourced.

Local Guam police practice, hate-crime charging, and any territory-level complaint mechanism for trans residents are not addressed by the sources and remain unverified.

VIR.name: U.S. Virgin Islands
VIR.summary:
U.S. Virgin Islands stands under the full the United States federal regime: the United States travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth and the X marker has been eliminated (January 2025 executive order), so a trans visitor arriving on the United States documents faces that mismatch at entry; airport screening follows federal procedure; the order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions here, so care access during a visit cannot be assumed; and in February 2025 the the United States State Department additionally announced visa denials for trans athletes seeking entry for women's sports.

A small US territory: federal document and airport policy applies, and the 2025–26 federal turn is felt through it (marker disputes, screening friction) with no local statute to soften it. Locally the record is quietly protective rather than hostile: the Attorney General ruled in 2017 that the human-rights law's sex provision covers transgender students — an official extension of territorial protection — and local media framed the community's position after the 2016 federal shock as 'losses... but reason for hope.'

Federal rollback above, a thin but genuinely welcoming local posture beneath.

ASM.name: American Samoa
ASM.summary:
American Samoa is an unincorporated United States territory and stands under the full federal entry-and-documents regime. Federal executive orders reach the territory through federal agencies: EO 14168 on binary sex classification in documents, federal facilities and care funding; EO 14187 on gender-affirming care funding; and EO 14201 on athletic participation, the last paired with a State Department visa restriction carrying an SWS25 marker.

Since the January 2025 executive order, all United States identity documents reflect sex assigned at birth. The State Department has stopped processing X-marker passports and markers that do not match sex assigned at birth; new and renewed passports are issued only as M or F on the basis of supporting documents; and passports already carrying an X marker remain valid until expiry. The X marker, available from 2022, has been eliminated for new applications. Trans and nonbinary travellers report passports confiscated or blocked, and the ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, with the policy contested in federal courts.

Marriage recognition is unsettled in practice. The Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended killing it, so the territory declined a formal ban before Obergefell. In July 2015 the territory's attorney general said applicability of the federal marriage ruling was still under review, while Puerto Rico, the US Virgin Islands, Guam and the CNMI moved to apply it. In January 2016 the newly confirmed District Court judge Fiti Alexander Sunia told the Senate he had not read Obergefell, that the district court does not deal with the ruling, and that he would not perform same-sex weddings absent a change in local law. A 2026 law review article by two attorneys practising in American Samoa concludes that Obergefell does apply and that the territory would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied, while recording that no same-sex couple has applied to date and setting out a litigation route through the High Court of American Samoa, with the Territorial Registrar as defendant, and then the US Department of the Interior. As of July 2024 an on-island survey by Miami University professor Daniel Hall was still testing whether the local ban would survive a 14th Amendment challenge, indicating that the ban is treated locally as operative and its durability as an open question, more than a year after the Respect for Marriage Act obliged recognition of marriages performed elsewhere.

Trans people in the territory have obtained protection through national enforcement machinery. In September 2023 the US Justice Department secured a settlement with the American Samoa Government resolving an employment-discrimination case involving harassment of a transgender employee, and in June 2023 a federal civil action had cited a hostile work environment in a transgender woman's lawsuit against the territorial government over her gender identity. In February 2023 a 51-year-old man was charged with sexual abuse of a 16-year-old transgender teen.

Social conditions differ from the legal picture. Fa'afafine, defined as people born male who embody both male and female traits, are described in university research material as a recognised and integral part of traditional Samoan culture, with colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of indigenous gender identities; the Society of Fa'afafine in American Samoa (SOFIAS) was formed in 2010 by merging the American Samoa Island Queens Association and the American 7s Association, re-anchored to cultural pride. Travel guidance describes homosexuality as widely accepted in Samoan culture, in contrast to Fiji, while noting that Samoan culture tends toward traditionalism and that reserved behaviour by people of all orientations is expected. Fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified at the 2003 committee hearing that Samoan fa'afafine do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing.
ASM.outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Obergefell v. Hodges is operative in American Samoa remains contested and unresolved: the territory's own officials have said they had not read the ruling or that it was under review, while a 2026 law review article by practitioners in the territory concludes it applies. No court in the territory has ruled on the question, and no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage licence, so the practical position is untested.

The constitutional durability of the local same-sex marriage ban was still being surveyed in July 2024 and no published result of that survey is available in this inventory. The scope of the SWS25 visa restriction attached to EO 14201 as applied to entry into American Samoa is not sourced here, nor is the current status of the ACLU's challenge to the passport policy in the courts.

Guidance from Lambda Legal and HRC is a secondary summary of a policy under litigation and may lag court developments. The February 2023 sexual-abuse charge involving a transgender teenager is reported as a charge only, with no outcome recorded in this inventory.

It defines fa'afafine as born male but embodying both male and female traits, 'a recognized and integral part of traditional Samoan culture', and frames colonial suppression followed by contemporary reclaiming of Pacific gender identities.

sources.title: American Samoa Senate rejects bill outlawing same sex marriages (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: American Samoa's Fono Senate voted down a bill that would have outlawed same-sex marriage in March 2003, after the House judiciary committee recommended the bill be killed. The bill was introduced by Representative Sua Carl Schuster, who wanted to preempt the kind of marriage lawsuits then unfolding in US states. At the committee hearing, fa'afafine resident Tifanny Poutasi testified that Samoan fa'afafine 'don't believe in marriages with other men', describing them as men expressing femininity through dress and speech who do not seek same-sex marriage, citing Christian upbringing. The territory therefore deliberately declined a formal marriage ban before Obergefell, and the hearing records contemporaneous local fa'afafine views on the question.

sources.title: American Samoa judge objects to same sex marriage (RNZ Pacific)
sources.summary: In January 2016 the American Samoa Senate unanimously confirmed former territory Attorney General Fiti Alexander Sunia as District Court judge, filling the seat left by Judge John Ward II's retirement. At his confirmation hearing Senator Tauolo Manaia Fruean, a retired associate judge of the High Court of American Samoa, asked whether Sunia had read Obergefell; Sunia replied he had not read the US Supreme Court decision and that the district court 'doesn't deal with this ruling', and said he would not perform weddings for same-sex couples unless local laws are changed. The exchange shows that eighteen months after Obergefell the territory's judiciary was operating on the premise that the ruling did not automatically apply.

sources.title: The Ambiguity that Isn't: Why Same-Sex Marriage Is Legal in American Samoa (Harootunian & Lawrence, American University JGSPL vol 33 iss 2 (2026) pp 163-207)
sources.summary: 2026 law review article by two attorneys practicing in American Samoa (American Samoa Legal Aid, with Freedom From Religion Foundation) concluding that Obergefell DOES apply in the territory despite local officials' statements, and that American Samoa would have to issue a marriage certificate to any same-sex couple that applied. It records that to date no same-sex couple has applied for a marriage license in the territory, and lays out the litigation roadmap: the High Court of American Samoa first (defendant the Territorial Registrar), then the US Department of the Interior. The article is the most recent dated authority on whether the 2015 ruling is operative in American Samoa, and it separates the law as written from the practical reality.

COK.name: Cook Islands
COK.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to the Cook Islands, while local criminal law governs conduct on the islands.

Sections 154 and 155 of the Cook Islands Crimes Act 1969 criminalised sexual activity between men and any indecent act with or upon another male, carrying maximum terms of seven years and five years respectively, with consent explicitly not a defence. Later coverage of the repeal cited a maximum of ten years for indecent acts between males. The penalty figures reported for the 1969 provisions differ across the sources, but all agree the offences were never enforced in living memory.

Parliament voted on Friday 14 April 2023 to strike the provisions from the Crimes Act through the Crimes Amendment Bill, effective 1 June 2023. A note attached to the bill cited growing acceptance of LGBT people in the Cook Islands, and the same bill added protections for victims of sexual abuse and assault. The repeal removed a colonial-era provision still on the statute books rather than an active prosecution threat.

Decriminalisation was stalled for years before 2023. A draft Crimes Bill, written with assistance from New Zealand, would have deleted sections 154 and 155, and a 2017 select committee recommended their removal; MPs subsequently backtracked on that recommendation. In 2020 parliament again deferred the bill's report by three months.

Same-sex marriage remains prohibited in the Cook Islands under the Marriage Amendment Act 2000. The islands' only LGBTI community organisation, the Te Tiare Association, campaigned for repeal across the whole period, and its members described the 1969 provisions as homophobia brought by colonisation into a society whose pre-contact history accepted same-sex relationships. The Cook Islands population was about 21,000 when the bill was drafted in 2017.
COK.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory addresses same-sex conduct only. It contains no information on the legal status of gender identity in the Cook Islands: no detail on legal gender recognition, on the marker requirements for Cook Islands residents travelling on New Zealand passports, or on how New Zealand identity-document procedures apply from the Cook Islands.

Nothing in the sources covers anti-discrimination protection, hate-crime provisions, restrictions or protections around bathrooms and other gendered facilities, or access to gender-affirming medical care for trans people in the Cook Islands.

The extension of New Zealand human-rights and human-rights-instrument protections to the Cook Islands is not addressed in the inventory; how much of New Zealand's framework applies to residents of a state in free association remains unresolved on this record.

Enforcement, sentencing and complaint-handling data after the 1 June 2023 repeal are not available here, as are entry and visa rules applying to trans visitors, or any reporting on anti-trans violence with dates or outcomes.

NIU.name: Niue
NIU.summary:
New Zealand nationality and passport rules apply to Niue; local criminal law governs conduct.

One of the world's smallest self-governing states, in free association with New Zealand, Niue carries neither criminalisation nor protection on LGBT matters. Colonial-era offences were removed with the age of consent reported equalised by 2011, and no audited source documents enforcement against queer people at all; equally there is no recognition of same-sex relationships and no non-discrimination statute — and the principal 1966 act still shows uneven ages of majority by sex (21 men/19 women) on its face into the 2010s.

Culturally, UN regional documentation lists Niue's fakafifine among the Pacific's pre-colonial third-gender identities — 'cultural treasure' framing that signals deep family embedding, coexisting with church-led conservatism. Legacy public-health law provided for HIV testing of visitors staying beyond about two months: rarely invoked, but on the books. With a population near 1,500, anonymity is impossible — the question is community reaction, not arrest, and it is quietly unresolved.
NIU.outOfScopeNotes: In free association with New Zealand; local deviations noted above.

sources.summary: The Niue Assembly passed the Niue (Sexual Offences) Amendment Act in May, in force in June, removing 'buggery', 'attempted buggery' and 'indecent assault on males' (Human Dignity Trust, Niue section). Those offences sat at ss.43-44 of the Criminal Law Code and carried up to 10 years. The law was inherited from New Zealand through the 1901 annexation, retained on self-governance in 1974, and survived New Zealand's own 1986 decriminalisation, which changed New Zealand law only.

UN Free & Equal Pacific information sheet (Aug 2015): FAQ on sexual orientation, gender identity and intersex status in the Pacific - documents the fakafifine of Niue among the diverse pre-colonial Pacific gender identities that are 'important parts of the cultural treasure of the region'.

Under the Niue Act 1966 (Part 21, Marriage of Minors), the age of majority is 21 for men and 19 for women. The age of consent was equalised in May 2011, per ILGA State-Sponsored Homophobia (May 2011). The sex-asymmetric age of majority remains on the books.

HKG.name: Hong Kong
HKG.summary:
Hong Kong is a special administrative region running its own legal system under a constitutional settlement, and trans claims here have been settled by courts rather than by statute. Same-sex conduct is not prohibited outright: the Crimes Ordinance instead set the age of consent for male-male sex at 21 against 16 for heterosexual acts, and the Court of Appeal's September 2006 judgment in Leung TC William Roy v Secretary for Justice (CACV317/2005), brought by a 21-year-old who had been in same-sex relationships since 16, examined whether that facially neutral disparity unjustifiably discriminated. The case is the landmark precedent on equal age of consent in Hong Kong.

In February 2023 the Court of Final Appeal ruled that full sex-reassignment surgery must not be a prerequisite for changing the gender marker on the compulsory identity card, a far-reaching win for the transgender men in the Henry Tse litigation. That ruling reversed a February 2019 High Court loss in the same case, where Judge Thomas Au's 59-page judgment made full confirmation surgery the only objectively ascertainable criterion and rejected self-ID as leading to uncertainty and arbitrariness. The men had already changed legal gender in Britain, and their counsel argued the surgical requirement was out of proportion to the aim.

Recognition stops at the card. Beyond the identity-card marker, legal gender recognition in Hong Kong continues to require full sex-reassignment surgery, so the 2023 win does not carry across to other official records. Relationship recognition is also absent: in September 2025 the Legislative Council voted down the government's own registered-partnerships bill 71–14 after court deadlines, and no ordinance covering sexual orientation and gender identity equality has been enacted.
HKG.outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not address entry, visa, or border-document screening as applied to trans visitors, and nothing here should be read as describing how a foreign passport or travel document with a changed marker will be handled on arrival. That question is unsourced.

No sourced incidents of violence against trans people in Hong Kong appear in the inventory, and hate-crime protection, healthcare access, and facilities or restroom rules are not covered by these sources. Their status is unresolved rather than known to be absent.

The current statutory age of consent in force after the 2006 Court of Appeal precedent is not separately confirmed by these sources; only the litigation and its standing as the landmark precedent on equal age of consent are documented.

The practical reach of the February 2023 identity-card ruling beyond the card, and the consequences of the September 2025 partnership-bill defeat for visiting partners of residents, are not sourced and remain unresolved.

MAC.name: Macau
MAC.summary:
A small southern Chinese territory with its own civil-law system of Portuguese derivation: nothing criminalises same-sex conduct or gender expression, and almost nothing protects them either. There is no legal gender-recognition pathway — the first organised push (2015) got only a hearing at the identification bureau, with the trans claimant speaking behind a screen; when government legislated on domestic violence in 2016 it knowingly excluded same-sex partners as non-'family', against a 2015 UN Committee-Against-Torture direction that protection be non-discriminatory — an exclusion a local association and an internationally known campaigner publicly accused the administration of choosing, warning it signals SOGI bias is justifiable.

For a visitor: zero legal risk, near-zero legal recourse, and the compression of a very small city where casinos, churches and old resident networks all know their own. The administration treats the subject as a non-issue — which is both the mercy and the void.
MAC.outOfScopeNotes: Territory of China; local deviations noted above. The 2026 official statement leaves reform timing unset; the employment-only protection's enforcement practice is undocumented; the April 2026 appeal by four trans residents has no reported outcome in the audited material.

ESH.name: Western Sahara
ESH.summary:
Western Sahara is a disputed territory under military administration by Morocco, and the territory stands under Morocco's penal code wherever its security services operate. Same-sex intimacy is criminalised, carrying six months to three years of imprisonment, and the broad discretion police hold in applying morality provisions is the instrument turned on visibly trans people.

The Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic, a partially recognised state and African Union member since 2016, claims sovereignty over Western Sahara and separately records homosexuality as illegal for men and women, and illegal there for decades. A July 2017 global legality roundup lists it as a criminalising jurisdiction, so both claimed frameworks record criminalisation.

Rights reviews document involuntary outing of trans people, discrepancies in expression at checkpoints and in registry records, an absence of gender-affirming healthcare, and no legal gender recognition; a 2021 route to recognition covers intersex people only. GMB.name: Gambia
GMB.summary:
Same-sex conduct has been a criminal offence in Gambia since the colonial era. The Criminal Code adopted in March 2025 removed the 2014 provision permitting life imprisonment for "aggravated homosexuality" and instead sets a five-year minimum sentence for "unnatural offences", defined in the statute as any homosexual act, with no stated maximum penalty; "gross indecency" carries three years. The offence attaches to conduct rather than to stated identity or expression.

The government of President Adama Barrow has not typically enforced these provisions. The US State Department's 2021 human rights report recorded no prosecutions under the statute while documenting significant societal stigma and police harassment of LGBT persons, and the 2020 report recorded arrests together with societal discrimination.

Official hostility was explicit under the previous long-term ruler. Human Rights Watch's September 2015 report "State of Fear" documents arbitrary arrest, torture and killings under Yahya Jammeh, including his anti-gay rhetoric and direct threats against LGBT people. Those findings describe the enforcement climate of the Jammeh regime rather than current practice.

Discrimination against LGBT people persists into the present political period. Freedom House rates Gambia "Partly Free" at 50/100 in Freedom in the World 2024, noting improved political freedoms after 22 years of Jammeh's rule while listing severe discrimination against LGBT+ people among the country's ongoing concerns.

Protection machinery exists on paper. The UK Home Office country information and policy note on sexual orientation and gender identity in Gambia, version 3.0 of February 2023, sets out a systematic assessment of risk, protection, internal relocation and certification for LGBT+ asylum claims, with country information on the law and its treatment.
GMB.outOfScopeNotes:
The source inventory contains no material on legal gender recognition, change of name or gender marker on passports or identity documents, entry or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status, access to gender-affirming care, facility access, hate-crime enhancement, or recognition of partners. These elements of the record are not sourced here and remain unresolved rather than negative.

No trans-specific violence, arrest or homicide figures appear in the inventory. The available reporting is framed around sexual orientation and homosexual conduct; whether the statute's language has been applied against trans people specifically is not established by these sources.

Enforcement since the March 2025 Criminal Code took effect is not covered. The inventory's most recent enforcement data points are the 2020 and 2021 US State Department reports, and the Outright International profile's statement that the provisions have not typically been enforced carries no post-March 2025 case data behind it.

The dating of the pre-2025 aggravated-homosexuality provision differs between sources: one reference attributes the life clause to 2014, while the 2020 US State Department report describes a maximum of life under a 2013 amendment. This discrepancy is not resolved by the inventory.

No source in the inventory addresses whether a trans visitor's documents, presentation or prior record would attract screening at ports of entry, and no official Gambian statement on the treatment of gender-diverse travellers is included.

GMB.tangentialFactors:
The legal change in March 2025 moved in two directions at once: it removed the life sentence introduced for aggravated homosexuality in 2014, yet raised the floor for any homosexual act to five years while leaving the ceiling unstated. The practical significance for a visitor turns on enforcement rather than on the length of the tariff, and enforcement has been irregular.

A political opening and a legal freeze coexist. Freedom House records gains in political freedoms under Barrow after more than two decades of authoritarian rule, while the criminal provisions targeting same-sex conduct remain on the books and LGBT discrimination remains a listed concern. The liberalisation of the wider political environment should not be read as an easing of the position of LGBT people.

The historical record is dominated by the Jammeh period. The most severe documented violence, including torture, killings and direct threats, belongs to the era covered by the 2015 Human Rights Watch report. Applying that description to current conditions would misstate the present enforcement picture, just as relying on the absence of prosecutions would understate the risk of arrest and police contact.

The 2020 and 2021 US State Department reports give a two-year window: arrests and discrimination recorded first, then no prosecutions but continuing stigma and police harassment. Together they suggest a regime of low-prosecution but persistent extralegal pressure.
